Title: How Duolingo reignited user growth
Creator: Jorge Mazal (former Duolingo CPO), Lenny's Newsletter
What they did: Duolingo built a growth model that put every user into a state (new, current, reactivated, resurrected, at-risk, dormant). It found that the current-user retention rate (CURR) had the biggest effect on DAU and made it the North Star for a new Retention Team. That team swapped friends-only leaderboards for weekly leagues of similarly engaged users, added a late-night streak-saver push, and treated notifications as a channel to protect: they tuned copy and timing freely, but sending more needed CEO sign-off.
Results: In simulations, CURR had '5 times the impact of the second-best metric' on DAU. Leagues raised learning time 'by 17%', tripled highly engaged learners (at least 1 hour a day, 5 days a week) and gave significant D1/D7 gains. Over four years CURR rose 'by 21%', daily churn among the best users fell 'by over 40%', and the share of DAU on a 7+ day streak rose almost 3x to more than half of DAU. Failures: a moves counter was 'completely neutral' and a referral program raised new users 'by only 3%'.
Takeaways: Current-user retention moved DAU five times more than anything; Weekly leagues beat friends-only leaderboards; Borrowed features fail when the context differs; Protect the push channel: tune, don't send more; Streak saver push was the first big streak win; Four years: CURR up 21%, DAU up 4.5x
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: add a 10 PM 'streak saver' push only when today's plan isn't done. Home/today's plan: add a weekly league of aspirants matched by last week's questions answered, opted in by default. Analytics: set up New/Current/Reactivated/Resurrected states in PostHog to find which rate drives DAU most.
Bottom line: Duolingo grew by protecting its current learners, not chasing new ones: leagues, a late-night streak saver and careful pushes lifted retention for four years.

Key points.title: Current-user retention moved DAU five times more than anything
Key points.detail: Duolingo put every user who ever used the app into exactly one daily bucket: new, current, reactivated (back after 7-29 days), resurrected (back after 30+ days), at-risk WAU, at-risk MAU and dormant. They then moved each rate between buckets by 2% a quarter for three years in a simulation. Current user retention rate (CURR) had '5 times the impact of the second-best metric' on DAU, because current users who stay come back into the same bucket and the effect compounds. For OnCourse, building these buckets in PostHog would show which rate to make a team's North Star.

Key points.title: Weekly leagues beat friends-only leaderboards
Key points.detail: The old leaderboard ranked you against friends, but in a mature app many friends are no longer active. Mazal had seen at Zynga's FarmVille 2 that matching people by similar engagement matters more than personal closeness. Duolingo matched users with others of similar engagement the prior week, added Bronze-to-Gold style leagues, opted everyone in, and needed no extra tasks beyond normal lessons. Learning time rose 17%, highly engaged learners (1 hour a day, 5 days a week) tripled, and D1 and D7 retention improved significantly.

Key points.title: Borrowed features fail when the context differs
Key points.detail: Two early bets failed. A Gardenscapes-style moves counter took 'a couple of months' and was 'completely neutral', because Duolingo answers involve no strategy, so the counter was 'a boring, tacked-on nuisance'. An Uber-style referral offering a free month of Plus raised new users 'by only 3%', because the best users already paid and could not use the reward. Mazal now asks three questions before copying: why it works there, whether it will translate, and what must change.

Key points.title: Protect the push channel: tune, don't send more
Key points.detail: Groupon's CEO warned Luis von Ahn that adding emails, up to five a day, lifted metrics until the channel suddenly stopped working. Users who opt out during a test stay opted out even after the test ends. So the team could freely test timing, templates, images, copy and localization, but sending more pushes needed 'strong justification and CEO approval'. Dozens of small wins, found through A/B tests and a bandit algorithm, added up to large DAU gains.

Key points.title: Streak saver push was the first big streak win
Key points.detail: An APM found that users who reached a 10-day streak were much less likely to drop off. The team knew this was partly selection bias but invested anyway. The first big win was a late-night streak-saver notification that warns users their streak is about to end. Calendar views, animations, streak freeze changes and streak rewards followed. Mazal explains that a longer streak gives a stronger reason to come back the next day.

Key points.title: Four years: CURR up 21%, DAU up 4.5x
Key points.detail: CURR rose 21%, which meant daily churn among the best users fell 'by over 40%'. Together with other bets, DAU grew 4.5x. The share of DAU on a 7+ day streak rose almost 3x to more than half of DAU. Focusing on CURR also meant deliberately not working on new-user retention, which had been the company's habit for years.

Title: How Duolingo's streak builds habit
Creator: Osman Mansur, Duolingo Blog
What they did: Duolingo added a celebration animation after a learner extends their streak, with special versions on milestone days. It also let learners equip up to two Streak Freezes at once instead of one.
Results: The animations 'increased the likelihood a brand new learner was still using Duolingo 7 days later by +1.7%'. Allowing two Freezes 'increased the relative number of active learners on Duolingo every day by +0.38%'. Learners who reach a 7-day streak 'are 3.6 times more likely to complete their course'.
Takeaways: Celebrating each streak extension kept new learners longer; Early streak days feel biggest, so design for them; Two streak freezes raised daily actives, not days off; Long streaks run on loss aversion, not novelty; A 7-day streak strongly predicts finishing the course
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: add a full-screen streak-extend animation after the first study action each day, with bigger versions at days 3, 7, 14 and 30. Streaks: let users hold up to 2 streak freezes and show them on the streak screen.
Bottom line: Celebrate every streak extension and give a little slack with freezes; both measurably kept new learners coming back.

Key points.title: Celebrating each streak extension kept new learners longer
Key points.detail: Duolingo added a new animation to the screen shown after you extend your streak, with a special version on milestone days. New learners who saw it were "+1.7%" more likely to still be using Duolingo 7 days later. The number looks small, but at Duolingo's scale it means thousands more learners stay. For OnCourse, the moment a student extends a streak should feel like a reward, and bigger on milestone days.

Key points.title: Early streak days feel biggest, so design for them
Key points.detail: Going from a 2-day to a 3-day streak is a 50% jump. Going from 200 to 201 days is only 0.5%. That is why new learners feel each new day as a real win, and why Duolingo's designers, animators and engineers work to make extending the streak "as satisfying as possible". The first week of a streak is where celebration pays off most.

Key points.title: Two streak freezes raised daily actives, not days off
Key points.detail: Breaking a streak feels demotivating, and fear of losing one can stop people from starting a streak at all. Duolingo let learners equip up to two Streak Freezes at a time instead of one. This "increased the relative number of active learners on Duolingo every day by +0.38%". The post cites a University of Pennsylvania and UCLA study: a little "slack" motivates people more than rigid rules.

Key points.title: Long streaks run on loss aversion, not novelty
Key points.detail: Once a streak gets long, the thrill of extending it wears off. Then loss aversion takes over: people practice even on lazy days to protect the progress they are proud of. The post notes that losing a streak does not mean losing what you learned. The streak just makes the progress feel worth guarding.

Key points.title: A 7-day streak strongly predicts finishing the course
Key points.detail: Learners who reach a streak of just 7 days "are 3.6 times more likely to complete their course". More than 6 million people were on a streak of 7 days or more when the post was written. For OnCourse, day 7 is a good first target to point students toward and to celebrate.

Title: Behind the product: Duolingo streaks | Jackson Shuttleworth (Group PM, Retention)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Jackson Shuttleworth)
What they did: Over 600 streak experiments. Duolingo changed the streak rule from hitting an XP goal to doing one lesson, and added a short explanation when a streak starts. It added a streak-goal picker (default 30 days, with an opt-out and easier options) and renamed the CTA to 'Commit To My Goal'. It also gave two free freezes at the start of a new streak, replaced paid Streak Repair with 'Earn Back', and shows Perfect Streak only after day 7.
Results: The roughly eight-word streak explanation added more than 10,000 DAUs and was a top-three CURR win. Going from 1 freeze to 2 or 3 was a 'huge DAU win' but hurt CURR, and 3 freezes were 'no better' than 2. 'One exercise counts' moved DAUs 'not one bit' and was shut down. Preselecting a harder goal 'lost pretty significantly'. 'Continue' to 'Commit To My Goal' was 'a massive win'. Practice reminders go out 23.5 hours after the last session; streak saver at 10 PM. About half of experiments lose.
Takeaways: An eight-word streak explanation was a top-three CURR win; Letting users pick their streak goal creates commitment; Give forgiveness early in a streak, less later; Base the streak on your app's real unit of use; Time reminders from yesterday's session, not a chosen time; Lead with the number; add concepts only after day seven
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding/first session: after the first question set, show 'Do one study session a day to grow your streak. Miss a day and it resets.' Streaks: add a goal picker (7/14/30 days, default 30, with an opt-out to an easier goal) and the CTA 'Commit to my goal'. Streaks: give 2 free freezes on a new streak, and replace any paid repair with 'Do 2 sessions today to earn your streak back'.
Bottom line: After 600+ streak tests: keep the rule simple, explain it in one line when it starts, let learners pick their goal, and make forgiveness free early.

Key points.title: An eight-word streak explanation was a top-three CURR win
Key points.detail: Jackson's first winning test at Duolingo was adding about eight words of copy at the bottom of the screen when a streak starts. He recalls it as roughly "Start a day to extend your streak, but miss a day and it resets." It added "over 10,000 DAUs" and was "a top three CURR win", because many users around the world simply did not understand how a streak works. For OnCourse, explain the streak rule in one plain sentence on the first-session completion screen.

Key points.title: Letting users pick their streak goal creates commitment
Key points.detail: Streak goals started with one message: you are about seven times more likely to finish the course with a 30-day streak, borrowed from a subscription upsell line. Tests of 14 and 50 days showed different lengths suit different users, so they set 30 days as the default with an opt-out that offers an easier goal. Adding the opt-out button alone was "almost just as big a win", and preselecting a harder goal "lost pretty significantly", because the act of choosing is where the engagement comes from. Changing the CTA from "Continue" to "Commit To My Goal" was "a massive win".

Key points.title: Give forgiveness early in a streak, less later
Key points.detail: Going from one streak freeze to two or three was a huge DAU win but hurt CURR, and three freezes were "no better" than two, since three days off makes people less likely to return at all. Giving two free freezes when a new streak starts, instead of making users buy them with gems, was one of the biggest wins, because short streaks are easy to let die before loss aversion kicks in at day seven. Paid Streak Repair was replaced by "Earn Back": do a few lessons soon after losing a streak to get it back, which felt earned and won on retention. Someone on the team guards the "sanctity of the streak" so it is never made meaningless.

Key points.title: Base the streak on your app's real unit of use
Key points.detail: The original streak needed an XP goal, so users who set a hard goal lost their streak even after several lessons. Changing it to one lesson a day was a huge DAU driver and users still cared. Making it even easier, one exercise, moved DAUs "not one bit" and only captured "the least engaged users imaginable", so it was shut down. For OnCourse, a streak day should mean one real study session, not one question.

Key points.title: Time reminders from yesterday's session, not a chosen time
Key points.detail: Duolingo sends two streak pushes a day. The practice reminder goes out 23.5 hours after you practised the day before; letting users set their own time lost, and more complex timing logic never beat it. A 10 PM "streak saver" goes only if the streak is not yet extended, and users see it as positive because they care about the streak. OnCourse could time its daily nudge from the user's last session and send one late-night save only when today's plan is not done.

Key points.title: Lead with the number; add concepts only after day seven
Key points.detail: UX research in India found the flame metaphor "did not resonate at all", so the redesign put the number first with an odometer animation, and the calendar was made more calendar-like to signal a daily habit. Perfect Streak (the streak turns gold if no freeze is used) is shown only after day seven, because adding extra concepts early "pretty universally" lost. Animations and haptics on the streak screen win partly because they make users pause and enjoy the moment.

Title: The Tenets of A/B Testing from Duolingo's Master Growth Hacker
Creator: Gina Gotthilf (ex-VP Growth, Duolingo), First Round Review
What they did: Duolingo moved sign-up behind a first lesson, then used three skippable soft walls (a subtle 'Later' replaced a red 'Discard my progress') before a hard wall. It also tested reminder copy (the personalised 'Hi, it's Duo' won), a Friday-only Weekend Amulet for protecting the streak, a badge collection, and in-lesson coaching from the owl with growth-mindset copy.
Results: Moving sign-up back 'led to about a 20% increase in DAUs'; later soft/hard wall work 'yielded an 8.2% increase in DAUs'. Winning reminder copy alone gave 'a 5% increase in DAUs'. Weekend Amulet: 'retention went up 2.1% and 4% D7 and D14'. Badges: '2.4% increase in DAUs' and '116% increase in friends added'. Owl coach: '7.2% increase in D14'. Red badge dot on the app icon: 'six percent increase in our DAUs'.
Takeaways: Letting people try a lesson before sign-up lifted DAUs 20%; Skippable soft walls make the final hard wall work; Goal-based reminders sent 23.5 hours later beat generic nudges; Badges worked only as a collection worth showing; Growth-mindset coaching in lessons lifted D14 by 7.2%; Streak protection paid for itself despite lost repair revenue
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: drop the account step before the first session. Pick exam, answer 5 real NEET PG questions, then ask to 'Save your progress' with a soft 'Later' option. Practice: add brief growth-mindset coach lines after wrong answers ('Tough one. Mistakes now are what stick on exam day').
Bottom line: Let people do a real lesson before signing up, then test small things like reminder copy and streak protection; each moved daily users by several percent.

Key points.title: Letting people try a lesson before sign-up lifted DAUs 20%
Key points.detail: Duolingo saw a big drop between visiting or downloading and signing up. They let users do a lesson and see the skill tree before asking for an account. "Simply moving the sign-up screen back a few steps led to about a 20% increase in DAUs." For OnCourse, students could answer real questions before creating an account.

Key points.title: Skippable soft walls make the final hard wall work
Key points.detail: Duolingo replaced a big red "Discard my progress" button with a subtle "Later" button. It now shows three soft walls that can be skipped, then a hard wall after several lessons. Gotthilf: "without those soft walls priming a sign-up as they're ignored, those hard walls perform significantly worse." Together these changes gave an 8.2% increase in DAUs.

Key points.title: Goal-based reminders sent 23.5 hours later beat generic nudges
Key points.detail: Streaks needed a daily goal, and the goal gave reminders a real reason: "You have a goal. Reach your goal today." Duolingo sends the reminder 23.5 hours after your last session, assuming the time you used the app today is a good time tomorrow too. They tested funny, imperative, word-example and quiz copy. The personalised "Hi, it's Duo" message won, and the winning copy alone gave a 5% increase in DAUs.

Key points.title: Badges worked only as a collection worth showing
Key points.detail: The first badge test gave users one badge for signing up, and it had no effect. The post-mortem found that signing up is not a source of pride, one badge doesn't matter, and people want to see a collection. The redesigned set of badges, with a home in the app, gave a 2.4% increase in DAUs, 4.5% more lessons finished, 13% more store purchases and 116% more friends added. The lesson: "viable" is the core of a minimum viable product.

Key points.title: Growth-mindset coaching in lessons lifted D14 by 7.2%
Key points.detail: Duo the owl pops up during lessons, for example after mistakes: "Even when you're making mistakes, you're learning." Praise like "Whoa, you're amazing" and growth-mindset copy like "Wow, your hard work is really paying off" both beat the control, but growth-mindset copy won. D14 retention rose 7.2%, even though some staff found the owl annoying. For OnCourse, encouragement after a wrong answer should praise effort, not talent.

Key points.title: Streak protection paid for itself despite lost repair revenue
Key points.detail: The Weekend Amulet, sold on Fridays, protects your streak if you skip Saturday and Sunday. It raised retention 2.1% at D7 and 4% at D14. Duolingo worried it would cut paid streak repair, so they tested that too and found the extra DAUs were worth more than the lost revenue. Gotthilf says to always weigh retention gains against monetization.

Title: Hi, it's Duo: The AI behind the meme
Creator: Kevin Yancey & Burr Settles, Duolingo Blog
What they did: Duolingo stopped picking practice-reminder templates at random. A bandit algorithm now chooses the best template for each user each day, rewarding lesson completion. Templates are compared only against others sent to the same type of learner, and recently seen ones get a recency penalty to counter novelty wear-off.
Takeaways: A bandit picks each learner's reminder by lesson completion; Reminders lose power when repeated, so space them out; Compare templates only against the same type of learner; The best reminder copy differs by course; New templates are tested small before joining the pool
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: write 10–15 reminder templates (exam countdown, weak-topic nudge, streak-at-risk, 'today's plan takes 12 min'), rotate them with a no-repeat-within-N-days rule, and judge each by study sessions started, segmented by exam (NEET PG vs USMLE).
Bottom line: Pick each learner's reminder by what gets them to finish a lesson, and keep the copy fresh by not repeating it.

Key points.title: A bandit picks each learner's reminder by lesson completion
Key points.detail: Duolingo used to pick practice-reminder templates from its pool at random. Its machine learning team built a bandit algorithm that learns which template is most likely to get each learner to finish a lesson that day. The "payout" is a completed lesson, not an open. For OnCourse, reminders should be judged by whether students actually study after them.

Key points.title: Reminders lose power when repeated, so space them out
Key points.detail: Using about 200 million reminders sent over 34 days, Duolingo confirmed a "novelty effect": a template the learner has never seen works best, then wears off. Normal bandits reuse the winner again and again, so they had to teach the system to demote recently seen templates. They spaced repeats using the same forgetting curve they use to model word learning.

Key points.title: Compare templates only against the same type of learner
Key points.detail: Some templates only fit certain learners, like those with a streak wager, or can only go out on Mondays. Learners with huge streaks practice no matter what, which makes templates aimed at them look better than they are. Duolingo scored each template only against others sent to the same type of learner. Without this, the data would reward the audience, not the copy.

Key points.title: The best reminder copy differs by course
Key points.detail: Some templates worked much better than others, and the winner changed by language. "Time for [language]" works very well for Chinese learners but is usually not the best option for English learners. So selection is tailored per course. For OnCourse, the best reminder for one exam or year group may not suit another.

Key points.title: New templates are tested small before joining the pool
Key points.detail: Following the principle "Test everything", new reminders go to a small group of learners first, and only the best are added to the pool for good. In the real-world test, more learners completed lessons more often within weeks. It especially helped tens of thousands of new learners come back. What the AI learned also feeds into writing better notifications.

Title: Learn How Calm Increased Retention 3X With Product Intelligence
Creator: Alicia Shiu, Amplitude
What they did: Calm's Daily Reminder was buried in Settings, and fewer than 1% of users found it. Calm tested showing new users a screen right after their first meditation that encouraged them to set a daily reminder.
Results: Users who set reminders showed 'an almost 3x increase in retention'. '40% of users who saw the prompt went on to set a daily reminder', and those users got 'an equal boost in retention' to organic finders, which suggests the effect is causal. The effect held '12+ weeks out'.
Takeaways: Asking for a reminder after the first session tripled retention; A buried feature showed almost 3x better retention; Surfacing it to new users proved the effect was causal; 40% of prompted users set a reminder; The gain lasted more than 12 weeks
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding/first session: after the first completed question set, show 'When do you want to study each day?' with a time picker, then the OS push permission. Settings: keep it editable, but the post-first-session prompt is the main entry point.
Bottom line: Ask new users to set a daily reminder right after their first session; those who did retained about 3x better.

Key points.title: Asking for a reminder after the first session tripled retention
Key points.detail: Calm tested a screen shown right after a new user finished their first meditation, encouraging them to set a daily reminder. People who set a reminder from this prompt got the same retention boost as those who had found the feature on their own: about 3x. For OnCourse, the moment right after a student's first completed session is the time to ask for a study reminder.

Key points.title: A buried feature showed almost 3x better retention
Key points.detail: The Daily Reminder lived deep in Settings, and fewer than 1% of users found it. On a hunch, Calm used Amplitude's behavioral cohorts to compare users who set a reminder with those who didn't. Setters showed "an almost 3x increase in retention". Small features hidden in settings are worth checking this way.

Key points.title: Surfacing it to new users proved the effect was causal
Key points.detail: The first result could have been power users finding Settings, since they would retain anyway. Showing the prompt to a random share of new users settled it: prompted setters retained as well as organic ones. The page says this shows the link is "causative, not just correlative". This is a cheap way to test any correlation you find in analytics.

Key points.title: 40% of prompted users set a reminder
Key points.detail: Four in ten users who saw the prompt went on to set a daily reminder. That turned a feature used by under 1% into one used by a large share of new users, which lifted overall new-user retention. Calm planned to roll the prompt out to all users.

Key points.title: The gain lasted more than 12 weeks
Key points.detail: In the comments, a reader asked whether the lift faded. Alicia Shiu replied that Calm focused on daily retention, but weekly and monthly retention also improved. They were still seeing the increase "12+ weeks out", which suggests a long-term effect.

Title: How We Doubled Headspace Course Starts (And Why Getting People to Meditate is Harder)
Creator: Irrational Labs (with Headspace and Purchasely)
What they did: Headspace tested five onboarding flows for new trial users. Control was a breathing exercise then the Today tab. The others were: default to the Basics course; a short quiz then Basics for everyone ('perceived fit'); a quiz with a real personalised match; and precommitment, where users also planned how, when and where they'd meditate.
Results: Course starts rose 'from a baseline of 31.25% in the control group all the way up to 62.97% in our perceived fit condition'. Asking questions alone gave '7.6 percentage points higher' starts than defaulting to Basics. Precommitment 'increased app opens by 7.5% and app open days by 4%'. But there was 'no statistically significant difference' in meditation days between control and any redesign.
Takeaways: A short onboarding quiz doubled course starts; Asking questions alone creates a sense of fit; Truly personalised matching didn't beat the beginner course; Planning when to practice raised app opens; More starts and opens did not mean more meditation; Measure the behavior that delivers value
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: ask 3 questions (exam and date, weakest subject, daily minutes), then start a 'Your first plan' session in that subject right away. Onboarding: add 'When and where will you study?' (e.g. 'After dinner, at my desk'). Home: on return, open with a one-tap 'Continue today's plan' card, not a busy dashboard.
Bottom line: A few onboarding questions and starting the course inside onboarding doubled course starts, but the habit only sticks if the way back leads straight to the task.

Key points.title: A short onboarding quiz doubled course starts
Key points.detail: Headspace, Irrational Labs and Purchasely tested five onboarding flows for new free-trial users. Putting a course inside onboarding, after a few quick questions, raised course starts from 31.25% in the control to 62.97% in the "perceived fit" version. The lesson: ask for the key action during onboarding, when motivation is highest.

Key points.title: Asking questions alone creates a sense of fit
Key points.detail: The "perceived fit" and "default to basics" flows both recommended the same Basics course. The only difference was asking a few questions first. That alone gave 7.6 percentage points more course starts. Irrational Labs calls this "idiosyncratic fit": people feel the plan was made for them. For OnCourse, two or three questions (exam, year, weak subjects) before the first study plan could do the same.

Key points.title: Truly personalised matching didn't beat the beginner course
Key points.detail: Flows that really matched users to a course based on their answers did not beat the Basics course. The matching logic always sent anyone who mentioned sleep to a sleep course, even though stress and anxiety were picked most often. The authors say "it's easy to be wrong and harder to be right". Good default beginner content is hard to beat.

Key points.title: Planning when to practice raised app opens
Key points.detail: The precommitment flow asked users which days they would meditate and what would trigger it, like "In the morning, to start my day". App opens rose 7.5% and unique app-open days rose 4%. This is an "implementation intention": a plan for when and how, which helps close the gap between intending and doing.

Key points.title: More starts and opens did not mean more meditation
Key points.detail: There was no statistically significant change in active meditation days for any flow. The precommitment effect faded after the first 2–3 days. Likely reasons: returning users landed on a busy Today page and couldn't find their course (a one-click return modal was designed but cut), and courses were longer than the short breathing exercise new users expected. For OnCourse, Home must lead straight back to the student's current plan.

Key points.title: Measure the behavior that delivers value
Key points.detail: The authors say to track the real value behavior, here meditation days, alongside starts and opens. Their last learning is that demanding habits may need stronger tools like streaks. A streak idea similar to Apple's daily rings was proposed but Headspace deprioritized it. For OnCourse, track study days or questions answered, not just sessions started.

Title: How Headspace Optimized Revenue by Gating Content — Shreya Oswal and Keya Patel
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat (David Barnard)
What they did: Headspace went from about 80% to eventually 100% of content locked, and moved from direct purchase to free trials (7 days for monthly, 14 days for annual). Onboarding swung from 10–15 screens to 3–4 and back to a middle length. The goal question changed from single-select to multi-select, and the paywall dropped lifetime for a two-plan setup ($12.99 monthly, $69.99 annual).
Results: Moving to 90–99% locked gave 'a pretty high lifting conversion'. Locking 100% gave 'a high double digit lift in paid subscribers'. Free trials gave a 'conversion lift that was in the double digits'. Multi-select goal question: 'a pretty significant lift', with less drop-off and more trial starts. Long onboarding helped week-1 engagement but cut conversion. Testing eight cheaper monthly prices was 'revenue negative'.
Takeaways: A multi-select goal question lifted trial starts; Onboarding length trades engagement against conversion; Locking all content gave a double-digit lift in subscribers; Nudging people to annual brought in lower-intent buyers; Price tests ended at $12.99 monthly and $69.99 annual; Personal, non-cash referral rewards beat give-and-get credits
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: make 'What do you want help with?' multi-select (MCQ practice, revision, weak subjects, mock tests). Paywall: test a 7-day trial on monthly vs 14-day on annual. Paywall: gate by depth (full Qbank, explanations, mocks), keeping a sample free in each subject.
Bottom line: Locking more content, adding trials and a multi-select goal question all lifted conversion; onboarding length trades engagement for conversion.

Key points.title: A multi-select goal question lifted trial starts
Key points.detail: Shreya changed the onboarding question about why people came to Headspace (sleep, anxiety, stress) from single-select to multi-select. It gave "a pretty significant lift": fewer people dropped off at that question and more started a free trial. Her view is that people felt more listened to, and most people do pick several reasons. For OnCourse, let students pick several goals or weak subjects.

Key points.title: Onboarding length trades engagement against conversion
Key points.detail: Keya's team moved onboarding from 10–15 screens down to 3–4, then back to the middle, "like an accordion". The long flow helped week-one engagement but fewer people converted. The very short flow sent people straight to an upsell; it worked on the numbers but felt against Headspace's mission. They settled in the middle, and the right answer depended on which metric they were chasing.

Key points.title: Locking all content gave a double-digit lift in subscribers
Key points.detail: In 2019 Keya tested 90%, 95% and 99% locked content and saw a "pretty high" conversion lift, with far less support backlash than feared. They kept one or two popular items free in each category. Later Shreya locked 100% of content and saw "a high double digit lift in paid subscribers", and trial users explored more content. Long-time free users got up to 75% off a year as a transition offer.

Key points.title: Nudging people to annual brought in lower-intent buyers
Key points.detail: Shreya tested eight lower monthly prices; more people chose monthly but it was "revenue negative". An annual-focused paywall did better with a simple "best value" label than with the dollar savings spelled out. But people nudged to annual often didn't stay after the free trial. Today monthly and annual get equal prominence, and some users like monthly as a regular check that they still use it.

Key points.title: Price tests ended at $12.99 monthly and $69.99 annual
Key points.detail: Headspace started with $9.99 monthly, about $99 annual and a lifetime plan. It tested annual prices from 49 to 99; 69 won on conversion and first renewal. Monthly went up to $12.99 to make annual look better, and lifetime was dropped. The paywall showed annual as a monthly cost and had an animated character, "Conversion Connie", pointing at it.

Key points.title: Personal, non-cash referral rewards beat give-and-get credits
Key points.detail: Research showed people refer Headspace to help a friend, and "give 10, get 10" made them worry about looking self-serving. A referral challenge offered top referrers a one-on-one session with their favourite teacher. Friends get a 30-day trial instead of the usual 14 days. Keya recalls a thank-you note from co-founder Andy meaning more to users than money.

Title: Blinkist – Using transparency to increase your conversion rate with Eveline Moczko
Creator: The Subscription League (Olivier Destrebecq), Purchasely
What they did: To fix 'trial anxiety' (users cancelling minutes after starting, or never starting for fear of being charged), Blinkist sent a day-5 push and email: 'you will be charged in two days'. Users who had already cancelled got a different message. Blinkist then advertised this reminder on the subscription screen, moved to a soft paywall with a 7-day trial, and dropped mandatory account creation before onboarding.
Results: No percentages in the episode. Moczko says trial retention rose even before the reminder was advertised, and after it went on the subscription screen the trial start rate 'went up like crazy'. Removing mandatory sign-up made personalised onboarding finally work and improved conversion, a net win even after losing email-driven conversions.
Takeaways: A promised trial reminder made trial starts jump; Dropping mandatory sign-up made personalised onboarding work; Indian users delete apps fast, so win them early; Retest old results; Germany rejected trials, then accepted them; Use a fast proxy metric for a slow North Star; Onboarding choices reveal the user's motivation
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: add 'We'll remind you 2 days before your trial ends' with the exact date. Renewal: send that push and email on trial day 5, and send already-cancelled users a 'make the most of your last days' message linking to their plan.
Bottom line: Promise to remind people before their trial ends, and say so on the paywall; it removes the fear that stops them starting.

Key points.title: A promised trial reminder made trial starts jump
Key points.detail: Blinkist called the problem "Trial Anxiety": users cancelled minutes after starting a trial, or never started for fear of being charged. On day 5 it sent a push and email: "Hey, you will be charged in two days." Users who had already cancelled got an encouraging message to make the most of their last two days. Trial retention rose even before it was advertised; once the reminder was shown on the subscription screen, trial opt-in "went up like crazy".

Key points.title: Dropping mandatory sign-up made personalised onboarding work
Key points.detail: For about two years, adding an onboarding that asked about interests always hurt conversion. Then Blinkist removed the required account-creation step, and the onboarding suddenly worked. It gave space to show the value before the subscription screen. Moczko calculated that even losing all later email-driven conversions, Black Friday included, it still made more money.

Key points.title: Indian users delete apps fast, so win them early
Key points.detail: Moczko says that in markets like India, users often delete an app after just a few taps because their phones have little storage. That means less time to convince them, and app size itself affects downloads. She also says Blinkist won't crack India without Indian authors in its catalog. Both points apply directly to OnCourse's audience.

Key points.title: Retest old results; Germany rejected trials, then accepted them
Key points.detail: The 7-day trial won globally, but German users saw it as a trap or a scam, so Blinkist launched everywhere except Germany. Two years later, after Netflix and Spotify had spread there, a retest was "a huge success". Her rule: never treat a past test result as the truth forever.

Key points.title: Use a fast proxy metric for a slow North Star
Key points.detail: Blinkist's North Star is "power customers": people with four content interactions in a month. That takes too long to measure in a test. So they use a proxy: does the user come back in the week after the 7-day trial? This lets them conclude an A/B test within two weeks.

Key points.title: Onboarding choices reveal the user's motivation
Key points.detail: Blinkist dropped personas for three motivations: Career Optimizers, Life Optimizers and Curious Explorers. Onboarding asks which categories you want to follow; picking leadership suggests a career optimizer, picking psychology or biography suggests a curious explorer. Content is then personalised. For habit, some users need external triggers, like Blinkist's Friday recommendation email.

Title: What the best subscription apps get right about paywalls
Creator: Daphne Tideman with Rosie Hoggmascall, RevenueCat Blog
What they did: Covers Blinkist's 'Honest Paywall' (a clear trial timeline, the features included, and a promise to remind users before the trial ends), plus Hoggmascall's test of where the paywall goes and what comes before it. Also covers Duolingo walking new subscribers through their benefits after purchase, and Headspace's clear cancellation instructions.
Results: Blinkist's Honest Paywall 'increased their conversion rate by 23% and dropped complaints by 55%'. Hoggmascall's test: 'A: welcome screen, onboarding, home, paywall – 2% trial opt in'; 'B: welcome screen, paywall, onboarding, home – 8% trial opt in'; 'C: welcome screen, new three part carousel, paywall, onboarding, home – 15% trial opt in'. SmartTales improved paywall conversion by 86% by changing ads and store listing, not the paywall.
Takeaways: A value carousel before the paywall raised opt-in to 15%; Blinkist's honest paywall: +23% conversion, -55% complaints; Judge a paywall by refunds, cancels and complaints too; Aftercare after purchase reminds new subscribers why they paid; Personalise the paywall by context and how often it's seen; Quick defaults: annual first, one choice, progressive disclosure
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: Today (full access) → Day 5 (reminder) → Day 7 (billing date and price). Onboarding: test a 3-card value carousel ('Daily plan to exam day', 'Qbank with explanations', 'Track weak topics') before the paywall. Post-purchase: show a 'Here's what you unlocked' screen.
Bottom line: An honest paywall (timeline, what's included, a reminder promise) and a short value story before it beat hiding the terms.

Key points.title: A value carousel before the paywall raised opt-in to 15%
Key points.detail: Rosie Hoggmascall tested three flows. Welcome, onboarding, home, then paywall gave 2% trial opt-in. Welcome then paywall then onboarding gave 8%. Welcome, a new three-part carousel, then paywall gave 15%. The carousel explained why to pay, even though it added screens.

Key points.title: Blinkist's honest paywall: +23% conversion, -55% complaints
Key points.detail: Blinkist's "Honest Paywall" was built on three parts: a clear timeline, the features included, and a promise to remind users before the trial ends. It "increased their conversion rate by 23% and dropped complaints by 55%". The article says trust is hard to build and easy to break, and worth it.

Key points.title: Judge a paywall by refunds, cancels and complaints too
Key points.detail: Optimising only for conversion can push teams into dark UX. Rosie tracks refund, cancellation and complaint rates as quality checks. She finds 20–30% of users cancel in the first three hours. MyFitnessPal's paywall was fine, but dense privacy screens before it made people tap through just to escape, which can raise cancellations later.

Key points.title: Aftercare after purchase reminds new subscribers why they paid
Key points.detail: Rosie finds that people surveyed after subscribing often can't name the app's main value. Good aftercare validates and celebrates the decision, shows what they now have, and nudges them to start. Duolingo shows a powered-up owl and walks through the five benefits again; Strava changes visuals after subscribing. For OnCourse, a single screen after purchase can do this.

Key points.title: Personalise the paywall by context and how often it's seen
Key points.detail: Rosie watches two numbers: how many times the paywall is viewed and the paywall-to-conversion rate. Early-stage apps should show the paywall more; later-stage apps sometimes show it so often it feels like spam. "The best paywalls feel like they speak to you", based on what the user was doing just before.

Key points.title: Quick defaults: annual first, one choice, progressive disclosure
Key points.detail: In a quick-fire round Rosie said: lead with the annual plan and make it one choice; use progressive disclosure; default to annual; highlight "Most popular", which beat highlighting the cheapest plan in her tests. Comparison tables only help for complex, high-price products like therapy. She also advises pricing high and discounting later, rather than pricing too low.

Title: 8 paywall test ideas to grow app revenue
Creator: David Barnard & Peter Meinertzhagen, RevenueCat Blog
What they did: Named examples: FitnessAI moved the paywall ahead of onboarding and added a silent demo video. Rootd moved its paywall to the start of onboarding. Mojo made yearly the default, hid monthly behind 'view all plans', and showed the annual price as a monthly amount. Duolingo tailors the paywall to the entry point (hearts from the shop, ad removal from an ad).
Results: FitnessAI: paywall views up 50%, 'install-to-trial conversions doubled' with trial-to-paid steady, 'leading to a doubling of revenue!'. Rootd: 'her revenue increased by 5x'. Mojo yearly default: '15-20% lift in yearly subscription take up' with only a slight rise in cancellations.
Takeaways: Track how many users ever see the paywall; Rootd's early paywall raised revenue 5x; Default to annual and show it as a monthly price; Visuals: trial timeline, real reviews, one coloured button; Match the paywall to where the user came from; Sell the outcome, in your users' own words
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: default-select annual, shown as '₹X/month, billed yearly', with monthly under 'See all plans'. Paywall: make the headline depend on the trigger (locked explanation → 'Unlock every explanation'; mock test → 'Take full-length mocks'). Paywall: add a 10–15 s silent screen recording of today's plan and a question with its explanation.
Bottom line: Show the paywall to more people earlier, default to the yearly plan, and match the headline to what the learner just tapped.

Key points.title: Track how many users ever see the paywall
Key points.detail: Superwall's Jake Mor says the metric almost every app ignores is "what percentage of your users are even seeing the paywall". In his app FitnessAI, he moved the paywall before onboarding and added a video. Paywall views rose 50%, install-to-trial doubled, trial-to-paid held steady, and revenue doubled. He suggests showing the paywall in every placement, then removing them one at a time.

Key points.title: Rootd's early paywall raised revenue 5x
Key points.detail: Rootd is a panic attack and anxiety app, and its founder feared a paywall would get in the way of users who needed relief. In 2020 she moved the paywall to the start of onboarding. Revenue rose 5x, with almost no negative feedback because "people are so used to seeing" paywalls. If an early paywall scares people, make the exit easy, for example "not right now" under the CTA.

Key points.title: Default to annual and show it as a monthly price
Key points.detail: Mojo hid the monthly plan behind a "view all plans" link and saw a 15–20% lift in yearly take-up, with only a small rise in cancellations. It also showed the annual plan as "$4.99 per month billed annually" instead of $59.99 a year. That raised revenue per paywall impression, especially in lower-income regions, which matters for OnCourse's Indian students.

Key points.title: Visuals: trial timeline, real reviews, one coloured button
Key points.detail: Blinkist added a free-trial timeline after exit surveys showed people didn't know when they'd be charged. Jake suggests a silent, high-quality product video, a Q&A section, and real App Store reviews with name and date. Make the purchase button the only coloured element so the eye goes there.

Key points.title: Match the paywall to where the user came from
Key points.detail: Duolingo's paywall changes with the entry point: from the shop it sells unlimited hearts, from an ad it sells removing ads. Apps can also use goals from onboarding to highlight the matching paid features, or offer a discount after five days or after someone closes the paywall. For OnCourse, a paywall opened from a locked mock test should talk about mock tests.

Key points.title: Sell the outcome, in your users' own words
Key points.detail: Copy is the cheapest thing to test. Jake suggests borrowing words from your best App Store reviews. For FitnessAI, "you're going to look your best and feel your best" beat "this is 20 times cheaper than a trainer". Personal Best's "payramp" CTA, "Redeem your free 2 weeks", made users feel they were gaining something.

Title: A Systematic Approach to Paywall Optimization — Live at App Promotion Summit NYC
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat (David Barnard, Jake Mor of Superwall, Darrell Stone of Citizen)
What they did: FitnessAI added a video to the paywall and moved it before onboarding, changing nothing else. It also put a cheaper plan in the App Store subscription group, so people see it when they go to cancel. Citizen shows two paywalls in onboarding (after sign-up, and again after the safety profile for non-subscribers) and tested crowdsourced copy ('never be alone').
Results: FitnessAI: 'conversion rates went up 80%', and installs reaching the paywall went 'from like 40% to 85%', with most converting further down the funnel. On the hidden cheaper plan, the transcript reads '10-15 of subscribers are on a plan that you can't even subscribe to in the app' (unit missing, likely %). Citizen: video was 'flat'; no other numbers.
Takeaways: Track the share of installs that ever see the paywall; FitnessAI: earlier paywall plus video lifted conversion 80%; A hidden cheaper plan wins back cancelling subscribers; Citizen shows a second paywall after a value step; Video helps most products; colour only the CTA; Tell users exactly what to do, and sell the outcome
Ideas for OnCourse: Analytics: track the share of installs that reach the paywall and aim for 80%+. Renewal: add a cheaper 'Qbank only' plan to the subscription group as a downgrade at cancellation. Onboarding: add a second paywall after the first completed plan session for users who skipped the first.
Bottom line: Measure how many installs ever see the paywall; moving it earlier and adding a second one after a value moment catches more buyers.

Key points.title: Track the share of installs that ever see the paywall
Key points.detail: Jake Mor calls this the most neglected metric. He rarely sees apps with over 80% of installs reaching the paywall, and gains in install-to-paywall carry through to install-to-paid. David Barnard guesses only 20–30% of his own users ever see one. Jake's usual winning setup: show it on app open and before locked features, both before and after onboarding.

Key points.title: FitnessAI: earlier paywall plus video lifted conversion 80%
Key points.detail: Jake added a video to FitnessAI's paywall and moved it before onboarding, changing nothing else, and "conversion rates went up 80%". Installs reaching the paywall went "from like 40% to 85%", and most of those users converted further down the funnel. His read: onboarding wasn't good, and motivated buyers weren't finishing it.

Key points.title: A hidden cheaper plan wins back cancelling subscribers
Key points.detail: When someone cancels in the App Store, they see every plan in your subscription group. Jake adds a discounted plan there that works as a built-in win-back. He says "10-15 of subscribers" (likely percent) are on a plan you can't buy in the app. David notes it doesn't trick anyone, since the cancel button is right there.

Key points.title: Citizen shows a second paywall after a value step
Key points.detail: Citizen treats onboarding as one story about personal and community safety. After sign-up comes the first paywall, where many convert. Those who don't fill in a safety profile, then see a second paywall; subscribers get a demo of what they bought instead. Darrell Stone says this framing lets the team test the key moments quickly.

Key points.title: Video helps most products; colour only the CTA
Key points.detail: Jake says the videos that work are high-quality screen recordings of the app in a phone, not live-action ads, so people see what they're buying. Darrell says video was flat for Citizen, so it doesn't always work. The CTA colour itself doesn't matter; what matters is that it's the only coloured thing on the page.

Key points.title: Tell users exactly what to do, and sell the outcome
Key points.detail: Jake says to be blunt, like "press the purple button below to start your free trial", and to borrow wording from answers to "why do you love this app?". Sell outcomes with emotion: "feel your strongest" instead of "an AI weightlifting coach". Citizen crowdsourced copy in team sessions and found "never be alone" resonated.

Title: Speak4Me: 27% higher conversion with a multi-step Duolingo-style paywall
Creator: Superwall
What they did: Speak4Me replaced a single-screen paywall with a trial checkbox with a three-step flow modelled on Duolingo. The flow walks users through premium features before showing pricing and trial options.
Results: The multi-step paywall 'achieved a conversion rate increase of +27% over the simpler checkbox-style paywall' and 'resulted in a +36% increase in proceeds'. No baseline or sample size given.
Takeaways: A three-step value flow lifted conversion 27%; The simple paywall couldn't show the premium features' depth; Extra steps are fine when each one sells; Thin evidence: no baseline, sample or duration
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: test a 3-step flow. Step 1 is your plan to exam day (personalised from onboarding), step 2 is what's unlocked (full Qbank, explanations, mocks, flashcards), step 3 is plans with the trial timeline.
Bottom line: Selling the value over three short steps before showing the price beat a single dense paywall.

Key points.title: A three-step value flow lifted conversion 27%
Key points.detail: Speak4Me, a text-to-speech app, A/B tested its single-screen paywall with a trial checkbox against a multi-step, Duolingo-style flow. The multi-step version gave "+27%" conversion and "+36%" proceeds. Proceeds grew more than conversion, so the extra steps didn't cost revenue.

Key points.title: The simple paywall couldn't show the premium features' depth
Key points.detail: The team found the first paywall "too basic" to explain premium voices, unlimited exports and other paid features. Their hypothesis was that three steps would show more features and make a better case. For OnCourse, if the paid plan has several benefits, one crowded screen may undersell them.

Key points.title: Extra steps are fine when each one sells
Key points.detail: The test was set up to see whether the added friction and complexity were worth it. They were. Superwall's summary: "Guiding the user through the value proposition, even with added complexity, drives conversion." Pricing and trial options came last, after the features.

Key points.title: Thin evidence: no baseline, sample or duration
Key points.detail: This is a short vendor case study. It gives only relative lifts, with no starting conversion rate, sample size or test length. Treat it as a direction to test, not a proven number.

Title: Pepper: 50% lifetime value increase with a timeline paywall
Creator: Superwall
What they did: Tweaking headers and highlights hadn't moved LTV, so Pepper built a two-step paywall with a timeline of what happens on each day of the free trial. It shipped first to 5% of users, then to over 50% after it beat every other design.
Results: 'The timeline paywall boosted LTV by half' (50% LTV increase), and 'LTV was sustained after moving the paywall to a larger user base'. No absolute figures given.
Takeaways: A trial timeline paywall raised lifetime value by half; Change the format when copy tweaks stop working; Test risky designs on 5% before scaling; Trial clarity brought better sign-ups, not just more
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: a second step after plan selection that shows a dated trial timeline ('Today: full access to your NEET PG plan · Day 5: reminder · Day 7: ₹X charged, cancel anytime'). Roll out to 5% first and track trial-to-paid and LTV, not only trial starts.
Bottom line: A paywall step showing what happens on each day of the trial raised lifetime value by half.

Key points.title: A trial timeline paywall raised lifetime value by half
Key points.detail: Pepper, a recipe app, built a two-step paywall that shows the free-trial commitment as a timeline of what happens each day. It "boosted LTV by half" and beat every other paywall they had tested. For OnCourse, a day-by-day trial timeline is a clear option to test.

Key points.title: Change the format when copy tweaks stop working
Key points.detail: Pepper had "design fatigue": many tests changing subheaders and highlights didn't move LTV. They suspected the whole format was wrong. The case study's lesson is that the answer "isn't always another minor copy tweak".

Key points.title: Test risky designs on 5% before scaling
Key points.detail: The timeline paywall was a "wild card", so Pepper first showed it to only 5% of users to limit any drop. Once it won, they scaled it to over 50% of users, and LTV held at that size.

Key points.title: Trial clarity brought better sign-ups, not just more
Key points.detail: Showing users the full trial lifecycle "built trust and led to higher-quality sign-ups". Because the gain was in LTV, not just trial starts, clarity seems to help people stay after they pay. No absolute numbers are given.

Title: The Subscription Growth Formula: Churn Math, Retention Wins, and Smart Product Bets — Dan Layfield
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat (David Barnard with Dan Layfield, ex-Codecademy)
What they did: Cancellation flows that route by survey answer: 'too expensive' gets a temporary discount or a hidden cheaper tier, 'negative experience' goes to support, 'too busy' gets a pause, which Codecademy used for people who learn in bursts. Also rewrote Codecademy's checkout error copy and added dunning emails for failed payments.
Results: Reason-based save offers: 'I've seen between a 10 and 20% drop in churn'. Codecademy's checkout error copy rewrite (about two days of work) 'very conservatively lifted checkout page conversion 1%'. Dunning emails: 'not a massive uplift'. At very low churn, 'if you get your churn rate all the way down to 2%, 50% might be payment based churn'. Good lifecycle email: '30% open rate and a net 2% click-through rate'.
Takeaways: Match the save offer to the cancellation reason; Polish every screen that all users pass through; Growth ceiling equals new users divided by monthly churn; Retention lasts as long as the user has the problem; Users decide on a trial within the first ten minutes; Measure retention by a core action, not payments
Ideas for OnCourse: Renewal: add a cancel flow with a reason survey. 'Exam done/postponed' offers a pause until the next exam cycle; 'Too expensive' offers a discounted period or a cheaper Qbank-only tier; 'Not using it' offers a reset plan. Renewal: before renewal, show a recap ('You did 1,240 questions, accuracy up 18% in Pharmacology').
Bottom line: Match the save offer to why someone is cancelling: a pause for 'too busy', a cheaper plan for 'too expensive'. It cuts churn 10–20%.

Key points.title: Match the save offer to the cancellation reason
Key points.detail: Big subscription companies like the New York Times, CLEAR and Zoom route cancellations by survey answer. "Too expensive" gets a temporary discount or a hidden cheaper tier (Zoom offered Layfield a $7 plan instead of $15). "Negative experience" goes to support. "Too busy" gets a pause, which Codecademy used because people learn in bursts. Layfield has seen "between a 10 and 20% drop in churn". For OnCourse, a pause fits students between exam cycles. (Time is the chapter start; this part comes near the end of it.)

Key points.title: Polish every screen that all users pass through
Key points.detail: Layfield says purchase flows and onboarding should be "polished to a mirror finish" because everyone goes through them. At Codecademy they rewrote checkout error messages so they said what went wrong and what to try next, like switching to PayPal. It took about two days and "very conservatively lifted checkout page conversion 1%", which lifts all new revenue. He also suggests one open question right after purchase and fresh-eyes walkthroughs.

Key points.title: Growth ceiling equals new users divided by monthly churn
Key points.detail: One divided by monthly churn gives average months retained: 20% churn means about five months, and halving churn doubles it. New users per month divided by churn gives your ceiling: 500 a month at 10% churn caps you at 5,000. Below the ceiling, numbers drift up on their own, which can make product work look better than it is.

Key points.title: Retention lasts as long as the user has the problem
Key points.detail: Layfield says the least discussed driver of churn is how long people have the problem you solve. Phone plans last for years; things like dating, fitness and language learning last months, so those apps need huge audiences. "A surefire recipe to die" is a short use case plus a small audience. Exam prep is a time-limited use case, so OnCourse has to plan for that.

Key points.title: Users decide on a trial within the first ten minutes
Key points.detail: Layfield tracks activation steps: sign-up, setup, the first "aha" moment, first 30 days, then long-term retention. He says people decide whether to start a trial "almost in session zero, probably within the first 10 minutes". Good emails get about a 30% open rate and 2% click-through, so once you lose someone in the product, it's hard to get them back.

Key points.title: Measure retention by a core action, not payments
Key points.detail: A user can pay for months without using the product and then churn. Layfield says to define a core action and chart what share of each cohort keeps doing it month over month. If that curve flattens for some group, you have product-market fit there. He also mentions the Sean Ellis test: 40% or more saying they couldn't live without the product.

Title: Lessons from Asia: turning local research into global experiments
Creator: Zan Gilani and Carrie Wang (Duolingo)
Bottom line: One word in onboarding ("test") scared experienced learners away from placement, and renaming it doubled placement and lifted retention.
What they did: Japanese learners with prior English avoided the placement test ("The word 'test' scares me"), started from the beginning and churned because it was too easy. Duolingo reworded "take a placement test" to "check your English level", then ran it globally; they also fixed an under-13 registration flow and moved and rewrote the notification opt-in prompt.
Results: Rewording "doubled placement tests taken and increased retention as well"; run globally it "improved placement completion and retention across the board." Under-13 learners registered at "62% compared with 90% for others" before the fix (no post-fix number given). Japanese learners were "50% less likely to opt into receiving reminder notifications" before the opt-in prompt changes (no post-change number given).
Takeaways: Renaming "test" doubled placement tests taken; Ask for notification opt-in at motivated moments; Country data exposed a global sign-up bug; Prefer global experiments to forking the app; Learners forced to start at the basics churn
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: rename any "diagnostic test" step to something like "Check where you stand" and let NEET PG repeaters skip ahead based on it. Today's plan: start returning-aspirant users at their level so the first session isn't too easy. Notifications: ask for reminder permission right after the first completed question set, not on launch

Key points.title: Renaming "test" doubled placement tests taken
Key points.detail: In Japan, some new learners who already knew English avoided the placement test. One said: "The word 'test' scares me. It makes me feel nervous." They started from the beginning and then churned because it was too easy. Changing "take a placement test" to "check your English level" doubled placement tests and raised retention, and it worked globally too. For OnCourse, words like "test" on a diagnostic may scare students off.

Key points.title: Ask for notification opt-in at motivated moments
Key points.detail: Japanese learners were 50% less likely to turn on reminder notifications, which are one of the biggest factors in forming a habit. Duolingo moved the opt-in prompt, rewrote the pitch, and added it in new moments, like getting promoted in the leaderboard or running out of hearts. These changes helped learners everywhere.

Key points.title: Country data exposed a global sign-up bug
Key points.detail: Vietnam's sign-up rate was about 15% below the world average. The cause was the special flow for under-13 learners: 62% registered, versus 90% for others. The flow was just as bad everywhere, but under-13s were 2.5x more common in Vietnam, so the problem showed there. Fixing it helped all under-13 learners.

Key points.title: Prefer global experiments to forking the app
Key points.detail: Duolingo does build custom local versions when needed, like WeChat sign-in in China and some India-specific changes. But forking adds complexity, slows development and testing, and custom versions can "silently break". So they turn local insights into global experiments, sometimes testing in one country first.

Key points.title: Learners forced to start at the basics churn
Key points.detail: The Japan finding shows a wider risk: experienced learners who skip placement end up in content that is too easy and leave. A placement step that feels safe keeps them. For OnCourse, students who already know a subject should be able to skip ahead without feeling tested.

Title: Improving the streak: Forming habits one lesson at a time
Creator: Anton Yu (Duolingo)
Bottom line: Making the daily habit easy to keep (one lesson extends the streak) beat tying the streak to an ambitious daily goal, especially for new learners.
What they did: Previously the streak only extended if the learner hit their daily goal (a number of lessons). Duolingo separated the two, so one lesson extends the streak and daily-goal progress is shown separately, and A/B tested it against the combined mechanic.
Results: Day 14 retention +3.3%; daily active learners +1%; share of daily learners on a streak +10.5% within 20 days, and +19% among new learners only; learners on a 7+ day streak up "over 40%". A year later "just over half" of daily learners had a 7+ day streak versus roughly a third before. Downside: fewer learners hit their daily goals. Before the change, "almost 40%" of learners active two days in a row without a streak had the "intense" goal.
Takeaways: One lesson extends the streak, separate from the daily goal; Ambitious daily goals kept the keenest learners off streaks; Early on, the habit matters more than daily volume; 7+ day streaks rose from a third to over half; A 7-day streak predicts coming back tomorrow
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: extend the streak with one completed question set or lesson, not the full daily plan. Today's plan: show progress toward the full plan separately from the streak so a partial day still counts. Onboarding: don't let an ambitious "hours per day" answer raise the bar for keeping the streak

Key points.title: One lesson extends the streak, separate from the daily goal
Key points.detail: Before, learners had to hit their daily goal to extend the streak. Duolingo A/B tested letting one lesson extend the streak, with goal progress shown separately. Results: Day 14 retention +3.3%, daily active learners +1%, and +10.5% more daily learners on a streak within 20 days (all relative). Among new learners, the share on a streak rose 19%.

Key points.title: Ambitious daily goals kept the keenest learners off streaks
Key points.detail: Learners with higher daily goals were less likely to be on a streak even when they used the app every day. Almost 40% of learners active two days in a row without a streak had the "intense" goal, the highest tier. The goal had become a barrier to the habit. For OnCourse, a big daily question target should not decide whether the streak survives.

Key points.title: Early on, the habit matters more than daily volume
Key points.detail: Fewer learners reached their daily goals after the change. But more built a daily habit and spent more total time learning. Duolingo's lesson: lowering barriers to a daily habit matters more than how much you learn each day, at least early on, "because we can't teach people if they stop using Duolingo."

Key points.title: 7+ day streaks rose from a third to over half
Key points.detail: A year later, just over half of daily learners had a streak of at least 7 days, compared with about a third before. The number of learners on a 7+ day streak rose by over 40%. That means millions more people learning every day for at least a week.

Key points.title: A 7-day streak predicts coming back tomorrow
Key points.detail: Learners who reach a 7-day streak are 2.4 times more likely to keep using Duolingo the next day than learners without a streak. People extend streaks in the hundreds or thousands even on the days they give birth or get married. The streak is a strong habit tool, which is why its rules matter so much.

Title: How lesson transparency helps learners reach their goals
Creator: Rachel Salvador (Duolingo)
Bottom line: Telling learners when a question is hard, and showing how they leveled up, made them study longer and come back more.
What they did: Duolingo added a small "this is a hard exercise" indicator at the top of harder adaptive exercises, and a level-up card explaining how proficiency improved after finishing a skill level.
Results: No figures reported. With the indicator, learners studied longer, spent more time on harder exercises, were more likely to come back the next day and more likely to start a Duolingo Plus trial. With the level-up card, study time and return frequency increased and "learners chased the harder content!" A learner quote: "If I make a mistake, I don't feel as bad, because you warned me that it was hard. If I get it right, I feel proud."
Takeaways: Labelling hard exercises made learners study more; A warning softens mistakes and makes wins feel earned; Explaining what a level teaches made learners chase harder content; Hidden personalisation works better when it is visible; No effect sizes were published
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: tag high-difficulty questions with a "Tough one, most aspirants miss this" label before the answer. Lessons: end each topic with a card showing what the learner can now do (for example, accuracy up on a subject). Practice: show the share of users who got a question right after a wrong answer to reduce discouragement

Key points.title: Labelling hard exercises made learners study more
Key points.detail: Duolingo's adaptive lessons already served harder exercises to learners who were doing well. They added a small indicator at the top of the screen saying, in effect, "this is a hard exercise". Learners spent more time studying, did more hard exercises, came back the next day more often, and were more likely to start a Duolingo Plus trial. For OnCourse, tagging tough questions could have the same effect.

Key points.title: A warning softens mistakes and makes wins feel earned
Key points.detail: One learner said: "The indicator raises the floor and the ceiling. If I make a mistake, I don't feel as bad, because you warned me that it was hard. If I get it right, I feel proud." The label changes how both outcomes feel, without changing the question.

Key points.title: Explaining what a level teaches made learners chase harder content
Key points.detail: Each skill level has a different purpose, from learning new words to speaking. Learners focused on moving down the course rather than leveling up. Duolingo added clear messages about improved proficiency when a level was finished. Learners studied more, came back more, and "chased the harder content", leveling up more often.

Key points.title: Hidden personalisation works better when it is visible
Key points.detail: The adaptive system was already working, but learners didn't know it was happening. Telling them what was happening and why it mattered tapped their intrinsic motivation, the reason they were learning in the first place. For OnCourse, saying why a question was picked, such as a weak topic, may raise effort.

Key points.title: No effect sizes were published
Key points.detail: The post reports directions only: more time, more returns, more trials. It gives no percentages or sample sizes. Treat these as ideas to test, not proven numbers.

Title: Duolingo's User Retention: 8 Tactics Tested On 300 Million Users
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: Duolingo gets new and returning users moving with a one-tap start, an easy first lesson and a quick win, then asks for a small commitment.
What they did: The comic walks through a lapsed user's return: a one-tap shortcut to start a lesson without choosing, an easy "happy path" review lesson, a welcome-back reward, a streak start, a 7-day streak wager for gems, and notifications that stop on their own. It also proposes (not a Duolingo feature) an exit-point screen after the daily goal.
Results: The streak wager "increased Day-7 retention by +14%." Resurrected users are "20% less likely than a new user" to be retained. "15-30% Duolingo students use the app to make international travel more enjoyable." The proposed exit-point screen's objective is "Increase Day-30 retention by 5%" (a hypothesis, not a result).
Takeaways: A one-tap start button beats choosing a lesson; Make the comeback lesson easy on purpose; Ask for a commitment right after a reward; Stacked pop-ups break momentum for fragile users; Give users a clear place to stop; Apps that stop notifying earn trust and returns
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: one large "Start today's plan" button that drops users straight into the first question with no selection step. Practice: make the first set for a new or returning user easier than their level so they get a quick win. Today's plan: after the plan is done, show a completion screen that says come back tomorrow, with extra practice as a low-emphasis option

Key points.title: A one-tap start button beats choosing a lesson
Key points.detail: The returning user opens Duolingo and finds a shortcut that starts a lesson in one tap, "without wasting my psych to choose one." The screen around it was a "rainbow" of colours competing for attention, and the author suggests an overlay to keep focus on the button (Hick's Law). Later the shortcut disappeared and they "got lost in all the lessons." For OnCourse, Home should have one obvious start action, and everything else should be visually quieter.

Key points.title: Make the comeback lesson easy on purpose
Key points.detail: The first question in the returning user's review lesson was "Leche", and the whole lesson felt much easier than before. Growth.Design calls this the Happy Path: "offer a 'simplified' experience with reduced difficulty, even if you have to cheat your user flows a bit." It helps activation for new users and retention for users coming back after a pause. OnCourse could serve a returning aspirant an easier first set so the session starts with a win.

Key points.title: Ask for a commitment right after a reward
Key points.detail: Right after the daily goal, Duolingo offered a bet of 50 gems on a 7-day streak. The case study explains that a small investment loads the next trigger (a reminder about the commitment) and that people value what they have invested in. Duolingo "confirmed that this specific 'Investment Wager' step increased Day-7 retention by +14%." The best moment to ask is just after a win, not before it.

Key points.title: Stacked pop-ups break momentum for fragile users
Key points.detail: Between lessons the user was hit with 100 gems, an "Up Your Progress Score" quiz and a podcast promo, and almost forgot the daily goal. The author says this "splash screen stacking" wastes attention at a fragile moment, and suggests hiding such prompts from beginners and returning users. Duolingo's resurrected users "are 20% less likely than a new user to be retained." OnCourse should keep returning users in a clean flow until the first goal is done.

Key points.title: Give users a clear place to stop
Key points.detail: After the daily goal, the screen still showed many unfinished lessons, so closing the app felt like abandoning something. The author proposes (this is not a Duolingo feature) a done-for-today screen: prime the user to come back tomorrow, remind them of progress, and keep extra practice as a low-emphasis option. Its stated objective, "Increase Day-30 retention by 5%", is a hypothesis, not a result. OnCourse's daily plan needs a satisfying finish screen.

Key points.title: Apps that stop notifying earn trust and returns
Key points.detail: After the user ignored reminders for days, Duolingo said it would stop sending them. That message made the author want to go back "to show that I am committed." The case study lists three benefits: users are less annoyed, fewer turn notifications off "forever", and the app can try again at a better time. It also warns against shaming copy, like a loading screen line that guilt-trips users.

Chapters.title: Triggers
