Title: Duolingo's new learning path (new home screen design)
Creator: Holly Munson, Anton Yu, Ananya Rajgarhia, AJ Noh (Duolingo)
Bottom line: Duolingo replaced a choose-your-own skill tree with one guided path because learners weren't sure they were using the app the right way.
What they did: The branching skill tree became a single linear path where each circle is one level; lessons from different skills are interleaved for spaced repetition, practice sessions and Stories sit inside the path, tips moved to a per-unit guidebook, crowns were removed and unit names became descriptive ("get directions" instead of "City 3"). Launched to all learners on November 1, 2022.
Takeaways: Learners doubted they were studying the right way; Review is built into the forward path; Unit names say what you will be able to do; Separate features were folded into one path; A longer-looking path needs an explanation; Migrate progress so no one loses work
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: show today's plan as one ordered path of steps (lesson, questions, flashcards) with a clear next step rather than a grid of subjects. Today's plan: interleave revision of earlier topics into the plan so review counts as progress. Lessons: name units by outcome ("Read an ECG for MI") rather than chapter numbers

Key points.title: Learners doubted they were studying the right way
Key points.detail: Duolingo says "we often hear from learners that they're not sure whether they're using Duolingo the 'correct' or 'best' way." The fix was to replace the skill tree, where learners chose what to do, with one path to follow step by step. The goal was that learners can be "confident that each step you take in Duolingo is truly the best step." OnCourse aspirants face the same doubt with many subjects, so a single next step on Home removes it.

Key points.title: Review is built into the forward path
Key points.detail: Lessons in the path are ordered using spaced repetition, so levels from different skills are mixed together. Some circles teach new concepts and some revisit older ones. Duolingo writes that review "shouldn't feel like you're 'going back' to 'old' lessons. Practice is also forward progress." For OnCourse, mixing revision of earlier topics into today's plan lets review count as progress.

Key points.title: Unit names say what you will be able to do
Key points.detail: Old units had names like "City 3" and "Travel 2." The new headers are more descriptive, such as "get directions" and "discuss destinations", and tapping a circle shows its topic. This tells learners what they gain, not where they are in a list. OnCourse could name units by outcome rather than chapter numbers.

Key points.title: Separate features were folded into one path
Key points.detail: Stories moved from their own tab into the path. Tips became a guidebook for each unit. Practice sessions now sit inside the path too, and crowns were removed because progress down the path replaces them. Quests and Practice Hub became bottom tabs. Fewer places to look means fewer decisions about what to do next.

Key points.title: A longer-looking path needs an explanation
Key points.detail: The path looks longer because each level is now spread out, and practice and stories were added. The FAQ says plainly it is "all the same content, just organized in a different way." A floating arrow jumps back to your current spot when you scroll away. When a redesign changes how progress looks, say so up front.

Key points.title: Migrate progress so no one loses work
Key points.detail: All lesson progress was carried over, though some learners start earlier in the path to finish levels they skipped. Legendary status was granted for a whole unit if more than 50% of its levels came from skills already at Legendary. For busy days, a quick practice session is one tap away. When OnCourse restructures content, honouring past work avoids anger from loyal users.

Title: Scaling Duolingo, embracing failure, and insight into Latin America's tech scene (Gina Gotthilf)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Gina Gotthilf)
Bottom line: Duolingo's growth team wasted months because they didn't use their own experiments, and lost Indian users by defaulting to the wrong language.
What they did: Gina describes a lean badge test ("You sign up and then you get a badge") that showed nothing because "no one is proud of signing up"; after dogfooding became practice, badges later became a growth lever. In India, Duolingo used the phone's UI language (often English) as the base language, so users were offered French, Spanish or German from English when they wanted to learn English, and left.
Results: She says "More than 50% of our AB tests didn't work out." Badges, once done properly, "impacted almost all metrics across the company positively" (no figures given). She helped grow Duolingo "from 3 million to 200 million users."
Takeaways: A mission line on the paywall raised payments; A badge for signing up proved nothing; In India, phone language didn't show what users wanted; Title and button should tell the whole story; A distinct voice: ask 'could another company write this?'; Copying Duolingo's screens without its data habits fails
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: ask the exam and preferred explanation language directly instead of inferring from device settings. Streaks: tie the first badge or celebration to a real study action (first 10 questions answered), never to account creation. Practice: have the team play through each onboarding variant on a real device before it ships

Key points.title: A mission line on the paywall raised payments
Key points.detail: When Duolingo tested screens that ask users to pay, it added a line like 'By paying for Duolingo, you're making language learning accessible to millions of people.' Gina says this 'actually improved the metric', because 'people cared enough to make the payment.' The mission was also built into social posts: one post a week on effectiveness and one on the mission. For OnCourse, a paywall could say what a subscription makes possible beyond the user's own prep, if that is true.

Key points.title: A badge for signing up proved nothing
Key points.detail: The growth team wanted badges because every top game had them, but Gina held the idea back for six months as too costly. They then ran a lean test: 'You sign up and then you get a badge.' It showed no effect, because 'no one is proud of signing up', there was nothing to collect and nothing to show others. They dropped badges for about eight more months, and later found they had never used their own variants. Done properly, badges 'impacted almost all metrics across the company positively.'

Key points.title: In India, phone language didn't show what users wanted
Key points.detail: Duolingo used the phone's UI language as the user's base language. In India most people set their phones to English, partly because typing in Hindi is hard. So the app offered French, Spanish or German from English, while people actually wanted to learn English, and they left. The team only saw this once they went to India. For OnCourse, ask users directly about language and exam rather than inferring it from device settings.

Key points.title: Title and button should tell the whole story
Key points.detail: On the Bloomberg campaign, Gina worked on landing pages while everyone else worked on ads, and once took a page 'from three to 12% conversion rate' in a day. Her rules: design for mobile first, keep the core copy and button above the fold, cut copy until it is shorter than seems needed, and make the title and button 'speak to each other' so people who read only those two get it. Images should support the message, not distract. She also says the second and third screens matter as much as the first, because that is where people leak out.

Key points.title: A distinct voice: ask 'could another company write this?'
Key points.detail: Duolingo checked every piece of copy by asking 'Could this have been written by other companies? ... What makes this Duolingo?' Gina wrote many of the passive-aggressive notifications, including 'This doesn't seem to be working. We'll stop sending them for now,' sent after five days of inactivity. The team even A/B tested the size of Sad Duo's puddle and the number of tears. When users made memes from it, Duolingo leaned in instead of backing off.

Key points.title: Copying Duolingo's screens without its data habits fails
Key points.detail: Founders often show Gina apps that look exactly like Duolingo because 'we used Duolingo' as the design. She compares it to copying the best student's answer on a maths test: you get the answer but not the method. What Duolingo really had was engineers and PMs watching how every change moved other metrics, forming hypotheses and checking statistical significance. She also says more than 50% of their A/B tests failed.

Title: Using behavioral science to improve your product (Kristen Berman, Irrational Labs)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Kristen Berman)
Bottom line: Easy questions in onboarding that make users think about the benefit raise conversion, hard open-text questions lower it, and the first key action should be booked during onboarding.
What they did: Kristen explains replacing benefit carousels with easy multiple-choice questions about what users want, removing an open-text question, and redesigning One Medical onboarding to ask a few health questions, then recommend one provider and a few appointment times so people book right after signing up.
Results: Trunk Club "has come out and said they did this and it increased conversion by 133%" (benefit questions in signup). TytoCare quiz: "53% of them went on to purchase versus 37% who didn't complete." Removing an open-text field "improved conversion by 40% page over page." One Medical: recommending one provider and a few appointment times "increased bookings by 20% during onboarding."
Takeaways: Easy questions about benefits raise signup conversion; Open-text questions are hard; removing one lifted conversion 40%; One Medical got the first booking done in onboarding; Budgeting, the most-requested feature, changed nothing; Define the behavior uncomfortably specifically; never 'log in'; Give a reason to act today, even a 'wrong' one
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: replace intro carousels with 2–3 tap questions (target exam, attempt year, weakest subject) that end in a recommended first session. Onboarding: drop any free-text fields and recommend one starting topic and one time slot instead of a subject list. Today's plan: if someone leaves mid-onboarding or mid-set, reopen exactly where they stopped

Key points.title: Easy questions about benefits raise signup conversion
Key points.detail: Asking a question puts an idea in someone's head; Kristen shows this by asking Lenny about her mother. In signup, questions like Apartment List's (studio or one-bedroom? patio or view?) make people think about the benefit, which helps them push through later friction. Trunk Club 'said they did this and it increased conversion by 133%'. On TytoCare's site, '53% of them went on to purchase versus 37% who didn't complete' the quiz. She suggests replacing the benefits carousel with questions like these.

Key points.title: Open-text questions are hard; removing one lifted conversion 40%
Key points.detail: Extra questions help only when they are easy, like a dropdown or multiple choice. Removing an open-ended text field 'improved conversion by 40% page over page'. The team had thought that question was easy, but 'most questions when you're asking people with an open text field, it's just not an easy question.' For OnCourse onboarding, keep every question to a tap.

Key points.title: One Medical got the first booking done in onboarding
Key points.detail: The team picked one behavior: book a doctor's appointment right after signing up. Otherwise, when users get sick months later, they forget the app and call their old doctor. Onboarding asked a few health questions (mental, sleep, physical), recommended one provider and said why, and offered a few virtual appointment times for tomorrow. Bookings during onboarding rose 20%. For OnCourse, this suggests finishing onboarding with one recommended first session at a set time.

Key points.title: Budgeting, the most-requested feature, changed nothing
Key points.detail: A fintech app's most-requested feature was budgeting. In a test with 10,000 people, two budgeting designs against a control that only showed spend gave 'zero change in average spend, zero change in spend variability.' Mapping every step (know your budget, know where you are in the month, make a plan, act on it many times a month) shows why it was unlikely to work. She calls this a 'behavioral diagnosis' and says to treat any work put on the user with suspicion.

Key points.title: Define the behavior uncomfortably specifically; never 'log in'
Key points.detail: The 3B model is behavior, barriers and benefits. The behavior must be an action, and 'the only wrong answer here is log in.' Her Peloton example: 'within seven days of somebody starting the app, they do two 10-minute workouts with two different instructors.' She says 'if you're not arguing with your teammates, you're doing it wrong.' She also suggests setting team incentives on this behavior, over a longer period, so tactics stay customer-friendly.

Key points.title: Give a reason to act today, even a 'wrong' one
Key points.detail: People are present-biased, so long-term benefits are not enough. Asana gets tasks logged partly through completion bias and teammates seeing work done. 'Right for Wrong' means doing the right thing for an immediate, unrelated reason, like pizza at the polls or an instructor's shout-out or a streak on Peloton. Adding a deadline to Kiva's borrower signup increased conversion; 'deadlines are a gift.' Wealthfront found that sending drop-offs back to where they stopped, not to the start, kept them going.

Title: Inside Duolingo's Unhinged Growth to a $500M Business (Cem Kansu)
Creator: Peter Yang with Cem Kansu (Duolingo)
Bottom line: Duolingo's core loop is the lesson on a linear home path with celebration at the end, and placing users at the right level matters a lot for retention.
What they did: Duolingo's head of product describes the core loop (a linear home path, a lesson, then celebration, streak extension and quests), streaks, leaderboards and push notifications as the main growth levers, and placement for learners who already know some of the language. He also describes temporarily changing the app icon to a "melting" or sick Duo for two to three weeks.
Results: No experiment numbers. He says growth "wasn't the case that one feature just changed all of our growth curves" but compounded over time, and that subscriptions now make up "more than 80%" of Duolingo revenue. On placement: "it certainly helps retention if you can kind of land the right person based on what they know to the right part of the courses."
Takeaways: Growth came from many stacked levers, not one feature; Passive-aggressive notifications work, and they know when to stop; The core loop is a game: path, lesson, celebration; Placing learners at the right level lifts retention; Charge for extras, never for learning itself; An "unhinged" app icon brings lapsed users back
Ideas for OnCourse: Lessons: end every lesson and question set with a celebration screen that shows the streak extended and progress toward today's plan. Onboarding: offer a short placement set so repeat NEET PG aspirants start at their level. Home: make the path to the next lesson the dominant element

Key points.title: Growth came from many stacked levers, not one feature
Key points.detail: Cem Kansu names streaks, leaderboards and push notifications as the top drivers to 100M monthly users. None of them changed the curve alone. They compounded over years of small improvements. Streaks existed from launch but were made more animated and visible again and again, and some users now have streaks over 1,000 days. Peter Yang notes daily users were still growing about 60% a year after a decade. For OnCourse: keep improving the streak and the weekly league steadily instead of hunting for one big feature.

Key points.title: Passive-aggressive notifications work, and they know when to stop
Key points.detail: Reminders are written in Duo's guilt-tripping voice. If a learner ignores them for several days, Duolingo stops sending them and ends with a message saying the reminders "don't seem to be working." Kansu compares it to a text from "a significant other that is kind of pissed off." For OnCourse: give reminders a voice, and end a run of ignored nudges with one honest last message instead of sending forever.

Key points.title: The core loop is a game: path, lesson, celebration
Key points.detail: Kansu calls Duolingo a game. The loop is a linear path on Home, then a lesson, then a celebration that extends the streak and fills quests. The path borrows from game design: you always know the next node to tap. For OnCourse: make the next lesson the dominant thing on Home, and end every question set with a reward screen that shows the streak and today's progress.

Key points.title: Placing learners at the right level lifts retention
Key points.detail: Onboarding has to handle people who already know some of the language. Kansu says placement is hard to get right, but "it certainly helps retention if you can kind of land the right person based on what they know to the right part of the courses." For OnCourse: repeat NEET PG aspirants should not start at chapter one. A short placement set can drop them where they are.

Key points.title: Charge for extras, never for learning itself
Key points.detail: The CEO had publicly promised no ads and no subscriptions. Kansu's team added them anyway, in order: ads first, then purchases like streak repairs, then a subscription that began as ad removal. The rule was that free and paid users learn the same. Subscriptions now bring in "more than 80%" of revenue, with perks like unlimited hearts and AI conversation. They A/B tested ad load, Plus versus Super naming, and even purchase-flow colors.

Key points.title: An "unhinged" app icon brings lapsed users back
Key points.detail: For about 2–3 weeks at a time, Duolingo swaps the app icon for everyone to a sick, wrinkly, melting or boogery Duo. Lapsed users think it is aimed at them personally and come back. Inside Duolingo, calling a change "unhinged" is a compliment. In one review the feedback was that "there weren't enough boogers." For OnCourse: mascot personality can be a retention tool, as long as it fits the brand.

Title: Why BoldVoice charged from day 1 and ignored the Duolingo freemium playbook (Anada Lakra)
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat, with Anada Lakra (BoldVoice)
Bottom line: Forcing a trial with a hard paywall raised trial starts but refunds rose faster, so BoldVoice gives the speech assessment and the whole first daily plan free before asking for a trial.
What they did: BoldVoice tested a hard paywall with no close button, and a version where closing the paywall gave a discount. They now let users who close the paywall take the speech assessment, see their results, and do the rest of day one's training for free, then require a 7-day trial from day two.
Results: Lakra: "Both of those look so promising on the trial numbers," but "The refund spiked by way more than the gain in start trials." (Quotes as given in RevenueCat's write-up of the episode; no exact figures given.)
Takeaways: Judge paywall tests on net revenue after refunds; Forcing people into trials costs more in refunds; Give a small free taste, then ask for the trial; Charging from day one tells you who your customer is; Everyone on the team does two user interviews a week; A free web tool went viral, then fed the app
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: make the full first daily plan free for every new user, with the paywall shown after day one is done. Onboarding: start with a short diagnostic whose results are shown free, as the first value moment. Paywall: measure trial tests on paid conversion and refunds, not trial starts

Key points.title: Judge paywall tests on net revenue after refunds
Key points.detail: BoldVoice now scores paywall tests on net revenue after refunds, per user who saw the paywall, on a matured cohort. That means waiting at least an extra week for trials to convert and two more weeks for refunds to settle. Anada Lakra says the hard part is patience, sitting on exciting data for a month or more. For OnCourse: never call a paywall test a win on trial starts alone.

Key points.title: Forcing people into trials costs more in refunds
Key points.detail: They tested a hard paywall with no X, and a version where closing the paywall showed a discount you couldn't close. Both "look so promising on the trial numbers," but "the refund spiked by way more than the gain in start trials." People who feel tricked ask for their money back when the charge hits and leave angry. Her rule: "Anything that kind of forces or tricks people into starting a trial, you'll pay it when it comes to refunds."

Key points.title: Give a small free taste, then ask for the trial
Key points.detail: If you close the paywall, you still get the speech assessment, the first daily plan and a coach video for free. On day two you need to start a 7-day trial to continue. David Barnard calls it a reverse trial. Lakra calls it a middle ground that keeps the onboarding paywall for people already ready to pay. For OnCourse: a free diagnostic plus one full day of the plan shows value before the ask.

Key points.title: Charging from day one tells you who your customer is
Key points.detail: BoldVoice launched during Y Combinator's summer 2021 batch at $10 a month with a one-week trial. "Charging for the product is a way to already figure out who that ICP is." They skipped Duolingo's freemium model on purpose: it suits huge numbers of hobby learners, while BoldVoice serves professionals whose alternative is a paid accent coach. She warns against mixing parts of different apps' playbooks into a "mishmash strategy."

Key points.title: Everyone on the team does two user interviews a week
Key points.detail: Automated invites go to a mix of long-time subscribers, new converters and people who didn't convert, and book whoever on the team has free time. Engineers demo unshipped features to a weekly super-user group. Because happy users are the ones who book calls, they add a three-question email survey and a short cancel-flow question. Without that, she says, you make happy people happier and the product gets narrower.

Key points.title: A free web tool went viral, then fed the app
Key points.detail: Their ML team built the Accent Oracle, an ungated web app that guesses where you're from after about ten seconds of speech. One Korean angel investor posted it on Threads, and "the next day we had 100,000 people in Korea try this thing." Showing a preview of fuller results waiting in the app lifted the number who downloaded it. Her lesson: you can't engineer virality, but you can add levers to something that already has it.

Title: This is not a playbook: how Mimo grew customer LTV by 65%
Creator: Ekaterina Gamsriegler (Mimo), RevenueCat blog
Bottom line: For Mimo, the biggest wins came from a transparent trial screen during onboarding and localising the app, not from retention tactics.
What they did: Mimo replaced its onboarding paywall with an "honest" Blinkist-style screen explaining how the trial works (plus trial-ending reminders), cut the trial from 30 to 14 days, raised the yearly price 20%, and localised into six languages after a two-language test.
Results: Honest paywall: "trial opt-in rates more than doubled" and trial-to-purchase rose 50% (the recap cites a 53% purchase-rate lift). Localisation: "D7 retention increased by +40% on average" in core markets and purchase rate rose 25–100%, with bigger gains where English adoption is lower. 20% price rise: higher ARPU with conversion unchanged. Churn and win-back tactics had no significant LTV impact. Over about three quarters: cLTV +65%, paid CAC -20%, monthly proceeds +35%.
Takeaways: An honest trial screen doubled trial opt-ins; Localising lifted retention most where English is weak; Match trial length to how fast users activate; Retention tactics matter little when revenue comes from new subscribers; Ad creative sets expectations for everything after; Sharing works only at moments users are proud of
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: test explanations and UI in Hindi and other regional languages for aspirants who prefer them, and measure D7. Paywall: show a plain timeline of the trial (today, reminder day, charge day). Renewal: send a reminder before the trial ends

Key points.title: An honest trial screen doubled trial opt-ins
Key points.detail: Mimo copied Blinkist's "honest trial paywall", a clear explanation of how the free trial works, because store reviews showed trial anxiety every day. "Trial opt-in rates more than doubled, and conversion from trial-to-purchase improved by 50%" (the summary later says purchase rate rose 53%). Trial-ending reminders did not have a strong negative effect on cancellations. Because most trials started in onboarding, more people paid full price, which lifted LTV.

Key points.title: Localising lifted retention most where English is weak
Key points.detail: Mimo localised into six languages after testing two. D7 retention rose by 40% on average in core markets, and purchase rate rose 25% to 100%. "The lower the market's adoption of English, the higher the activation metrics moved." Better reviews then raised store conversion and lowered blended CAC. For OnCourse, regional-language support may matter most for aspirants less comfortable in English.

Key points.title: Match trial length to how fast users activate
Key points.detail: Mimo ran 30-day trials for a long time; opt-ins were high, but so were cancellations by day 30. Users thought they had used up the content, or never built a habit. Shortening to 14 days and showing how much content there is helped. RevenueCat data shows over 55% of 3-day trials cancel on day 0 or 1, versus 31% of 30-day trials, and 7 or 14 days often suits education apps.

Key points.title: Retention tactics matter little when revenue comes from new subscribers
Key points.detail: Mimo built payment-failure reminders, trial reminders, lifecycle messages and cancellation flows. "None of it significantly moved the needle on LTV," because most revenue came from new subscriptions and churn cohorts were small. The author says subscriber retention work pays off once recurring revenue is a big share, or churn starts to exceed new subscribers. Before that, it may solve a problem that does not exist yet.

Key points.title: Ad creative sets expectations for everything after
Key points.detail: Mimo's early ads were playful cartoons with good click rates. But they signalled "game" and "easy" rather than "serious learning tool", which lowered the intent of people who downloaded. Switching to professional, coding-focused imagery changed who entered the funnel. Seasonal and discount cohorts showed a similar trap: high volume, then churn months later.

Key points.title: Sharing works only at moments users are proud of
Key points.detail: Mimo added share-to-stories at streaks, league promotions and other milestones, and many users shared daily. The same feature failed in Playgrounds, where users were not proud of their projects. A rebuilt referral programme tripled the k-factor, but "a triple from 0 was still pretty much 0." OnCourse should place share prompts only at real achievements, like a mock test score.

Title: The Longest Onboarding Ever (Noom)
Creator: Jacob Rushfinn, Retention.Blog
Bottom line: Noom's 90+ screen onboarding works by explaining why it asks each question and giving value (a predicted goal date, a profile) before the paywall.
What they did: A teardown of Noom's 96+ screen onboarding: it explains why each question is asked, uses a progress bar and conversational copy, adds encouragement after sensitive answers, breaks questions up with social proof and study stats, repeats the value proposition on 5+ screens, varies question formats, keeps text to about a sentence, predicts the goal-weight date and adds a behavioural profile quiz before a paywall with a countdown timer.
Takeaways: Tell users why you ask each question; Show specific value before the paywall; Repeat what makes you different, many times; Pair an emotional story with a hard stat; Keep each screen to one sentence and vary formats; Expensive plans need urgency and reassurance
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: add a one-line "why we ask" under each personalisation question. Onboarding: end with a personalised prediction (for example, syllabus coverage by a date given daily minutes) before the paywall. Paywall: show a short topper testimonial next to an outcome stat

Key points.title: Tell users why you ask each question
Key points.detail: The common line is "We'll ask some questions to personalize your experience." Noom goes further and explains why it asks each one, for example why it wants to know about your lifestyle. After sensitive answers like weight it adds encouragement: "Thank you for sharing! That's an important (and hard) first step!" OnCourse could add a one-line reason under each onboarding question.

Key points.title: Show specific value before the paywall
Key points.detail: Noom predicts the date you will hit your goal weight, runs a quiz that tells you your "behavioral profile", and gives quick diet tips, all before asking for money. The author's point: users think "If you're this helpful before me giving you money then I can't wait til I pay!" For OnCourse, a personal prediction (such as syllabus coverage by a date) could come before the paywall.

Key points.title: Repeat what makes you different, many times
Key points.detail: Noom shows "Noom creates long-term results through habit and behavior change, not restrictive dieting" in different forms on 5+ screens. The author warns: "If a user makes it through your new user experience without understanding why you're different/better, you've failed." Onboarding is where OnCourse's main difference should be stated, more than once.

Key points.title: Pair an emotional story with a hard stat
Key points.detail: Between questions, Noom takes breaks with social proof: testimonials, partner brand names, and stats from studies. It shows an emotional testimonial and then follows with a study figure. The author ties this to Aristotle's pathos (emotion), ethos (credibility) and logos (logic). OnCourse could put a topper's short story next to an outcome number.

Key points.title: Keep each screen to one sentence and vary formats
Key points.detail: Noom uses a progress bar so people know what to expect. It keeps to "one sentence max per screen so you can tap through and read at a glance." It also changes question styles to fight visual fatigue across 96+ screens. Long onboarding can work if each screen is fast.

Key points.title: Expensive plans need urgency and reassurance
Key points.detail: At about $100 per 2 months, Noom starts a countdown timer when you reach the paywall, playing on the effort you just put into your plan. The paywall is long so it can include all the reassurances a buyer needs. The onboarding also includes a refer-a-friend step framed as an "accountability buddy" and asks "How did you hear about us?" The higher the price, the more trust you must build.

Title: Growing a Mindset with the Right Words (Khan Academy x PERTS experiment)
Creator: Rebecca Butler, EdSurge
Bottom line: One growth-mindset sentence above practice problems raised mastery on Khan Academy, while generic encouragement did nothing.
What they did: Stanford's PERTS and Khan Academy randomly showed 250,000+ students one of three message types above fraction problems for two months (Jan–Feb 2013): growth mindset ("If you make a mistake, it's an opportunity to get smarter!"), standard encouragement ("Some of these problems are hard. Just do your best.") or science facts, against a no-message control.
Results: Growth-mindset messages increased concepts mastered by 3%; the other message types had "no statistically significant effect."
Takeaways: One growth-mindset line raised mastery by 3%; Generic encouragement did nothing; Growth mindset turns effort into a good sign; Each student saw one message type for two months; Longer mindset sessions showed bigger effects
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: after a wrong answer, show a short line that treats the mistake as learning ("Getting this wrong now is how it sticks for exam day"), and A/B test it against no message. Flashcards: use the same framing when a card is marked "Again"

Key points.title: One growth-mindset line raised mastery by 3%
Key points.detail: PERTS (a Stanford research centre) and Khan Academy placed messages above fraction problems for over 250,000 students in January and February 2013. Growth messages like "If you make a mistake, it's an opportunity to get smarter!" "increased the number of concepts that students mastered by 3%." It is a tiny change in copy with a measured effect on learning. OnCourse could test the same idea above practice questions.

Key points.title: Generic encouragement did nothing
Key points.detail: Two other message types were tested: standard encouragement ("Some of these problems are hard. Just do your best.") and science facts ("An elephant brain weighs 7/2 as much as a human brain"). Both had "no statistically significant effect." So it is not just any friendly line that helps. The words must change how the student sees effort and mistakes.

Key points.title: Growth mindset turns effort into a good sign
Key points.detail: PERTS associate director Carissa Romero explains that growth-mindset students believe effort and the right strategies make them smarter: "Their main goal is to learn." Students with a fixed mindset see needing effort "as evidence of failure" and give up more easily. This is why copy that frames a wrong answer as learning can keep a struggling aspirant going.

Key points.title: Each student saw one message type for two months
Key points.detail: Students were randomly assigned one of three message types, plus a fourth control group with no message. The message type stayed constant over the two months, and researchers measured proficiency. That design makes the comparison clean. OnCourse can copy the setup: one variant per user, measured on learning, not clicks.

Key points.title: Longer mindset sessions showed bigger effects
Key points.detail: In other PERTS studies, at-risk high school students who did a single 30-minute online mindset session earned As, Bs or Cs at a 14% higher rate over the semester. Community college math students saw a 12% rise in satisfactory grades. The article stresses the low cost of these interventions. A short onboarding module on how practice builds ability might be worth testing.

Title: Finding hidden growth opportunities in your product (Albert Cheng: Duolingo, Grammarly, Chess.com)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Albert Cheng)
Bottom line: Once an app matures, returning and resurrected users matter as much as new ones, so design a real comeback experience and protect beginners from early failure.
What they did: Duolingo used social push notifications (a friend just joined) and re-placement tests to bring back lapsed learners, and briefly tracked screenshots in the app to find shareable moments (streak milestones, funny challenges, top-3 leaderboard finishes) and then invested illustrators and animators in them. Chess.com is testing a guided learn-to-play flow for self-declared beginners and hiding ratings for the first five games.
Results: At Chess.com, new and resurrected users are 'about similar size' in the active base, with roughly 80% of daily or weekly actives being existing users (Cheng's estimate). Over 75% of Chess.com new users call themselves new or beginners, fewer than a third win their first game, and 'when you lose a game, user retention is 10% worse than when you win a game'. Cheng calls D1 retention of 30 to 40% 'quite solid' for a consumer app. At Chess.com, showing best moves and an encouraging coach after a loss in Game Review "grew game reviews by 25%, subscriptions by 20%". At Grammarly, showing free users a taste of paid suggestions meant "our upgrade rates nearly doubled".
Takeaways: Encourage after a loss instead of showing mistakes; Let free users taste paid features inside real use; Make the moments people already screenshot much better; Protect beginners from early failure signals; Design a real comeback flow for returning users; Gamification has three parts: core loop, metagame, profile
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: show users back after 14+ days a 'welcome back' quick diagnostic that re-places them in their plan instead of a backlog of missed tasks. Practice: for a first-time user's first session, serve an easier calibrated set and hide accuracy percentages until they have done 3 sessions. Streaks: track which screens users screenshot and invest in the share card for those (e.g., mock-test score, milestone streak).

Key points.title: Encourage after a loss instead of showing mistakes
Key points.detail: Chess.com's Game Review was built so players could study their mistakes after a loss. The data showed '80% of people that review their games actually do so after a win.' So after a loss the coach now shows your brilliant and best moves and says something like 'Losing, just part of learning, keep it up.' That change 'grew game reviews by 25%, subscriptions by 20%', and lifted retention. For OnCourse, a post-test review after a bad score could lead with what the student got right before the wrong answers.

Key points.title: Let free users taste paid features inside real use
Key points.detail: Grammarly's free users only saw spelling and grammar fixes, so they thought that was all Grammarly did. The team mixed a few paid suggestions (tone, clarity, full rewrites) into free users' writing, capped and refreshed over time. Cheng calls it 'a reverse free trial but in real time.' Upgrade rates 'nearly doubled.' His rule: make the free product 'a reflection of everything that your product can offer.' For OnCourse, free users could get a small daily taste of premium explanations or analytics inside their normal practice.

Key points.title: Make the moments people already screenshot much better
Key points.detail: Duolingo's virality team briefly tracked screenshots in the app to find where users already shared. The hotspots were streak milestones, funny challenges, and reaching the top three of a leaderboard. They then put illustrators and animators on those exact moments, which 'worked amazingly well.' The lesson is to amplify what people already want to share, not push sharing elsewhere. For OnCourse, find which screens students screenshot (mock scores, streaks) and design rich share cards for them.

Key points.title: Protect beginners from early failure signals
Key points.detail: Over 75% of Chess.com's new users call themselves new or beginners. Fewer than a third win their first game, and 'when you lose a game, user retention is 10% worse than when you win a game.' Chess.com is testing a guided learn-to-play flow for self-declared beginners and hiding ratings for the first five games. Cheng says first steps in learning are 'fraught with a lot of self-doubt,' so design around them. For OnCourse, first sessions could use easier sets and hide accuracy scores until a student has some wins.

Key points.title: Design a real comeback flow for returning users
Key points.detail: At Chess.com, roughly 80% of daily or weekly actives are existing users, and new and resurrected users are 'about similar size.' A mature app builds up huge numbers of dormant users, so the return experience deserves real design. Duolingo used social pushes ('one of your best friends just started using Duolingo') and offered a new placement test so returning learners land at the right level. For OnCourse, a student back after weeks away needs a quick re-placement, not a pile of missed tasks.

Key points.title: Gamification has three parts: core loop, metagame, profile
Key points.detail: Cheng credits Jorge Mazal with this model. The core loop is the daily lesson: do it, get rewards, extend the streak, get a push tomorrow. The metagame is the long-term goal, such as Duolingo's path, leaderboards and achievements. The profile reflects your investment over time. Nailing all three gives a long learning journey. OnCourse can check each screen against this: the daily plan is the loop, rank and syllabus coverage are the metagame, and the profile shows stored progress.

Title: How to Time Reactivation Campaigns for Maximum Impact (Jackson Shuttleworth, Duolingo)
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat (David Barnard with Jackson Shuttleworth)
Bottom line: Win-back has a short window: after 3 to 4 days away a daily-habit user is hard to recover, so the first week of reminders, then weekly email, then personal or social reasons to return carry the load.
What they did: Duolingo sends a practice reminder on each of the first 7 days a user skips, then stops; it schedules the next reminder 23.5 hours after the user's first practice of the day instead of a time picked at onboarding. Lapsed users then get a weekly progress-report email, long-lapsed users get a Year in Review and seasonal (back-to-school, New Year) pushes, and active users are prompted to nudge friends who have been gone for months.
Results: No lift percentages. Shuttleworth says efficacy 'has dropped significantly' by day 7, that after day 3 to 4 without a return 'it is just going to be tough sledding', that the 23.5-hour timing consistently beat other strategies, that 55 or 60% of users have a friend on the app, and that friend-to-friend resurrection is 'one of our best-performing' win-back campaigns. Messages from leaderboard strangers get a 'much higher click-through rate' than app reminders.
Takeaways: Win back users within three to four days; Schedule reminders 23.5 hours after today's first session; Friends bring lapsed users back better than the app; Switch to email with a weekly progress report; Give long-lapsed users delight, not product news; Test notification copy constantly
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: schedule tomorrow's study reminder about 23.5 hours after today's first session, and send a daily reminder for 7 days after a miss, then stop. Renewal: send lapsed users a weekly email with their questions done, accuracy and days to exam compared with last week. Notifications: let active users tap 'nudge' on a study-buddy who has been inactive for a while, with prewritten copy.

Key points.title: Win back users within three to four days
Key points.detail: Duolingo sends a practice reminder on each day a user misses, then turns them off at day seven. Shuttleworth says "even by day seven, the efficacy has dropped significantly," and "if they're not coming back by day three or four... it is just going to be tough sledding." He adds that even one or two days away makes return much harder. OnCourse should put most reminder effort into the first few days after a miss.

Key points.title: Schedule reminders 23.5 hours after today's first session
Key points.detail: Many apps ask users at onboarding when they want reminders. Shuttleworth says the chance you are free at that time forever "is just zero." What "was always a winner" was scheduling the next reminder 23.5 hours after the user's first practice of the day. They tested many strategies and "this is the one that continues to win."

Key points.title: Friends bring lapsed users back better than the app
Key points.detail: About 55 or 60% of Duolingo users have a friend on the app. Prompting active users to nudge friends who have been gone for months is "one of our best-performing" win-back campaigns, because "it's Jackson saying, 'Hey, come back and learn with me.'" Even messages from leaderboard strangers get a much higher click-through rate than app reminders. Returning users can then be eased into Friend Streaks.

Key points.title: Switch to email with a weekly progress report
Key points.detail: For users gone a few weeks, Duolingo sends a weekly progress email comparing this week with last week. Email has more space than push and reaches people who may have uninstalled. They test framing that is hopeful, a challenge, or a little passive-aggressive. Just showing XP and time spent, with supportive copy, "gets a lot of the bang for the buck."

Key points.title: Give long-lapsed users delight, not product news
Key points.detail: For users gone for months, Duolingo's Year in Review shows fun stats, even for someone who "used it for a few days in April." Outreach works much better when it is personal or tied to a time of year, like back to school or New Year's resolutions, than when it is "here's a product update." OnCourse has natural moments too, like exam-date countdowns and result season.

Key points.title: Test notification copy constantly
Key points.detail: Duolingo has machine-learning systems that pick the right copy for each user; PMs just add variants. "We test so much copy, like a disgusting amount of copy." The practice reminder has been under experiment for six years. Churned users are the ones you understand least, so they need the most testing.

Title: How to Turn Gamification Into a Retention Powerhouse (Anton Derlyatka, Sweatcoin)
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat (David Barnard and Jacob Eiting with Anton Derlyatka)
Bottom line: A balance that keeps growing works better as progress than a counter that resets to zero each day, and optional rewards help retention only up to a small daily cap.
What they did: Sweatcoin turned validated steps into an in-app currency (1 coin per 1,000 steps, with a daily cap) that accumulates rather than resetting daily, avoided guilt-based nudges, and tested optional rewarded videos worth 1 coin at once per day versus up to three or more per day.
Results: Allowing rewarded video one to three times a day improved retention and engagement, while allowing it more often than that made retention drop. About 20% of users engage with ads. Derlyatka says users would pay 1 to 5 cents for others' coins but would sell their own for 50 cents to $1, and that moving retention by 1% is a 'massive uplift' at 60 to 80 thousand daily onboards.
Takeaways: A growing balance beats a counter that resets daily; Cap bonus rewards at a few per day; People value their own earned coins far more; Build the invite into the main earning screen; Skip guilt and use positive reinforcement; Gamification needs a genuinely good core
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: show a lifetime 'questions mastered' count that only grows, alongside the daily goal that resets. Practice: cap bonus XP rounds (e.g., 'bonus review') at 1 to 3 per day rather than unlimited. Notifications: drop guilt-framed copy in favour of progress-framed copy and A/B test it.

Key points.title: A growing balance beats a counter that resets daily
Key points.detail: Derlyatka contrasts Fitbit, where "you got 10,000 steps, next morning, zero," with Sweatcoin's balance that "keeps on growing." He says the balance "serves as a progression system": his own 15,000 coins make him want to reach 20,000. Jacob Eiting adds that when the experience grows with time and effort invested, it creates hooks that help retention. OnCourse could pair a resetting daily goal with a lifetime count that only grows.

Key points.title: Cap bonus rewards at a few per day
Key points.detail: Sweatcoin offered an optional rewarded video worth one coin, at first once a day, then tested three times a day. Between one and three times, retention and engagement improved; allowing more made retention drop. Only about 20% of users engage with these ads. For OnCourse, bonus rounds should have a small daily limit.

Key points.title: People value their own earned coins far more
Key points.detail: Asked what they would pay for someone else's Sweatcoins, users said 1 to 5 cents. Asked what they would sell their own for, they said 50 cents to a dollar. Derlyatka separates rational value from emotional value, and a business-school dean warned that making it a real crypto coin could break the "magic." Earned progress feels worth far more than its market value.

Key points.title: Build the invite into the main earning screen
Key points.detail: After Y Combinator rejected them for slow growth, the team set a goal of 300 new users a day. The "today" screen gave two ways to earn: start walking or invite a friend, paid in their own currency, so referrals cost no cash. Users who brought 30+ invites unlocked a secret marketplace section, which grew into an influencer hub. Earning itself became the referral loop.

Key points.title: Skip guilt and use positive reinforcement
Key points.detail: Derlyatka says "we are born to be lazy" and about 70% of people lack intrinsic motivation to exercise. Sweatcoin avoided "guilt trip based" messages like "lazy bum, stand up, do a 5K" and pitched "you walk anyway, why don't you try and earn something useful?" With 60,000 to 80,000 people onboarding daily, moving retention by 1% is "a massive uplift."

Key points.title: Gamification needs a genuinely good core
Key points.detail: "In order for gamification to work well, there's got to be an underlying experience that's actually good for the people and they know it." If gamification just pushes people to watch more ads, it may work short term but not long term. He credits Duolingo for layering simple mechanics on top of something good, learning a language. Exam prep is a good core, so OnCourse can use game mechanics with less risk.

Title: 5 product lessons we learned from building Friend Streak
Creator: Jackson Shuttleworth, Duolingo blog
Bottom line: A shared streak with a friend needs no direct interaction to motivate daily practice, and the biggest lever is getting the first invite sent, not serving power users.
What they did: Duolingo built Friend Streak, letting a learner share a streak with up to 5 friends, designed the UI for multiple friends from day one, used a data analysis of retention gain per extra streak instead of testing 6 or 7 slots, and focused iteration on the first-invite step, which was the largest funnel drop-off.
Results: Learners with at least one Friend Streak are 22% more likely to complete their daily lesson, and the likelihood rises with more Friend Streaks (correlational). 57% of users have at least one friend on Duolingo. The analysis found users with large friend groups were few and already retaining well by 5 streaks.
Takeaways: A shared streak needs no direct interaction; Optimise the biggest drop-off: the first invite; Use data analysis instead of costly slot tests; Design the UI for many friends from day one; A hacky local prototype can win buy-in; Ship V1 as if it is the only version
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: add a 'study buddy streak' with up to 3 classmates preparing for the same exam, which grows only when both finish today's plan. Onboarding: prompt users to invite one batchmate right after their first completed session, and measure invite-send rate as the key metric.

Key points.title: A shared streak needs no direct interaction
Key points.detail: Friend Streak lets you share a streak with up to 5 friends. Shuttleworth says it is "the first social feature we've seen, on any app, that doesn't require you to actually do anything with another learner" and compares it to "studying next to a friend at the library." Learners with at least one Friend Streak are 22% more likely to complete their daily lesson (a correlation). OnCourse could offer a passive study-buddy streak.

Key points.title: Optimise the biggest drop-off: the first invite
Key points.detail: The team broke a successful Friend Streak into 6 funnel steps and found that sending the first invite was the biggest hurdle. "If we made a 1% gain at that step, we'd have a much larger population exposed" than by optimising for power users with 5 streaks. They keep iterating on the invite. For OnCourse, invite-send rate would be the metric to watch.

Key points.title: Use data analysis instead of costly slot tests
Key points.detail: Rather than A/B testing 6, 7 or unlimited streak slots, the team analysed how much retention improved from each extra Friend Streak and how many users were at each level. Users with large active friend groups were few and already retained well by 5 streaks. So raising the cap was not worth it yet. Existing data can answer some questions faster than a test.

Key points.title: Design the UI for many friends from day one
Key points.detail: A one-friend design would have locked them into patterns that need a big redesign later. They designed for multiple friends from the start so they could test different limits without redesigning each time. But they also chose not to build more scale than they could justify, since more slots add UI, backend and testing cost.

Key points.title: A hacky local prototype can win buy-in
Key points.detail: The first internal version stored everything on your own device, so the friend did not even know about the streak. Even so, it was fun, and staff loved it. That excitement won early leadership buy-in and exposed edge cases early. A cheap fake can test whether a feature changes behaviour before building the backend.

Key points.title: Ship V1 as if it is the only version
Key points.detail: Duolingo CEO Luis told the team to stop saying "MVP" and call first launches "V1", meaning complete and ready for users. The key goal was that Friend Streak makes you want to do your daily lesson. That required nudges, notifications, and a design "separate yet related" to the personal streak. 57% of users already have at least one friend on Duolingo.

Title: How Streaks keep Duolingo learners committed to their language goals (Streak Wager and Weekend Amulet)
Creator: Kai Herng Loh, Duolingo blog
Bottom line: Letting learners bet on their own consistency, and letting them take planned breaks without losing their streak, both raised retention in A/B tests.
What they did: Duolingo tested a Streak Wager (spend in-game currency after a lesson to bet you keep your streak 7 more days, win double if you do) and a Weekend Amulet (equipped on Fridays to protect the streak if you skip the weekend).
Results: Streak Wager: statistically significant rises in Day-1, Day-7 and Day-14 retention, with Day-7 retention up most, by +14%. Weekend Amulet: daily actives normally fall 5 to 10% on weekends; learners offered the amulet were 4% more likely to come back a week later and 5% less likely to lose their streak.
Takeaways: A streak wager lifted Day-7 retention by 14%; Planned breaks protected streaks and raised returns; Bingeing predicts quitting more than steady pacing; The streak is tied to a goal the learner sets; Losing a streak can be very discouraging
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: offer a '7-day commitment' after the first completed plan, staking earned coins for a double payout on day 7. Today's plan: let users mark a rest day in advance (e.g., Sunday) that protects the streak, instead of only offering freezes after a miss.

Key points.title: A streak wager lifted Day-7 retention by 14%
Key points.detail: At the end of a lesson, Duolingo offered a "Streak Wager": spend in-game currency to bet you keep your streak 7 more days, and win double if you do. Day-1, Day-7 and Day-14 retention all rose significantly, with Day-7 up most, by 14%. The author says this makes sense because day 7 is when the reward arrives. Set the payoff date at the retention point you care about.

Key points.title: Planned breaks protected streaks and raised returns
Key points.detail: Duolingo use peaks midweek and drops 5 to 10% on weekends. The "Weekend Amulet", equipped on Friday, kept the streak if you skipped the weekend. Learners offered it were 4% more likely to come back a week later and 5% less likely to lose their streak. "By giving learners the option to take a break, they're actually more likely to do more in the long run."

Key points.title: Bingeing predicts quitting more than steady pacing
Key points.detail: Duolingo's research found that learners who binge on lessons were much more likely to abandon the app than those who pace themselves. Streaks help because they treat learning "as more of a marathon than a sprint." For OnCourse, a modest daily plan that people finish may beat letting motivated users do huge sessions early.

Key points.title: The streak is tied to a goal the learner sets
Key points.detail: New learners pick how much time they want to spend each day, and meeting that goal keeps the streak. The streak shows as a flame on the home screen top bar, and Duolingo sends personalised email reminders about it. Letting users choose the daily goal makes the streak feel like their own commitment.

Key points.title: Losing a streak can be very discouraging
Key points.detail: Many learners are proud of their streaks and "highly averse to losing it"; one former employee kept a 1,296-day streak after leaving. But the post admits "losing a streak can be very discouraging," which is why the team built ways to take breaks. Any OnCourse streak needs a plan for what happens when it breaks.

Title: Megastudies improve the impact of applied behavioural science (StepUp megastudy with 24 Hour Fitness)
Creator: Katherine L. Milkman, Angela Duckworth et al., Nature (2021)
Bottom line: The best of 53 tested habit nudges was a small reward for coming back right after a missed session, and almost none of the effects lasted once the programme ended.
What they did: Thirty scientists tested 54 four-week digital programmes on 61,293 gym members. The baseline involved planning workouts, a text reminder 30 minutes before each planned workout and micro-incentives; the top arm added a bonus of 125 points (US$0.09) for returning to the gym after a missed workout.
Results: 45% of interventions significantly increased weekly gym visits by 9% to 27%. The missed-workout bonus produced 0.40 more weekly visits per participant, 'a 27% increase in exercise' versus placebo control, and 16% more than planning, reminders and micro-incentives alone. 'Only 8% of interventions induced behaviour change that was significant and measurable after the four-week intervention.' Forecasts by impartial judges failed to predict which interventions would work best.
Takeaways: A tiny comeback bonus after a miss worked best; Experts could not predict which nudges would win; Most effects faded once the programme ended; Planning, reminders and micro-rewards gave a 9% base; Social norms and framing choice also ranked top five; Test many ideas at once in one population
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: when a user misses a planned day, give bonus XP for completing the very next day's plan ('Comeback bonus'). Notifications: test several reminder variants at once instead of one at a time, since intuition about winners is unreliable.

Key points.title: A tiny comeback bonus after a miss worked best
Key points.detail: The top intervention gave 125 points (US$0.09) for returning to the gym after a missed workout. It added 0.40 weekly visits per person, "a 27% increase in exercise" versus the placebo control, and 16% more than planning, reminders and micro-rewards alone. A 225-point version also made the top five, at 23%. For OnCourse, a small 'comeback bonus' after a missed day is worth testing.

Key points.title: Experts could not predict which nudges would win
Key points.detail: 301 lay people, 156 public health professors and 90 behavioural-science practitioners each predicted the effects of interventions. Their forecasts had no real link to actual results (pooled r = 0.02). On average predictions were 9.1 times too optimistic. This is the case for testing many ideas instead of trusting intuition.

Key points.title: Most effects faded once the programme ended
Key points.detail: During the four weeks, 45% of the 53 interventions significantly raised gym visits, by 9% to 27%. In the four weeks after, "only 8% of interventions induced behaviour change that was significant and measurable." Each extra visit during the programme gave about 0.3 extra visits later. Short nudges alone do not build lasting habits.

Key points.title: Planning, reminders and micro-rewards gave a 9% base
Key points.detail: The baseline asked people to plan workout dates and times, texted reminders at those times, and paid 300 points (about US$0.22) per visit. That alone added 0.14 weekly visits, a 9% increase. All 24 interventions that worked were built on top of this base. Plan, remind and reward is a solid starting point.

Key points.title: Social norms and framing choice also ranked top five
Key points.detail: Telling people that most Americans exercise and the share is growing added 24%. Larger incentives of 490 points (US$1.75) per visit added 25%. Letting people choose gain-framed or loss-framed rewards added 19%. The authors warn top results are probably inflated because they were picked as winners.

Key points.title: Test many ideas at once in one population
Key points.detail: In this 'megastudy', 30 scientists from 15 universities designed 54 four-week programmes for 61,293 members of 24 Hour Fitness. Everything was measured the same way over the same period, so results are directly comparable and null results get published. Few of the 20 preregistered hypotheses held up. OnCourse can run several notification variants side by side, not one at a time.

Title: Effectiveness of Behaviorally Designed Gamification Interventions With Social Incentives for Increasing Physical Activity (STEP UP trial)
Creator: Mitesh S. Patel et al., JAMA Internal Medicine (2019)
Bottom line: Points you can lose, levels you can drop from, and a small weekly leaderboard raised activity most, and competition was the only social design whose effect lasted after the game stopped.
What they did: 602 adults were randomised to control or a 24-week game: a precommitment pledge, 70 points credited each Monday with 10 lost for each missed daily goal, five levels starting at silver so a drop felt like a loss, weekly fresh starts, and daily progress updates. The game had three social arms: a support sponsor emailed weekly, collaboration in teams of 3 where a random member's miss cost the team points, and competition with a weekly leaderboard email in groups of 3.
Results: Versus control during the intervention, daily steps were up 920 (competition), 689 (support) and 637 (collaboration). In the 12-week follow-up only competition stayed significant, at 569 more steps (P = .009); support (428, P = .04) and collaboration (126, P = .49) did not meet the adjusted threshold. Share of days the goal was met during the intervention: competition 0.41, support 0.36, collaboration 0.36, control 0.25.
Takeaways: Competition was the only effect that lasted; Points you already have and can lose; Start users mid-ladder so a drop feels like a loss; Fresh starts re-engage people who are struggling; Teams of strangers worked worst; Let users pick a stretch goal and ramp up
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: put users in weekly groups of 3 to 5 aspirants at similar levels with a leaderboard of plans completed. Streaks: credit a weekly allowance of 7 'plan points' every Monday and deduct one per missed day, with levels starting mid-ladder.

Key points.title: Competition was the only effect that lasted
Key points.detail: During the 24-week game, daily steps rose versus control by 920 (competition), 689 (support) and 637 (collaboration). In the 12-week follow-up with no game, only competition stayed significant, at 569 more steps (P = .009). Support (428, P = .04) and collaboration (126, P = .49) did not meet the adjusted threshold. Competition was a weekly leaderboard email in groups of 3.

Key points.title: Points you already have and can lose
Key points.detail: Every Monday each person got 70 points, 10 for each day. Missing the step goal on a day cost 10 points. The design uses prospect theory: losing feels worse than gaining feels good. OnCourse could credit a weekly allowance that shrinks with missed days.

Key points.title: Start users mid-ladder so a drop feels like a loss
Key points.detail: There were five levels: blue, bronze, silver, gold and platinum. Everyone started at silver, so falling to bronze in week one felt like a loss. Moving up needed 40 points, down from 50 in an earlier study, to be more forgiving. The ladder gives a reachable next level and a sense of status.

Key points.title: Fresh starts re-engage people who are struggling
Key points.detail: Every week began with a fresh 70 points. At weeks 8 and 16, people stuck in blue or bronze got an email resetting them to silver and inviting them to adjust their goal. This uses the fresh start effect around dates like a new week. OnCourse could offer a reset after a bad stretch instead of leaving users at the bottom.

Key points.title: Teams of strangers worked worst
Key points.detail: In the collaboration arm, 3 strangers formed a team; each day one random member's miss cost the whole team points. It had the smallest effect and declined over time. An earlier trial in families found collaboration added 953 steps. The authors suggest competition works better when people have no prior connection.

Key points.title: Let users pick a stretch goal and ramp up
Key points.detail: People first wore the device to set a baseline. Then they chose a goal 33%, 40% or 50% above it, or any goal at least 1,500 steps higher. Goals ramped up by 25% a week over 4 weeks, and everyone signed a pledge. Choosing the goal and ramping into it made the target feel achievable.

Title: Fitness and Nutrition App 8fit Leverages Braze to Promote User Workout Streaks
Creator: Braze
Bottom line: Streak messages that adapt to whether a user kept or broke their streak, sent across push, email and in-app, raised weekly class views and completions.
What they did: 8fit sent personalised push, email and in-app messages using each user's own workout record, split users into those who kept their streak (congratulations) and those who lapsed (prompts to restart), nudged users close to losing a streak to complete at least one class per week, and gave badges for extending streaks.
Results: Weekly class views 'went up by 40%'; a '17% increase in weekly class completions' (also labelled an increase in users completing classes); free-to-paid conversion 'rose to 13%' (absolute rate, no baseline given). Vendor-reported case study.
Takeaways: Branch streak messages by kept versus broken; Nudge before the streak breaks, with a weekly bar; Put each user's own record in the message; Reported gains: 40% views, 17% completions; Free trial classes were used to drive upgrades
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: send different evening messages to users who already finished today's plan (celebrate plus tomorrow's preview) and those at risk (one 10-question set saves your streak). Notifications: include the user's own numbers, such as days studied this week and topics left, in streak messages.

Key points.title: Branch streak messages by kept versus broken
Key points.detail: 8fit used Braze's Decision Split Steps to separate users who kept a streak going from those who had not. Streak keepers got congratulations and encouragement. Lapsed users got a nudge to pick things up again. The same evening message should not go to both groups.

Key points.title: Nudge before the streak breaks, with a weekly bar
Key points.detail: Users at risk of losing a streak were encouraged to "not break the chain by taking part in at least one class a week." Badges and awards rewarded extending a streak. A weekly minimum is easier to keep than a daily one. OnCourse could test a weekly streak for users who can't study every day.

Key points.title: Put each user's own record in the message
Key points.detail: With Liquid templating, 8fit filled each message with the user's personal workout record. It sent push, email and in-app messages together, all tied to the same streak goal. The product manager says he could set this up without taking developers' time. Personal numbers make a reminder feel relevant.

Key points.title: Reported gains: 40% views, 17% completions
Key points.detail: "Weekly class views went up by 40%, with a corresponding 17% increase in weekly class completions." Free-to-paid conversion "rose to 13%." The case study gives no baseline, control group or test design, and it is written by the vendor. Treat the numbers as a direction, not proof.

Key points.title: Free trial classes were used to drive upgrades
Key points.detail: 8fit also wanted the streak dynamic to push free users to paid, so it offered free trial classes as an incentive. The idea is to let free users taste premium content while they are building a habit. OnCourse could offer a premium session as a streak reward for free users.

Title: Scaled-Up Social Psychology (Chapter 5: growth mindset messages in Khan Academy fractions exercises)
Creator: David Paunesku, Stanford PhD dissertation (2013), with Khan Academy
Bottom line: One line of copy above each practice problem framing effort and mistakes as how you get smarter raised mastery, while generic 'just do your best' encouragement did nothing.
What they did: Khan Academy randomised 265,082 learners on all fractions exercises to no header, standard encouragement ('Some of these problems are hard. Just do your best'), science trivia, or growth mindset headers such as 'Remember, the more you practice the smarter you become!' and 'If you make a mistake, it's an opportunity to get smarter!'
Results: Relative to no header, the growth mindset group earned proficiencies at a rate 2.9% higher (z = 3.212, p < .01). Neither standard encouragement nor science statements changed the rate (z < 1).
Takeaways: Mindset headers raised the proficiency rate 2.9%; 'Try harder' messages had zero effect; Measure copy by mastery, not clicks; A 3% gain matters because it is free at scale; Users may tune out repeated messages
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: after a wrong answer, show rotating growth-framed lines ('Mistakes now are marks saved on exam day') and A/B test them against no message, measured by questions mastered. Lessons: replace 'You can do it!' style banners with copy about effort building memory.

Key points.title: Mindset headers raised the proficiency rate 2.9%
Key points.detail: Khan Academy put header messages above every problem in all fractions exercises for 265,082 learners. Growth-mindset headers, such as "Remember, the more you practice the smarter you become!", raised the rate of earning proficiencies by 2.9% versus no header (z = 3.212, p < .01). It is one sentence of copy, tested at huge scale.

Key points.title: 'Try harder' messages had zero effect
Key points.detail: Standard encouragement like "Some of these problems are hard. Just do your best" had an estimate of 0.000, and science trivia had no effect either. The author explains why: both ask for effort, but "only growth mindset messages transform the meaning of effort" into something that builds ability. Copy must say that effort makes you smarter, not just ask for it.

Key points.title: Measure copy by mastery, not clicks
Key points.detail: The outcome was proficiencies earned, where proficient means more than a 94% chance of getting the next problem right. So the test measured learning, not engagement with the message. A version that added a link to read about brain growth did no better than the plain message. OnCourse should judge practice copy by accuracy and topics mastered.

Key points.title: A 3% gain matters because it is free at scale
Key points.detail: The author admits "the absolute size of the gain (3%) may appear small," but calls it practically significant since it can be added anywhere at almost no cost. The sample was over 1,000 times larger than the biggest earlier growth-mindset study (n = 138). Small copy wins add up across every question.

Key points.title: Users may tune out repeated messages
Key points.detail: Every problem showed a header, and the author notes students "may 'tune out' these messages after repeated exposure." Future tests were proposed with intermittent messages, or messages timed to hard moments, such as "when they hit a streak of problems on which they are struggling." OnCourse could show such copy after a run of wrong answers, not on every question.

Title: On or Off Track: How (Broken) Streaks Affect Consumer Decisions
Creator: Jackie Silverman and Alixandra Barasch, Journal of Consumer Research (2023)
Bottom line: Showing a broken streak in a log lowers people's willingness to continue, below showing no log at all, and letting them repair it recovers most of the loss.
What they did: Study 1 was a field study of 980 university employees in a 30-day challenge to walk 7,000+ steps a day, using their real step data. Studies 2 to 7 were lab experiments where participants used app-like behaviour logs that showed the same past behaviour as an intact streak, a broken streak (an X), a repairable broken streak, or no log, and researchers measured whether they repeated the behaviour.
Results: Exercise study (Study 2): 66.23% continued with an intact streak versus 57.86% with a broken one. When a broken streak was highlighted in the log, 45.21% continued versus 60.90% when it was not. Study 7: 93.14% continued with an intact streak, 68.66% with a broken streak and 85.20% with a repairable broken streak. In a pilot survey, 59% of app users had 'gone out of their way' to maintain a streak. Study 1 (field data, correlational) points the same way in real step counts.
Takeaways: Showing a broken streak is worse than no log; Letting users repair a streak recovers most of the loss; Self-blamed breaks hurt more than external ones; Keeping the streak becomes a goal in itself; Field data showed the same pattern; Define streaks loosely to keep them intact
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: after a miss, don't show a red X on the calendar; show the days studied this month and a 'repair by finishing 2 plans today' option. Home: when the streak is broken, lead with total study days and progress to exam rather than a zeroed streak counter.

Key points.title: Showing a broken streak is worse than no log
Key points.detail: In a vocabulary study, 65.84% continued with an intact streak, 47.98% with a broken one, and 54.73% with no log at all. In another, a broken streak highlighted in the log cut continuation to 45.21%, versus 60.90% when it was not highlighted. The actual past behaviour was the same; only the display changed. OnCourse should avoid a big red X or a zeroed counter after a miss.

Key points.title: Letting users repair a streak recovers most of the loss
Key points.detail: In Study 7, 93.14% continued with an intact streak, 68.66% with a broken one, and 85.20% when told the next game would "repair" the streak to 4 in a row. Repair did not fully close the gap, perhaps because a repaired streak feels less valuable. A separate study found 46% would watch an ad to repair a broken streak. A repair option is worth building into OnCourse streaks.

Key points.title: Self-blamed breaks hurt more than external ones
Key points.detail: In Study 6, 53.17% continued with an intact streak, 42.00% when the break was caused by the app, and 28.87% when users felt they caused it. The authors suggest companies could "shoulder some of the responsibility" for a break. Copy like 'busy day? Let's pick up again' may soften a miss.

Key points.title: Keeping the streak becomes a goal in itself
Key points.detail: Across studies, people were more likely to continue when the log showed an intact streak, even with identical real behaviour. Sense of accomplishment explained the effect; negative emotion did not. In the pilot, 59% of app users said they had "gone out of their way" to keep a streak, and 27% did things offline to keep it.

Key points.title: Field data showed the same pattern
Key points.detail: Study 1 used data from 980 university employees in a 30-day, 7,000-step challenge in fall 2018. People were more likely to hit the goal on a day that would extend an intact streak than after a broken one. This is correlational, so the six lab studies (2 to 7) were used to show cause. The research is not only online experiments.

Key points.title: Define streaks loosely to keep them intact
Key points.detail: The authors suggest counting a broader range of actions toward a streak and considering weekly rather than daily streaks. They also suggest not sending alerts when a streak breaks. The trade-off: a looser streak may feel less meaningful. For OnCourse, counting any study action (questions, flashcards, a video) toward the streak may keep more users on track.

Chapters.title: The question
