Title: What can machine learning teach us about habit formation? Evidence from exercise and hygiene
Creator: Anastasia Buyalskaya, Hung Ho, Katherine Milkman, Xiaomin Li, Angela Duckworth, Colin Camerer, PNAS (2023)
Bottom line: A gym habit typically takes months to form, not 21 days, and the strongest predictor of the next visit is how long it has been since the last one.
What they did: Researchers used machine learning on more than 12 million gym check-ins (over 30,000 gymgoers across four years) and more than 40 million hospital handwashing events to trace when each person's behaviour became predictable, that is, habitual.
Results: 'It typically takes months to form the habit of going to the gym but weeks to develop the habit of handwashing'. For the gym, the median time to form the habit was "122 to 226 d or about 4 to 7 mo". Time since last visit was an important predictor for 76% of gymgoers, and 69% tended to go on the same days of the week. More predictable (habitual) gymgoers were less responsive to an intervention to boost attendance.
Takeaways: Gym habits take months, not 21 days; Time since the last visit predicts the next one; Same weekdays help build the habit; Simple, frequent actions form habits in weeks; Habitual users respond less to nudges; Frequency is not the same as habit
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: ask users to pick fixed study weekdays during onboarding and anchor reminders to those days. Notifications: trigger outreach based on days since last session rather than calendar dates, and focus incentives on users in their first 2 to 3 months.

Key points.title: Gym habits take months, not 21 days
Key points.detail: Researchers traced when each person's gym visits became predictable, using over 12 million check-ins. The median time to form a gym habit was 122 to 226 days, about 4 to 7 months. The paper rejects the popular "magic number" of days. For OnCourse, a few weeks of streak mechanics will not create a study habit on their own.

Key points.title: Time since the last visit predicts the next one
Key points.detail: The most important predictor was how long since the last gym visit. For 76% of gymgoers, the longer the gap, the less likely they were to go on a given day. Attendance in the past 7 days was a positive predictor for 82%. OnCourse should trigger outreach by days since last session and act early.

Key points.title: Same weekdays help build the habit
Key points.detail: A "day-of-week streak" mattered: 69% were more likely to go on the same weekdays they had gone before. Monday and Tuesday positively predicted attendance for 57% of people, which fits the "fresh start" effect. OnCourse could let users pick fixed study days and anchor reminders to them.

Key points.title: Simple, frequent actions form habits in weeks
Key points.detail: Hospital handwashing habits formed in about 9 to 10 shifts, or roughly 220 washing opportunities. The strongest predictor was how well the worker washed on their last shift (positive for 100% of workers). The authors suggest gym habits are slower because the behaviour is less frequent and more complex. Small, daily study actions may stick faster than big sessions.

Key points.title: Habitual users respond less to nudges
Key points.detail: Using the StepUp megastudy, the authors found that more predictable gymgoers responded less to the intervention (r = −.48, P < .001). Less habitual people were more sensitive to nudges. OnCourse should aim incentives and reminders at users still forming the habit, not long-time regulars.

Key points.title: Frequency is not the same as habit
Key points.detail: Two members went to the gym about equally often in March 2018. One was highly predictable (AUC = 0.946) and the other not at all (AUC = 0.546). The paper finds frequency and predictability are unrelated. A user who studies often at random times may not have a habit yet.

Title: Kudos make you run! How runners influence each other on the online social network Strava
Creator: Rob Franken, Hidde Bekhuis, Jochem Tolsma, Social Networks (2023)
Bottom line: Getting lightweight recognition (kudos) from clubmates makes people exercise more and more often, and people drift toward the habits of those they cheer for.
What they did: Researchers built longitudinal network and activity data for five Strava clubs tied to real Dutch running clubs (329 members, 11 one-month periods) and modelled how giving and receiving kudos related to running behaviour.
Results: 'Receiving kudos induced runners to run more and more often.' Runners adjusted toward the running of the people they gave kudos to, but unexpectedly became more like kudos-friends who ran less, not more. Observational network study with no product change; sample limited to five Dutch clubs.
Takeaways: Receiving kudos made runners run more and more often; People drift toward those they give kudos to; Less active peers pulled people down; Real-life clubs are the unit of influence
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: add a cohort feed for an exam batch where peers can send one-tap 'kudos' on finished daily plans. Notifications: tell users when a batchmate cheered their session ('Priya cheered your 50-question set').

Key points.title: Receiving kudos made runners run more and more often
Key points.detail: Researchers followed five Strava clubs linked to real Dutch running clubs, 329 members in total, across 11 one-month periods. They found that "receiving kudos induced runners to run more and more often." A one-tap sign of recognition from peers was linked to more activity. OnCourse could let batchmates send a one-tap cheer on a finished daily plan.

Key points.title: People drift toward those they give kudos to
Key points.detail: Athletes tended to adjust their running to that of their "kudos-friends", the people they gave kudos to. So the peers you choose to cheer for shape your own behaviour over time. In a study group, who you follow matters.

Key points.title: Less active peers pulled people down
Key points.detail: The authors expected the most active kudos-friends to be most influential. "If anything, the reverse was true": runners came to resemble kudos-friends who ran less and less often. Social features can lower effort as well as raise it. OnCourse should watch whether peer groups drag down activity, not assume they lift it.

Key points.title: Real-life clubs are the unit of influence
Key points.detail: The clubs studied were online extensions of real running clubs, not random strangers. The study is observational network analysis (using SIENA), not a product experiment, and is limited to five Dutch clubs. It was published in Social Networks (2023, vol. 72). Cohorts tied to a real batch or coaching group may be the best place for OnCourse social features.

Title: How Clarity and Personalization Help Drive Duolingo's Growth — Anmol Tiwari, Duolingo
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat (David Barnard) with Anmol Tiwari
Bottom line: Duolingo treats the paywall as a place to give clarity rather than persuade, and found that shorter trials, repeated trial chances and letting users pick their reminder day all raised conversions.
What they did: Moved from a two-week trial (used until around the end of 2024) to a 7-day trial and changed how many trials users get, including a no-strings 3-day 'free taste' of Super/Max framed as a reward after a lesson. Tested letting users choose which day they get the trial-ending reminder instead of a fixed reminder about two days before expiry.
Results: On the trial change: "overall net, we saw more conversions over time", and going from 14 to 7 days "basically doubled our experimentation velocity". The pick-your-reminder-day test increased confidence and had users wait until "that fifth day or sixth day to decide"; no percentage uplift was given. Building the upsell into onboarding questions (e.g. learning with or without ads) was "one of our biggest wins last year."
Takeaways: The paywall's job is clarity, not persuasion; Letting users pick their reminder day built trust; Upsells built into onboarding questions won big; Cutting the trial to 7 days doubled test speed; A no-strings 3-day 'free taste' works as a reward; Track day-zero cancellations as an intent signal
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: next to the existing trial timeline, let the student pick the day they get the trial-ending reminder (e.g. day 5 or 6) and confirm it on screen. Practice: after a strong session, offer a 3-day no-strings premium 'earned' preview instead of a generic upsell. Onboarding: fold the premium question into the exam-plan questions (e.g. 'Do you want full mock tests and analytics?') rather than a standalone pitch.

Key points.title: The paywall's job is clarity, not persuasion
Key points.detail: Anmol Tiwari says: "our goal is not to persuade users to try this. Our goal is to give them clarity and confidence to purchase." In practice that means a timeline of what happens on each day of the trial, and plain numbers on refunds when someone switches plans. For OnCourse, the trial timeline and a clear refund line on the paywall do more than stronger sales copy.

Key points.title: Letting users pick their reminder day built trust
Key points.detail: Duolingo used to send one trial-ending reminder about two days before the trial expired. They tested letting users choose which day the reminder comes. The extra step drew attention to the fact that a reminder was coming, so people felt safe waiting until "that fifth day or sixth day" to decide whether they were getting value. No uplift number was given.

Key points.title: Upsells built into onboarding questions won big
Key points.detail: Instead of dropping the standard Super Duolingo upsell into onboarding, they asked it as an onboarding question: learn with or without ads, learn faster or at your own pace. Tiwari calls this "one of our biggest wins last year" and says new users are far more likely to convert. OnCourse could ask about mock tests and analytics as part of the exam-plan questions.

Key points.title: Cutting the trial to 7 days doubled test speed
Key points.detail: Duolingo ran a two-week trial until around the end of 2024, then tested 7 days. Net conversions went up over time when paired with changes to how many trials users get. The bigger win: results arrive in 7 days, not 14, which "basically doubled our experimentation velocity" and let them kill losing tests faster.

Key points.title: A no-strings 3-day 'free taste' works as a reward
Key points.detail: Users get several trial chances across their lifecycle, plus a 3-day 'free taste' of Super or Max with no card and no auto-charge. It is framed as "you just earned this" and was moved from a chest on the path to after a lesson, because earning it after a lesson felt more rewarding. They also give single-feature tastes, like one Max video call. When it ends, a drawer says "Your X benefits have ended" with options to continue or resubscribe.

Key points.title: Track day-zero cancellations as an intent signal
Key points.detail: Tiwari calls day-zero cancellation "such an important kind of thing to track" because it shows whether users really have intent, and once they cancel it is hard to win them back. He also notes paid trials (about $1) are the norm in China because people are wary of auto-renewal. Losing trust shows up as poor conversion or complaints like "I didn't expect this charge."

Title: BoldVoice removed the X from its paywall. Trial starts jumped. Refunds jumped more.
Creator: RevenueCat (write-up of Sub Club episode with Anada Lakra, BoldVoice)
Bottom line: Forcing or tricking people into a trial lifts trial starts but costs more in refunds, so judge paywall tests on net revenue after refunds.
What they did: BoldVoice, an accent-coaching learning app, tested a hard paywall with no dismiss button and a discount offer that appeared on dismiss and could not be closed. It now lets users who dismiss the paywall get a speech assessment, first daily plan and a coach video, then offers a 7-day trial on day two; the lead offer is an annual plan around $150/year.
Results: No percentages given. Lakra: "Both of those look so promising on the trial numbers" but "The refund spiked by way more than the gain in start trials." Tests are now judged on net revenue after refunds per exposed user on a matured cohort, waiting at least an extra week for trials to convert and two more for refunds to settle.
Takeaways: Inescapable paywalls raised trials but refunds rose more; Judge paywall tests on net revenue after refunds; Give a narrow free taste, then ask on day two; Everyone does two user interviews a week; Don't mix playbooks from apps with different users; Default to annual so ads pay back fast
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: keep a visible close button and measure paywall tests on net revenue after refunds and renewal, not trial starts. Onboarding: if a student dismisses the paywall, give them a diagnostic mini-test and their first Today's plan, then re-offer the trial on day two. Today's plan: show the day-two trial offer inside the plan they already started.

Key points.title: Inescapable paywalls raised trials but refunds rose more
Key points.detail: BoldVoice tested a hard paywall with no X, and a discount offer that appeared on dismiss and could not be closed. Both looked good on trial starts, but "The refund spiked by way more than the gain in start trials." Anada Lakra: "Anything that kind of forces or tricks people into starting a trial, you'll pay it when it comes to refunds." Keep the close button on the OnCourse paywall.

Key points.title: Judge paywall tests on net revenue after refunds
Key points.detail: BoldVoice now scores paywall tests on net revenue after refunds, per exposed user, on a matured cohort. That means waiting at least an extra week for trials to convert and two more weeks for refunds to settle. Lakra's worst change of the year was over-optimizing the paywall: "Optimize them for a little bit and then move on to the actual product."

Key points.title: Give a narrow free taste, then ask on day two
Key points.detail: If a user dismisses the paywall, they still get the speech assessment, their first daily plan and a coach video. On day two they are offered a 7-day trial to continue. Lakra calls it a middle ground that keeps the onboarding paywall for people who are ready to pay. For OnCourse, this could be a diagnostic test and a first Today's plan before a day-two offer.

Key points.title: Everyone does two user interviews a week
Key points.detail: Automated invites book a 15-minute call with a mix of long-time subscribers, recent converters and non-converters, and slot in whoever on the team is free. Every person, engineers included, does at least two a week. Because happy users book more calls, they add a three-question email survey and a short cancellation flow to hear from unhappy users.

Key points.title: Don't mix playbooks from apps with different users
Key points.detail: BoldVoice charged from day one ($10/month, one-week trial) to find who really had the problem. It now leads with an annual plan around $150/year, with a $200/year tier. Lakra refuses to copy Duolingo's freemium model because her users are professionals whose alternative is a paid accent coach: "totally different ICP, different value proposition, different willingness to pay."

Key points.title: Default to annual so ads pay back fast
Key points.detail: BoldVoice runs at $10M ARR with 10 people. Defaulting users to the annual plan means paid acquisition pays back within the trial window, so each channel's return is clear the same week. An ungated web tool, the Accent Oracle, went viral when an investor posted it on Threads and 100,000 people in Korea tried it the next day.

Title: How Removing the Free Trial Grew Monthly Subs 2000% — Nancy Anderson, Natal
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat (David Barnard) with Nancy Anderson
Bottom line: Removing the free trial from the monthly plan can lift paid starts sharply when users already trust the product before the paywall.
What they did: Natal, a pregnancy fitness app, removed the free trial from its monthly option (an idea borrowed from Zumba) and kept it as a permanent offering. It also raised prices during a growth quarter and added pre-tax HSA payment at web checkout, where the free trial is offered "only on our annual subscription".
Results: "I think our monthly subs went up by 2,000% and our quarterly went up by 46%, our annual went up by 21%" (no baseline, timeframe or sample given). Nancy: "20% increase in ARR growth in Q1" (Barnard: "you all grew 20% in the first quarter"), while they also raised prices. Trial conversion rate "is like 68%" versus an industry average she puts at 38%; download to trial about 17% versus a 6% health and fitness average.
Takeaways: Removing the monthly free trial lifted monthly subs 2,000%; Trust before the paywall shows in every funnel number; Real coaches answer every message within 24 hours; Too many programs caused decision fatigue; A guided first step drives activation; No free workouts, to protect perceived value
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: test offering the free trial only on the annual/exam-cycle plan and a no-trial monthly plan, watching paid starts and refunds. Onboarding: build trust before the paywall with a personalised exam plan and visible human support response times.

Key points.title: Removing the monthly free trial lifted monthly subs 2,000%
Key points.detail: Natal copied an idea from a Sub Club episode with Zumba and removed the free trial from its monthly option. Nancy Anderson: "I think our monthly subs went up by 2,000% and our quarterly went up by 46%, our annual went up by 21%." No baseline or timeframe was given, and they made it permanent. Her read: trust was built before the paywall, so many people "don't even want or need a trial."

Key points.title: Trust before the paywall shows in every funnel number
Key points.detail: Anderson credits trust, not paywall tricks, for strong numbers: 93% of web checkout visitors download the app, trial conversion is "like 68%" against a 38% industry average she cites, and download-to-trial is 17% against a 6% health and fitness average. The app costs about $25 a month. David Barnard's line: "Your paywall is only as good as a story leading up to it."

Key points.title: Real coaches answer every message within 24 hours
Key points.detail: For eight years every DM, comment, email and in-app post has been answered by a human within 24 hours, often by physical therapists and trainers, not support reps. It costs more, but Anderson says it is what makes people feel safe before they are asked to pay. OnCourse could show real faculty response times inside the app.

Key points.title: Too many programs caused decision fatigue
Key points.detail: Natal merged four apps into one, and its biggest fail of the year was having five to seven postpartum rehab programs with no clear starting point. "When women come in and they're overwhelmed or confused of where to start, they don't start." Onboarding of about 10 to 15 questions now asks your phase (trying to conceive, pregnant, postpartum) and cuts about 50 programs down to about 15.

Key points.title: A guided first step drives activation
Key points.detail: A free posture assessment, reviewed by a real expert, ends with which program to start and which routines to add. Anderson says 68 to 70% of women who do it complete their first workout. In the in-app community, 31% come back on day 2. For OnCourse, a diagnostic that ends in one clear first session could do the same job.

Key points.title: No free workouts, to protect perceived value
Key points.detail: Natal never posts free workouts or lead magnets, because Anderson thinks they attract the wrong audience and devalue the experts' work. The posture assessment is free but not promoted, so coaches are not swamped. She also added pre-tax HSA payment at checkout, which saves eligible users roughly 30 to 40%.

Title: How a Single Paywall Experiment Generated $50M — Jeff Morris, Chapter One, Ex-Tinder
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat (David Barnard, Jacob Eiting) with Jeff Morris
Bottom line: Where the paywall entry points sit can matter more than the paywall itself; Tinder's biggest win was a new entry point in the top nav.
What they did: Around 2018 Tinder tested a toggle at the top of the app that let users enter a new subscription tier from the top nav bar, a 'throwaway' A/B test. Every subscription feature also had its own paywall entry point tracked for taps, conversion and incremental revenue, with pricing localized by geography (LATAM and India paid less).
Results: Described as "a single experiment that generated $50 million in revenue" at roughly "50 million monthly actives"; no conversion lift or duration given.
Takeaways: A new top-nav entry point earned $50 million; Track taps, conversion and revenue per entry point; One or two features drive most subscriptions; Design paywalls with the same care as features; Ask for payment after the magic moment; Hard paywalls can fake product-market fit
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: test a persistent premium entry point in the header (e.g. 'Unlock full mock tests') and track taps and conversion per entry point. Practice: put the paywall right after the moment of value, such as after a score breakdown, not before the first question. Paywall: lead with the one or two features that drive most upgrades (e.g. grand tests, analytics).

Key points.title: A new top-nav entry point earned $50 million
Key points.detail: Around 2018 Tinder tested a toggle at the top of the app that let users enter a new subscription tier from the top nav bar. It was "kind of a throwaway AB test" that generated about $50 million, at roughly 50 million monthly actives. The design team had not wanted the top nav. Jeff Morris: "you should constantly be thinking about where users can access your premium features."

Key points.title: Track taps, conversion and revenue per entry point
Key points.detail: Every subscription feature at Tinder had its own paywall entry point, and a daily dashboard showed taps, conversion rate and incremental revenue for each. They treated screen space as "real estate." Low numbers meant either the entry point was too hidden or the feature wasn't worth paying for. OnCourse could tag every premium entry point and compare them the same way.

Key points.title: One or two features drive most subscriptions
Key points.detail: Morris sees "a power law to subscription features where one or two features are probably going to drive the majority of your new subscriptions." Tinder had two to three power features. Features whose paywalls didn't convert were made free, but they never moved a free feature behind the paywall. Lead the OnCourse paywall with the one or two features students really pay for.

Key points.title: Design paywalls with the same care as features
Key points.detail: In 2017 Tinder added a gold shimmer animation to a paywall that took a couple of days of engineering. Morris: "I see a lot of paywalls that look like they were designed by a PM." He also warns that too many paywalls make a mature product feel spammy.

Key points.title: Ask for payment after the magic moment
Key points.detail: At Tinder they waited for someone to get a match and have a conversation before asking them to pay. Morris warns against asking for a card before users get a successful outcome, citing a website builder whose free users hit bugs and were pushed to pay. For OnCourse, show the paywall after a score breakdown, not before the first question.

Key points.title: Hard paywalls can fake product-market fit
Key points.detail: Barnard and Morris discuss how apps that launch with a hard paywall think they have product-market fit because people pay, "but then they bleed customers out the back end." With annual plans you may not see bad retention for 12 months. Morris also says Tinder priced by geography, since India and LATAM grew fast but had lower willingness to pay.

Title: The Hidden Cost of Underpricing Your Subscription — Patrick Rills, Lose It!
Creator: Sub Club by RevenueCat with Patrick Rills
Bottom line: Retest prices that lost before; doubling the annual price broke even on conversion and opened room for deeper lifecycle discounts.
What they did: Lose It! had charged $39.99/year since 2012 and had tested everything from $5 to $120 a year. In late 2024 it retested about $80 across iOS, Android, new, existing and reactivated users, rolled it out in 2026, grandfathered existing subscribers, and uses a lifecycle sale system where the discount depends on where the user is in their journey.
Results: Testing ~$80 "broke even," which "had never happened before"; the full rollout "results have been exactly our experiment results." Retention stayed "very stable." At $80 "we can do more steep discounting" and "the bigger the percent, usually the higher the conversion."
Takeaways: Retest prices that lost before; A higher list price funds deeper discounts; Rising ad costs forced the price rethink; A strong free tier kept retention stable; Grandfather existing subscribers instead of risking churn; Prices tell users how valuable the product is
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: retest a higher annual list price paired with a lifecycle discount (e.g. bigger % off for students near their exam date). Renewal: keep current subscribers on their old price and show a 'your price changes if you lapse' note when they turn off auto-renew.

Key points.title: Retest prices that lost before
Key points.detail: Lose It! charged $39.99/year from 2012 and had tested everything from $5 to $120 a year without beating it. In late 2024, with phones and competitors getting pricier, they retested and the higher price "broke even," which "had never happened before." They repeated it on iOS, Android, new, existing and reactivated users and kept getting similar results.

Key points.title: A higher list price funds deeper discounts
Key points.detail: Lose It! has a homegrown lifecycle sale system that sets how much discount a user gets at each point in their journey. At $40 there was little room for 50% or 75% off, but at $80 "we can do more steep discounting." Patrick Rills: "the bigger the percent, usually the higher the conversion," even when the dollar price ends up higher. OnCourse could pair a higher list price with discounts timed to the exam calendar.

Key points.title: Rising ad costs forced the price rethink
Key points.detail: Acquisition costs rose on every channel, and Meta restricted how health and wellness apps can advertise. Lose It! had relied on organic App Store rank but needs paid acquisition to grow. "At a $40 price point, it's much harder than at an $80 price point to get the ROAS that you need." AI feature costs were another reason.

Key points.title: A strong free tier kept retention stable
Key points.detail: Rills says retention stayed "very stable" after the increase. Lose It! ran free from 2008 to 2012 and keeps the free product good enough that "you can do everything you need to do to lose weight" without paying. Fewer people go premium, but the free tier keeps everyone else engaged.

Key points.title: Grandfather existing subscribers instead of risking churn
Key points.detail: They did not raise prices for current subscribers. Apple's opt-in flow for price rises felt "confusing and cumbersome," couldn't be A/B tested, and the churn rate was an unknown risk. One idea they plan to test: when a grandfathered user turns off auto-renew, show a "Are you sure?" message saying the price will be different if they come back.

Key points.title: Prices tell users how valuable the product is
Key points.detail: The product team pushed for the increase because main competitors charge around $80 and they felt their work was just as good. Rills: "what are prices, if not information about how something valuable is?" One month after full rollout, results were "exactly our experiment results."

Title: Explore Retention Messaging in App Store Connect (WWDC26 session 309)
Creator: Apple (App Store server team)
Bottom line: iOS now lets apps show a message, image, offer or plan switch on the App Store cancel page, and offers saved the most subscribers.
What they did: Apple added Retention Messaging: a message shown on the App Store cancellation page that can be text only, text plus image, or text plus a retention offer, with real-time server-chosen messages and same-group plan switches available via an API. The App Store auto-picks the best eligible offer.
Results: "Subscriptions that have adopted Retention Messaging experience an average save rate increase of +1.4 points equivalent to an 82% increase, with promotional offer messages achieving the highest observed save rate at +5.5 points equivalent to a 223% increase. Note that we have observed varying results across developers." (Save rate = % who keep their subscription after reaching the cancel confirmation page.)
Takeaways: Offers on the cancel page saved the most subscribers; Three formats: message, message plus image, or message plus offer; The App Store picks the best eligible offer for you; Real-time messaging adds plan switches and per-user choices; Always set up App Store Connect messages as the fallback; Everything can be tested in sandbox first
Ideas for OnCourse: Renewal: set up a retention message on the cancel page that reminds students what they lose before their exam (mock tests, saved progress) with an image. Renewal: for annual subscribers cancelling right after their exam, offer a switch to a cheaper monthly or next-cycle plan via real-time messaging.

Key points.title: Offers on the cancel page saved the most subscribers
Key points.detail: Apple defines save rate as the % of subscribers who keep their subscription after reaching the cancel confirmation page. Apps using Retention Messaging saw "an average save rate increase of +1.4 points equivalent to an 82% increase." Promotional offer messages did best: "+5.5 points equivalent to a 223% increase." Apple adds that results vary across developers. For OnCourse: an offer is worth testing first on the iOS cancel page.

Key points.title: Three formats: message, message plus image, or message plus offer
Key points.detail: Every retention message needs text. An image and an offer are optional. The demo used the headline "Launching Next Month: Guided Yoga" with a line on what the subscriber would miss. When the customer is eligible for an offer, the offer replaces the image. For OnCourse: write a message about what a student loses before their exam, such as mock tests and saved progress.

Key points.title: The App Store picks the best eligible offer for you
Key points.detail: In App Store Connect you can attach several retention offers to one message. The App Store "will automatically choose the best offer for eligible customers," so you can add multiple offers without picking per user. There is a new offer type for this, recorded as offerType 5 in the transaction data, so you can track redemptions.

Key points.title: Real-time messaging adds plan switches and per-user choices
Key points.detail: With real-time Retention Messaging, Apple calls your server when someone tries to cancel. You can reply with a message, a promotional offer, or a switch to another plan in the same subscription group. The demo offered an annual Yoga+ plan. A new monthly plan with a 12-month commitment can also be offered as a switch. For OnCourse: a student cancelling after the exam could be offered a cheaper plan instead of leaving.

Key points.title: Always set up App Store Connect messages as the fallback
Key points.detail: Real-time needs a fast server, and you must pass a performance test in sandbox before going live. If your server is slow or sends a bad reply, the App Store falls back to your App Store Connect message, then to the API's default message. Apple says to set up App Store Connect messaging even if you use real-time. Real-time access needs an interest form; App Store Connect messaging is open to all.

Key points.title: Everything can be tested in sandbox first
Key points.detail: Retention messages show up when you cancel a sandbox subscription. You can check that offer fields like offer identifier, discount type and period appear in the signed transaction. App Store Connect also shows a live preview of the message as you type, with or without each offer.

Title: Early Apple Retention Messaging benchmarks from 22M messages
Creator: Margarita Loktionova, RevenueCat
Bottom line: Most apps throw discounts at cancelling users, but almost nobody accepts them, so match the message to the cancel reason and limit who sees discounts.
What they did: RevenueCat analysed 21,960,020 retention messages across 309 apps (March 22 to September 20, 2026) to benchmark save rates, setups and offer acceptance on Apple's cancellation page.
Results: Median save rate "17%", or "17 in 100 subscribers" (a quarter of apps above 27 in 100, top 10% at 42 or more). 87% of apps regularly show a discount or plan-switch offer, yet acceptance was about 1.1% for promotional offers and 0.6% for plan switches. Adopters' median cancellation decline after launch was 3.6% vs 7.3% for matched apps; with 64 apps the gap "could easily be chance."
Takeaways: Cancel-screen offers are almost never accepted; Save rate overstates what the message does; No clear effect on cancellation rates yet; Match the message to the cancel reason; Keep discounts away from trial users and past redeemers; Bigger apps adopted first
Ideas for OnCourse: Renewal: ask one cancel-reason question in-app (exam done, too expensive, not using) and show a matching message instead of a blanket discount. Renewal: keep discounts away from trial users and anyone who already redeemed one so cancelling isn't a shortcut to a lower price.

Key points.title: Cancel-screen offers are almost never accepted
Key points.detail: 87% of the 309 apps regularly show a discount or plan-switch offer when users try to cancel. Yet subscribers accepted only about 1.1% of promotional offers and 0.6% of plan switches (June to September data). Most 'saves' happen without any offer: the user just doesn't cancel within 24 hours.

Key points.title: Save rate overstates what the message does
Key points.detail: The median save rate was 17%; a quarter of apps were under 10%, a quarter over 27%, and the top 10% at 42% or more. But someone who cancels a few days later still counts as saved, some would have stayed anyway, and the metric doesn't track renewal. Track renewals and revenue, not just saves.

Key points.title: No clear effect on cancellation rates yet
Key points.detail: Across 64 apps with 500+ paying customers, cancellation rates fell 3.6% after launching Retention Messaging versus 7.3% at comparable apps without it. With only 64 apps, "a gap this size could easily be chance." Both groups were already trending down before launch.

Key points.title: Match the message to the cancel reason
Key points.detail: Low acceptance doesn't mean the discount should be bigger: "Price may not even be the issue." Use cancellation surveys, support chats and usage to learn why people cancel, then test a discount for cost, a different plan for changed needs, or a reminder of features they missed. For OnCourse, 'exam done' and 'too expensive' need different messages.

Key points.title: Keep discounts away from trial users and past redeemers
Key points.detail: If everyone who opens the cancel screen gets a discount, people learn that starting to cancel is a shortcut to a lower price. RevenueCat lets you exclude users still in a free trial and those who already redeemed an offer; setting it up directly in App Store Connect doesn't allow this targeting.

Key points.title: Bigger apps adopted first
Key points.detail: 44% of App Store apps making $1M+ a month on RevenueCat have tried Retention Messaging, 17% of those making $100K to $1M, and under 5% of smaller apps. Apps need Apple's approval, must pass a performance test, and each message must be approved.

Title: 17% Revenue Boost with Transaction Abandon Paywalls - A Case Study
Creator: Superwall
Bottom line: Showing a discounted paywall to people who start checkout but back out recovered meaningful revenue without raising refunds.
What they did: 18 companies showed a discounted paywall to users who started a transaction but didn't confirm it with Face ID, running campaigns for at least two weeks and comparing against all recent installs.
Results: Transaction abandon paywalls "account for 17% of total revenue." Variant (87,403 users who abandoned) converted at 6.3% vs 8.9% for control (438,144 recent installs); refund rate 3.3% vs 6.8%. "Approximately 20% of total paywalled users will encounter a transaction abandon paywall." Some apps "received scrutiny from Apple."
Takeaways: Abandoned-checkout discounts made 17% of revenue; Only about half who start a purchase finish; Refunds went down, not up; Apple has pushed back on this tactic
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: when a student cancels the App Store/Play purchase sheet, show a one-time discounted annual offer with the same trial timeline. Paywall: log purchase-sheet cancels separately from paywall dismisses to size how many start a purchase but don't finish (Superwall says only "around 50%" finish).

Key points.title: Abandoned-checkout discounts made 17% of revenue
Key points.detail: Across 18 companies, a discounted paywall shown to users who started a purchase but didn't confirm it with Face ID accounted for 17% of total revenue. The variant group (87,403 abandoners) converted at 6.3% and earned $80,590; the control (438,144 recent installs) converted at 8.9% and earned $394,960. Superwall admits it is hard to know how many would have bought anyway.

Key points.title: Only about half who start a purchase finish
Key points.detail: Superwall cites that "only around 50% of users complete in-app purchases once they start." About 20% of all paywalled users end up seeing a transaction abandon paywall. That is a large group of people who showed clear intent and then hesitated, often over price.

Key points.title: Refunds went down, not up
Key points.detail: The refund rate was 3.3% in the variant versus 6.8% in the control. Superwall argues users who get a better deal are less likely to ask for money back, so the data doesn't point to accidental purchases or a dark pattern.

Key points.title: Apple has pushed back on this tactic
Key points.detail: A few apps in the group got scrutiny from Apple, which says the tactic leads to "unintentional purchases." It can cause App Review problems, so OnCourse should check store rules before showing a discount after a cancelled purchase sheet.

Title: The ultimate guide to price localization
Creator: Daphne Tideman (with Jacob Rushfinn), RevenueCat
Bottom line: Store-default prices for India are far above what successful apps charge; build your own price index and test, judging on LTV.
What they did: Jacob Rushfinn compared localized prices across 10 apps against Apple's suggested prices and describes what apps did: Duolingo charging more in Spain and France, Flo cutting prices sharply in Brazil, and Impulse dropping its annual plan in Brazil.
Results: For India, "Apple recommends pricing about 21% lower than the U.S., but most apps actually go 50–80% lower." Signal of mismatch: "If your conversion rate in India is five times lower than in Canada, Australia, or US, well, there's some mismatch." Flo's pricing work coincided with 45% overall growth: 35% in English-speaking markets and 80% in non-English-speaking ones. About 40% of brands in a webinar poll still use store defaults.
Takeaways: Most apps price India 50–80% below the US; Store default prices ignore purchasing power; Compare conversion by country to spot mismatches; Build your own index from about ten apps; Adjust plans, not just prices, by market; Test bold price gaps and judge on LTV
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: compare India vs US paywall-to-purchase rates; if India is several times lower, test a price 50–80% below US for NEET PG. Paywall: build a price index from Indian exam-prep competitors and show plans in rupees per month of prep.

Key points.title: Most apps price India 50–80% below the US
Key points.detail: Jacob Rushfinn compared localized prices across 10 apps with Apple's suggestions. For India, "Apple recommends pricing about 21% lower than the U.S., but most apps actually go 50–80% lower." For the UK Apple suggests 26% higher, while most apps price about 10% lower. This matters directly for OnCourse's rupee pricing.

Key points.title: Store default prices ignore purchasing power
Key points.detail: Apple and Google set local prices from exchange rates, taxes and price patterns, not what users can pay or how much they value the app. A webinar poll found about 40% of brands still use these defaults. Duolingo charges more in Spain and France than in the US because people there use it to learn English for work, so they value it more.

Key points.title: Compare conversion by country to spot mismatches
Key points.detail: Rushfinn: "If your conversion rate in India is five times lower than in Canada, Australia, or US, well, there's some mismatch." Compare download-to-purchase rates and ARPU across your top 10 to 20 markets. If engagement and retention are healthy but conversion is low, price is the likely cause.

Key points.title: Build your own index from about ten apps
Key points.detail: Pick around ten apps with global success, a similar business model, a nearby category and a similar audience, and include local competitors. Check prices through a VPN in local stores, and keep separate tables for iOS, Android and web. For OnCourse, that means Indian exam-prep apps, not just global brands.

Key points.title: Adjust plans, not just prices, by market
Key points.detail: Impulse, a brain-training app, dropped its annual plan in Brazil and kept weekly and lifetime. Flo cut prices sharply in Brazil, which became its third-largest market and stayed profitable partly because ads there were cheaper. Cheaper or shorter plans can suit lower purchasing power.

Key points.title: Test bold price gaps and judge on LTV
Key points.detail: Fix your main market's price first with big swings, such as $39 versus $69, not $39 versus $43. Pricing tests take 3 to 6 months to show the effect on retention and LTV. Keep legacy prices for existing users. Flo's pricing work coincided with 45% growth: 35% in English-speaking markets and 80% in others.

Title: Experiment: Free-trial Timeline Page vs. Long-form Feature/Benefit Page
Creator: Jeffrey Bunn (Clearful)
Bottom line: A trial timeline paywall boosted trial starts but hurt retention versus a long-form benefits page, so combine both and check downstream metrics.
What they did: Clearful A/B tested its long-form pricing page (features, benefits, testimonials, social proof, FAQ) against a Blinkist-style free-trial timeline page with a push prompt offering a reminder before the trial ends (sent two days before renewal).
Results: "54% increase in trial starts (yay) with worse retention for all users in the test (uh-oh)." The vast majority of new trialists converted to Pro and push opt-ins rose; retention fell even among people who saw the page but didn't start a trial. No retention figures given. In a follow-up post, trial-user push opt-ins were "nearing 100%" and trial-to-paid conversion "didn't drop."
Takeaways: A trial timeline page lifted trial starts 54%; But retention got worse, even for non-buyers; Long-form pages build understanding that supports retention; Next test: timeline on top of a long-form page
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: keep the existing trial timeline at the top but add scrollable proof below it (topper testimonials, what's in the question bank, FAQ on cancelling). Paywall: A/B test on 30-day retention and renewal, not just trial starts.

Key points.title: A trial timeline page lifted trial starts 54%
Key points.detail: Clearful tested its long-form pricing page against a Blinkist-style free-trial timeline page, plus a push prompt offering a reminder before the trial ends. Result: a "54% increase in trial starts." Most new trialists converted to Pro, with no drop in paid conversion, and push opt-ins went up.

Key points.title: But retention got worse, even for non-buyers
Key points.detail: Retention fell for everyone in the test, including people who saw the timeline page and did not start a trial. Jeffrey Bunn found this "the most fascinating part." No retention numbers were shared. The paywall shapes how people understand the app, not just whether they buy.

Key points.title: Long-form pages build understanding that supports retention
Key points.detail: The working idea is that the long-form page, with features, benefits, testimonials, social proof and FAQ, gives users a better sense of the product and more confidence it is right for them. For OnCourse, a timeline alone may get trials while hurting how well students understand what they are paying for.

Key points.title: Next test: timeline on top of a long-form page
Key points.detail: Clearful planned to put the timeline at the top of the long-form page and test it against the original, hoping to keep higher trial starts and opt-ins while undoing the retention drop. This post doesn't report that result. OnCourse can try the same layout: timeline first, proof and FAQ below.

Title: How ABBYY increased annual subscription revenue by 58.5% with paywall A/B testing
Creator: Adapty
Bottom line: Highlighting the annual plan with a savings badge and a longer trial, and making each plan its own button, doubled annual plan choice.
What they did: ABBYY tested its paywall with benefits in a gallery and the monthly plan highlighted against a version with benefits in one list, the annual plan on a coloured button with a 'save 71%' badge and a 14-day free trial, and each plan as its own tappable button.
Results: "the users would choose the annual plan twice more often than the monthly option"; "the conversion rate from views to purchases increased from 1.37% to 1.54%"; "the revenue from annual subscriptions also increased by 58.5%".
Takeaways: Highlighting annual doubled annual plan choice; View-to-purchase conversion rose from 1.37% to 1.54%; Put the trial on the plan you want to sell; A list of benefits and tappable plans replaced a gallery
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: highlight the full-exam-cycle plan with a 'save X%' badge and attach the trial only to it. Paywall: replace any benefit carousel with a short list and make each plan card a direct purchase button.

Key points.title: Highlighting annual doubled annual plan choice
Key points.detail: ABBYY wanted to sell more annual plans. Version B highlighted the annual plan with a coloured button and a "save 71%" badge, where version A highlighted monthly. Users then chose "the annual plan twice more often than the monthly option" and annual subscription revenue rose 58.5%.

Key points.title: View-to-purchase conversion rose from 1.37% to 1.54%
Key points.detail: Overall conversion from paywall views to purchases went from 1.37% to 1.54%. The bigger effect was on plan mix, not on how many people bought. The case study doesn't say how long the test ran or how many users saw it.

Key points.title: Put the trial on the plan you want to sell
Key points.detail: In version B only the annual plan offered a 14-day free trial. That gave the annual plan a second reason to win besides the discount. For OnCourse, attach the trial to the full-cycle plan.

Key points.title: A list of benefits and tappable plans replaced a gallery
Key points.detail: Version A showed benefits as a gallery with one button to proceed. Version B grouped benefits into a single list and made each plan its own button. Several changes shipped together, so the test can't say which one mattered most. Adapty says its paywall tests take about 10 minutes to launch.

Title: How long should your free trial be? Data from 17,000+ apps
Creator: Margarita Loktionova, RevenueCat
Bottom line: Longer trials tend to come with higher conversion and much higher first renewal, especially on annual plans, but pick length by time-to-value and test it.
What they did: RevenueCat analysed trial length against trial conversion and first renewal across 17,000+ apps (August 2025 to July 2026), split by plan type, category and region.
Results: Annual plans: conversion from 24% (≤4-day trials) to 44.6% (17–32 days); first renewal from 18.3% to 47.5%. Monthly: conversion 39.6% (≤4 days), 45.9% (5–9), 46.6% (10–16), 43.7% (17–32); first renewal 62.8% at 5–9 days to 77.5% at 17–32. Monthly plans in India & Southeast Asia peak at 5–9 days. Education top apps favor 5–9-day trials. Author calls it "a correlational pattern."
Takeaways: Annual plans gain most from longer trials; Monthly in India and Southeast Asia peaks at 5–9 days; Short trials are common but renew worse; No-trial plans renew worse on weekly and monthly; Choose trial length by time to value and habit
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: test a 7-day vs 14-day trial on the annual plan, measured on first renewal, since students need time to finish a few mocks. Renewal: report renewal rate by trial length cohort so trial changes are judged on renewal.

Key points.title: Annual plans gain most from longer trials
Key points.detail: On annual plans, moving from trials of 4 days or less to 17–32 days goes with conversion rising from 24% to 44.6% and first renewal from 18.3% to 47.5%. The share of trial users who paid and renewed went from 3.5% to 18.5%. The author notes buyers of annual plans may just need more time before a big commitment.

Key points.title: Monthly in India and Southeast Asia peaks at 5–9 days
Key points.detail: On monthly plans, conversion in India and Southeast Asia, Middle East and Africa, and Latin America is highest with 5–9-day trials and lower at 17–32 days. Overall monthly conversion is 39.6% at 4 days or less, 45.9% at 5–9, 46.6% at 10–16 and 43.7% at 17–32. This is the most relevant benchmark for OnCourse's monthly plan.

Key points.title: Short trials are common but renew worse
Key points.detail: Among the 100 apps with the most trial starts per category, short trials dominate. Education, Health & Fitness and Travel favor 5–9 days. But monthly first renewal climbs from 62.8% at 5–9 days to 72% at 10–16 and 77.5% at 17–32. Popular doesn't mean best.

Key points.title: No-trial plans renew worse on weekly and monthly
Key points.detail: First renewal without a trial is 35.9% weekly and 49.5% monthly, below every trial group. Annual is different: 26.6% with no trial beats trials of up to 9 days but trails longer ones. Lower renewal doesn't always mean less profit, since a no-trial offer can earn more per buyer.

Key points.title: Choose trial length by time to value and habit
Key points.detail: The guide asks four questions: how long users need to judge the app, whether habit or motivation drives use, how much the audience trusts recurring billing, and what free access costs. RevenueCat calls the data "a correlational pattern," since people still in a trial on day 25 were likely to pay anyway. OnCourse should test trial length and judge on renewal.

Title: Writing for Interfaces (WWDC22)
Creator: Kaely Coon and Jennifer Bush, Apple
Bottom line: Make each screen say one clear thing, and label every button with the action it performs.
What they did: Apple's UX writers set out the PACE framework (Purpose, Anticipation, Context, Empathy) with before/after rewrites of real iOS screens. One example: an ambiguous 'Confirm Cancellation' alert with 'Cancel'/'Confirm' buttons became 'Cancel Platinum Subscription?' with 'Cancel Subscription' and 'Keep Subscription'.
Takeaways: Buttons should name the action, never Yes/No; Each screen has one purpose; cut what doesn't serve it; Errors should say what's wrong and how to fix it; Empty states should explain how the space gets filled; Keep one voice, but change tone with the moment; Anticipate the next step and make it the default
Ideas for OnCourse: Copy: Rewrite every alert and sheet so the buttons name their action (e.g. 'End session' / 'Keep practicing' instead of 'Yes' / 'No'). Flashcards: Replace empty states like 'Nothing here' with what fills them, e.g. 'No saved cards. Bookmark a question during practice and it shows up here.' Streaks: Keep the celebratory tone for milestones only and make the copy for missed days calm and factual.

Key points.title: Buttons should name the action, never Yes/No
Key points.detail: A made-up alert titled "Confirm Cancellation" had buttons "Cancel" and "Confirm," so you couldn't tell which ended the plan. The rewrite says "Cancel Platinum Subscription?" with "Cancel Subscription" and "Keep Subscription," and a body of "You'll continue to have access until June 21, 2022." The rule: if you only read the button labels, you should still understand the choice. For OnCourse: "End test" / "Keep going," not "Yes" / "No."

Key points.title: Each screen has one purpose; cut what doesn't serve it
Key points.detail: A draft iPhone overheating screen explained causes and had a huge emergency button. The shipped version just says "Temperature," lets the thermometer image show it's hot, uses one sentence, and has a button labelled "Emergency." People don't read screens in order, so the header and button must make sense alone. When a flow has several steps, give the whole flow and each screen a purpose.

Key points.title: Errors should say what's wrong and how to fix it
Key points.detail: The bad example: "Oops! you can't do that," error code 1234567, "Sorry, bad input," and two buttons that seem to do the same thing. They say "oops" can sound patronizing and "sorry" insincere. The better version names the billing problem, says to add a new payment method, and offers "Add Payment Method" and "Not Now."

Key points.title: Empty states should explain how the space gets filled
Key points.detail: A made-up restaurant app said "Nothing strike your fancy?" which is whimsical but may not translate and gives no guidance. Apple Podcasts says "No Saved Episodes" and "Save episodes you want to listen to later, and they'll show up here." Empty states can also teach or celebrate, like finishing a to-do list. For OnCourse: empty bookmarks or notes screens should say how to add the first item.

Key points.title: Keep one voice, but change tone with the moment
Key points.detail: Decide your app's voice first: what it would and wouldn't say, and a list of common terms. Then vary tone. Apple Watch's fall alert is calm: "It looks like you've taken a hard fall." The Activity app celebrates "You set a personal record for your longest daily Move streak: 35 days!" Use exclamation points sparingly, since "they can look silly when they're frequent." For OnCourse: celebrate streak milestones, but stay calm on missed days and errors.

Key points.title: Anticipate the next step and make it the default
Key points.detail: When you edit a weekend alarm, the Clock app's first option is "Change Next Alarm Only," because that's usually what you mean. If you wake before the alarm, iPhone asks "It looks like you're awake. Would you like to turn off your alarm?" Think of the app as one side of a conversation and always ask "What comes next?"

Title: Designing Fluid Interfaces (WWDC18)
Creator: Chan, Nathan de Vries and Marcos, Apple Human Interface team
Bottom line: Motion should respond instantly, be interruptible, and follow the gesture's momentum, so the interface feels like an extension of the hand.
What they did: Apple's HI team explains the principles behind the iPhone X gesture interface: no latency, motion that can be redirected mid-gesture, spatial consistency, and springs described by damping and response instead of duration. It also covers projecting a flick's momentum to pick where an element should land.
Takeaways: Describe springs with damping and response, not duration; Start at 100% damping; bounce only for momentum; Project momentum to decide where a flicked item lands; Taps: highlight on touch-down, commit on touch-up; Make every motion interruptible and remove all latency; Things should leave the way they came in
Ideas for OnCourse: Motion: Define 2-3 shared spring presets (e.g. no-bounce for taps, slight bounce for swipe-dismiss) in the design system and use them everywhere instead of ad-hoc durations. Flashcards: Make the card swipe follow the finger one-to-one and use release velocity to decide know/don't-know, so a quick flick counts. Practice: Make answer options highlight on press-in, so a learner can slide off to change their mind before committing.

Key points.title: Describe springs with damping and response, not duration
Key points.detail: Nathan de Vries says mass, stiffness and damping are hard to design with. Apple reduces them to two values: damping (100% means no overshoot, 0% oscillates forever) and response (how quickly it heads to the target). They avoid the word duration because a spring is always ready to move somewhere else. The technical names are damping ratio and frequency response. For OnCourse: define a few named spring presets in the design system.

Key points.title: Start at 100% damping; bounce only for momentum
Key points.detail: Tools shouldn't add needless motion, so start with no overshoot. Add bounce when the gesture itself has momentum, or it can feel "broken or unsatisfying." In Music, tapping the mini player opens Now Playing at 100% damping, but swiping it down to dismiss uses 80% for "a little bit of bounce and squish." Bounce can also hint: the iPhone X flashlight button bounces on a tap to teach that a firmer press is needed.

Key points.title: Project momentum to decide where a flicked item lands
Key points.detail: In FaceTime, the small self-view can be flicked to any corner. Picking the nearest corner on release felt wrong, because a quick flick snapped back. Instead they project where it would coast using the scroll view's deceleration rate, then send it to the corner nearest that projected point. They share the function on stage. For OnCourse: a flashcard flick should count as a swipe even if the finger barely moved.

Key points.title: Taps: highlight on touch-down, commit on touch-up
Key points.detail: Marcos shows the Calculator button. Highlight immediately on touch, but only confirm when the finger lifts. Add an extra margin around the hit area so small movements don't cancel. Dragging off the button cancels, and dragging back re-highlights it. He also warns that adding double-tap delays every single tap by about half a second.

Key points.title: Make every motion interruptible and remove all latency
Key points.detail: People are very sensitive to lag, so look for delays in taps and presses too, not just swipes. On iPhone X you can redirect mid-gesture: head home, then change your mind and go to multitasking. "The thought and gesture happen in parallel," which is faster than thinking first. To detect the pause that opens multitasking, they watch for a spike in finger acceleration instead of waiting on a timer.

Key points.title: Things should leave the way they came in
Key points.detail: A pushed screen slides in from the right and goes back to the right, so you can also drag it there yourself. If it slid in and left downward, it would feel like you were sending it somewhere. Animations can also teach gestures: tapping X in Safari slides the tab left, which hints that you can swipe it left. Chan's closing advice is to build interactive demos, since one is "worth a million static designs."

Title: Explore Navigation Design for iOS (WWDC22)
Creator: Sarah McClanahan, Apple
Bottom line: Tabs should mirror your information hierarchy. Push to go deeper, and use modals only for self-contained tasks.
What they did: Using a fictional cycling app, the session shows how an overloaded first tab was split by modelling the content's natural relationships, and warns against a catch-all Home tab that duplicates actions found elsewhere. It sets rules for push (always when a chevron is shown) and modals (preferred action plus Cancel, and a sparing X).
Takeaways: A Home tab that repeats other tabs' actions confuses people; Don't load everything onto the first tab; Never switch tabs for people; keep the tab bar visible; Push to go deeper; a chevron always means push; Modals suit self-contained tasks, with Cancel plus a named action; Use an X only on modals with no input
Ideas for OnCourse: Navigation: Audit whether Home repeats actions that already live in Practice or Lessons, and keep Home as a launch point rather than a second copy. Practice: Present a custom test builder as a bottom modal with 'Cancel' and 'Start test', not an X, since the learner has made choices. Lessons: Use push for chapter, then topic, then lesson, with the back button showing the previous title, and keep the tab bar visible.

Key points.title: A Home tab that repeats other tabs' actions confuses people
Key points.detail: Teams add a catch-all Home tab to boost features people aren't finding, such as repeating "New Itinerary" there. Sarah McClanahan says this makes "the tab where every feature is fighting for real estate" and breaks the link between content and how to act on it. Repeating content, like songs on several tabs, is fine; repeating actions is not. Her advice: "consider removing the Home tab altogether." For OnCourse: check that Home launches into Practice and Lessons instead of copying them.

Key points.title: Don't load everything onto the first tab
Key points.detail: The demo cycling app crammed a map, filters, an itinerary editor and route lists into its first tab. Filtering a map and editing an itinerary are different mindsets, so people scroll and struggle to parse it. They fixed it by asking why people use the app and following natural relationships: all places, then a city, then a route. That made Places a self-contained tab, with Itineraries as its own.

Key points.title: Never switch tabs for people; keep the tab bar visible
Key points.detail: When an action exists in two tabs, tapping it can throw the user into another tab, which is "jarring and disorienting." "Never force someone to change tabs automatically." Keep the tab bar on screen as people go deeper, and keep each tab's state, so they can compare content across tabs. Slopes is praised for opening on its Logbook tab with short, clear labels.

Key points.title: Push to go deeper; a chevron always means push
Key points.detail: A push slides the next screen in from the right and mirrors the hierarchy: more specific content and fewer options as you go in. The back button shows the previous screen's title, so people never have to remember where they came from. Any row with a chevron must push. Use push for things people move between often, like Messages threads, where modals would feel heavy.

Key points.title: Modals suit self-contained tasks, with Cancel plus a named action
Key points.detail: Use a modal for a simple task, a multi-step task like adding a transit card, or full-screen content like a workout video. The right button is the preferred action, a short verb in bold, disabled until required fields are filled. "Cancel" on the left abandons the task. If the user has entered data, confirm before discarding. Avoid stacking modals over modals.

Key points.title: Use an X only on modals with no input
Key points.detail: An X works on an App Store Today article because there's nothing to save. On a filter sheet, an X is a problem: after picking filters, will closing apply or discard them? Labelled actions in the navigation bar are clearer. For OnCourse: a custom test builder sheet should use "Cancel" and "Start test," not an X.

Title: Make Your App Visually Accessible (WWDC20)
Creator: Drew Haas, Apple
Bottom line: Never rely on color alone, design for large text from the start, and respect the system's motion and contrast settings.
What they did: An Apple accessibility engineer walks through a demo app, adding symbols to color-coded items, checking contrast (4.5:1 by default, 7.5:1 in the high-contrast variant), and switching layouts from horizontal to vertical at accessibility text sizes. He also turns off parallax and slide transitions when Reduce Motion is on.
Results: Contrast example in the demo: 4.5:1 by default ('generally the lowest acceptable ratio'), 7.5:1 in the high-contrast variant
Takeaways: Never use color alone; pair it with a shape; Aim for 4.5:1 contrast, plus a high-contrast version; Design for large text from the start; Respect Reduce Motion: cut idle animation, parallax and autoplay; Bold Text only works if you use system text styles; Reduce Transparency turns blurs solid for readability
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: Mark right and wrong answers with a check or cross icon as well as green and red, so color-blind learners can tell them apart. Design system: Add a contrast check (at least 4.5:1) to every text and background token pair in light and dark, and let answer rows wrap to vertical layouts at large Dynamic Type sizes. Motion: Gate celebration and confetti animations behind React Native's AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled.

Key points.title: Never use color alone; pair it with a shape
Key points.detail: For color-blind or low-vision users, emphasis made with color only "can get lost." Drew Haas's Starstruck demo gave each constellation its own symbol as well as its own color. He recommends SF Symbols (over 1,500) and supporting the Differentiate without Color and Button Shapes settings. For OnCourse: right and wrong answers need a check and cross, not just green and red.

Key points.title: Aim for 4.5:1 contrast, plus a high-contrast version
Key points.detail: Xcode's contrast calculator gave white on his purple 4.5:1, "generally the lowest acceptable ratio for most cases." For Increase Contrast he darkened the background to reach 7.5:1. The general rule: colors get darker in light mode and lighter in dark mode when contrast goes up. System colors adapt automatically; custom colors need their own high-contrast variants.

Key points.title: Design for large text from the start
Key points.detail: "My biggest tip is to think about these early on." Don't truncate as text grows; wrap labels and use the full width. In Starstruck, rows sit side by side at normal sizes, but at accessibility sizes the stack flips to vertical with leading alignment, and labels never limit their line count. Symbols should scale with the text too.

Key points.title: Respect Reduce Motion: cut idle animation, parallax and autoplay
Key points.detail: Parallax and big animations can cause motion sickness. With Reduce Motion on, users expect apps to suppress small idle animations, parallax, autoplaying video or GIFs, and slide transitions. iOS 14 added Prefer Cross-Fade Transitions, which swaps slides for fades. For OnCourse: confetti and celebration animations should check this setting.

Key points.title: Bold Text only works if you use system text styles
Key points.detail: The Bold Text setting is for people who need heavier type everywhere, since thin and even default weights can be hard to read. System font styles respond to it automatically. Custom text styles may not, so you have to check the setting and update them yourself.

Key points.title: Reduce Transparency turns blurs solid for readability
Key points.detail: Text over a blurred background can have uneven contrast and make some readers dizzy. With Reduce Transparency on, system blur and vibrancy become one solid color. Custom blurs need to check the setting too. His closing ask: turn these settings on yourself and look at your app.

Title: Implementing Dark Mode on iOS (WWDC19)
Creator: Kurt and Tyler, Apple UIKit team
Bottom line: Dark mode is not an inversion. Build it on semantic color names and elevation levels so screens adapt without per-mode code.
What they did: Apple's session shows converting a demo app by swapping hard-coded colors for semantic ones (system background, label, secondary label) and giving brand colors and images their own dark variants. It explains that elevated layers such as sheets get lighter backgrounds in dark mode to separate them from the black base.
Takeaways: Name colors by role, not by value; Dark mode is not an inversion of light mode; Raised layers get lighter backgrounds in dark mode; Brand colors and images need their own dark versions; Learn the system before customizing; You can lock one screen to dark
Ideas for OnCourse: Design system: Replace raw hex values in components with role tokens (surface/base, surface/elevated, text/primary, text/secondary) that resolve per theme. Design system: Make bottom sheets and modals use a lighter elevated surface in dark mode, not the same black as the screen behind. Lessons: Give illustrations and diagram images dark-mode variants, or put them on a light card, so they don't glare.

Key points.title: Name colors by role, not by value
Key points.detail: Apple's dark mode uses semantic colors whose names say what they're for: "label" for text, "system grouped background," "system blue." Each has a light and dark value, and UIKit swaps them automatically. "You don't have to think about what mode you're in." In the demo, a hard-coded white background and black text were swapped for system background and label, and the screen worked in both modes. For OnCourse: components should use role tokens, not raw hex values.

Key points.title: Dark mode is not an inversion of light mode
Key points.detail: "Dark mode is not just a simple inversion of light mode. It's more subtle than that." System background is pure white in light and pure black in dark, with secondary and tertiary backgrounds stacked on top for hierarchy. Text has four levels, from primary for titles to secondary for subtitles and so on.

Key points.title: Raised layers get lighter backgrounds in dark mode
Key points.detail: The same system background looked black on the main screen but lighter grey in a presented card. Dark mode has two levels: base for full-screen content and elevated for layers on top, like sheets or iPad split view. Elevated backgrounds are lighter "to distinguish them from the black background underneath." Foreground colors don't change. For OnCourse: sheets in dark mode need a lighter surface than the screen behind them.

Key points.title: Brand colors and images need their own dark versions
Key points.detail: In the demo, the green logo color got a yellow dark variant, and a sunny beach header got a sunset version for dark mode, both set in the asset catalog with no code. The same works for the launch screen. For OnCourse: diagrams and illustrations need dark variants, or a light card behind them.

Key points.title: Learn the system before customizing
Key points.detail: Apple's dark design has three parts: colors, materials (blurs with vibrant text on top) and built-in controls, all made to work together. "Before you touch a single line of code, learn this design system and figure out how to take advantage of what it provides." Blurs come in thick, regular, thin and ultra-thin, and vibrancy has four text styles, all adapting to dark mode.

Key points.title: You can lock one screen to dark
Key points.detail: They made the "Learn More" screen always dark, even when the rest of the app is light, by overriding the interface style on that view controller. Everything inside it follows. A whole app can also be locked to light or dark with one setting. One common bug: styled text drawn without a color shows as black, which disappears in dark mode.

Title: Discoverable Design (WWDC21)
Creator: Jiabao Li and Mylène Dreyer, Apple
Bottom line: Make features obvious from the screen itself instead of explaining them in onboarding slides.
What they did: Apple designers redesign a fictional recipe app: they drop a hamburger menu for a tab bar, place features by how often they're used, label ambiguous icons, keep gestures as shortcuts next to visible buttons, and rewrite a feedback control over three rounds of testing until its consequence was clear ('Suggest toast like this').
Takeaways: People skip onboarding, so teach in context; Rank features by importance and frequency, then give space; Label icons that could mean several things; Solve the blank page with example inputs; Use gestures as shortcuts, never as the only way; Make feedback labels say what will happen
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: Replace feature-tour slides with in-context hints on the first practice session, e.g. a one-time label on the bookmark and the explanation toggle. Home: Label recommended content with its reason, e.g. 'Because you missed 4 cardiology questions'. Flashcards: Keep visible 'Again' and 'Got it' buttons even if swiping works, and make the first tap animate in the swipe direction to teach the gesture.

Key points.title: People skip onboarding, so teach in context
Key points.detail: Jiabao Li admits "I always skip through these onboarding screens," and even readers won't remember them later. Toasty's camera teaches instead: an outline shows where to hold the toast, the shutter stays disabled with a note that it's looking for toast, the outline changes at the right angle, and a haptic marks the moment to shoot. For OnCourse: swap feature-tour slides for hints on the first practice session.

Key points.title: Rank features by importance and frequency, then give space
Key points.detail: They listed every feature and ranked them. The hamburger menu failed in testing: closed, "people don't know what's inside." Six tabs were too many. The main and most frequent features went into two tabs, the photo-to-recipe button sat at the top of Recipes, search went top for less frequent use, and settings went behind the profile icon.

Key points.title: Label icons that could mean several things
Key points.detail: Even familiar icons are vague: is that a book or a newspaper? Labels clarified the tabs as browse and saved recipes. A camera icon could mean photo, document scan or QR code, so they labelled it "New." Standard patterns like the back chevron need no extra hint, but unique designs need words.

Key points.title: Solve the blank page with example inputs
Key points.detail: People know how to use search but "draw a blank on what to write." They call this the blank page problem. Toasty shows example ways to search, by ingredients, places or friends, so people learn the options at a glance. For OnCourse: suggest example searches like a topic, a subject or a past exam.

Key points.title: Use gestures as shortcuts, never as the only way
Key points.detail: Gestures are invisible, so every gesture needs a visible button too. Toasty shows a Like icon but also allows double-tap. Tapping the back button plays a slide-down animation, which hints that you can also swipe down. Showing slivers of the next and previous recipes hints that you can swipe sideways. For OnCourse: keep visible flashcard buttons even if swiping works.

Key points.title: Make feedback labels say what will happen
Key points.detail: A heart for "show me more like this" was read as "add to favorites." Thumbs up and down made people think others would see their like. The final label, "Suggest toast like this," made the effect clear. Recommendations got a reason ("Because you added avocado toast") and a visible "edit suggestion" button instead of a hidden More menu. For OnCourse: label recommendations with why they appear.

Title: How we redesigned the Linear UI
Creator: Linear
Bottom line: A small team redesigned the chrome in about six weeks by cutting visual noise, generating themes from three variables, and dogfooding behind a flag.
What they did: Linear refreshed its sidebar, tabs, headers and inbox, and rebuilt its themes on an LCH generator using three inputs (base, accent, contrast) instead of 98 hand-set variables per theme. That also made high-contrast themes possible. They deliberately left navigation alone and rolled the change out through a feature flag with an old/new toggle, then a private beta, then general availability.
Results: About six weeks with a small dedicated team; themes went from 98 hand-defined variables to 3 inputs; no usage metrics reported
Takeaways: Themes now come from three inputs, not 98; A contrast input gives high-contrast themes for free; They cut navigation from scope on purpose; Stress-test the direction before building; Ship behind a flag with an old/new toggle; A redesign needs a dedicated team, done fast
Ideas for OnCourse: Design system: Generate OnCourse's light and dark palettes from a small set of base, accent and contrast values so dark mode and a high-contrast mode come from the same source. Design system: Ship visual refreshes behind a PostHog flag with an internal old/new toggle before rolling out. Navigation: Keep restyling separate from navigation changes, and test each on its own.

Key points.title: Themes now come from three inputs, not 98
Key points.detail: Linear moved its main light and dark themes onto its LCH-based theme generator. "Instead of having to define 98 specific variables for each theme, we defined three: base color, accent color, and contrast." LCH is perceptually uniform, so colors with the same lightness look equally light, which keeps generated themes consistent.

Key points.title: A contrast input gives high-contrast themes for free
Key points.detail: The generator has a contrast variable that sets how contrasty a theme is, which "allows us to automatically include super high-contrast themes for users who need it for accessibility reasons." They also darkened text and neutral icons in light mode and lightened them in dark mode, and limited how much blue fed into the color system for a more neutral look.

Key points.title: They cut navigation from scope on purpose
Key points.detail: Karri Saarinen explored navigation but set it aside because changes would need major engineering work and change how people use the product: "This felt like an unnecessary risk." The redesign focused on the 'inverted L' chrome: sidebar, tabs and headers. For OnCourse, restyle and re-navigate in separate projects.

Key points.title: Stress-test the direction before building
Key points.detail: Before implementation they tested the concept on environment (macOS, Windows and browser), appearance (light, dark and custom themes) and hierarchy (list, board, split and other views). They checked every main view: Inbox, Triage, My Issues, Project, Cycles, Roadmap and Search. This kept the scope from blowing up.

Key points.title: Ship behind a flag with an old/new toggle
Key points.detail: After a week of work at an offsite, the new UI went behind a feature flag for everyone at Linear. A toggle in the internal toolbar switched old and new UI instantly so teams could compare. Then came a private beta, rollout to a percentage of workspaces each day, and general availability.

Key points.title: A redesign needs a dedicated team, done fast
Key points.detail: "It's always better to do a redesign quickly," or every new feature adds design debt. Linear put a small dedicated team on it and "couldn't treat it as a side project"; it took about six weeks. Designers and pairs of engineers worked in a daily back-and-forth.
