Title: Expressive Design: Google's UX Research (Material 3 Expressive)
Creator: Google Design
Bottom line: Bolder color, shape, size and motion helped people find key actions faster, but only when basic usability stayed intact.
What they did: Over three years Google ran 46 studies with more than 18,000 participants (eye tracking, surveys, usability tests) comparing expressive designs with standard Material. In one example, the email Send button was made bigger, moved above the keyboard and given a secondary color.
Results: 46 studies, 18,000+ participants; key UI elements spotted up to 4x faster; preference for expressive designs up to 87% among 18-24-year-olds; modernity perception +34%; age gaps in fixation time largely disappeared for users 45+; scattered layouts and removing text labels hurt usability
Takeaways: Expressive designs helped people find key actions 4x faster; Bigger Send button near the thumb was seen 4x faster; Breaking familiar patterns hurt usability; Older users caught up with younger ones; Young users strongly prefer expressive design, but not all; The finding rests on 46 studies and 18,000+ people
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: Make 'Submit' and 'Next question' larger and anchored at the bottom in the thumb zone, in a distinct color from the answer options. Home: Give the single 'Start today's plan' action clear size and color emphasis rather than equal weight with other cards. Design system: Keep text labels on icon buttons in the practice toolbar, since removing labels reduced usability in Google's tests.

Key points.title: Expressive designs helped people find key actions 4x faster
Key points.detail: In an eye-tracking lab, people used 10 apps in both Material 3 Expressive and standard Material 3 versions. They spotted key UI elements "up to four times faster" in the expressive versions, and the time to tap key actions dropped by seconds. Color, size, shape and containment pull attention to what matters.

Key points.title: Bigger Send button near the thumb was seen 4x faster
Key points.detail: In an email app test, the Send button was made larger, placed just above the keyboard and given a secondary color, instead of sitting small in the top toolbar. Participants' eyes found it four times faster. For OnCourse, put Submit and Next in a large, distinct button near the keyboard or thumb.

Key points.title: Breaking familiar patterns hurt usability
Key points.detail: A playlist with album art scattered helter-skelter looked modern but scored worse on usability. Removing text labels from email actions also reduced usability. "No amount of expressive design will beat basic functionality." Keep labels on OnCourse's practice toolbar icons.

Key points.title: Older users caught up with younger ones
Key points.detail: Older adults usually take longer to find key elements. With the expressive versions, age differences in fixation time largely disappeared, and users 45+ performed on par with younger ones. Larger buttons and high-contrast containment also helped people with different movement and vision abilities.

Key points.title: Young users strongly prefer expressive design, but not all
Key points.detail: Preference reached up to 87% among 18-to-24-year-olds, and expressive designs scored 34% higher on modernity and 32% higher on subculture. But "a strong minority of users preferred calmer, less intense versions," and unfamiliarity lowered some scores. OnCourse's students are in the high-preference age group.

Key points.title: The finding rests on 46 studies and 18,000+ people
Key points.detail: Over three years Google ran 46 studies with more than 18,000 participants, using eye tracking, surveys, focus groups, experiments and usability tests. They started with single components, such as how big a button can be before it crowds the screen. Test with timed tasks, not just preference.

Title: How Duolingo's World Characters lip sync
Creator: Jasmine Vahidsafa and Kevin Lenzo, Duolingo
Bottom line: Duolingo made characters feel alive at scale by driving Rive state machines with data, not hand-animated video.
What they did: Duolingo ran its text-to-speech audio through its own speech models to get word and phoneme timings, mapped them to 20+ mouth shapes per character, and ran mouth and body animation as parallel states in a Rive state machine. The app downloads the audio and timings and drives the animation live, so characters react to taps and to right or wrong answers.
Results: 10 characters, 40+ languages, 100+ courses, 20+ mouth shapes per character; no engagement metrics reported
Takeaways: State machines scale where hand animation can't; Speech models give timing for each mouth shape; Separate body and mouth layers run together; Sending timing data beats shipping video; Characters react to right and wrong answers
Ideas for OnCourse: Motion: Use Rive (it has a React Native runtime) for any mascot or feedback animation, with states for idle, correct and incorrect driven by app events instead of Lottie clips per outcome. Practice: Add a small reacting element (icon or character) that responds to correct and incorrect answers, so feedback feels warm without extra screens.

Key points.title: State machines scale where hand animation can't
Key points.detail: Duolingo teaches 40+ languages across 100+ courses with thousands of sentences, so hand-animating lip sync for 10 characters was "completely out of the question." They used Rive's State Machine to control which animation states run and how they blend, turning a small set of assets into near-unlimited combinations with small files for Android, iOS and web.

Key points.title: Speech models give timing for each mouth shape
Key points.detail: The text-to-speech tool didn't provide timings, so Duolingo runs the generated audio through its own speech recognition and pronunciation models to get the timing of each word and phoneme. Each sound maps to a viseme (mouth shape). They built tools to generate, audit and correct these timings at scale.

Key points.title: Separate body and mouth layers run together
Key points.detail: Each character has animation states for general poses and separate states just for the mouth, running at the same time. Every character got 20+ mouth shapes designed to fit their personality and the Duolingo look. The key design test was whether the shapes looked believable when animated.

Key points.title: Sending timing data beats shipping video
Key points.detail: At runtime the app downloads the audio and timing data and drives the animation live. This is "much less than sending down a little movie" and lets characters react: tap a word and they say it, finish early and they stop. They also blink and nod while idle.

Key points.title: Characters react to right and wrong answers
Key points.detail: At the end of a challenge the state machine moves to a final state that shows the character's reaction to a right or wrong answer. The goal was "lively, engaging study buddies." For OnCourse, a small element that reacts to correct and incorrect answers could make feedback warmer without extra screens.

Title: Shape language: Duolingo's art style
Creator: Megan Barker, Duolingo
Bottom line: A minimal style built from a few rounded shapes let a small team make hundreds of clear, friendly illustrations a year.
What they did: In 2018 Duolingo moved from flat, sharp, muted art on gray to bright, rounded vector illustrations on white, and the UI followed with rounded buttons. The rules: use the fewest shapes needed, exaggerate key details almost to caricature, leave white space around artwork, and angle lines toward UI elements to guide the eye.
Results: No metrics reported; the team produces 'hundreds' of illustrations a year. Qualitatively, animated skill icons held attention longer than static ones
Takeaways: Unclear art makes learners fail; Pick a style a small team can produce fast; Use white space so art reads on small screens; Humor lowers the fear of mistakes; Lines and motion point attention at the UI; Duolingo moved from flat and sharp to bright and round
Ideas for OnCourse: Design system: Define a small illustration kit (2-3 base shapes, a fixed palette, a stroke rule) so devs and non-illustrators can make empty-state and milestone art that stays on style. Lessons: Keep medical diagrams minimal with exaggerated key features and generous white space so they stay legible on phones.

Key points.title: Unclear art makes learners fail
Key points.detail: Because Duolingo is an education app, confusing visuals can make learners answer wrong or get lost in the UI: "Our failure becomes our learners' failure." They use the fewest details needed to make the point, since too few confuse and too many distract. This applies to every diagram in OnCourse.

Key points.title: Pick a style a small team can produce fast
Key points.detail: In the early days only a few designers could illustrate, yet they had to make hundreds of illustrations, icons and marketing pieces a year. Moving to a minimal style and vector software sped up production and made art scale across phone and tablet sizes without losing quality.

Key points.title: Use white space so art reads on small screens
Key points.detail: After finding the key shapes, they give them room to be clearly silhouetted, which is the first step to quick recognition. Artwork is framed with white space so it supports the lesson "and never interrupts it."

Key points.title: Humor lowers the fear of mistakes
Key points.detail: "A big hurdle of language learning is getting over the fear of making mistakes." Duolingo exaggerates key details almost to caricature and finds small stories in sentences, like turning "I like this shirt" into a quirky scene. Playful visuals make learners look forward to practice.

Key points.title: Lines and motion point attention at the UI
Key points.detail: Artists rotate lines and angles to steer the eye toward UI or text, and use animation because eyes go to motion. Animated skill icons held attention longer than static ones, and longer attention makes learners more likely to start a lesson.

Key points.title: Duolingo moved from flat and sharp to bright and round
Key points.detail: Early designs were static, hard-edged shapes on light gray. In 2018 the art team tried brighter, rounder art for Duolingo KIDS, and the main app followed with a redesign of vibrant colors and rounded buttons on white.

Title: Behind the Design: Headspace
Creator: Apple Developer (interview with Jeff Birkeland, Headspace)
Bottom line: Headspace replaced category tabs with a Today tab that offers one-tap activities by time of day, and moved the full library into Explore.
What they did: Following user research, Headspace removed core tabs for meditation, focus, movement and sleep, and made a Today tab that offers activities of varying lengths for morning, afternoon and night without showing categories. The deep catalogue moved into an Explore tab with purpose-named collections.
Results: No redesign-specific metrics; the app has 100M+ users in nearly 200 countries and won a 2023 Apple Design Award
Takeaways: Headspace swapped category tabs for a Today tab; Keep the surface simple and the depth one tab away; Name collections by purpose; A warm brand makes hard topics approachable
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: Make the first tab a short, time-aware set of one-tap sessions (e.g. 10-minute warm-up, main block, evening review) rather than a list of subjects. Navigation: Move the full subject and system catalogue into a Browse/Explore tab so Home doesn't carry the taxonomy. Lessons: Name collections by goal ('High-yield for the last 30 days') as well as by subject.

Key points.title: Headspace swapped category tabs for a Today tab
Key points.detail: Earlier versions had core tabs for meditation, focus, movement and sleep. User research convinced the team to drop them and focus on a Today tab with one-tap activities of different lengths for morning, afternoon and night, "without bringing up specific categories." For OnCourse, Home could be today's sessions, not a list of subjects.

Key points.title: Keep the surface simple and the depth one tab away
Key points.detail: The Explore tab holds the full library, including the old category sections. Jeff Birkeland: "There's still simplicity at the surface. But there's an incredible depth of content underneath." He adds that "it's not a very long trip into an extensive archive."

Key points.title: Name collections by purpose
Key points.detail: Collections carry plain purpose names like Unlocking Creativity and Mindful Eating, which helps people find the right content faster. OnCourse could name collections by goal, like a last-30-days high-yield set, alongside subject names.

Key points.title: A warm brand makes hard topics approachable
Key points.detail: Birkeland says the team aims to "demystify" mindfulness, and that "the root of our success from the very beginning was creating a warm feel and brand." The illustration style and colors are part of that. The app has been used by more than 100 million people in nearly 200 countries and regions.

Title: 35 years of product design wisdom from Apple, Disney, Pinterest and beyond (Bob Baxley)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Bob Baxley)
Bottom line: Write a few opinionated design tenets that settle repeat debates, and stay low-fidelity until the concept is clear, because the first realistic picture anchors everyone.
What they did: At ThoughtSpot, Baxley set three tenets every team had to memorize: documentation is a failure state; start simple and let users opt into complexity; the whole product should feel like it came from a single mind. The team worked in 'block brain diagrams' (chunky blocks, simpler than wireframes) for weeks so feedback stayed on the concept, then an agency produced high-res comps in a day from the design system. When redesigning a checkout, he ran a 'reality check' study where users went through checkout on eBay, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon, and learned that the shipping quote mattered almost as much as price.
Results: Apple's online store had "six designers for a store that ran in 30 some odd countries, 12 and a half thousand instances of the store doing billions of dollars of revenue." Once block frames were locked, the agency "could do the full high-res comps in a day."
Takeaways: Design tenets are decision rules, not nice-sounding principles; Keep three memorable tenets so distant teams decide alike; Delay the first realistic picture, the 'primal mark'; Low-fidelity 'block brain diagrams' keep feedback on the concept; Watch people use other products, not just yours; Every screen creates an emotion, so choose it on purpose
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: write 3 OnCourse tenets that settle repeat debates (for example 'start simple, opt into complexity' for Practice filters) and check every crit against them. Design process: start new flows as block diagrams and only build an AI or Figma prototype once the concept is agreed. Design process: run a 'reality check' session where NEET-PG students use Marrow or PrepLadder to practise MCQs while we watch what they care about.

Key points.title: Design tenets are decision rules, not nice-sounding principles
Key points.detail: Baxley says principles like 'simple, clear, beautiful' don't help decisions because "nobody would ever argue the opposite." A tenet picks a side in a real trade-off. His model is Steve Jobs's brief for Keynote: make ugly presentations hard, focus on cinematic transitions, and choose "innovation over PowerPoint compatibility." To find yours, look for the debate your team keeps having, settle it once, and write it down. For OnCourse, a tenet could settle repeat arguments like how much to show on the Practice screen.

Key points.title: Keep three memorable tenets so distant teams decide alike
Key points.detail: At ThoughtSpot, with many engineering teams in India, he moved "from a mindset of control to one of choreography." He set three tenets everyone had to memorize: "documentation is a failure state"; start simple and let users opt into complexity (unlike Tableau, which felt like "flying the space shuttle"); and the product should feel like it "came from a single mind." He says you can't have more than three or four, because people must remember them without a handbook. In design debates the team asked: are we really starting simple here?

Key points.title: Delay the first realistic picture, the 'primal mark'
Key points.detail: Borrowing from art, he calls the first mark on the canvas the 'primal mark': everything after it reacts to it. As soon as a picture looks even slightly real, "everybody kind of goes, oh, that's the thing," and options shrink to one. AI prototyping tools make this worse, because they give back your first-order idea based on existing solutions. Stay in conversation long enough to reach a second, third and fourth idea, which can happen in one meeting. He sees AI prototypes as a production tool for once the idea is clear.

Key points.title: Low-fidelity 'block brain diagrams' keep feedback on the concept
Key points.detail: High-res mockups pull feedback toward colours and shapes, which he compares to judging "the special effects of a movie that has a really bad story." ThoughtSpot used 'block brain diagrams', chunky blocks even simpler than wireframes, sometimes for weeks, which made PMs nervous. Then, thanks to a strong design system, an agency "could do the full high-res comps in a day." The hard part is the thinking, not the polish.

Key points.title: Watch people use other products, not just yours
Key points.detail: When you watch people use your own product, bias gets in the way: you want to see the good parts and urge them to click the button. In a checkout redesign he ran a 'reality check' study where users went through checkout on eBay, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. They learned that the "ship quote is almost as important as price." He also watches self-checkout at Target, chip-card payments, and his kids' friends' home screens. For OnCourse, this means watching students practise MCQs on competing apps.

Key points.title: Every screen creates an emotion, so choose it on purpose
Key points.detail: He sees software as a medium like film or music, because every app makes him feel "confused or empowered." When execs said visual choices were "a matter of opinion," he pushed back: blue or red will cause a certain feeling, so decide what users should feel first. His Toast example: the payment device can make a grandmother paying the bill "look like a superhero" or "look like a fool." He also says "every time we make a demand on the audience, that's a failure on our part."

Title: Figma's CEO: Why AI makes design, craft, and quality the new moat for startups (Dylan Field)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Dylan Field)
Bottom line: When AI makes software cheap to build, design and craft decide who wins, so get users to real value fast, fix the blockers that stop adoption, and still ship something a little awesome.
What they did: A month before FigJam's launch, the team felt the product was boring, so they chose to make fun its differentiator and ran a one-day design sprint that produced about 20 ideas, including Cursor Chat. Figma had a team called Blockers that removed, one by one, the missing table-stakes features stopping adoption, and Field pushes every launch to shorten time to value (for example, getting a new user from a blank canvas to a multiplayer moment). Figma pulled its first AI feature, 'Make Design', after it produced near-copies of Apple's Weather app; Field called it a preventable QA failure and pushed the team toward evals. With Figma Make, he wants prototypes built from the real design system, because ideas get dismissed when they 'don't look right'.
Results: Fixing blockers: 'Each time we saw improvement in retention, improvement in activation... you could literally see the change in the graph' (no figure given). FigJam was built in 'around six-ish months'. Figma started in August 2012 and 'summer of 2017 we made our first money.' Figma's survey: '72% of respondents said AI powered tools like Make are one of the top reasons behind the expansion of roles'; non-designers doing design tasks went 'from 44% to 56%'; '53%' said you still need deep knowledge to do a task well with AI; about '16% or 17%' of designers saw AI as a threat to their role. After the Adobe deal fell through, 'a little bit over 4% of the company' took the 'Detach' severance offer.
Takeaways: Good enough is now mediocre; design is the differentiator; FigJam won by making fun its differentiator; A 'Blockers' team fixing basic gaps lifted retention; Shorten time to value to the product's special moment; Prototypes beat mocks, and mocks beat words; Figma pulled an AI feature after a QA failure
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: put playful touches (celebrations, streak animations) in low-stakes moments, and keep the MCQ-solving screen in Practice calm and out of the way, the way Figma kept fun in FigJam but not in Figma Design. Onboarding: measure time from install to the first solved question with an explanation, and keep a 'blockers' list of what stops students reaching it; fix those before adding features. Design process: build AI prototypes with OnCourse's real components so reviews judge the idea, and test any AI explanation feature against a set of real questions before launch.

Key points.title: Good enough is now mediocre; design is the differentiator
Key points.detail: Field says AI makes code cheap, so value moves up the stack to design: "We're no longer in this era of good enough is fine. Good enough is not enough. It's mediocre." He calls AI output "the realm of law of averages", which is why craft beats it. For OnCourse, generic-looking screens will look like every AI-built prep app, so a distinct look and careful details are part of the product, not polish.

Key points.title: FigJam won by making fun its differentiator
Key points.detail: FigJam was built in about six months, but a month before launch it felt boring: "the soul isn't there." At a board meeting they chose to "differentiate by making FigJam fun", ran a one-day design sprint with about 20 ideas, and Cursor Chat came out of it. He adds that context matters: fun suits a brainstorm tool, but in Figma Design quirky touches would get in the way. For OnCourse, play belongs in low-stakes moments like streaks and celebrations, not on the screen where a student is solving an MCQ.

Key points.title: A 'Blockers' team fixing basic gaps lifted retention
Key points.detail: Figma once had a team literally called Blockers that removed, one by one, the missing table-stakes features stopping people from adopting the product. With each fix, "you could literally see the change in the graph" for retention and activation. But he warns that only fixing basics leaves you without a reason to care, so ship "something that's a little bit awesome" too. For OnCourse, keep a running list of what stops students from finishing a first session and treat it as seriously as new features.

Key points.title: Shorten time to value to the product's special moment
Key points.detail: Field pushes every launch to cut the time until a new user feels what is special. In Figma Design that means getting someone from a blank canvas to making something, and ideally to a live multiplayer moment, as fast as possible. He later names "time to value" as his motto. For OnCourse, the first session should reach its 'aha' (a solved question with a great explanation, or a plan built for my exam date) within the first minute.

Key points.title: Prototypes beat mocks, and mocks beat words
Key points.detail: He says that in his product reviews "prototypes beat static mocks and static mocks beat lots of words", and that PMs no longer ask designers to "draw this thing out", which frees designers to explore deeper. He also stresses building prototypes from the real design system, because ideas get filtered out when they "don't look right"; consistent visuals let an idea be judged on its merits. For OnCourse, prototype in OnCourse's real components so reviews judge the idea, not the styling.

Key points.title: Figma pulled an AI feature after a QA failure
Key points.detail: Figma's first AI feature, renamed 'Make Design' ("wrong name"; it was meant as a first draft), turned "make me a weather app" into something close to Apple's Weather app. Because it was just an LLM assembling existing pieces, Field called it "preventable... a QA failure" and pulled it. His lesson: when the input space is wide, test it hard and build real evals, because "it's easy to go on vibes for too long." For OnCourse, any AI explanation or tutor feature needs a test set of real questions before launch.

Title: How to see like a designer: The hidden power of typography and logos (Jessica Hische)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Jessica Hische)
Bottom line: Train your eye by naming the feeling a typeface gives you and then working out why, and test every brand asset at its smallest real size first.
What they did: For the Lenny's Podcast refresh, Hische kept the colour and handwritten feel fans already knew, and designed the podcast avatar early because it was the main use; detailed versions failed when shrunk to avatar size. She scopes each round (broad look first, then weight, letter height, detail), lets clients mix and match options, and hands files over early so they can be tried in real use. For Jeni's Ice Cream she fixed a misread in the wordmark that only fresh eyes noticed.
Takeaways: Design for the smallest real use first; Name the feeling a font gives, then find why; Make type and illustration look like one hand made them; Misreads need fresh eyes to catch; Visual styles signal an industry, for better or worse; Good assets teach their own use
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: test icons and illustrations (streak flame, badges, app icon) at their smallest real size, such as a notification icon or tab bar, before polishing the large version. Design process: run a quick font-feeling exercise with the team, labelling candidate typefaces as calm, serious or friendly, to pick type that feels trustworthy for exam prep. Streaks: check that the streak illustration, numbers and type look like they came from the same hand, rather than an icon from a library next to custom type.

Key points.title: Design for the smallest real use first
Key points.detail: For Lenny's refresh, the podcast avatar was the main use, so Hische designed brand assets alongside the logo from the start instead of finishing a big logo first. Some versions "felt a little bit too detailed to shrink down that much", and the challenge was keeping them full enough at large sizes that they didn't look "pulled from an icon library". For OnCourse, check the app icon, streak flame and badges at notification and tab-bar size before polishing the large version.

Key points.title: Name the feeling a font gives, then find why
Key points.detail: Her exercise: page through fonts on MyFonts or your font folder, screenshot ones you react to, and write the first feeling ("calm", "exciting") without overthinking. Then compare groups: the calm ones might share lighter weight, generous spacing, rounded edges and rounder bowls. Even slightly rounding Helvetica's corners makes it feel softer and printed, because ink bleeds into paper. For OnCourse, run this with the team to pick type that feels trustworthy and calm for exam prep.

Key points.title: Make type and illustration look like one hand made them
Key points.detail: Lenny's old logo was teased as "clip art fireplace" because the icon and type felt like separate parts. Hische says a simple icon is fine if the rest of the brand is just as simple, but mismatched pieces read like "hot ham water" instead of a soup. She also says to blur your eyes or take your glasses off to judge the overall colour and cohesion. For OnCourse, check that illustrations, icons and numbers in streaks and results look like one family.

Key points.title: Misreads need fresh eyes to catch
Key points.detail: Jeni's Ice Cream had put its apostrophe over the i, and with the looped J the wordmark looked like it said "penis". The team was too close to see it, so Hische says to show work to many people who don't know the letterforms. A new brand needs legibility "at a super fast glance" until it has years of equity. For OnCourse, test new labels, icons and short copy with students who have never seen them.

Key points.title: Visual styles signal an industry, for better or worse
Key points.detail: Some industries take over a style for a time, so using it aligns you with them. A certain kind of script reads as wedding invitations, and Lenny jokes that FinTech must be green. Brand designers map competitors' visuals and then choose to blend in (instantly read as that category) or diverge on purpose. For OnCourse, audit what NEET and medical prep apps look like and decide where to match and where to stand apart.

Key points.title: Good assets teach their own use
Key points.detail: Hische says you shouldn't need a "500-page brand book"; if you do, the brand or logo is probably too complicated. Her goal is a logo "so easy to use that you don't have to be an extremely skilled designer to design well with it", so anyone with some taste can use it right. She also gives Lenny a 'wardrobe' of pieces that recombine. For OnCourse, components and illustration kits should be hard to misuse by engineers and marketers.

Title: Inside Linear: Building with taste, craft, and focus (Karri Saarinen)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Karri Saarinen)
Bottom line: Ship rough versions to yourselves within about a week, refine with a few opted-in customers, and save the polish pass for general release, which you check yourself by trying every state.
What they did: Linear teams put a feature into production in roughly the first week, visible only internally, then open it to a few opted-in customers (for example Vercel for roadmap changes) before polishing for general release. Before launch Saarinen tries every state himself; testing threaded comments with different message lengths showed janky animation and scrolling, so the release was pulled back until fixed. Linear runs no A/B tests and sets no feature metric goals, and relies on everyone talking to customers in shared Slack channels. During the year-long private beta they invited about 10 people a week from a survey-based waitlist, fixed what each cohort hit, then invited the next cohort.
Results: After about a month the waitlist had "maybe 4,000 people"; by June–July 2019 there were "100, 200 users on it and maybe about 10 companies." At public launch with pricing, "maybe one company didn't subscribe, but everyone else subscribed to that paid plan." On the optional pay-what-you-want slider, Saarinen says some paid "$28 per seat and some people pay $1," but then says "20 was probably the maximum that people could pay", so the $28 is likely a slip.
Takeaways: Ship rough in week one, polish only at release; Try every state with real content before launch; Opinionated defaults beat flexible settings; Small eng-design teams who own projects catch the details; Invite beta users in small cohorts; No A/B tests; everyone talks to customers instead
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: ship new screens behind a flag to the team first, then to a small opted-in student cohort, and only then do the polish pass before full release. Design process: before release, try every state with real content: long question stems, long explanations, images and empty states in Practice and Lessons. Practice: give one strong default session (for example 10 mixed MCQs from weak topics) instead of asking students to configure it.

Key points.title: Ship rough in week one, polish only at release
Key points.detail: Linear tells teams to "put it into the app and ship it to production" in about the first week, visible only internally. Next they find one to ten opted-in customers (for example Vercel for roadmap changes) and accept some jank because "it's not finished." Polish and craft get attention at general release. Saarinen says the perfection mindset makes it "hard to put anything out". For OnCourse, build new screens behind a flag for the team, then a small student cohort, then polish.

Key points.title: Try every state with real content before launch
Key points.detail: Before release Saarinen goes into the product himself and clicks through different states. Threaded comments looked fine in demos, but with different message lengths the animations were "janky" and the screen didn't scroll right, so the release was pulled back until fixed. For OnCourse, test long question stems, long explanations, images and empty states in Practice and Lessons, not just the demo path.

Key points.title: Opinionated defaults beat flexible settings
Key points.detail: He believes productivity software should be opinionated: flexible tools make every team spend time working out how to use a feature 10 different ways. Linear gives one good default workflow so people spend less time on the tool. His mantra is "design something for someone", because designing for everyone gives a generic result. For OnCourse, give one strong default session instead of asking students to configure filters first.

Key points.title: Small eng-design teams who own projects catch the details
Key points.detail: Linear has one PM; each project has a lead who can be an engineer or designer. Saarinen says craft happens when the people building look at the feature all day. Engineer Andreas, unasked, built macOS-style dynamic "safe zones" so users can move diagonally into a submenu without it closing. For OnCourse, give the designer and engineer on a feature real ownership and time to fix small annoyances.

Key points.title: Invite beta users in small cohorts
Key points.detail: Linear's waitlist used a short survey (tools used, company size, why Linear) and reached about 4,000 people in a month. Saarinen invited about 10 people a week by personal email, then asked for feedback, because inviting everyone would mean everyone hits "the same bug". Each cohort's problems were fixed before the next was invited, for a year of private beta. For OnCourse, roll out big changes in waves and fix what each wave hits.

Key points.title: No A/B tests; everyone talks to customers instead
Key points.detail: Linear runs no A/B tests and sets no metric goals for features; success is when "customers agree that the problem is solved." He calls it "magic and science": the science is user research, weekly customer calls and shared Slack channels everyone reads, and the magic is using intuition once everyone understands customers. He warns people often lean on data out of fear of making the wrong call. For OnCourse, this suits Linear's B2B retention model; OnCourse should keep tests but give everyone direct exposure to student feedback.

Title: Building beautiful products with Stripe's Head of Design (Katie Dill)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Katie Dill)
Bottom line: Quality is growth: give named owners the most important user journeys, have them walk the whole journey as a user every quarter, and score it together.
What they did: Stripe picked 15 critical user journeys, each owned by an engineering, product and design leader. Every quarter they 'walk the store' end to end (from a Google search to the website, docs and dashboard), write a friction log with screenshots tagged from 'nice touch' to 'P0 bug', and give a colour score against a rubric of utility, usability, desirability and 'surprisingly great'. Scores are then calibrated in a product quality review with leaders. Dill also has designers drop screenshots or prototypes of work in progress into a shared Google Slides deck (now monthly) sent to the whole company, so overlapping work is spotted early.
Results: Stripe's research found "99% of the top e-commerce sites have errors in their checkout flow"; improving checkout quality gave "a 10.5% increase in business' revenue from an older form of checkout to a newer form of checkout." Onboarding quality fixes that made products easier to understand led to activations increasing (no figure given). A clearer invoice-status button reduced support contacts (no figure given).
Takeaways: Named owners walk 15 critical journeys every quarter; Friction logs with colour scores, not numbers; Quality is growth: checkout fixes lifted revenue 10.5%; Share examples where quality moved a metric; A shared deck of work in progress prevents collisions; Sketch the 11-star end state, then ship toward it
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: name 5 critical OnCourse journeys (install to first MCQ, daily plan to session done, broken streak to return, paywall to purchase, renewal) and have a designer, engineer and PM walk each one every quarter with a friction log and a red/yellow/green score. Onboarding: walk it starting from the Play Store listing and first notification, not just the in-app screens, to catch mismatches between what the listing promises and what the first screens show. Design process: keep a monthly shared deck of in-progress screens so Home, Practice and Paywall work doesn't drift apart.

Key points.title: Named owners walk 15 critical journeys every quarter
Key points.detail: Stripe noticed products get worse after launch as other teams ship, like redoing one room so the rest of the house looks worse. So it picked 15 critical user journeys, each with an engineering, product and design leader who 'walks the store' quarterly, starting from a Google search through the website, docs and dashboard. At minimum the engineer, PM and designer walk it together, because each spots different problems. For OnCourse, name 5 journeys (install to first MCQ, broken streak to return, paywall to purchase) and walk them as a trio.

Key points.title: Friction logs with colour scores, not numbers
Key points.detail: Walkers fill a friction log template with screenshots, tagging moments from "nice touch" to "P0 bug". They give a summary score against a rubric of utility, usability, desirability and "surprisingly great". Stripe chose colours over numbers so people don't argue "is it really a six or is it a seven?" Scores are calibrated in a product quality review (PQR) with leaders, like calibrating performance reviews. For OnCourse, a red/yellow/green score per journey is enough.

Key points.title: Quality is growth: checkout fixes lifted revenue 10.5%
Key points.detail: Dill rejects 'growth versus quality'. Stripe's research found "99% of the top e-commerce sites have errors in their checkout flow", and moving from an older to a newer, higher-quality checkout gave "a 10.5% increase in business' revenue." Onboarding fixes that made products easier to understand also raised activation (no figure given). For OnCourse, polish on paywall and onboarding screens is a growth lever.

Key points.title: Share examples where quality moved a metric
Key points.detail: Customers kept contacting support because a nice-looking but unclear button hid the status of their invoices. Making it clearer cut support contacts. Dill says every company has stories like this, and sharing them breaks the false belief that quality work doesn't move numbers. She also says to define 'impact' in performance reviews so long-term quality work counts. For OnCourse, collect before/after cases from PostHog and support tickets to justify polish work.

Key points.title: A shared deck of work in progress prevents collisions
Key points.detail: "A picture tells a thousand words and a prototype saves a thousand meetings." Designers drop screenshots or prototypes into a Google Slides deck, now monthly (it was biweekly), sent to PMs, engineering leads and executives. It catches two teams designing the same surface or projects "on a path to collide". They use Slides, not Figma, so every function can flip through. For OnCourse, a monthly deck keeps Home, Practice and Paywall work consistent.

Key points.title: Sketch the 11-star end state, then ship toward it
Key points.detail: Dill sees a "fear of bold ideas" because small changes are easy to measure in a quarter, but incremental fixes to one owned area rarely improve the whole journey. Her rule is "reach for the stars and land on the moon": sketch the ideal journey (Chesky's 11-star experience), then ship it in steps and learn from each. She stresses this is not a deck that sits on a shelf. For OnCourse, draw the ideal exam-prep journey before planning the next quarter's screens.

Title: From managing people to managing AI: The leadership skills everyone needs (Julie Zhuo)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Julie Zhuo)
Bottom line: Diagnose with data, treat with design: data tells you where the problem is, but the fix still has to be designed, and working well with AI starts with a sharp definition of what success looks like.
What they did: At Sundial, Zhuo removed planned PM roles and asked engineers and designers to own product definition themselves, using AI to cover gaps like front-end work, with a specialist reviewing. Her team uses ChatGPT as a tutor: she feeds in a course curriculum and asks for a version suited to how she learns (analogies, examples), then explains concepts back so it can correct her. She treats TikTok posts, tweets and customer interviews as data alongside metrics, and argues chat-style products need new measures, such as grouping user intent with an LLM, because there are no tab clicks to count.
Takeaways: Diagnose with data, treat with design; Picking metrics and judging +5% is judgment; Define success so precisely a machine could grade it; Without a PM, engineers own product definition; Use AI as a personal tutor, then explain back; Chat products need new ways to measure intent
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: before each redesign, write the PostHog finding that shows where the problem is (for example the step where onboarding drops), then explore design fixes; don't let the metric dictate the solution. Design process: when prompting AI prototyping tools, write explicit success criteria first (who the screen is for, the one action it must drive, what failure looks like). Design process: count Play Store reviews and support tickets as research data and tag them by theme alongside analytics.

Key points.title: Diagnose with data, treat with design
Key points.detail: Zhuo and her co-founder repeat this to every customer: data "is not a tool that's going to tell you what you should build", but it shows whether you have a problem and where. The fix still needs a creative design process. She counts TikTok posts, tweets and customer interviews as data too, not just A/B tests. For OnCourse, start each redesign with the PostHog finding that locates the problem, then explore design fixes freely.

Key points.title: Picking metrics and judging +5% is judgment
Key points.detail: She warns about the "false precision of numbers": choosing which metrics to look at is "an art, not a science", and so is deciding whether a 5% lift is good. She agrees with designers that "you can't make a really great product by thinking you can A/B test your way into it", but says the best designers she has met are "obsessed" with understanding what users really do. For OnCourse, use data to understand students, not to make the call for you.

Key points.title: Define success so precisely a machine could grade it
Key points.detail: The top skill for managing both people and AI is being "crystal clear on what does success look like." Big-company misalignment usually comes from people picturing different outcomes, and vague goals like "lots of people hear it" aren't enough. Evals matter because they turn success into objective criteria. For OnCourse, write the screen's one goal and what failure looks like before prompting an AI prototyping tool or briefing a teammate.

Key points.title: Without a PM, engineers own product definition
Key points.detail: Sundial planned PM roles but found that when a PM or designer exists, engineers delegate product thinking to them. Without one, "communication's up to me" and getting value to users is in everyone's charter. Engineers also take on front-end work with AI help and a specialist reviewing. It's slower at first, but she says the investment pays off in more well-rounded people. For OnCourse, this argues for giving engineers direct exposure to student problems.

Key points.title: Use AI as a personal tutor, then explain back
Key points.detail: Zhuo feeds a 12-week course curriculum into ChatGPT and asks it to customise the program to how she learns (examples, analogies, "explain like I'm five"). An engineer used it to learn when a root-cause analysis is useful, not just how. She then explains concepts back so it can critique her, from "that's close" to "you were completely wrong." For OnCourse, this explain-back loop is also a product idea for students revising a topic.

Key points.title: Chat products need new ways to measure intent
Key points.detail: Clicks used to reveal intent (a shopping tab click meant shopping), but in conversational products "it's just all conversation." Teams now need an LLM or ML model to bucket user intent and new ways to judge whether a short or long conversation was a good one. She also notes fast-growing AI companies run on "good vibes" without instrumentation until growth stalls. For OnCourse, any AI tutor feature needs intent tagging from day one.

Title: Mastering onboarding (Lauryn Isford)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Lauryn Isford)
Bottom line: Replace feature tooltips with a guided setup wizard that builds something real for the user, personalise by how people learn rather than by job title, and teach advanced features later.
What they did: Airtable rebuilt onboarding over 12–18 months: a 'Guided Onboarding' wizard asks simple button questions on the left (what project, what to track) while the user's workflow builds itself on the right; most old tooltips were retired. They then personalised it by learning and building style (for example database-savvy builders versus visual learners) instead of by role, and added 'The Mole', a panel that pops up from the bottom with tips as users explore, for ongoing education. The activation metric was strict: week-4 multi-user active, backed by individual week-2/week-4 retention and a 'Build' sophistication score.
Results: The wizard, The Mole and personalisation together "drove a 20% lift in activation rate for Airtable" over "about a six to eight month period"; the guided wizard was "the most impactful thing we did." One generic wizard was meant to cover "more than 90% of customers." She suggests a good activation metric is one only "five to 15%" of users reach, because it correlates more strongly with long-term retention.
Takeaways: A guided setup wizard beat tooltips for activation; Personalise by learning style, not job title; A good activation metric only 5–15% reach; Show what a feature does, don't name it; Don't push premium features in onboarding; A reverse trial gives full premium, then free
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: turn setup into a guided builder where the student taps exam, exam date and weak subjects on one side and sees their Today's plan fill in live, instead of tooltips over Home. Onboarding: ask one question about how the student likes to study (questions first or lessons first) and route them to Practice or Lessons as their first session. Paywall: test a reverse trial where new students get full premium for 7 days and then drop to free, so they see what they would lose.

Key points.title: A guided setup wizard beat tooltips for activation
Key points.detail: Airtable's 'Guided Onboarding' wizard asks easy button questions on the left (what project, what to track) while the user's workflow builds itself on the right. Together with personalisation and 'The Mole' tips panel, it drove "a 20% lift in activation rate" over six to eight months, and the wizard was "the most impactful thing we did." Most old tooltips were retired, though she says the pattern suits complex products with high setup effort. For OnCourse, let students tap exam, date and weak subjects while their plan fills in live.

Key points.title: Personalise by learning style, not job title
Key points.detail: One generic wizard covered "more than 90%" of users at first. When they personalised, grouping people by learning and building style worked better than role (marketing, product, operations). Some users know databases and like to build, others need a more visual path, and a template example isn't always the best way to teach. For OnCourse, ask whether a student prefers questions first or lessons first, not just their year.

Key points.title: A good activation metric only 5–15% reach
Key points.detail: Airtable's north star was 'week-4 multi-user active': in the fourth week, more than one person on the team is active and contributing. She prefers a strict metric that "maybe for most companies five to 15%" reach because it correlates more strongly with long-term retention. They added supporting metrics: individual week-2 and week-4 retention, and a 'Build' sophistication score. For OnCourse, pick an activation event tied to long-term retention, not one most students hit on day one.

Key points.title: Show what a feature does, don't name it
Key points.detail: A tooltip saying "This is automations" is "an announcement of something awesome that Airtable built", not help for a new user. Better is to explain how it helps their workflow, or offer a one-touch turn-on that does the work and shows the value. Only show it to the segment who need it. For OnCourse, onboarding copy should say what a student gets ("we'll revise your weak topics"), not feature names.

Key points.title: Don't push premium features in onboarding
Key points.detail: Teams are tempted to push premium features in onboarding because their use predicts payment. Isford says that serves the company, not the user's first steps. She relies on guardrail metrics instead: an onboarding change that dropped revenue 10% would get caught and investigated. For OnCourse, teach the free core loop first and let premium value show up later.

Key points.title: A reverse trial gives full premium, then free
Key points.detail: A reverse trial starts everyone on the premium plan for a limited time (7, 14 or 30 days), then drops them to a free-forever plan. You get to show everything the product can do while still keeping users who never pay. She prefers it when you value user growth over short-term revenue, since you "only get a couple moments" to ask for a credit card. For OnCourse, test 7 days of full premium for new students before they drop to free.

Title: Career frameworks, A/B testing, onboarding tips, selling to engineers (Laura Schaffer)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Laura Schaffer)
Bottom line: Onboarding questions that reassure users they are in the right place can raise conversion, and the scariest step should be tucked inside something familiar instead of being step one.
What they did: At Twilio, Schaffer A/B tested adding four signup questions (coding language or 'not a developer', product, use case) against a bare email-and-password form, expecting a drop. Later, a step-by-step onboarding checklist started with 'get a phone number', which scared developers new to telecom; in a deliberately rough test, users were sent to a docs page in their coding language with the phone number step tucked inside the code sample ('putting the pill in a hot dog'), and it converted better. The 'not a developer' answer later revealed a growing group of non-coders, which led to Quick Deploy on CodeExchange, a no-code way to get a working demo.
Results: Adding the signup questions, with no personalisation behind them, "improved conversion by 5%, just improved signups." The docs-page version of onboarding "converted better" even though it sent users away from the console (no figure given). Citing Microsoft and Netflix data, she says "80 plus percent" of experiment ideas fail.
Takeaways: Signup questions that reassure users raised signups by 5%; Hide the scary step inside something familiar; If it's not embarrassing, you've gone too far; Kill weak ideas with fake doors and mockups first; Agree the confidence level and hypothesis before testing; The 'not a developer' answer revealed a new user group
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: add 2–3 tappable questions (exam, attempt year, weakest subject) and A/B test them against the current flow, since questions that confirm the app fits the student may lift completion rather than hurt it. Practice: if the first session opens on a hard timed mock, test starting with a short untimed set from the student's strongest subject, with the timed mock coming later. Design process: when a funnel step drops, pull session recordings of that exact event from PostHog before redesigning.

Key points.title: Signup questions that reassure users raised signups by 5%
Key points.detail: At Twilio the signup form asked only for email and password, because people believed developers hated friction. Schaffer quietly added four dropdowns: coding language (with an 'I'm not a developer' option), product, and use case. She expected a drop, but with no personalisation behind it signups 'improved conversion by 5%'. Users told her the questions were comforting: new users are 'looking for the bogeyman', and seeing their language listed told them 'I'm in the right place'. For OnCourse, asking a student their exam and attempt year can work the same way, as long as the options match what they are already worried about.

Key points.title: Hide the scary step inside something familiar
Key points.detail: Twilio's step-by-step onboarding started with 'get a phone number', which scared developers who knew nothing about telecom. In a rough test they sent users out of the console to a docs page in their own coding language, with the phone number step tucked inside the code sample. She calls this 'pilling a hot dog'. Even with no easy way back to the console, it converted better. When a logical step doesn't convert, look for the step that feels scary to the user and wrap it in something they already know.

Key points.title: If it's not embarrassing, you've gone too far
Key points.detail: Schaffer tells her teams the first version of a test should be embarrassing. Kicking new users out of onboarding to a docs page was 'nuts', but if it had failed it would have been a cheap lesson. She says it is always better to iterate than to redesign in one go, because roughly 80% of ideas fail (she cites Microsoft and Netflix data). Lenny adds that full redesigns he has launched were negative almost every time.

Key points.title: Kill weak ideas with fake doors and mockups first
Key points.detail: A/B tests are the most expensive way to check an idea: they need design, engineering and weeks of run time. Schaffer validates ideas earlier with painted-door tests (offer the concept before it exists) and with designer mockups shown to users. Only ideas that survive those steps go on to a full A/B test. This lowers the failure rate of the tests you do run.

Key points.title: Agree the confidence level and hypothesis before testing
Key points.detail: She is happy to accept a confidence level below 95% if it lets the team run twice as many experiments, because product teams are not making medical decisions. The rule is that this must be decided before the test starts, with a clear hypothesis, so nobody bends the data afterwards. When accepting more risk, back the result with qualitative feedback, for example asking users from both versions whether they felt confident or stuck.

Key points.title: The 'not a developer' answer revealed a new user group
Key points.detail: The signup question later showed a growing number of people who said they were not developers but still wanted to build with Twilio. Sales said that if these people could get to their first $1 of spend, they could grow them to much more. Twilio built Quick Deploy on CodeExchange, a way to deploy a working app with no code, which she describes as a 'create your own demo' experience. Signup answers are worth tracking over time because they can show a new audience before it shows up anywhere else.

Title: How to grow a subscription business (Yuriy Timen)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Yuriy Timen)
Bottom line: Mostly about acquisition channels for subscription apps. The design lesson is that onboarding for complex prosumer products almost always pays off: ask for relevant information up front and tailor the first screen, so new users don't face the whole product at once.
What they did: For complex prosumer editors (Airtable, Canva, Whimsical, InVideo), Timen pushes onboarding that gathers relevant information up front and customises the landing experience, so users are guided to what they came to do instead of being 'left to their own devices' in the full editor. Canva's first big growth loop was long-tail programmatic SEO on 'make' and 'template' keywords (for example wedding invitation templates). Grammarly leaned heavily on performance marketing and lacked built-in network effects, so referral loops were 'an uphill battle'. Laika, a premium fresh dog food subscription, still made give-one-get-one referrals work because the brand is so loved. He also treats paid search ads as a quick way to A/B test headlines and positioning.
Results: Through onboarding, earlier-stage companies "can two to four X activation rates easily"; Series B and later companies "can still probably get to 20 to 30% lift at activations." For prosumer SaaS, a healthy visit-to-free-signup rate is "in that 20 to 35% range" (40 to 50% with a narrow, strong-fit audience early on). Free-to-paid conversion: "anything under 5% is not going to work long term"; "ideally like more than 7%." Most $5 to $7 a month consumer subscriptions have LTVs that "cap out at 50 to 60 bucks." These are his benchmarks from advising, not measured experiments.
Takeaways: Tailored onboarding is almost always a big opportunity; Free-to-paid under 5% won't work long term; Customer research always pays off; Give a tactic a fair test before dropping it; Paid ads double as fast tests of messaging; Referral loops need network effects or a loved brand
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: ask what the student is preparing for and where they are weak, then land them on a cut-down Home with one suggested first session instead of every tab and feature at once. Paywall: track free-to-paid conversion against Timen's 5% floor and 7% target, and treat anything below it as a prompt to work on activation before pricing. Design process: run a round of student interviews before redesigning a major flow and share the findings with the whole team so everyone works from the same picture.

Key points.title: Tailored onboarding is almost always a big opportunity
Key points.detail: Timen says onboarding is worth investing in 'almost always', especially for complex prosumer tools like Airtable, Canva, Whimsical and InVideo. The gap is between dropping a new user into the full editor, 'left to their own devices', and asking for relevant information up front so you can guide them without showing the whole product at once. He says earlier-stage companies 'can two to four X activation rates easily', and Series B and later can still get '20 to 30% lift'. For OnCourse, asking what a student is preparing for and landing them on one clear first task follows the same idea.

Key points.title: Free-to-paid under 5% won't work long term
Key points.detail: For prosumer subscription products he gives benchmarks from his advising work. A healthy visit-to-free-signup rate is '20 to 35%', or 40 to 50% early on with a narrow, strong-fit audience. For free-to-paid, 'anything under 5% is not going to work long term', and 'ideally like more than 7%'. These are his rules of thumb, not measured experiments, but they give a target for judging paywall and activation work.

Key points.title: Customer research always pays off
Key points.detail: Asked which investments reliably pay back, Timen says getting to know customers through interviews, surveys and panels 'always pays off'. In seed to Series B companies, the first proper research push brings clarity, focus and momentum that 'can galvanize the team'. Over-reliance on paid acquisition is what tends to backfire.

Key points.title: Give a tactic a fair test before dropping it
Key points.detail: 'The only thing that's worse than a channel or a tactic that you tried not working' is concluding it doesn't work without a fair shot. He often hears 'we tried YouTube, it doesn't work', then finds the attempt was never designed to succeed. He recommends focus with guardrails, for example a minimum number of impressions, two to three creative angles and a target click-through range, so the team knows when to keep going or stop. The same applies to design experiments: decide up front what a fair test looks like.

Key points.title: Paid ads double as fast tests of messaging
Key points.detail: Timen sees two reasons to run paid ads: as a profitable channel, or as a quick way to learn about messaging, positioning, designs and features. 'It's hard to get faster learnings at scale than A/B testing headlines' in Google search. The mistake is spending large budgets in a muddled middle where the spend is neither efficient nor set up as experiments.

Key points.title: Referral loops need network effects or a loved brand
Key points.detail: Viral and referral loops work best when the product gets more useful as more people use it, as with Airbnb, Airtable, Whimsical or Dropbox's file sharing. At Grammarly, writing wasn't a multiplayer task, so engineering virality was 'an uphill battle'. The exception is a much-loved brand: Laika, a premium fresh dog food subscription in Australia, makes give-one-get-one referrals work without network effects.

Title: Nickey Skarstad (Airbnb, Etsy, Shopify, Duolingo) on translating vision into goals, operationalizing product quality, second-order decisions, brainstorming, influence, and much more (Nickey Skarstad)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Nickey Skarstad)
Bottom line: Pair every growth metric with a quality metric, and don't be afraid to slow onboarding down if it gets people to their first real success faster.
What they did: At Etsy, Nickey's team owned seller onboarding and first pushed to open as many shops as fast as possible; that hurt the downstream metric of sellers getting a first sale, so they added friction that made sellers more thoughtful about their listings, which got them to a first sale faster (the quality metric was roughly 'first sale in seven days'). On Airbnb Experiences, the top-line goal was the review rate, a quality metric balanced against bookings, and the team dogfooded experiences constantly to catch bad ones. For reviews she uses three cross-functional check-ins (first principles, approach plus a technical review, ready to ship) instead of separate design and engineering reviews where feedback stays in silos, and she puts first principles and a second-order-effects line into spec templates.
Takeaways: Etsy added onboarding friction to get sellers a first sale; Balance every growth metric with a quality metric; Review work together at three check-ins; Dogfood constantly to catch bad experiences; Slow down on one-way doors, move fast on two-way; Write first principles and second-order effects into specs
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: measure success by 'first correct practice session within 1 day' rather than raw sign-up completion, and test adding a short exam-and-subject setup step if it gets students to a better first session. Design process: start each feature crit with a short first-principles check (what we solve for, what matters, what doesn't) before any screens, then do a second check on approach with engineering present. Design process: have the team dogfood the app daily on real NEET-PG question sets and log quality issues, the way Airbnb staff took Experiences.

Key points.title: Etsy added onboarding friction to get sellers a first sale
Key points.detail: Nickey's team owned Etsy's seller onboarding and first pushed to open as many shops as fast as possible. That hurt a downstream metric: sellers getting their first sale. A sale on day one tells a seller 'I could make money doing this', while waiting 7 to 30 days makes them feel 'I'm terrible at this'. So they added friction that made sellers more thoughtful about their listings, and it got them to a first sale faster (the metric was roughly 'first sale in seven days'). For OnCourse, a short setup step is worth testing if it leads to a better first study session.

Key points.title: Balance every growth metric with a quality metric
Key points.detail: On Airbnb Experiences, the top-line goal was the review rate, not bookings. Bookings and revenue mattered, but the team was 'obsessed with making sure every person who booked actually had a good experience'. She describes growth and quality as a seesaw: the closer to balance, the more successful the business is in the long run. Lenny adds that Airbnb's supply team only counted a new listing once it got its first booking.

Key points.title: Review work together at three check-ins
Key points.detail: Nickey has seen reviews fail when each function runs its own, so design feedback and technical problems stay in silos. She prefers cross-functional reviews with a clear pre-read, at three points: first principles (what are we solving for, what matters most), approach (what we will build, plus a technical or architecture review), and ready to ship. She says agreeing on first principles is 'almost the most important thing' because it saves teams from hearing late that they solved the wrong problem.

Key points.title: Dogfood constantly to catch bad experiences
Key points.detail: The Experiences team took experiences all over the world all the time. Within minutes of arriving they knew whether it would be a five-star experience, and they took what they learned back to the team: 'We were on an experience last night, and it did not go well. What do we do about it?' She says pushing teams to use the product themselves gives them the motivation to fix quality problems.

Key points.title: Slow down on one-way doors, move fast on two-way
Key points.detail: Decisions that are hard to reverse and limit future options deserve time, debate and buy-in; reversible ones should ship fast to keep autonomy and speed. Her one-way-door examples are the quality standards that defined a good Airbnb experience, which the product, policies and host education were built around, and Etsy's rules on what counts as handmade. Even changing an Airbnb listing title length affects every host and many screens.

Key points.title: Write first principles and second-order effects into specs
Key points.detail: To build second-order thinking into the process, add a line to the spec template that asks for it, and write first principles for each change: what we care about, why, and what isn't important. She picked this up at Shopify, where first principles are used everywhere. The principles section is where people argue most, which is good, because the debate happens before design or engineering starts.

Title: The full-stack PM | Anuj Rathi (Swiggy, Jupiter Money, Flipkart) (Anuj Rathi)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Anuj Rathi)
Bottom line: Design for the new user who is 'lazy, vain and selfish', and carry the exact promise that brought them in from the ad straight through onboarding.
What they did: At Swiggy, the team stopped onboarding new users with 'here is everything we do' and reframed it around 'what is in it for you', continuing the exact marketing message and promotion that triggered the download (for example the rupee offer) into the splash and onboarding, in language users understand. At Jupiter Money they treat a user who uses one product as having found value there, and introduce the next product later instead of pushing everything up front. Anuj runs 'show don't tell' reviews: a wall of every screen and touchpoint built around one concrete person (not a persona) at a specific moment, such as 11:00 with a given trigger, and about half his product reviews focus on that journey. He also asks teams to write three divergent PR/FAQs before picking and recommending one.
Takeaways: Design for new users who are lazy, vain and selfish; Carry the ad's promise straight into onboarding; Lead with one hook, introduce other products later; Walk every screen against one real person and moment; Write three divergent options, then recommend one; Think more and ship better when forced to choose
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: match the first screens to the acquisition message (for example 'NEET-PG daily plan' vs 'MCQ practice') so the promise that brought the student in is the first thing they see, and save other features for later. Home: lead new users with one hook (today's plan or first practice set) and introduce flashcards and lessons only after they finish a first session. Design process: before a crit, build a 'show don't tell' wall for one concrete student (name, year, exam date, time of day, what triggered the open) and walk every screen and copy line against it; bring three divergent directions with one recommendation.

Key points.title: Design for new users who are lazy, vain and selfish
Key points.detail: Anuj borrows Scott Belsky's framework. New users are lazy ('blow my mind away, otherwise I'm not going to pay attention'), vain ('I have a habit... do you really expect me to change it?') and selfish ('show me what's in it for me'). Teams look at their product all day and assume users care as much as they do, but most people barely know it. He says designing copy, onboarding and the 'first warm welcome' for this user makes a bigger difference than core features built for loyal users.

Key points.title: Carry the ad's promise straight into onboarding
Key points.detail: At Swiggy the team stopped opening onboarding with 'we are a food delivery app, a grocery delivery app' and asked 'what is in it for you'. They traced what brought each user in: the trigger, the marketing message and the offer (for example a rupee discount). Then they continued that same message from the splash screen through onboarding, in language users understand, and it 'instantly started showing us results'. For OnCourse, the first screens should repeat the promise of the ad or referral that brought the student in.

Key points.title: Lead with one hook, introduce other products later
Key points.detail: At Jupiter Money, a neobank with savings, credit cards, mutual funds and gold, many users use only one service. Anuj says that means they found value there and aren't interested in the rest yet. PMs should understand the category consumer as well as marketers do, pick the hook product, and choose 'the right time when I introduce them to this other one rather than being very greedy about letting the new user try everything'.

Key points.title: Walk every screen against one real person and moment
Key points.detail: Anuj's 'show don't tell' is a wall of every screen and touchpoint, built around a person, not a persona: for example 'Lenny, 30 years old', with his recent history, fears and needs. Then: 'It's 11:00. What triggered this app open, and then what happened?' 'Each pixel, and each copy, and each word' must serve that moment, and about half of his product reviews are spent on it. It also covers waiting states, like the 30 minutes before food arrives or a delivery bike with a puncture.

Key points.title: Write three divergent options, then recommend one
Key points.detail: Anuj asks teams to write three fully thought-through PR/FAQs that go different ways, for example two membership tiers versus three, or a points-based tier programme instead. This shows stakeholders their ideas were considered, makes the trade-offs visible, and gives leaders a real choice. He agrees with Lenny that the PM must still recommend one and explain why.

Key points.title: Think more and ship better when forced to choose
Key points.detail: His contrarian view: if you must choose between speed and excellence, choose excellence. 'Most experiments should be thought experiments' because many are obviously going to fail, and running them wastes company time. A launch that won't work for a 'lazy, vain and selfish' user isn't a viable MVP, however fast it ships.

Title: How to build a high-performing growth team | Adam Fishman (Patreon, Lyft, Imperfect Foods) (Adam Fishman)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Adam Fishman)
Bottom line: Onboarding is the one screen flow 100% of users touch and when they are most motivated, so use it to deliver the brand's promise and set opinionated defaults that lead people toward what works.
What they did: At Patreon, creators connected their social accounts during onboarding; a data-science model flagged high-potential creators by audience size and engagement and sent them to a human who coached them. That human help lifted early revenue, and the team then built what the humans did into the product as 'opinionated defaults': three-tier pricing recommended (sweet spot three to five tiers, $3 or $5 entry rather than $1), with extra friction when creators tried to change those defaults, while keeping the choice. They judged onboarding changes with fast proxy metrics (speed to first patron and first $100 processed) plus qualitative sampling, instead of waiting 90 days. Adam only reworks onboarding when there is a new, hard-earned insight about users, not for redesign's sake.
Results: Connecting the right creator with a human at the right time 'would improve the first month of revenue or the second month of revenue that a creator made on the platform by 25%', learned 'through a lot of experimentation'; second-month payments were a key LTV input, so overall value improved by about the same amount. More generally, he says he has seen companies 'shift their curve outward by 10, 15, 20 percentage points' on cohort retention from onboarding and activation work.
Takeaways: Onboarding is the one flow every user touches; Use opinionated defaults: easy right path, harder wrong path; Learn with human help first, then build it in; A small conversion dip can be right if retention rises; Judge onboarding changes with early proxy metrics; Only redo onboarding when you've learned something new
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: use opinionated defaults for study setup (for example pre-select a recommended daily MCQ target and plan length based on exam date) and add a confirm step when a student picks an unrealistic target, without blocking it. Today's plan: track an early proxy like 'completed first full day's plan within 48 hours' to judge onboarding changes instead of waiting for 30-day retention. Design process: before automating a feature, have mentors or the team hand-guide a small group of new students, note which advice works, and then design those patterns into the product.

Key points.title: Onboarding is the one flow every user touches
Key points.detail: Adam calls onboarding 'the only part of your product experience that a hundred percent of people are ever going to touch'. It is also the first chance to deliver on your brand's promise ('your brand is the promise... your product experience is your delivery of that promise'), and the moment users are most motivated. Because motivation is high, you can add some friction and learn about users. He has seen onboarding and activation work shift cohort retention curves out 'by 10, 15, 20 percentage points'.

Key points.title: Use opinionated defaults: easy right path, harder wrong path
Key points.detail: Patreon learned what worked across hundreds of thousands of creators: three pricing tiers (three to five is the sweet spot) and a $3 or $5 entry tier rather than $1. They made these the defaults and added friction when creators tried to change them, but never removed the choice. A creator could still set up one tier or 40, it was just harder. For OnCourse, a pre-filled study target based on exam date, with a confirm step for unrealistic changes, follows the same idea.

Key points.title: Learn with human help first, then build it in
Key points.detail: In Patreon's onboarding, creators connected social accounts. A data-science model scored audience size and engagement, and high-potential creators were routed to a human who coached them. Connecting the right creator with a person at the right time raised first or second month revenue 'by 25%', and because second-month payments drove LTV, overall value rose about the same. The team then built what the humans did into the product. Start by guiding a small group by hand, then design the advice that worked into the flow.

Key points.title: A small conversion dip can be right if retention rises
Key points.detail: 'If you're doing it right, sometimes conversion should actually decrease a little bit,' because the people who drop out often weren't a fit and would have churned. The risk is cutting conversion so much that retention gains don't make up for it, so watch both metrics in every onboarding test. He believes onboarding's biggest effect is on retention, by connecting people to value and forming a habit early.

Key points.title: Judge onboarding changes with early proxy metrics
Key points.detail: Don't wait 90 days for retention data. At Patreon the proxies were speed to first patron and to the first $100 processed, which predicted how big a creator would become and how well they'd retain. They also sampled new creators by hand to check the right people were getting through. OnCourse could use something like 'finished the first day's plan within 48 hours' as its proxy.

Key points.title: Only redo onboarding when you've learned something new
Key points.detail: Adam 'very strongly' dislikes redesigning for redesign's sake. Small tweaks rarely move the needle once onboarding is in decent shape. Revisit it when you gain 'a new hard-earned insight' about users or your growth model, as Patreon did after learning the right tier structure. At larger companies, a team that owns activation should come back to onboarding for a quarter or two each year.
