Title: Unorthodox frameworks for growing your product, career, and impact (Bangaly Kaba)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Bangaly Kaba)
Bottom line: Most growth sits between onboarding and habit, and you find it by doing planned 'understand work' and using your own product as a brand-new or next-wave user.
What they did: At Instagram the team found new users followed mostly celebrities, then posted to no one and left after 7 to 9 months; the 'connections pivot' recommended real friends first at sign-up. They fixed 'account access churn' with one omnibox login field (email, phone or handle), an SMS prompt after two failed tries on a trusted device, and an offer to save login details at log-out. Because the sign-up flow logged only start and finish, the first job was logging all 8 steps to find the drop-offs. At Instacart, people's orders were mostly the same but reordering took 7 or 8 clicks and all-or-nothing, so they made reordering easy.
Results: Instagram teams ran '12 to 20 experiments a quarter a team' and '60 to 70% of them were positive and shippable'. Account access churn lost '10, 12 million people a year'; the fix 'helped drive 15, 20 million extra monthly active users a year'. After the connections pivot, retention 'doubled over the course of a year and a half'. Launching Instagram web 'increased Instagram's growth by 10%'. Registration conversion would drop 'by 15%' in new markets with nothing broken. At Instacart, 'after five times... 90% of your order was the same'.
Takeaways: Most growth sits between onboarding and habit; Connect new users to friends before celebrities; Make the way back easy instead of removing behaviour; Use the product as a brand-new, next-wave user; Plan 'understand work' as real roadmap items; Make the repeat action easy: Instacart's reorder
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: log every step of sign-up and the first session as its own event so each drop-off can be seen, not just started vs finished. Practice: in the first sessions, give a quick visible reward (score vs peers, a right-answer explanation) so a new student's first effort gets a response rather than nothing. Design process: each designer tests key flows monthly on a fresh account as a next-wave student (first-time NEET-PG taker on a low-end Android phone, slow data) and logs what breaks.

Key points.title: Most growth sits between onboarding and habit
Key points.detail: Asked where he usually finds growth, Bangaly says 'somewhere in the onboarding to habit-building experience'. Many teams don't know what their aha moment is, and if new users don't stay, 'you just have a leaky bucket and it doesn't matter how big your top funnel is'. He focuses on making the first month, two months and three months great, then layering several growth loops that compound.

Key points.title: Connect new users to friends before celebrities
Key points.detail: Early Instagram treated every follow as equal, so new users mostly followed celebrities. Rob Andrews spotted users retaining and then dropping after 7 to 9 months: when they finally posted, none of their friends followed them, so they were 'posting into an echo chamber' and felt bad. The 'connections pivot' recommended real friends first at sign-up and saved celebrities for later, and retention 'doubled over the course of a year and a half'. For OnCourse, a new student's first effort needs a visible response.

Key points.title: Make the way back easy instead of removing behaviour
Key points.detail: Instagram was losing '10, 12 million people a year' who logged out and could not get back in. Users in South and Southeast Asia logged out on purpose, to save prepaid data or share a phone, so the team kept logout. They added one omnibox login field for email, phone or handle, an SMS prompt after two failed tries on a trusted device, and an offer to save login details when logging out. The fix drove '15, 20 million extra monthly active users a year' and led to a multiple-accounts team.

Key points.title: Use the product as a brand-new, next-wave user
Key points.detail: Power users see a different, better product because of their history, so Bangaly has teams dogfood on fresh accounts as the 'adjacent user'. In hypergrowth, cohort curves can decline even when nothing is broken: Instagram's registration conversion would drop 'by 15%' when it entered markets like India or the Philippines, where people used different phones and understood the app differently. For OnCourse, test key flows on a fresh account as a first-time student on a low-end Android phone.

Key points.title: Plan 'understand work' as real roadmap items
Key points.detail: He replaces 'identify, justify, execute' with Facebook's 'understand, identify, execute'. Understand work, such as logging, funnels, analysis and field visits, is written into the roadmap with a named owner. When he joined Instagram, the 8-step sign-up flow logged only start and finish, so the first job was logging every step. At YouTube his teams started at 40% understand work and moved to 15 to 20%. Instagram teams ran '12 to 20 experiments a quarter' and '60 to 70%' were positive and shippable.

Key points.title: Make the repeat action easy: Instacart's reorder
Key points.detail: Instacart data showed that 'after five times... 90% of your order was the same', yet reordering took seven or eight clicks and you had to reorder the whole basket, not single items. Making the next order easy was key to retention. He also asked whether the app reflected the real job, like making Taco Tuesday, rather than making people search for tortillas, tomatoes and avocado one by one.

Title: How to build your product strategy stack (Ravi Mehta)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Ravi Mehta)
Bottom line: Write strategy down with wireframes, not just words, and when data shows odd behaviour like big spenders, phone those users before you guess why.
What they did: For Tripadvisor trip planning, the strategy doc wasn't done until it had wireframes, because words alone gave everyone a different picture (for example, which 4 or 5 tabs go in the nav bar). At Tinder a small group of users spent hundreds of dollars a month on Super Likes and Boosts; the team assumed they were rich, but calls showed they were movers, salespeople or new in town who compared the cost to the cost of dating. That led to Tinder Platinum and a pricier Super Like with a note that lets you message before matching. Tinder also mostly avoided search filters to keep matching casual and surprising.
Results: A Super Like makes the recipient 'three times more likely to match with you'. 'A really significant percentage of a la carte revenue... was coming from a very small single digit percentage of users', spending '$200 or $300' against an average ARPU of '$30'. The super like with a note was priced 'much higher than we thought the pricing was going to be'.
Takeaways: A strategy doc isn't done until it has wireframes; Tinder's big spenders weren't rich, they were in a hurry; People judge price against what they'd otherwise spend; Tinder held back on filters to keep matching serendipitous; The strategy stack: mission, strategy, product strategy, roadmap, goals; If you don't know what moves a metric, aim to learn first
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: compare the price to what students already spend on coaching (for example the fee for one coaching module or test series), not to other apps, and test that line. Design process: find the top 1 to 2% of paying or most active students in PostHog and run five phone calls to learn why they pay before redesigning Paywall or Renewal. Design process: every strategy or feature brief ships with low-fidelity wireframes of the main screens and the tab bar, so the team agrees on what goes where before building.

Key points.title: A strategy doc isn't done until it has wireframes
Key points.detail: At Tripadvisor, the trip-planning strategy doc was not allowed to be finished without wireframes. Ravi's reason: when strategy is only words, 'everyone takes away a different interpretation'. His litmus test is the nav bar: most mobile apps fit only four or five tabs, and two people reading the same strategy will pick different ones. For OnCourse, any feature brief should come with rough screens and the tab bar, so the team agrees on what goes where before building.

Key points.title: Tinder's big spenders weren't rich, they were in a hurry
Key points.detail: A small single-digit percentage of users drove a big share of a la carte revenue (Super Likes and Boosts), spending '$200 or $300' a month against an average ARPU of about $30. The team assumed they were wealthy show-offs. Phone calls showed they were military people, salespeople and people new to a city who badly wanted to meet someone. The data showed what was happening; only talking to users showed why.

Key points.title: People judge price against what they'd otherwise spend
Key points.detail: Those heavy spenders did not compare Tinder to other subscriptions. They compared it to the cost of dating: 'If I go on a few dates a month, that's probably a couple hundred dollars.' This led to Tinder Platinum and to a Super Like with a note, which lets you message someone before matching. It was priced 'much higher than we thought the pricing was going to be'. For OnCourse, the useful comparison may be coaching fees or test series, not other apps.

Key points.title: Tinder held back on filters to keep matching serendipitous
Key points.detail: Most dating apps let you filter by job, income, religion, height and more. Tinder mostly resisted this because it did not want to feel like 'a search engine for people'. Users say they met people they 'never would've met otherwise'. A missing feature can be a deliberate choice that follows from the strategy.

Key points.title: The strategy stack: mission, strategy, product strategy, roadmap, goals
Key points.detail: Ravi splits strategy into five layers: company mission, company strategy, product strategy, roadmap and goals. You define strategy from the top down and debug it from the bottom up. If you keep missing goals, check the roadmap, then the product strategy, then the company strategy. Tinder and Hinge show this: both serve dating, but Hinge is 'designed to be deleted' while Tinder wants to make single life fun, so their products differ.

Key points.title: If you don't know what moves a metric, aim to learn first
Key points.detail: Ravi puts goals after the roadmap. He compares setting a goal first to planning a road trip as 'drive 250 miles' with no destination. His 'frontier of understanding' has four kinds of risk: understanding, dependency, execution and strategic. If you don't know why students stay, set a goal to find out (talk to users, analyse data) before you commit to moving retention.

Title: Inside Etsy's product, growth, and marketplace evolution (Tim Holley)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Tim Holley)
Bottom line: Small, quick-to-read signals and one-line copy can move conversion a lot, and saved items plus timely pushes close the habit loop.
What they did: Etsy added one line to the cart, 'Etsy offsets carbon emissions from every delivery', and saw a big conversion lift they didn't expect. They show 'signals and nudges' (for example 'only one left', fast-reply sellers) and buyer review photos so shoppers can decide quickly among 100 million unique items. For retention they used the habit loop around Favorites: an updates feed plus push notifications when a favorited item goes on sale or is about to sell out. Teams run with five leads: product, engineering, design, insights (research and analytics) and marketing.
Results: On the cart text line: 'we just saw huge uplift that we really, really didn't expect' (no figure given). Tim agreed with the stat that '80% of experiments fail'. Lenny's intro: Etsy grew from 'around 500 million in GMV to over 13 billion in GMV' during Tim's time there.
Takeaways: One line about values in the cart lifted conversion; Short, glanceable signals help people choose among millions; Favorites feed a habit loop of trigger and reward; Buyer photos build trust when there's no known brand; Retention tests need 30, 60 or 90 days; Use the buyer experience to steer what sellers do
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: A/B test one plain line of copy that says what OnCourse stands for (for example explanations written by doctors who cleared NEET-PG) next to the buy button. Notifications: turn bookmarked or wrong-answer MCQs into triggers ('5 questions you got wrong last week are due for revision') with a link straight into Practice. Practice: show short signals on each question or set ('asked in NEET-PG 2023', '62% got this wrong') so students can quickly see why it matters.

Key points.title: One line about values in the cart lifted conversion
Key points.detail: Etsy added a single line to the cart: 'Etsy offsets carbon emissions from every delivery.' Tim says 'we just saw huge uplift that we really, really didn't expect' (no figure given). He thinks about effort against reward, and a one-line copy change that reads 'almost like marketing copy' can have an outsized effect. For OnCourse, test one plain line near the buy button about what the app stands for.

Key points.title: Short, glanceable signals help people choose among millions
Key points.detail: With over 100 million unique items, Etsy leans on 'signals and nudges' from behavioural economics. Snippets like 'there is actually only one of these' or a badge for sellers who reply to messages fast put buried facts right into the buyer's decision. Tim calls these 'quick summaries, the easy glanceable information'. For OnCourse, short facts on a question or set (asked in a past exam, how many got it wrong) could do the same job.

Key points.title: Favorites feed a habit loop of trigger and reward
Key points.detail: A favorite shows intent, so Etsy uses it as a trigger. When a favorited item goes on sale or is about to sell out, Etsy says so in an 'updates feed' and through push notifications. Tim calls that 'a pretty great notification to get', because it's about something the user already chose. Bookmarked or wrongly answered MCQs could be OnCourse's version of favorites.

Key points.title: Buyer photos build trust when there's no known brand
Key points.detail: Etsy buyers often buy from one-person shops they have never heard of. Reviews matter more there, especially 'buyer review photos' that show the item in a real hand or home, so the next buyer can judge size and colour. This has 'long been a track that has been very fruitful'. Proof from real peers matters most when the maker is unknown.

Key points.title: Retention tests need 30, 60 or 90 days
Key points.detail: After the 2020 surge of new buyers, Etsy shifted to driving frequency. That pushed an A/B-testing culture 'out of our comfort zone': instead of a purchase in one visit, you ask whether people come back in 30, 60 or 90 days. Tim also admits that testing nearly everything can miss the point for bigger new bets. Judge streak or reminder changes over weeks, not one session.

Key points.title: Use the buyer experience to steer what sellers do
Key points.detail: Etsy tells sellers what helps, backed by data (for example, more photos lead to more sales), and changes the advice by season. It also 'uses the buyer experience to signal what matters'. When search highlights photos or fast replies, sellers see what they need to improve. Lenny adds that Airbnb pushed Instant Book by showing only instantly bookable listings by default in search.

Title: Superhuman's secret to success | Rahul Vohra (CEO and founder) (Rahul Vohra)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Rahul Vohra)
Bottom line: Design features like toys people want to play with, not points and badges, and pick one clear position (for Superhuman, speed) that every detail supports.
What they did: Superhuman designs with game-design principles (goals, emotions, toys, controls, flow) instead of gamification: its snooze 'time auto-completer' accepts playful input like '2d', 'in a fortnight and a day' or 'never' (with a shrug emoji), so people explore it for fun. For years every new user went through 1:1 concierge onboarding (about 20 onboarders at peak) before a self-serve flow was built. They tested 15 font families on printouts and chose Adelle Sans, with line length fixed at roughly 90 to 120 characters for reading speed. Price ($30/month) came from a Van Westendorp survey of about 100 early users, and roadmap came from the Sean Ellis 'very disappointed' survey, focusing on 'somewhat disappointed' users who love the main benefit.
Results: Stanford reward study he cites: children with no reward spent 17% of their time drawing, those expecting a reward spent 8%. Facebook's viral factor was 'about 0.7'; LinkedIn address-book import had a lifetime viral factor of 'about 0.4'. Companies under 40% 'very disappointed' struggled to grow. The median answer to 'starting to get expensive' was $30 per month. Write with AI is used '37 times per week' per user; AI-written emails grew 'four times' over 2024. Users get through email 'twice as fast' and save 'four hours or more every single week'; a consulting firm measured '3.3 hours per person per week'. Rahul's time on product/design went from '6 to 7%' to '60% to 70%' of his week after hiring a president.
Takeaways: Rewards can halve motivation, so make the action fun; Build features as toys people explore for fun; Hands-on onboarding of early users creates super fans; Grow fit by fixing objections from 'somewhat disappointed' users; Price where it 'starts to get expensive' if you're premium; Own one clear position and test it at parties
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: make a small interaction a 'toy' (for example a playful, forgiving input or a surprising answer reveal) instead of adding more points or badges. Streaks: check that rewards do not replace the joy of learning; lead with progress on mastery, keep badges secondary. Design process: run the Sean Ellis 'how would you feel if you could no longer use OnCourse?' survey and build for 'somewhat disappointed' users who value the same core benefit as fans.

Key points.title: Rewards can halve motivation, so make the action fun
Key points.detail: Rahul cites a 1970s Stanford study. Children aged three to four who expected a certificate for drawing later drew only 8% of their free time, against 17% for children who expected no reward. 'The very presence of a reward halved their motivation.' His view is that gamification (points, levels, badges) fails, and when it seems to work, the core experience was already built like a game. For OnCourse, streaks and badges shouldn't crowd out the satisfaction of getting questions right.

Key points.title: Build features as toys people explore for fun
Key points.detail: Superhuman designs around five game-design areas: goals, emotions, toys, controls and flow. Its snooze 'time auto-completer' accepts '2d', '3h', 'in a fortnight and a day', '8am in Tokyo' and even 'never' (with a shrug emoji). In onboarding, people kept testing where it would break. Rahul's test for a toy: does it invite playful exploration, is it fun without a goal, and does it give pleasant surprises?

Key points.title: Hands-on onboarding of early users creates super fans
Key points.detail: For years nobody could use Superhuman without a one-to-one onboarding session, with about 20 onboarders at peak. Rahul says it beat benchmarks on engagement, retention, product-market-fit score, NPS and virality. It also meant engineers could skip building a self-serve first-run experience. They moved to self-serve once the market got wide enough and some people simply didn't want a call, and building that was 'terrifying'.

Key points.title: Grow fit by fixing objections from 'somewhat disappointed' users
Key points.detail: Ask 'How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?' Sean Ellis found that companies under 40% 'very disappointed' struggled to grow. Ignore the 'not disappointed' group and don't over-serve the fans. Focus on 'somewhat disappointed' users who value the same main benefit as the fans (for Superhuman, speed), and politely ignore the rest. Each planning cycle, spend half the time on what fans love and half on those users' objections.

Key points.title: Price where it 'starts to get expensive' if you're premium
Key points.detail: Superhuman ran a Van Westendorp survey with about 100 early users using four price questions. Most startups price at the 'bargain' answer. A best-in-category product should use the 'starting to get expensive' answer, whose median was $30 a month. They then checked market size: $100M ARR would need about 300,000 subscribers at that price. Rahul says to settle positioning before price.

Key points.title: Own one clear position and test it at parties
Key points.detail: Rahul interviewed hundreds of Gmail and Outlook users, and many said their email apps were too slow. Speed was a free position, as almost no software since Chrome had sold on it, and incumbents struggle with speed. His 'cocktail party test' is to listen to how people pitch your product. The pitch for Superhuman was simply that it's 'really fast'. The custom Adelle Sans font and line length fixed at 90 to 120 characters for reading speed both support that position.

Title: Pricing your AI product: Lessons from 400+ companies and 50 unicorns | Madhavan Ramanujam (Madhavan Ramanujam)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Madhavan Ramanujam)
Bottom line: Keep pricing simple enough that a customer can explain it back, tell it as a value story, and do not give away the 20% of features that drive 80% of willingness to pay.
What they did: Madhavan describes 'beautifully simple pricing': test it by asking customers to explain your pricing back to you, and frame price as value, as Superhuman did with $30/month told as 'a dollar a day' to get 'four hours of productivity back in the week'. He recommends showing options (good, better, best) so the talk moves from price to value. His '20-80 axiom' warns that the 20% of the product that drives 80% of willingness to pay is often the easiest to build and gets given away free. To stop churn, acquire the kind of customers who stay, rather than throwing offers at people who are already leaving.
Results: A founder who offered '100K plus 10% of incremental value, or 500K fixed' saw the 500K option negotiated to 400K, about '4X the deal'. About '5% of companies' are in a true outcome-based pricing model; the best recover '25 to 50%' of the value they create versus '10 to 20%' in classic SaaS. Prices for things you consume rise '3 to 5%' a year; revisit your pricing at least once every two years (about half that for AI companies).
Takeaways: Simple pricing means customers can explain it back; Don't give away the 20% that drives willingness to pay; Show good-better-best options to move talk to value; Stop churn by acquiring users who won't leave; Land and expand needs a fence around the free tier; Raise prices regularly; the fear is mostly internal
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: restate the plan price as a small daily amount tied to a concrete outcome (for example, per day of NEET-PG prep), and test it against the plain total. Paywall: check which few features drive most of the willingness to pay (likely the Today's plan or the full question bank) and keep them out of the free tier. Onboarding: use the answers of users who renew to shape who onboarding targets and what it promises, so the app pulls in the users least likely to churn.

Key points.title: Simple pricing means customers can explain it back
Key points.detail: Madhavan's test for 'beautifully simple pricing' is to ask early customers to explain your pricing back as if they were selling it for you. If they can't, it isn't simple. Good pricing also tells a value story. His example is Superhuman's $30 a month framed as 'a dollar a day' to get 'four hours of productivity back in the week'. The Subway $5 footlong is another. For OnCourse, a per-day price tied to prep could be tested against the plain total.

Key points.title: Don't give away the 20% that drives willingness to pay
Key points.detail: His '20-80 axiom': '20% of what you build drives 80% of the willingness to pay', and that 20% is often the easiest part to build. Founders ship it almost free, then chase features that drive little willingness to pay. He suggests MVP should mean 'most valuable product'. For a freemium app, decide carefully which core feature goes behind the paywall.

Key points.title: Show good-better-best options to move talk to value
Key points.detail: One product at one price makes the whole conversation about price. With three options, a budget-minded buyer says what they like in the higher tier, and you can ask why. One founder offered '100K plus 10% of incremental value, or 500K fixed'. The 500K was negotiated to 400K, about '4X the deal'. Tiers on a paywall work the same way: the middle and top plans frame the choice.

Key points.title: Stop churn by acquiring users who won't leave
Key points.detail: Offers made when someone is already cancelling are 'too late'. They might stay six more months, then leave. Instead, look at which customers stay longest, find what they have in common, and spend acquisition money on getting more of them. For OnCourse, the profiles of students who renew should shape onboarding and marketing.

Key points.title: Land and expand needs a fence around the free tier
Key points.detail: 'If you land, make sure to expand.' If the entry product gives 'the farm away', there's nothing left to sell later. Decide where the fence sits, by features or by usage, so the free experience pulls people in but leaves room to upgrade. This connects to the 20-80 axiom: the fence should keep the most valuable part behind it.

Key points.title: Raise prices regularly; the fear is mostly internal
Key points.detail: Revisit pricing at least once every two years, and about twice as often for AI companies. Prices of things people consume rise '3 to 5%' a year. His 'price paralysis axiom' says reluctance to raise prices is 'internal and emotional', not 'external and logical'. He quotes Warren Buffett: if you need a 'prayer session' before a 10% increase, 'you have a terrible business'.

Title: Making time for what matters | Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky (Authors of Make Time, Character VC) (Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky)
Bottom line: Pick one daily 'highlight', put barriers between you and infinity-pool apps, and reflect on each day as an experiment; for product work, go from idea to tested prototype in five days.
What they did: Make Time's system has four steps: choose one daily Highlight (by urgency, satisfaction or joy), written on a sticky note and given a 60 to 90 minute block; Laser, which uses speed bumps such as deleting apps, logging out and turning on two-factor auth, because 'willpower is never going to win'; Energize; and Reflect, treating each day as an experiment with curiosity, not self-judgment. They name 'infinity pools', apps with endlessly refreshing content, and the 'busy bandwagon'. The Design Sprint, refined over hundreds of sprints at Google Ventures, goes from zero to a prototype tested with customers in five days. Jake's Google Meet side project had stalled for a year and a half until one focused week turned it into a working prototype colleagues used.
Takeaways: Infinity pools are built to pull people back; Willpower never wins; add speed bumps instead; Pick one daily highlight and give it 60–90 minutes; Write the goal down to create a reflection loop; Reset expectations with a reason, and slow the loop; One cleared week turned a stalled idea into Google Meet
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: lead with one 'highlight' task for the day (one block of 60 to 90 minutes) and let students pick it by urgency or satisfaction, with the rest of the plan secondary. Notifications: make reminders point to the student's chosen highlight and avoid infinity-pool patterns like endless feeds; offer one quiet focus block with no prompts. Design process: run a five-day design sprint for one big open question (for example, the Renewal flow), ending with a clickable prototype tested with real students.

Key points.title: Infinity pools are built to pull people back
Key points.detail: Their name for any endlessly refreshing source: 'if you can pull to refresh or if it streams, it's an infinity pool.' That covers email as much as Instagram. Combined with the 'busy bandwagon', the feeling that you should always be busy, it becomes 'a flywheel, but bad'. These products are engineered to be 'friction-free'. For a study app, the question is whether OnCourse is the infinity pool or the thing students want to make time for.

Key points.title: Willpower never wins; add speed bumps instead
Key points.detail: John: 'willpower is never going to win… you're not going to white-knuckle your way through.' He disabled Facebook and Instagram, stays logged out of Twitter and LinkedIn, uses a Chrome extension that hides the LinkedIn feed, and turned on two-factor login just as a speed bump. Jake has kept email off his phone since 2012. Friction and defaults shape behaviour more than intent, which matters both for distractions and for the study habit OnCourse wants to build.

Key points.title: Pick one daily highlight and give it 60–90 minutes
Key points.detail: Each morning (or the night before) ask what you'd want to call the highlight of the day. Choose it by urgency, satisfaction or joy, then protect a 60 to 90 minute block, 'the rough time we think it takes to really get in the zone'. Jake calls it 'the anchor of everything'. If you get one thing done you're proud of, the day feels good even when the rest is messy. For OnCourse, Today's plan could lead with one chosen focus block.

Key points.title: Write the goal down to create a reflection loop
Key points.detail: Write the highlight on a sticky note and put it where you'll see it. 'Even if you don't see it again, just writing it down is a big deal.' At day's end, Reflect treats the day as 'an experiment that you ran', with 'curiosity about your day instead of self-judgment'. The 'Groundhog Day' idea: if you missed it, try again tomorrow. A visible goal plus a gentle end-of-day check-in is a good pattern for study apps.

Key points.title: Reset expectations with a reason, and slow the loop
Key points.detail: Add an email signature like 'I'm checking email twice a day because I'm working on an important project', and say people can text if it's urgent. They cite the photocopier-line study: saying 'because', even with a weak reason, made people far more willing to let someone cut in. Replying slower also slows the whole back-and-forth. Jake says the real benefit is changing your own expectations.

Key points.title: One cleared week turned a stalled idea into Google Meet
Key points.detail: Jake's side project had gone nowhere for a year and a half. In one focused week in Stockholm, the team skipped the perfect PRD and pitch, built a working prototype and got colleagues using it. That became Google Meet and led to the Design Sprint: zero to a tested prototype in five days, refined over hundreds of sprints at Google Ventures. It's a model for testing a big OnCourse question with real students quickly.

Title: How Airbnb innovates with design (Teo Connor)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Teo Connor)
Bottom line: Airbnb made the app feel alive again by adding touch, motion and personal touches, and by moving to real-code prototypes early.
What they did: Airbnb rebuilt checkout so the price and book button stay at the top, and cut four lines of legal copy to one. New users now get a short welcome tour built from a screenshot of their own screen, so it feels personal. The team added haptics, 3D icons, a confetti moment and a playful guest counter with an Easter egg, and moves from Figma to engineering prototypes in real code early. New visual elements like the 3D icons start in one product area and only join the design system once they prove themselves.
Takeaways: Pin price and book button; cut legal copy hard; A first-run tour feels personal when it uses your screen; Judge interactions in real code, not static Figma; Haptics, confetti and Easter eggs show users you care; New visual ideas earn their way into the system; Two-stage reviews align teams before the CEO sees work
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: replace generic tips with a short first-run tour that points at the student's own Today's plan and their real first task. Paywall: keep the price and the main button pinned and visible, and cut the fine print to one line. Design process: prototype key motion (streak celebration, answer feedback) in real code on a phone before signing it off.

Key points.title: Pin price and book button; cut legal copy hard
Key points.detail: Airbnb's old checkout had grown through years of add-ons until the price and book bar sat 'way way way down' a long page. The redesign keeps the price and book bar at the top at all times, and cut four lines of legal copy down to one, which Teo calls one of the 'big big innovations'. She says this only happened because the company moved from divisions, where each team owned a slice of the page, to one functional team that could make bold cuts. For OnCourse, the paywall and plan screens should keep price and the main button always visible and fight for every line of fine print.

Key points.title: A first-run tour feels personal when it uses your screen
Key points.detail: Before, Airbnb treated a brand-new user exactly like an expert. The new welcome tour is 'short and snappy', not a full takeover, and shows new users the map, filters and booking. It takes a screenshot of what the user is actually looking at, so the tour is built on their own screen and 'feels personal from the off'. For OnCourse, a first-run tour should point at the student's real Today's plan and first task, not at generic sample screens.

Key points.title: Judge interactions in real code, not static Figma
Key points.detail: Teo says the team used to spend a long time designing flat screens in Figma, but 'you only understand when a design is going to work when you see it on device'. Now they go from static designs and early Figma prototypes 'quickly into real engineering prototypes', using specialist prototypers on the engineering team. The host passport animation was the first case: it had to be 'super fluid' or it would be 'awful', so it went into code early. For OnCourse, motion like streak celebrations and answer feedback should be judged on a phone in code before sign-off.

Key points.title: Haptics, confetti and Easter eggs show users you care
Key points.detail: Airbnb is adding haptic feedback, a reusable confetti moment for welcome and celebration screens, flipping group-travel postcards and 3D elements from its ad campaigns. For hosts, the team could have shipped a plain plus/minus guest counter that was already in Figma, but built a playful one where you click through little people, with a llama Easter egg at the end. Teo says these touches show 'we really care about the product', especially in host tools that 'hadn't had much love for a really long time'.

Key points.title: New visual ideas earn their way into the system
Key points.detail: New elements like the 3D icons start in one project (the listings tab), then other teams try them, and only once they spread and prove themselves do they become official in the design system, 'with some guard rails around how much or where'. A central team watches every project to keep things coherent and spot trends. Teo also plays guardian: if a special treatment is used too much it loses its surprise, so she sometimes says 'too much of that right now'.

Key points.title: Two-stage reviews align teams before the CEO sees work
Key points.detail: Work is first reviewed inside design every week or two with Teo and a director, to unblock ideas and share context from other tracks. Then a cross-functional VP review with product marketing and engineering checks things like whether engineering can build it in time (checkout has many payment methods). Only then does the team present to Brian Chesky, as a team, already aligned. Her advice for new leaders: listen first, don't hide problems and don't get defensive.

Title: Make your designs memorable (Rafa Conde)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Rafa Conde)
Bottom line: Moments that make people feel something are memorable, but a forced intro video cost Retro signups, so make emotional moments easy to skip.
What they did: At Retro, Rafa built a short intro slideshow (about 7 seconds) that plays before sign-up, with a haptic on each photo. It starts fast and slows down, with street noise fading into piano, to match the message 'slow down'. Testing showed it lost signups, so the team made it easy to skip and made it respect the phone's mute switch. He shares every idea as a short, entertaining video (under 10 minutes, ideally 5) with music, humor and B-roll of a real phone in hand: 'Make an ad. Sell this idea.'
Results: Showing the intro video first 'lost like 20% or 30% of signups'. Measured at the end of onboarding, the drop was smaller ('the numbers get a little bit softer').
Takeaways: A forced intro before sign-up cost 20–30% of signups; One motif should drive visuals, haptics and sound; Pitch ideas as a short, entertaining video ad; Film a real phone in hand, not a screen recording; Don't let rare edge cases lower the ceiling; Collect small delightful details and use empty states
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: if we add an emotional intro, put it after sign-up or make it skippable with one tap, keep it under 10 seconds and respect silent mode. Design process: share new prototypes as a short narrated video of a real phone in hand, not just Figma frames. Practice: use haptics that match the pace of a session, for example a light tap per answer and a slower, deeper one when the set is done.

Key points.title: A forced intro before sign-up cost 20–30% of signups
Key points.detail: At Retro, Rafa built a short emotional intro that played before the sign-up button, and at first you had to tap and hold to skip it. Testing showed 'we lost like 20% or 30% of signups' among people who saw it first. Measured at the end of onboarding the drop was smaller ('the numbers get a little bit softer'). The team made it easier to skip and stopped ignoring the phone's mute switch. For OnCourse, anything placed before sign-up must be skippable with one tap and respect silent mode.

Key points.title: One motif should drive visuals, haptics and sound
Key points.detail: The intro is a slideshow of photos with a haptic on each new photo and no transitions ('snap snap snap'), with one slow zoom over the whole thing. A co-worker noticed you could feel the pace through the haptics and suggested starting fast and ending slow, to match the message 'slow down'. After that every choice followed the motif: street noise and chatter fade out halfway so only a calm piano is left. The whole thing is only about 7 seconds. Rafa says once you find the motif, 'everything else was just working around that'.

Key points.title: Pitch ideas as a short, entertaining video ad
Key points.detail: Rafa ends most explorations with a 'medium production' video shared on Slack, because video transfers an idea with the least loss. His rules: under 10 minutes, ideally 5; add a light soundtrack and change it when you move to a new point; add humor so people want to watch. 'Don't just design the feature and share mock-ups. Don't just make a prototype and do a screen recording... Make an ad. Sell this idea.' For OnCourse, share new Practice or Home ideas as short narrated videos, not just Figma links.

Key points.title: Film a real phone in hand, not a screen recording
Key points.detail: Rafa found that a screen recording of the Retro intro had some emotional weight, but filming someone holding the phone and watching it 'is different. It's more real.' He loads builds on his device and records himself using it at a slight angle, and shoots B-roll, like walking in and sitting at his desk, to act out the story he is telling. He uses Hand Mirror to drag his face into frame, CleanShot or ScreenFlow for recordings, and Final Cut to edit.

Key points.title: Don't let rare edge cases lower the ceiling
Key points.detail: Rafa and Ridd discuss unlearning old rules like 'don't make users scroll' or 'labels everywhere'. Ridd says it is easy to let the not-happy paths 'lower the ceiling' for the users you care about most, and he now downplays the 1% case if it lets him make something special. Rafa's example is Apple removing the home indicator bar: designers worried 'how will people know?', but real users adapted. His point: 'trust the user a little bit more'.

Key points.title: Collect small delightful details and use empty states
Key points.detail: Rafa's advice is to stay open to 'wouldn't it be funny?' or 'wouldn't this be cool?' ideas, try them quickly, but not force them. He calls empty states great places for these moments. He keeps notes of small details he notices elsewhere, like a hand-drawn signature at the end of a blog post, which he later reused in his own case study. In his side project Hand Mirror, the Plus toggle shakes and says no if you try to turn it off, and tapping the name cycles through joke names.

Title: Why Amo's Design Hits Different (Julien Martin)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Julien Martin)
Bottom line: Pick one core visual idea and let it shape the whole app, and design the feedback for every tap, not just the confetti.
What they did: At Amo, Julien's team spent about 4 months on a polished, luxury 'black gem' look, then dropped it because it felt cold and not fun. They found the core idea in animated real-person avatars, which led to a messy 'fridge collage' sticker style used across all their apps. In Bump, friends are shown on an iPod-style wheel under your thumb, and each face animates when it reaches the center. Zenly greeted users with cheeky mood messages and created gestures like the edge-zoom on the map.
Results: Ridd puts Zenly at 'like 40 million users'. No experiment results.
Takeaways: Find the one 'atom' that sets the whole look; Design the reaction to every tap, not just confetti; Physical metaphors turn browsing into play; Too much novelty loses people, so step back; Zenly greeted users with cheeky, playful messages; Feature creep turned Zenly into a 'Christmas tree'
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: design the feedback for every tap (selecting an option, a correct answer, a wrong answer) with a small animation and a careful haptic, not only the end-of-set screen. Streaks: give the streak one strong visual idea that also appears on Home and in Notifications, instead of a generic flame. Home: try a cheeky, rotating greeting that reflects the student's real state (exam countdown, yesterday's score).

Key points.title: Find the one 'atom' that sets the whole look
Key points.detail: Julien's first direction for Amo was a luxury look where buttons felt like tapping a black, shiny onyx gem. After about 4 months they dropped it: 'It was cold. It was not warm.' He says Zenly's style had grown from just a logo and a first icon set, a 'halo effect'. For Amo, the atom became the avatar: the real you, animated like a short GIF. People said it looked like a collage slapped on a fridge, which became a messy sticker-collage brand used across all the apps.

Key points.title: Design the reaction to every tap, not just confetti
Key points.detail: 'You don't have to build everything to be functional.' Delight 'doesn't have to have confetti' or saturated colors. Instead always ask: 'what happens when I tap this button? What's the reaction? What's the feedback?' It might be a tiny animation, a carefully tuned haptic or a change on screen. Julien says users may not be able to explain why, but this shapes how they judge quality. He also argues for spending four days instead of two to raise the bar. For OnCourse, this means designing feedback for selecting an option and for right and wrong answers, not only the end-of-set screen.

Key points.title: Physical metaphors turn browsing into play
Key points.detail: Find My and Life360 list friends in panels like a contact list. Bump instead borrowed the Rolodex and old phone dials: friends sit on an iPod-like wheel at the bottom of the screen under your thumb. Faces are still until they reach the center, then animate, which 'creates really nice anticipation'. His test for the whole app: 'If you're smiling when you use this app, even after the 45 days, you know you created something really special.'

Key points.title: Too much novelty loses people, so step back
Key points.detail: Zenly invented patterns like the edge zoom on the map, where you slide your thumb along the screen edge; once learned, other maps feel wrong. But Julien admits many Amo and Zenly features confused people: 'What's happening? I don't understand.' When users won't use it or pay for it, you are doing something wrong, so you step back and adjust instead of brute-forcing your 'DNA'. They also designed for word of mouth: moments people screenshot or show friends at school.

Key points.title: Zenly greeted users with cheeky, playful messages
Key points.detail: Zenly built a game-like 'world' DNA: blue screens everywhere, a colorful ice-cream logo and carefully designed transitions. Every time you opened the app it greeted you with a mood message, sometimes 'a bit ballsy', like 'you look great, you looked better yesterday', or saying it was rainy in the middle of July. Julien admits it was sometimes over-designed, but says it helped Zenly become popular in Japan, South Korea, Indonesia and Eastern Europe.

Key points.title: Feature creep turned Zenly into a 'Christmas tree'
Key points.detail: By the end Zenly had so many competing calls to action, colors and a busy dynamic map that the team called it a Christmas tree, and they kept doing redesigns to tone it down. So Amo started as a suite of separate apps, each tackling one problem, that still clearly felt like Amo. The third app, Bump, was meant as a small thank-you location app but became the main product. For OnCourse, this is a warning about piling features onto Home.

Title: What it takes to design an award-winning product (Balint Orosz)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Balint Orosz)
Bottom line: Craft tests ideas in the real product with real data, because fake data in tests gives misleading answers.
What they did: At Skyscanner, Balint showed that people testing with fake data picked the variant with $1,000 flights, which real buyers would hate, so Craft now prototypes in the real app and runs beta programs. Craft 3's Quick Add came from an old chat-style capture prototype, revived 5 days before launch and taken from Figma to an interactive build in about two days. For tasks, a beta of a flexible 'objects' feature showed users mostly built projects and tasks, so after reading thousands of comments the team rolled back four months of work and built tasks around documents. Designers own product decisions (there are no PMs) and engineers name spacing and animation values in code so designers can tweak them.
Results: Objects beta: 'like 2,000 users'; '90% of them were creating two type of object types', projects and tasks. Tasks: 'four months to figure this out and then we built it in two months'. Average user spends 'two three hours a day' in Craft.
Takeaways: Tests with fake data and fake intent mislead; Save delight for core moments; keep 'skip' screens plain; Act on fragile ideas fast; Quick Add proved it; Ask why users want a feature before building it; Let the user's own content become the design; Build primitives and readable code, not button libraries
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: test Practice and Today's plan ideas with real students using their own question history in a beta build, not fake data in Figma. Practice: try a one-tap, chat-style quick capture for doubts or notes during a session, and sort them later. Onboarding: keep one-time screens (permissions, OTP) plain and save motion and personality for daily moments.

Key points.title: Tests with fake data and fake intent mislead
Key points.detail: At Skyscanner, Balint tested two variants, one showing $100 flights and one showing $1,000 flights, and the $1,000 version won. Real customers come only for the cheapest flight, so a buyer with real intent would call it 'the worst product I have ever seen'. Since then Craft uses Figma only for early sketching, prototypes most things in the real product with real data, and runs beta programs. For OnCourse, test Practice ideas with real students on their own question history.

Key points.title: Save delight for core moments; keep 'skip' screens plain
Key points.detail: Balint splits screens into 'skip pages' that people want to get past, like the iPhone SIM PIN screen you see 'once ideally in your lifetime', and core interactions that deserve a positive emotional loop. Too many animations feel unharmonized, but none makes the app 'way too dry'. Because users spend 'two three hours a day' in Craft, he wants it to feel like a decorated home office. For OnCourse, keep OTP and permission screens plain and spend motion on daily practice moments.

Key points.title: Act on fragile ideas fast; Quick Add proved it
Key points.detail: About 5 days before the Craft 3 launch, the planned context-sensitive plus button 'doesn't feel right', said the head of design. Balint dug up a 5–6 year old screen recording of a chat-style capture prototype: tap plus, type like in chat, decide where it goes later. Within 3–4 hours there was a Figma prototype, the next morning an interactive one, and after about two days of iteration it shipped. 'Ideas are super fragile': act on them almost in the moment or they fade. Quick Add is now growing into a bigger project.

Key points.title: Ask why users want a feature before building it
Key points.detail: Users kept asking for databases. Craft built a flexible 'objects' feature and ran a beta with about 2,000 users, then found '90% of them were creating two type of object types': projects and tasks. After reading thousands of comments, the head of design proposed rolling back four months of work. They rebuilt tasks around documents, where tasks already have context, kept the existing checkbox, and added an inbox for quick capture. It took 'four months to figure this out and then we built it in two months'.

Key points.title: Let the user's own content become the design
Key points.detail: Craft is mostly text, so it can't lean on cover art like Netflix or Spotify, and a strong brand would fight users' content. So 'we should put your content everywhere as a design element': colorful documents make the app colorful, and opening a document casts 'ambient lighting' from it across the window. Japanese users add cover images so their grid looks like a Pinterest board, while Balint's looks like plain documents.

Key points.title: Build primitives and readable code, not button libraries
Key points.detail: Craft avoids heavy components because 'if you have a button that has 25 properties, when you're at the 26th it's just going to fall apart'. Instead it has shared primitives: a synced animation engine, a one-line faded clipping for long labels, and a one-line colorful material that picks up document colors. Engineers keep spacing, animation curves and colors well named in code so designers can tweak them. The trade-off is a few too many corner radii, but a new segmented control takes 'one or two hours'.

Title: Mastering the pillars of great visual design (Anthony Hobday)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Anthony Hobday)
Bottom line: Visual design follows learnable rules, and a few of them (alignment, grouping, fewer colors, careful brightness) give big gains fast.
What they did: Anthony collects the unwritten rules behind good interfaces. For color: give each palette color a different brightness so they don't clash, avoid flat black, avoid yellow, and use colors for meanings the product defines (red = delete) rather than cultural meanings. He limits himself to black, white and one color, warns that packing too much into one view causes confusion, and uses tricks like a 10% black border that works on any background and gradients with more stops so they don't go muddy. For type pairings, the easy path is copying experts (Typewolf, one foundry's paired fonts); the hard path is comparing letter by letter across about 100 pairings.
Takeaways: Give each palette color a different brightness; Use colors for meanings your product defines; Black, white and one color makes a bolder design; Dense screens confuse; communicate more with less; Font pairing: copy experts now, study letters later; Small techniques: see-through borders and eased gradients
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: give correct, wrong and selected states clearly different brightness, not just different hues, and keep each color's meaning the same everywhere. Home: count the accent colors on Home and Today's plan and cut back to one main accent so the key action stands out. Design process: keep a shared library of saved visual techniques and look at it during crits.

Key points.title: Give each palette color a different brightness
Key points.detail: Anthony learned from a book on interface visuals that colors with the same perceived brightness tend to clash. So when he builds a palette of four or five colors, he makes each one a different brightness. He avoids flat black (and flat white where he can), calls blue the safe choice, and avoids yellow because it is the brightest hue and clashes with white; dark yellow just turns brown, so he shifts toward orange. For OnCourse, correct, wrong and selected states should differ in brightness, not only hue.

Key points.title: Use colors for meanings your product defines
Key points.detail: He separates connotative colors, whose meaning comes from culture (red means danger), from denotative colors, whose meaning the product sets (red means delete). He tries not to mix the two, and prefers denotative color because 'color becomes this really useful practical tool' instead of something users have to interpret. For OnCourse, keep each color's meaning the same on every screen.

Key points.title: Black, white and one color makes a bolder design
Key points.detail: Big palettes of many hues and shades tend to 'average out to something relatively bland'. Anthony prefers black, white and just one color, which gives that color much more impact and makes the design more striking, even when the color is blue. He also uses extreme constraints like a one-column layout to force more creative solutions. For OnCourse, count the accent colors on Home and cut back to one main accent so the key action stands out.

Key points.title: Dense screens confuse; communicate more with less
Key points.detail: Beyond basic mistakes in alignment and grouping, Anthony sees designers pack too much into one view because they enjoy the work and want to say everything. If users 'can't find your bearings, that's a huge problem'. Density is fine when an app needs it, but it is a harder skill, so until you have that skill, 'pull back on what you want to communicate' and 'try harder to actually communicate more with less'.

Key points.title: Font pairing: copy experts now, study letters later
Key points.detail: 'Easy mode' is to copy experts: read Typewolf's weekly email, which lists sites with great type and the typefaces they use, or pick a sans and a serif from the same foundry that were designed to work together. 'Hard mode' takes years: zoom in on good pairings and compare the same letters (for example the 'a') across display and body faces to see what is similar and what contrasts, over something like 100 pairings.

Key points.title: Small techniques: see-through borders and eased gradients
Key points.detail: A 10% opacity black border works on any background, because it darkens whatever is behind it instead of fighting it. Gradient easing adds about eight hand-tuned stops so a two-stop gradient doesn't show a hard line in the middle or pass through a 'muddy brown valley'. He also likes stepped background transitions, bands of gray between dark and light sections, and subtle shapes that point the eye to the next section.

Title: Designing Snapchat and the future of music (Jack Brody)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Jack Brody)
Bottom line: Use what users already work around to back your product bets, and let designers keep going with ideas others call bad, as long as they deeply believe in them.
What they did: At Snap, Jack led Memories and Snap Map. He says both 'didn't necessarily come from this emergent behavior', but seeing it made the team more sure: people saved snaps to their camera roll (Memories, whose flashbacks became a reason people still open the app every day), and people posted 'come hang' location snaps and deleted them once they left (Snap Map). Gesture-only navigation was fast for early users, but Snap went too far hiding the UI and new users struggled. At Suno, each prompt returns two songs, which shows that results vary and gives preference data to improve the model.
Results: At Snap the design team was 'about a dozen' product designers in a company of '5500 people'. No experiment results.
Takeaways: User workarounds show demand and where the friction is; Flashbacks of saved history keep people coming back; Gesture-only navigation was fast, but new users struggled; Two AI results teach variability and gather preferences; Let designers champion ideas others call bad; Keep design small and central; work 20% outside your area
Ideas for OnCourse: Streaks: add 'on this day' flashbacks (topics mastered, scores a month ago) so a student's history becomes a reason to come back. Practice: when showing AI explanations or generated questions, try offering two versions and record which one the student picks. Design process: look at what students do outside the app (screenshots of questions, notes in other apps) and build for that.

Key points.title: User workarounds show demand and where the friction is
Key points.detail: Jack says if users go through friction to hack a product into doing something, the desire is strong, and removing the friction lets more people do it. Snap saw people saving snaps to their camera roll before sending, which led to Memories. For Snap Map, people posted 'come hang' snaps with location geofilters to their story, then deleted them once they left. He notes these behaviors 'solidified' conviction rather than being the only origin. For OnCourse, watch what students do outside the app, like screenshotting questions.

Key points.title: Flashbacks of saved history keep people coming back
Key points.detail: Memories became 'stored value' for users. Jack has heard 'a million times' from people who say they use Snapchat less, 'but I still use it almost every day because I get these flashbacks from my memories', and they could never give that up. He calls this the 'retentive power' of Memories. For OnCourse, 'on this day' flashbacks of topics mastered or past scores could make a student's history a reason to return.

Key points.title: Gesture-only navigation was fast, but new users struggled
Key points.detail: Snap's swipe-based navigation was built for speed: open to the camera and move around fast. It came from a culture of questioning conventions ('you have to start by doing them differently'), and parts of it later became standard elsewhere. But as the audience broadened, 'we probably over rotated on some of this hide the UI' approach, and the new-user experience was harder than it should have been.

Key points.title: Two AI results teach variability and gather preferences
Key points.detail: Every Suno prompt returns two songs. This teaches users that the same prompt gives different outputs, which isn't intuitive for a machine. It also collects preference data: which one you listen to longer, like or dislike. At Suno's scale, that feeds the loop that makes the model better. Jack frames the moat as model advantage, then data advantage, then network advantage. For OnCourse, showing two AI explanations and recording the pick could do both jobs.

Key points.title: Let designers champion ideas others call bad
Key points.detail: Jack expects designers to get feedback early and often, but accepts a designer ignoring all of it, even 'this is a dumb idea', if they have 'deep, deep conviction' and the idea fits the mission. He accepts it may fail. The limits: he must respect the person's judgment, and someone who keeps ignoring feedback and keeps being wrong is a problem. His reasoning: ideas everyone agrees with have probably been done already, and Snapchat itself was called a bad idea.

Key points.title: Keep design small and central; work 20% outside your area
Key points.detail: When Snap had 5,500 people, it had only about a dozen product designers, in one central team rather than embedded in squads. A shared design meeting where everyone shows work builds context across areas, so projects don't drift toward separate local maximums. Jack expects about 20% of a designer's output to be outside their focus area, and moves designers to new areas every so often to bring fresh ideas.

Title: Lessons from the founding designer at Linear (Adrien Griveau)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Adrien Griveau)
Bottom line: Early on, design on top of what is live, build with engineers from day one, and fix bugs users see before building new features.
What they did: Adrien designs by taking screenshots of the live app and changing them, instead of keeping a large design system, which he says slows small teams down. He shares a rough direction early, engineers build it, and they go back and forth on screenshots of the build. Features go first to staff, then to opt-in users, then to everyone. Every feature must work with the mouse; keyboard shortcuts are added on top, following a consistent set of rules. Bugs users hit come before new work, and every engineer does support.
Results: Adrien estimates that once a feature reaches everyone, '80 90% of the time' it already handles most cases. No experiment results.
Takeaways: Design on screenshots of the live product; Share rough ideas early; most work is thrown away; Release in stages and fix live bugs first; Mouse first; shortcuts are a layer on top; Listen for user problems, not their solutions; Write real copy, not lorem ipsum
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: design changes on screenshots of the live OnCourse app with real student data, and treat production as the truth. Design process: release new Practice or Flashcards changes first to staff, then to a small opt-in group of students, before everyone. Flashcards: make every action work by tap first, then add swipe shortcuts on top for power users.

Key points.title: Design on screenshots of the live product
Key points.detail: Adrien says big design systems slow down a team of one or two designers: time spent on the system is time not spent improving the product, and the UI may change anyway. Linear kept only basic font sizes and colors in Figma. For small changes he takes 'a screenshot of the app and just design on top of it', because recreating a screen with 1,000 realistic issues takes forever. 'The source of truth is what is in prod.' He worries when candidates show button files instead of live work.

Key points.title: Share rough ideas early; most work is thrown away
Key points.detail: '80% of my job is going to the trash.' His designs are often just a few screens that open a direction. Engineers start building something scrappy very early, and they go back and forth on screenshots of the build: 'actually, you did that, it looks better than what I did.' It is not a top-down spec handoff. This also shows quickly when an idea is too much or could be simpler.

Key points.title: Release in stages and fix live bugs first
Key points.detail: Features ship internally first, since the whole company uses Linear daily and anyone, even sales, can push back. Then they go to opt-in users through the changelog, then to everyone. By then '80 90% of the time' the feature already handles most cases. There is no QA team; when users hit a problem in production, fixing it becomes the top priority, ahead of new features. For OnCourse, try new Practice changes with staff, then a small opt-in group of students.

Key points.title: Mouse first; shortcuts are a layer on top
Key points.detail: Most people don't use shortcuts at first, so every feature must work with the mouse alone. Shortcuts are 'the cherry on the cake' added after. Adrien even avoids shortcuts himself sometimes so he doesn't forget the clicking path. Changing a shortcut later is very hard, so you need your own shortcut 'philosophy' and should check conflicts in each context; copying another tool's scheme 'will end up in a nightmare'. For OnCourse Flashcards, make every action work by tap, then add swipes.

Key points.title: Listen for user problems, not their solutions
Key points.detail: Linear is opinionated: the 'Linear method' gives teams a workflow, with little customization. Customers often suggest fixes like 'this button should do that'. Adrien listens, but looks for the common problem behind different requests, and says the answer is often simpler or elsewhere. Because everyone uses the same issues, statuses and labels, a 'feature request' can sometimes be solved just by showing existing data differently.

Key points.title: Write real copy, not lorem ipsum
Key points.detail: Adrien wants 'makers, not executioners': people who do whatever the product needs, even outside their role. His example: 'Do you use lorem ipsum or do you try to come up with real text?' Real sentences that users might write change the design. He also says building your own small product teaches copy, marketing and distribution, and that the best designers find engineers to build their crazy ideas.

Title: Defining the visual language for DoorDash (Kathryn Gonzalez)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Kathryn Gonzalez)
Bottom line: Start a design system only when there is a real problem, build it from what the product already uses, and sell infrastructure work in small steps.
What they did: Kathryn was DoorDash's first designer and first front-end engineer, and every employee did deliveries to see the problems firsthand. She started the design system in 2017 when the team had about 10 front-end engineers and 8 designers, and timed its first version (tokens, buttons, modals) to the rebrand so it would get used. Components were picked from what the UI already used most (mostly modals). Later, each area (merchant, consumer, Dasher) got its own design-system partner and 'local systems', for example charts for merchants.
Results: By the middle of the year after the rebrand, 'everything on the website was using the design system'. Team size when it started: 'about 10 front-end engineers', '50 engineers overall', 'eight people' in design.
Takeaways: Build first components from what the UI already uses; Ride a rebrand to get the design system adopted; Pitch infrastructure as small steps, not six months; Different users need different kinds of craft; Local systems partners catch blind spots in other areas; Keep tokens one-to-one; let higher layers stay loose
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: before adding components, list what OnCourse screens really use most and standardize those first. Design process: tie token and component cleanup to a visible launch (a Home or Paywall redesign) so engineers adopt it. Design process: have each designer spend time with real NEET-PG students during a study day, the way DoorDash staff do deliveries.

Key points.title: Build first components from what the UI already uses
Key points.detail: Kathryn did not predict what the system should hold. She looked at what made up '90% of our UI'. At the time that was mostly modals, so a good modal came first. Every component or token had to tie back to the real problem: quality was slipping as the team grew. For OnCourse, audit which cards, sheets and buttons appear most across screens and standardize those before inventing new ones.

Key points.title: Ride a rebrand to get the design system adopted
Key points.detail: She started the system in full in mid-2017, when the founders had just decided to rebrand by year end. Her MVP was backward-compatible tokens, so every existing surface could take on the new brand, plus core components like buttons and modals. The rebrand shipped on the system, and 'by middle of the following year everything on the website was using the design system'. That win earned buy-in to extend it to iOS and Android. Tie cleanup work to a visible launch so engineers have a reason to adopt it.

Key points.title: Pitch infrastructure as small steps, not six months
Key points.detail: Pitching 'I'm just going to do infrastructure work for the next six months' usually fails. There is almost always a smaller version of the change that is cheap and clearly worth it to an executive. Small steps also teach you which part to start on and what to iterate on next. A good story ties the work to a business or product problem, not to 'the product is chaotic'.

Key points.title: Different users need different kinds of craft
Key points.detail: At DoorDash, merchants needed dense, real-time information to run a restaurant, so the system invested in data visualization and charts for them. Consumers got the visual richness, which merchants did not need. Craft is not one bar; it depends on who you design for. For OnCourse, a dense performance analytics view and a calm daily-plan screen can follow different rules.

Key points.title: Local systems partners catch blind spots in other areas
Key points.detail: From 2021 to 2022 DoorDash added design system partners for areas like merchant and consumer, who own 'local systems' on top of the global one. Without them, the global team drifts to the biggest, most urgent partner, usually consumer mobile. Partners bring patterns back, and the team connects groups solving the same thing (like how finances show for Dashers and merchants) before standardizing. It is not 'once it happens twice, add it to the system'.

Key points.title: Keep tokens one-to-one; let higher layers stay loose
Key points.detail: Her answer to design debt is 'embrace the chaos'. Quoting another design systems leader, she calls design systems a practice of reducing entropy, which always goes up. Making code, Figma and the product match fully is a losing battle. But the base primitives, like tokens, should match as closely as possible. Layers above that can be looser, and some things should live outside the system.

Title: The art of designing for delight (Jenny Wen)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Jenny Wen)
Bottom line: Delight means going beyond what people expect, often in everyday high-traffic moments, not confetti on a finish screen.
What they did: For FigJam's launch, the team shipped just the basic whiteboard tools plus features unique to FigJam (cursor chat, emotes, high-fives) instead of trying to match every competitor feature. Cursor chat came from a daily build-and-try cycle with two engineers and a PM, testing each version in real meetings. Jenny starts projects by listing every open question, picks the few that unlock the rest, and explores the extremes ('how expressive?') to find the middle. She swapped Amazon's press-release exercise for writing pretend tweets reacting to features, to find what people would share.
Takeaways: Confetti is table stakes; add delight to everyday moments; Delight means exceeding expectations, including in nervous moments; The best delight anticipates needs, like a good waiter; Launch with features only you have, not parity; List every open question, then crack the key ones; Measure delight through reactions; write pretend tweets
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: instead of more celebration on the results screen, find an everyday moment to improve, such as already showing the right next set after a wrong-answer streak. Onboarding: support nervous moments (first mock test, choosing the exam date) with reassuring copy and guidance, like a supportive friend. Design process: run a 'pretend tweet' exercise where the team writes how a student would share a new feature.

Key points.title: Confetti is table stakes; add delight to everyday moments
Key points.detail: Jenny says adding delight only to celebrations 'is kind of tired'. Everyone has a confetti or a fun animation after you finish something, so it is now expected. Real delight is in high-traffic, mundane moments that show extra care, like Andy Allen's weather app where you can flick and spin the temperature while checking the weather. For OnCourse, polish the question-to-question flow or the daily plan before adding more to the results screen.

Key points.title: Delight means exceeding expectations, including in nervous moments
Key points.detail: She defines delight as going 'above and beyond someone's expectations', not a sparkle or a cheeky illustration. In a utility tool like Shopify, that means finding moments when a merchant wants to celebrate, feels nervous or feels unsure. For a first-time store setup, the product can hold their hand 'almost like a supportive friend'. OnCourse has many such moments: the first mock test, picking an exam date, a bad score.

Key points.title: The best delight anticipates needs, like a good waiter
Key points.detail: The most delightful work starts with a designer asking 'wouldn't it be smart if we did X', not 'wouldn't it be nice if we animated it'. It anticipates a need and solves it slightly out of scope. Her analogy: you drop your fork and the server is already handing you a new one. Ridd's summary: extend what the product can do in unexpected ways instead of 'throwing glitter on what you already have'.

Key points.title: Launch with features only you have, not parity
Key points.detail: FigJam launched with only the core whiteboard tools (shapes, stickies, text) plus fun features unique to it: cursor chat, emotes and high-fives. A first launch is a special moment you can't redo, so chasing parity with other whiteboards made no sense. 'Instead of filling the existing check boxes we actually created some of our own checkboxes.' Things like resizable stickies, timers and voting came in the weeks after.

Key points.title: List every open question, then crack the key ones
Key points.detail: On a big ambiguous project she writes down every question, big ('what is the relationship between Figma and FigJam') and small ('how do you manipulate text'). Then she picks the few that, once solved, make the rest easy, based on Coda CEO Shishir's article on 'eigenquestions'. Her design files list each question at the top with options below. She explores spectrums by pushing extremes (utilitarian vs over-the-top expressive) to find the middle, and always keeps one 'straw man' option she believes in to avoid analysis paralysis.

Key points.title: Measure delight through reactions; write pretend tweets
Key points.detail: Delight won't show up in an A/B test. It shows up in what people say on Twitter and to friends, often as an 'oh my gosh' reaction, so keep your ear to the ground. She reworked Amazon's press-release exercise into a tweet template: the team brainstorms features and writes the tweets people would post about them. This finds what people would love and share. Ask how a student would describe a new OnCourse feature to a friend.
