Title: What makes a software product feel great (Janum Trivedi)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Janum Trivedi)
Bottom line: Netflix's whole-app motion and polish refresh was A/B tested and improved all core business metrics, which shows that how an app feels affects the business.
What they did: At Netflix, Janum and designer Ben Johnson spent about 9 months on an iOS refresh: a zoom transition from artwork to the detail page, and backgrounds colored from each title's artwork using about 200 lines of tuned color code. They tested the whole refresh together (control, full refresh, and refresh without the zoom) instead of piece by piece, so it wouldn't feel patched together. For Arc's download animation he used real physics so the arc and shadow worked from any click position. His ladder for good motion: animations you can interrupt, that keep their momentum when they change direction, that stretch at edges, and that always respond.
Results: Netflix A/B test of the iOS refresh: 'statistically significant'; 'all core business metrics are positive by a substantial margin' (no exact numbers given).
Takeaways: Netflix's motion refresh lifted all core business metrics; Test a full redesign as one package; A ladder for motion that feels great; Good details respect muscle memory; Tune spring values per animation; don't standardize them; Model real physics to make an animation work anywhere
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: make answer feedback and moving to the next question interruptible, so fast students can tap ahead without waiting for animations to finish. Flashcards: use springs that keep the swipe's speed so cards fly off and snap back naturally, tuned for each gesture. Design process: if we redesign Home, A/B test the whole new look together against the old one, not screen by screen.

Key points.title: Netflix's motion refresh lifted all core business metrics
Key points.detail: Janum and designer Ben Johnson spent about 9 months on a refresh of the Netflix iOS app. It added a zoom transition from artwork to the detail page and backgrounds tinted from each title's artwork. They expected metrics to be slightly red or neutral, but the A/B test came back 'statistically significant' with 'all core business metrics positive by a substantial margin' (no numbers given). His takeaway: 'feel is product quality, just like stability, performance'. People drop products that feel bad as soon as they aren't forced to use them.

Key points.title: Test a full redesign as one package
Key points.detail: Netflix tested three groups: control, everything on, and everything on except the zoom transition (in case its engineering was broken). They chose not to ship the refresh surface by surface. 'As soon as we start breaking this refresh up it's no longer a refresh, you've just kind of created this Frankenstein's monster.' Ridd notes that piece-by-piece tests might have read neutral and killed the whole project.

Key points.title: A ladder for motion that feels great
Key points.detail: Level one is fire-and-forget: you must wait for the animation to finish, which feels slow because you think faster than the software. Level two makes it interruptible, so tapping the background reverses a rising modal at once. Level three keeps momentum when direction changes ('retargeting'), using springs instead of jerking back. Beyond that, handle what happens past the edges (iOS rubber-banding tells you 'this is the end, not a bug') and make the UI always respond to touch. For OnCourse Practice, students should be able to tap ahead without waiting for feedback animations.

Key points.title: Good details respect muscle memory
Key points.detail: On iOS, people start typing while the keyboard is still sliding up. The designers knew this, so key taps count as if the keyboard were already in place. If you had to hit the moving key exactly, 'people will lose their mind'. He calls Apple's WWDC 2018 talk 'Designing Fluid Interfaces' the 'holy text' for these principles. He also says Disney's 12 principles of animation apply to UI, like the Netflix tiles dipping before they expand.

Key points.title: Tune spring values per animation; don't standardize them
Key points.detail: He is 'not really in the standardization camp' for animation constants. The last step of design is tuning: change one number by 0.02 and try again, until you have 'a big file of tuned constants, don't touch it'. A spring that moves something 50 points feels different from the same spring moving it across the screen. Real tuned motion 'is not going to match what your design system says'.

Key points.title: Model real physics to make an animation work anywhere
Key points.detail: For Arc's download animation, Bézier curves with a timing curve felt off, because 'you're doing physics motion with not physics curves'. He treated it as a high school projectile problem (his sister, a math teacher, helped) and simulated gravity every frame. That worked from any click position and gave him velocity to drive the shadow and a squishy spring landing. At Netflix the same lesson held for artwork-tinted backgrounds: a mock is easy, but the real system took about 200 lines of tuned color code.

Title: The trick to AI prototyping with your design system (Lewis Healey and Kyler Hall)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Lewis Healey and Kyler Hall)
Bottom line: AI prototypes look right when you start people from a pre-coded template of your app's shell plus short, AI-written design system instructions, not from a blank prompt.
What they did: Atlassian's design system team built Figma Make and Replit templates where the top nav and side nav are already coded, so the AI only edits the content area. They wrote a 2,000–3,000 line guidelines file (cut from a 5,000-line one) with a 'translating from Tailwind' section per component, plus 'recipes' (code blob plus instructions) for things like the Rovo chat box or dark mode. They used 'sticker sheets' and bounding-box prompts to learn what the AI's vision misses, and then taught people to upload smaller, zoomed-in screenshots. Guidelines are generated from the real component code so docs stay in sync.
Results: Starting from the coded nav template cut navigation errors from 'maybe like half of the prototypes' to 'nearly zero'; instructions alone gave about '50 60% accuracy' on one-shot screenshot recreation; people had been spending 'two or three hours' getting the nav pixel perfect.
Takeaways: Pre-code the app shell so AI edits, not invents; Map generic Tailwind patterns to your own components; Give AI three clean examples, not every variant; Test what the AI's vision actually sees; Remove common failure points with copyable commands and recipes; Adoption came from simple formats and leaders demoing prototypes
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Build a coded OnCourse prototype template with the real tab bar, header and Practice/Lessons card components, so AI prototypes start inside the app shell. Design process: Keep a short AI guidelines file for OnCourse components with 2–3 clean examples each and a 'if you see this generic pattern, use this component' map. Design process: When recreating a screen from a screenshot, crop to one section at a time.

Key points.title: Pre-code the app shell so AI edits, not invents
Key points.detail: Atlassian's AI tools kept hallucinating the top nav and side nav, which have many imports and icons. So the design system team built Figma Make and Replit templates with the nav already coded. The AI is 'very very good at just changing the code that already exists'. Navigation errors dropped from 'maybe like half of the prototypes' to 'nearly zero', and people stopped spending 'two or three hours' perfecting the nav. The chrome matters most in customer tests because a wrong shell distracts people, while the content area can be rougher.

Key points.title: Map generic Tailwind patterns to your own components
Key points.detail: Uploading their full documentation failed: the file was truncated and the AI didn't know how to use the components. Models are trained on shadcn and Tailwind, so each component in their guidelines file has a 'translating from Tailwind' section. It says, in effect, 'if you see these class names, it should be this React code'. This helps with odd names like Atlassian's 'Lozenge', which the AI would never guess is a badge. The file also says to use the design system and tokens first, then Tailwind for gaps.

Key points.title: Give AI three clean examples, not every variant
Key points.detail: Each component gets a few examples written only for AI, 'just basically the three relatively basic versions'. Giving all variants made it mix them: 'I can do this mixed with this mixed with this... no, you really can't'. They aim for the 80% of common uses, not every case. The guidelines were cut from about 5,000 lines to 2,000–3,000 and show only 20–30 of 100+ components. They are generated from the real component code, because docs in five places had drifted apart.

Key points.title: Test what the AI's vision actually sees
Key points.detail: Instructions alone got about '50 60% accuracy' recreating a screenshot in one shot. Lewis borrowed the idea of printer calibration sheets: he made 'sticker sheets' of components and asked the AI to describe them and draw bounding boxes. It missed weak borders, skipped the colored background of small icon tiles, guessed font sizes wrong, and dropped elements lower down in complex screenshots. So he taught people to upload smaller, zoomed-in sections instead of a whole screen.

Key points.title: Remove common failure points with copyable commands and recipes
Key points.detail: Asking 'change logo to Jira' pulled an old Jira logo from training data. A config object of constants wired to the nav, plus a copyable command to paste, cut those hallucinations. For smaller add-ons they built 'recipes': a code blob with instructions, like adding the Rovo chat box or switching to dark mode, which needs theming code. These avoid the 'one or two extra prompts' that make people lose confidence.

Key points.title: Adoption came from simple formats and leaders demoing prototypes
Key points.detail: With about 11,000 employees, 'if you build it they do not come'. What worked: a 3-minute Loom UI tour saying what each button does, an AI Builder Week where the president had everyone put tools down, and a 500-person Replit masterclass. A Slack bot sends group DMs to inactive users, which people answer, unlike channel posts. Leaders sharing their own prototypes in design reviews and Looms spread it further: 'my boss's boss is doing this, maybe I should'.

Title: Doing UX research with AI (Noam Segal)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Noam Segal)
Bottom line: Start research from the risk the team is worried about, turn it into a few tight learning goals, and share findings as short stories that show the user's pain, not bullet points.
What they did: Noam (research lead at Airbnb, Meta, Twitter, Wealthfront) frames research as risk reduction: ask the PM what risk the study addresses, then derive a short, limited list of learning goals. He uses an interview guide, not a script, because the value is in follow-up questions, and pilots interviews first. He builds rapport by spending 3–5 minutes asking about something in the participant's background. His stack: Sprig (in-product surveys, replays, usability tests), Dscout (diary studies) and an AI interviewer like Genway to get qualitative 'why' at scale.
Takeaways: Start research from the risk, then limit learning goals; Show the pain behind each insight; Use an interview guide, never a script; Spend 3–5 minutes on rapport; it pays back; Quant shows what happens; qual explains why; Late usability tests can still find big wins
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Before any OnCourse study, write the risk (e.g. 'students quit after day 3 of Today's plan') and 3 or fewer learning goals, then check every guide question against them. Design process: Share research back as a 1-minute story with a clip of a student struggling, then the insight. Onboarding: Use an in-app survey plus session replays to find where new students drop off, then interview a few of them about why.

Key points.title: Start research from the risk, then limit learning goals
Key points.detail: Noam calls research 'an exercise in risk reduction' or confidence building. First ask the PM what risk the study addresses and whether it is real. Then turn that risk into a 'crisp and clear and constrained' set of learning goals, and check every guide question against them before you start. 'Research is not an exercise in curiosity'; it is about specific pain points in an experience. For OnCourse, a study might start from 'students drop off after day 3 of the plan'.

Key points.title: Show the pain behind each insight
Key points.detail: His 'pain-insight equilibrium': an insight is far more compelling when the pain that led to it is just as clear. Telling executives 'we need this feature' is the TL;DR version that people don't act on. Video of a user 'really really struggling', with frustration on their face, 'does something to us that no Slack message could ever do'. Stories need a hook like Mr Beast's first 30 seconds, and a micro story can still fit in a minute or a Slack message.

Key points.title: Use an interview guide, never a script
Key points.detail: 'The magic moment in interviews is always in the follow-up question', and those are never in your guide. A script over-standardizes and kills that. You can only ask a good follow-up if you are listening, not thinking about your next question. Useful follow-ups: ask why again, ask people to clarify, and ask about an emotional reaction you noticed. He recommends Steve Portigal's book 'Interviewing Users', and piloting interviews with colleagues first.

Key points.title: Spend 3–5 minutes on rapport; it pays back
Key points.detail: An interview is not a natural situation for people. His habit is to ask about something specific in the participant's background, because people keep things around that matter to them. It shows interest in them beyond the interview and finds a shared point of connection. Take 'three, four, even five minutes' instead of 30 seconds, because 'the other 25 minutes of the interview will be so much more effective'.

Key points.title: Quant shows what happens; qual explains why
Key points.detail: Quant can show a drop-off after level 3 of Duolingo math, or clients on a marketplace giving freelancers bonuses mid-job, but never why. Until now you chose between shallow data at scale and rich data from about five people. AI interviewers like Genway can run qualitative interviews 'at essentially an infinite scale'. His startup stack: Sprig (in-product surveys, replays, usability tests), Genway, and Dscout for diary studies.

Key points.title: Late usability tests can still find big wins
Key points.detail: He rejects calling usability testing 'tactical' or 'just validating'. Tests near launch often find problems in usability, copy or the call to action. Fixing them can have 'an outsized incredible impact', even 'millions of dollars worth of additional revenue'. Research should also come into every crit early, not only at the end. For OnCourse, a quick test of paywall or onboarding copy before release is worth doing.

Title: Designing Claude Code (and what's coming next) (Meaghan Choi)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Meaghan Choi)
Bottom line: Let AI do the polish and small fixes so you spend your time on the hard part: the mental model and 'shape' of the product, and decide when polish is worth it.
What they did: Meaghan, design lead on Claude Code, uses HTML artifacts as a mini decision log: Claude pulls research and data to the top, states the goal, shows 3–4 design versions, and links to side explorations with the chosen option marked. Once an idea is mid-fidelity she has Claude rebuild it with real components and it becomes a PR. Through Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) she gets draft PRs with before/after screenshots for UI fixes, plus a weekly cleanup job. She stacks nicer PRs on top of engineers' PRs and is building an automated reviewer that asks her usual questions (who is this for, does it match the design system, does it need a name).
Results: She says 'more than half of my code is done like this now' (via Claude Tag in Slack).
Takeaways: Know when to shape the idea vs polish it; Use one HTML artifact as a mini decision log; Make quality shared instead of gatekeeping it; Decide which UI stays fixed and which adapts; Just because you can build it doesn't mean ship it; Hand small UI fixes to Claude with before/after screenshots
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: For each feature, make one HTML artifact with the goal, PostHog data, 3–4 options and the chosen one marked, and share that instead of a Figma link. Design process: Write down the questions Sainath asks in review (who is this for, which existing component, does it need a name) and turn them into an AI review step for engineers' PRs. Design process: Label each prototype 'testing the shape' or 'testing polish' so crits judge the right thing.

Key points.title: Know when to shape the idea vs polish it
Key points.detail: Meaghan says a key skill is knowing when to use AI for execution and when to 'go deep and do the thinky work'. Many people ask Claude to execute when the shape itself is wrong, and 'Claude is not good today at telling you if your idea is wrong'. Experiments that test a mental model can look rough on purpose; polishing them wastes time if the shape turns out wrong. She expects her designers to know which is which. For OnCourse, label each prototype as testing the concept or testing the polish.

Key points.title: Use one HTML artifact as a mini decision log
Key points.detail: She asks Claude to pull research and data (from BigQuery, Slack and docs), summarize it at the top, state the goal, and lay out three to four design versions. Side artifacts hold deeper explorations, like five entry points, and link back with 'I chose option A' marked. This works better than a Figma file for execs, who rarely open a canvas. Once it feels mid-fidelity, she has Claude rebuild it with the real components, and it grows into a pull request.

Key points.title: Make quality shared instead of gatekeeping it
Key points.detail: Her goal is to 'lower the floor and raise the ceiling' so engineers and PMs own quality too. She stacks nicer PRs on top of engineers' PRs, which doesn't slow them down or erase their work. She is building an automated reviewer that asks her usual questions: who is this for, does it match the design system, should it be a product or a feature, does it need a name. She says to frame it as teaching and adding, not stopping people.

Key points.title: Decide which UI stays fixed and which adapts
Key points.detail: She is more and more sure we will still need many fixed interfaces. Things like a login screen or billing settings should stay stable so people don't relearn them. 'A lot of people don't want everything to be customized. The right things should be customized and adaptive.' For adaptive parts, design how people can tell something is adaptive, and whether they are customizing the tool or its output.

Key points.title: Just because you can build it doesn't mean ship it
Key points.detail: With AI, everything feels easy to build, so teams build everything, which adds bloat and complexity. 'Not every idea is good or necessary. Sometimes adding it is worse.' She lists discernment, her word for taste, as a core skill: what to build, how to shape it, and when to say 'that was actually bad, let's not do it'. This applies directly to adding features to a study app.

Key points.title: Hand small UI fixes to Claude with before/after screenshots
Key points.detail: In Slack, through Claude Tag, she asks for fixes like removing a stray drop shadow. Claude finds the code, opens a draft PR (so CI doesn't run) with before and after screenshots, then merges and pings engineers for review once she approves. 'More than half of my code is done like this now', and a weekly job proposes cleanup PRs. Once, Claude filled a gap in her mockup with its own design call and said why, and 'it was right'.

Title: Our AI design workflows have changed (again) (Kyle Zantos)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Kyle Zantos)
Bottom line: Use cheap HTML files from your AI agent as review tools: side-by-side options, before/after animations with sliders, and approve/deny lists that paste back into the agent.
What they did: Kyle has the agent run design audits with several skills and output one HTML doc listing every proposed change with approve/deny/discuss options and a 'copy all' button to paste back; for motion it shows current vs proposed animation. Ridd prototypes 4 layouts in HTML, dictates feedback while clicking, and repeats; he shipped a fidget-spinner hover effect in about 5 minutes after three rounds. Ridd also had Claude render every toast, dialog and error message on one HTML page with inline editing, to write all system copy together. Ridd now records Supercut videos talking over designs (like a handoff to an engineer) and gives them to the agent with the Paper frame.
Results: Ridd says the agent's accuracy from his Supercut video feedback is '80 90%'.
Takeaways: Turn AI audits into an approve/deny HTML review page; Explore wide and cheap in HTML before building; Write all system copy together on one page; Talk over designs on video, like a handoff; An auto review loop makes variations hit a basic bar; Spend more time planning in HTML and Paper
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Generate one HTML page with every OnCourse toast, error, empty state and notification text, edit them together, and paste the changes back. Design process: For motion work (streak flame, answer feedback in Practice), ask for before/after versions side by side with sliders for duration and easing. Design process: Record a short video walking through a Paper/Figma frame and hand it with the frame link to the coding agent.

Key points.title: Turn AI audits into an approve/deny HTML review page
Key points.detail: Kyle chains several skills (from Emil Kowalski and Jakub Krehel) into one audit run. An orchestrator sends sub-agents to run each skill, removes duplicates, and outputs one HTML doc. Every proposed change has approve, deny or discuss options, and a 'copy all' button pastes his answers back into the session. For motion, the doc shows the current and proposed animation side by side. His standing rule: 'give me the closest possible representation of the real thing'.

Key points.title: Explore wide and cheap in HTML before building
Key points.detail: Ridd asks Claude to prototype a component four ways, then dictates feedback while clicking around ('I like layout 2, change this, show me four more'). For a commit chart he wanted to feel 'like a fidget spinner', he had no words for it, so he asked for many effects, cut the bad ones and zoomed in on 'disperse'. He shipped it 'in about 5 minutes based off of three rounds of HTML prototypes'. Static design tools work for concepts, but 'when you have to feel it, it just doesn't cut it'. This fits OnCourse motion like answer feedback or streak animations.

Key points.title: Write all system copy together on one page
Key points.detail: Inspired by Raphael Schaad of Cron, who kept every toast, dialog, error and notification in one Figma file, Ridd had Claude render all his system messages on one HTML page. It has inline editing, so he can type changes and send a prompt back. Doing this in Figma was a lot of manual work; in Claude it was a one-shot. They note a content team could own this page. For OnCourse, it is a quick way to make error, empty-state and notification copy consistent.

Key points.title: Talk over designs on video, like a handoff
Key points.detail: Ridd records Supercut videos and gives them to the agent through Supercut's MCP, which matches his words to video frames. He puts 'like 15 pieces of feedback' in a six or seven minute ramble, and puts the accuracy at '80 90%'. For a build, he selects a Paper frame with annotations, adds a four-minute Supercut talking it through 'exactly the same as handoff', and says 'build this'. He also records 40-minute product sessions and has the agent turn his comments into tickets and a UX audit.

Key points.title: An auto review loop makes variations hit a basic bar
Key points.detail: Kyle got tired of five predictable variations full of obvious errors he had to point out 'like you would tell an intern'. In Terminal Graph he set up a pipeline: five different styles, an audit by an independent sub-agent using chosen skills, then refinements, repeated for three rounds. Browser nodes show V1, V2 and V3, so he can see where the review is too weak. He built it only by describing what he wanted to the agent and giving it the tool's docs.

Key points.title: Spend more time planning in HTML and Paper
Key points.detail: Both have moved from tweaking the real app (prompt, wait, prompt, wait) to going wide cheaply in HTML, then nudging layouts in Paper, then a full build. Ridd: 'it's much slower to manipulate the real thing than it is to kind of dial it in'. He now writes fewer long prompts but does bigger builds. They compare it to engineers who spend 70% of their time planning before agents build.

Title: Takeaways from interviewing 100+ design teams about their process (Brian Lovin)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Brian Lovin)
Bottom line: Healthy design teams share rough work early in an open feed, say what they will do each week, and cut features nobody uses.
What they did: At Campsite, Brian's team 'calls their shot': Monday kickoff, Friday recap and a daily bullet list in Slack, plus 'radiating intent' (I'm doing this, speak up if not). They built Linear and GitHub issue creation because customers asked, moved the button out of an overflow menu when nobody used it, then deleted it, and zero people complained. He shares design updates like tweets in a feed so the team builds 'ambient awareness', which at Facebook (Pixel Cloud) helped him spot related work and duplicates. When asking for feedback he says what he wants feedback on and what he doesn't.
Results: Issue creation: 'nobody used it… a handful' of issues even after making the button prominent; after deleting it 'zero people complained'.
Takeaways: What users ask for isn't always what they use; Say what feedback you don't want; Share rough work like tweets to build ambient awareness; Sharing gets scarier as the audience grows; Call your shot, then radiate intent; Pick the format for the audience
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Post every rough OnCourse exploration (including discarded ones) to one shared channel, short and unpolished, so PMs and engineers see the process. Design process: When sharing for feedback, add one line on what you want comments on and one on what you don't. Home: Check PostHog usage for each Home card or entry point and remove ones almost nobody taps.

Key points.title: What users ask for isn't always what they use
Key points.detail: Customers asked Campsite to create Linear and GitHub issues from a post, and the team wanted it too. They built it with full syncing, but 'nobody used it… a handful' of issues. They moved the button out of a three-dot overflow menu onto every post, and still nobody used it. They deleted it and 'zero people complained'. Brian's rule: 'everything added to an interface dilutes everything else', so check usage and cut. For OnCourse, look at PostHog taps on each Home entry point and remove the ones almost nobody uses.

Key points.title: Say what feedback you don't want
Key points.detail: The usual advice is to say what feedback you want. Brian adds the opposite: say what you don't want. His examples: 'I don't want comments on these icons', 'I know this color is wrong, please don't talk about it.' This means thinking about who you want feedback from and what context they need before you post. It keeps feedback focused and saves the reviewer's time.

Key points.title: Share rough work like tweets to build ambient awareness
Key points.detail: You don't read every tweet, but scrolling a feed leaves 'breadcrumbs' about what people are doing. Brian wants design updates shared the same way: short, unpolished, and fine to scroll past. At Facebook he browsed the internal tool Pixel Cloud daily from the payments team. He spotted other designers building Commerce things and offered work they could reuse, '1 plus 1 equals 3'. Teams on Campsite also find duplicate work this way. Ridd adds that discarded explorations are often the most useful thing to see.

Key points.title: Sharing gets scarier as the audience grows
Key points.detail: A five-person design team with shared trust will post scribbles and rough screenshots. Once PMs, engineers and the CEO join as viewers, people get anxious about showing unpolished work. Brian says remote work made this worse, so designers retreat into Slack DMs. He finds many design leaders want more work-in-progress shared but won't ask, because it costs 'social and political capital'. His view: if a leader won't put 'skin in the game' and say 'this is a thing we do now', the culture won't change.

Key points.title: Call your shot, then radiate intent
Key points.detail: Campsite does a Monday kickoff, a Friday recap and a daily bullet list in a Slack updates channel. Saying what you will do in front of peers forces you to be specific, instead of 'just working on this project'. 'Radiating intent' means saying 'I am going to do this, speak up if you don't want me to', rather than asking permission. Brian says this small shift is what lets great teams move fast. A third habit, 'everybody shovels snow', means doing grunt work like tidying files and bug-hunting preview builds.

Key points.title: Pick the format for the audience
Key points.detail: Brian's quick guide: executives probably need a deck, PMs a doc, another designer a screenshot or prototype, and an engineer a prototype. He says you learn this by noticing when a different format got better results with a certain person. Elsewhere he warns that flashy landing pages with Bento grids often leave people not knowing what the product does. Campsite built its landing page in 24 hours, focused on words you read as you scroll.

Title: Designing with a growth mindset (Kate Syuma)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Kate Syuma)
Bottom line: Onboarding is a journey to setup, aha and habit moments, not a tooltip tour; test small changes you can explain instead of big redesigns.
What they did: At Miro, Kate's growth team tested adding an animated, product-like preview to the sign-up flow to show value; users tried to interact with the visuals, got distracted and dropped at each step, so they removed it and conversion improved (she now thinks they should have tested a quieter version). They learned that big bets changing many things at once were hard to read, while small personalization changes had clear, explainable effects. She defines activation by working backwards: find retained or paying users, find the early actions they share, and keep the aha moment simple (e.g. create one piece of content). Her study of 80+ companies found most still rely on step-by-step tooltips users skip.
Results: In her research of 'more than 80 companies', 'more than 60% of companies' rely on step-by-step tooltips. Miro sign-up test: the animated preview made users drop 'on each step a little bit'; removing it 'worked way better' (no figure given).
Takeaways: Adding product previews to sign-up made people drop off; Define activation backwards, starting from the habit; Split big bets into small tests you can explain; Most companies still lean on tooltips users skip; Growth teams own whole flows, not features; People value what they help create (IKEA effect)
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: Keep sign-up steps plain; don't add animated previews of Practice or Lessons inside the flow, show value right after sign-up instead. Onboarding: Define OnCourse's habit moment from retained students in PostHog (e.g. finish Today's plan X days in week 1), then design onboarding to reach the first MCQ set fast. Notifications: Plan the first 2 weeks of push and email as part of onboarding, tied to the setup, aha and habit steps.

Key points.title: Adding product previews to sign-up made people drop off
Key points.detail: Miro's growth team believed users didn't finish sign-up because they couldn't see the product. They added animated, product-like visuals to the sign-up steps. Users tried to interact with them, but they weren't interactive, so people got distracted and 'dropped on each step a little bit'. Removing it all 'worked way better'. Kate now thinks the fix was too radical and they should have tested a quieter, less interactive version. For OnCourse, keep sign-up plain and show value right after it.

Key points.title: Define activation backwards, starting from the habit
Key points.detail: Kate uses three moments: setup, aha and habit. She says start from the last one, which feels counterintuitive. Find engaged or paying users, look at what they did early on through data or regression analysis, and work back to find the aha moment. Then keep it simple, for example 'create one piece of content for a specific use case'. She warns this needs enough users and data, so it is not for the very earliest stage. For OnCourse, find what retained students did in week 1 and design onboarding to reach it.

Key points.title: Split big bets into small tests you can explain
Key points.detail: Later at Miro, the team ran big experiments that changed many things at once. It was then very hard to tell what worked and, more importantly, what didn't. Kate's lesson: break big bets down and test a prototype or small version first, instead of spending a quarter building. Small changes are easier to read because 'you can connect the dots'. She says even a small personalization change had a clearer effect than a whole new tutorial or sign-up flow.

Key points.title: Most companies still lean on tooltips users skip
Key points.detail: Kate and a former colleague researched onboarding at 'more than 80 companies'. 'More than 60%' relied on step-by-step tooltips, which users click through with 'next, next, next, done'. Other common mistakes: treating onboarding as only the first session, not investing in emails and lifecycle messages, and giving everyone the same flow even though personalization works best. She says onboarding is a journey that can take weeks for complex products.

Key points.title: Growth teams own whole flows, not features
Key points.detail: A growth team optimizes for learning, so it experiments and iterates a lot. An activation team thinks across the website message, the sign-up flow, personalization, the first aha moment, what to trigger in the product, and which emails to send afterwards. It defines activation in data, watches where the biggest drops happen, researches why, and keeps running experiments until the number moves. Kate uses Canva as a hypothetical example of finding a product's core value.

Key points.title: People value what they help create (IKEA effect)
Key points.detail: Kate learned user psychology through more than 100 user interviews in one year and the growth.design psychology course. She points to the IKEA effect: people are more engaged with things they invested in or made themselves. She worries that AI products which do everything with one button lose that sense of belonging. Step-by-step tooltips also miss it, because they are not 'learn by doing'. For OnCourse, let students set or build part of their plan themselves.

Title: Plaid's culture of craft, tips for CRIT, and lessons from early Facebook (Christophe Tauziet)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Christophe Tauziet)
Bottom line: Craft comes from process: many from-scratch explorations, open work, varied crits, and a final polish review by the same senior panel before build.
What they did: Plaid added 'polish reviews': a fixed panel of about four senior ICs, including a content designer, nitpick every Figma file in the 24–48 hours before engineering starts (spacing, consistency, copy like noun vs verb buttons). Designers can call 'design jams' where others help explore a problem for an hour or more. Crits are 7–10 people and switch formats: traditional, silent crit (5 minutes of Figma comments to music), and no-context crit where the work must speak for itself. Christophe pushes designers to start each exploration on a blank artboard (like a Facebook designer who, for the first screen of an onboarding, made 20 blank artboards and designed each version from scratch) and to share short face-on Loom videos with their opinion and doubts.
Results: Polish review panel comments per file dropped from '20 30 comments' a year earlier to 'five six seven' now. Best crit size: 'between seven and 10'.
Takeaways: Run a final polish review before engineers start; Start each exploration on a blank artboard; Keep crits to 7–10 people and vary the format; Ask why instead of saying 'I like', and never vote; Name a ritual so asking for help is easy; Share short videos that show your face and your opinion
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Add a 24-hour polish review before handoff where the same 2 people check spacing, components and copy on every screen. Design process: Run a no-context crit on Paywall and Onboarding screens, since students won't get an explanation either. Design process: For the next new screen, make 10 versions each starting from blank before picking one.

Key points.title: Run a final polish review before engineers start
Key points.detail: Plaid created a fixed panel of about four senior ICs who know the design system well, including a content designer. They get every Figma file in the last 24 to 48 hours before engineering starts and nitpick: margins, consistency with other screens, typos, buttons that use a noun instead of a verb. Partners first complained it added two days, but it now catches questions engineers would ask later, like why one font is 16px and another 18px. A year ago files got '20 30 comments'; now it's 'five six seven', because designers learned from the feedback.

Key points.title: Start each exploration on a blank artboard
Key points.detail: Duplicate-and-tweak keeps you anchored on your first idea and stuck in a 'local maxima'. Christophe's favorite Facebook colleague would make 20 empty artboards for the first screen of a new onboarding and design each from scratch. She once made around a hundred very different app icons for one photo app. He says every designer he gave this advice to came back saying 'I'm a different designer now'. It's 'pure process', not skill. Ridd calls the duplicate habit 'iteration theater'.

Key points.title: Keep crits to 7–10 people and vary the format
Key points.detail: Three people give too little feedback; at 20 only the same two people speak. The best size is 'between seven and 10'. Plaid switches formats: a traditional crit; a silent crit where the designer gives 3 minutes of context, then everyone drops Figma comments for 5 minutes to music; and a no-context crit where the work must speak for itself, like it will for real users. Christophe also pushes designers to share early, even a napkin sketch, before they get too attached to defend the work.

Key points.title: Ask why instead of saying 'I like', and never vote
Key points.detail: Christophe prefers candid feedback without sugar-coating, once trust is built. He dislikes feedback that starts with 'I like', because it turns into a taste contest. He bans voting on a favorite design: 'this is design by committee'. Instead, debate pros and cons and iterate on fixable cons. Senior designers start with questions, like 'why is this button rounded?', which teaches the designer to ask themselves that next time.

Key points.title: Name a ritual so asking for help is easy
Key points.detail: At Plaid any designer can call a 'design jam'. Others come and explore the problem with them for one, two or five hours. This spreads context, so later feedback is sharper. Helpers often go back to their own project and start over with a better idea. Ridd points out that naming it removes the social cost of writing 'I'm stuck, can someone help?'

Key points.title: Share short videos that show your face and your opinion
Key points.detail: Plaid designers post short Loom or Screen Studio videos of their work in public channels, so PMs and engineers can follow along and flag problems early. Christophe's tips: keep it to about three minutes, say what feedback you need, give your own opinion and doubts, show your face, and explain why. He says a 3-minute video beats a three-page doc, and that people who followed the process rarely push to cut scope later. He also calls a prototype 'worth a thousand meetings'.

Title: Make landing pages that convert (Erik Kennedy)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Erik Kennedy)
Bottom line: A sales page lives or dies on its headline and subheads; write them to state the main value and answer objections, and use real, ugly testimonials over polished ones.
What they did: Erik's headline rule: 'the most succinct statement of the greatest value for the greatest number of your customers', so any plausible buyer sees they are the target. Subheads should tell about 90% of the story and never be bare labels like 'Our process'. He lists likely objections up front and answers each with a matching testimonial (Clout Monster pairs 'even with no prior connections' with a customer who had none). He prefers small, contained animations (Lemonade's subtly moving hero) over scroll-jacking, and agreed when Ridd showed Formcarry's animated icons inline with headings, and uses tricks like frame breaks and the 'SLUB' label style (smaller, lighter, uppercase, bold). Ridd shares that on an education product, swapping raw Facebook-group screenshots for designed testimonial cards made the page convert worse, and putting the screenshots back recovered it.
Takeaways: The headline must make readers see they're the target; Subheads should tell 90% of the story; Raw, ugly testimonials beat polished ones; Pick testimonials that remove a specific doubt; Put the phrase that wows people in person up top; Small contained animations signal quality without distraction
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: Rewrite the headline as the single biggest benefit for most NEET-PG students and make each feature row a full claim, not a label. Paywall: Add testimonials that answer common objections (e.g. 'I started late', 'I'm repeating the exam') as real WhatsApp or review screenshots, not redesigned cards. Renewal: Lead with the outcome students mention most in interviews.

Key points.title: The headline must make readers see they're the target
Key points.detail: Erik says the headline matters most, then the subheads; if they fail, the body text doesn't matter. His rule: 'the most succinct statement of the greatest value for the greatest number of your customers'. Every plausible buyer should read it and think 'I'm the target market'. He calls a landing page a 'blindfolded sales pitch' to someone who can't ask questions and can leave at any second. He notes Lemonade's 'Forget everything you know about insurance' fits the brand but doesn't meet this rule.

Key points.title: Subheads should tell 90% of the story
Key points.detail: If someone reads only the H1 and subheads, they should understand what you offer. Erik says subheads can be '10, 20 x more important' than body text. Ridd's pet peeve is subheads that are just labels like 'Our process'. Erik's fix is to make a claim: 'our easy three-step process', 'rated 4.9 stars'. For an OnCourse paywall, each feature row should be a full benefit, not a label.

Key points.title: Raw, ugly testimonials beat polished ones
Key points.detail: On an education product, Ridd replaced raw screenshots from a Facebook group with nicely designed testimonial cards. Conversion dipped. When he put the 'ugly' screenshots back, it went right back up. The raw versions felt more authentic. Erik adds that obviously unedited proof, like embedded tweets or a Twitter icon, signals 'somebody hit enter on this'. For OnCourse, use real review or WhatsApp screenshots rather than redesigned quotes.

Key points.title: Pick testimonials that remove a specific doubt
Key points.detail: Clout Monster, a press consulting site, pairs each claim with a matching customer. 'Even when they had no idea where to start' sits next to someone who had no idea where to start. 'Even with no prior connections' sits next to someone with none. Erik's first Landing Page Academy worksheet asks you to list the objections you'll hear again and again and answer them on the page. Superlative quotes like Runway's 'unlike any other product' also tell readers they don't need to compare.

Key points.title: Put the phrase that wows people in person up top
Key points.detail: When you explain the product in person and keep seeing the same phrase or feature make people go 'oh, wow', that should be higher on the page. 'The same things that sell something in real life are going to sell something on a landing page.' Erik also says to write like 'a clear, helpful, confident person talks', and to say true things competitors can't say. 'A better way' could be said by anyone.

Key points.title: Small contained animations signal quality without distraction
Key points.detail: Lemonade's hero looks like a static illustration, but a few parts move subtly, which makes the site feel high quality. Erik thinks anything 'hard to do in Figma' reads as rare and well made. He advises most teams to skip scroll-jacking and keep animation contained within sections, like Formcarry's small animated icons beside headings. He adds cheap tricks: frame breaks where an image spills out of its box, and the 'SLUB' label style (smaller, lighter, uppercase, bold). Free animations on LottieFiles can work well.

Title: Crafting interfaces with uncommon care (Josh Puckett)
Creator: Dive Club (Ridd with Josh Puckett)
Bottom line: Use AI's speed to go deeper on a few essential moments, not to add scope; a personal, playful onboarding token people make themselves gets shared.
What they did: For Interface Craft's onboarding, Josh gave each buyer a library card they pick from an infinite canvas of color combos and sign themselves; people spent minutes on signatures and shared them, which made it spread. He moved from a 5-card picker (felt limited) to the canvas, and later added one 'magic' slider that changes hue, saturation and lightness at once and a Lissajous (infinity-shaped) slider that controls three graphic settings, with no labels, to invite play. Buttons morph in place (Edit name becomes Done, input auto-focuses, other content fades) instead of opening dialogs, and the card is dragged into a slot with sound, inspired by Mailbox's coin. He sketches rough interaction storyboards in Figma, pastes them as images into AI tools, and tries many versions fast.
Results: He launched January 13 and opened the library February 10, about 4 weeks later; there are '14 color combinations' on the card canvas. No conversion numbers given.
Takeaways: A token people make themselves gets shared; Use AI speed to go deeper, not to add scope; Edit in place instead of opening dialogs; Combine several controls into one to invite play; Give the token a real use later; Sketch interactions roughly and let AI build versions
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: Let students create a personal 'exam card' (name, target exam, signature or color) and reuse it later on Streaks and the profile. Streaks: Add one tactile moment (drag, sound, haptic) when a streak milestone is claimed, kept to that single spot. Design process: Sketch interaction storyboards as grey boxes in Figma and paste them into the coding agent to try 5+ versions in an hour.

Key points.title: A token people make themselves gets shared
Key points.detail: When people pre-bought Interface Craft before any content existed, Josh gave each one a library card to pick and sign. He first tried five cards to choose from, but it felt limited, so he moved to an infinite canvas of 14 color combinations. People spent minutes on their signatures, drew smiley faces and scenes, and shared recordings. Josh says that co-creation made it feel personal and is why it went viral. For OnCourse, a student-made 'exam card' could be shared and reused later.

Key points.title: Use AI speed to go deeper, not to add scope
Key points.detail: Josh's main point: now that tools let us explore faster, 'instead of creating more scope', take the essential scope and 'execute it to a bar' people haven't seen. He quotes the Shaker furniture rule 'make it as well as you can and make it as simple as you can' and Bruce Lee's 'hack away at the inessential'. He also uses 'conceptual range then depth': list many ways to do something, pick one, then go very deep. He spent as much time on the scratch-off gift card as on the rest of onboarding.

Key points.title: Edit in place instead of opening dialogs
Key points.detail: Josh calls the usual approach, a pop-up to edit your name, 'very unconsidered'. On the card, tapping Edit name turns that button into Done, fades the other content, auto-focuses the input, and changes the label to 'type to edit'. He first had the signature button clear the signature, then saw it was a destructive action that didn't look destructive, so he added a separate erase option. He credits Benji (benji.org) and the Family crypto wallet for 'morphing interfaces'.

Key points.title: Combine several controls into one to invite play
Key points.detail: When members returned, Josh gave them two big, unlabeled sliders. One changes hue, saturation and lightness at once. The other is a 'Lissajous slider' shaped like an infinity sign that controls frequency, phase and amplitude of the card graphic. Three separate sliders felt 'too messy'. He says customers don't want a Lightroom-style panel because it feels like work, and the lack of labels makes people curious to touch things.

Key points.title: Give the token a real use later
Key points.detail: Josh worried a library card you never see again would feel 'lame'. Inspired by Mailbox's waitlist coin, which you dropped into a machine to get access, he made members drag their card into a slot, like a subway ticket. With sound designer Josh Dunsterville he added sounds and a snap-back if you don't drag far enough. For the scratch-off gift card he made three scratch sounds that change with direction. For OnCourse, a streak or milestone token could be 'used' in a satisfying gesture.

Key points.title: Sketch interactions roughly and let AI build versions
Key points.detail: Josh storyboards interactions as rough grey boxes in Figma, copies them as PNG, and pastes them into Claude or v0 as 'a storyboard of what I want'. He says the frames should be even rougher, just color blocks, because only the interaction matters. A first five-card prototype took about five minutes to build and reject. He quotes Kanye's 'five beats a day for three summers': make many versions to build taste. He thinks Figma is still useful for intent, but 'Figma's a lie' for final fidelity.

Title: How Swiggy Designs 0-1 Products (ft. Swiggy Designer)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with a Swiggy designer)
Bottom line: A small Swiggy team shipped whole new apps in one to two weeks by reusing the existing design system, generating mascots, food images and videos with AI, and still fixing every AI flaw by hand.
What they did: For Swiggy's cuisine filter images (90 to 100 cuisines), the team moved from Blender and Cinema 4D to Adobe Firefly, then ChatGPT image and Nano Banana Pro. They kept images consistent by giving a silhouette (same bowl, plate, glass, isometric angle) as a reference plus prompts like 'garnished with a single coriander leaf on top'. Snacc (Gen Z, own kitchen) took two weeks from idea to launch with one week for all design: they swapped the Swiggy primary token from orange to a fluorescent green (hex CAFE33) in a separate DLS, used a ginger cat mascot for every error and empty state, and sat next to engineers to check feasibility screen by screen. Motion is handed off as Lottie JSON through ImageKit links, or as a Jitter or After Effects video with easing and duration values, then a 'PP session' tests on a real phone to fix 2px and easing mismatches.
Results: Snacc went from idea to launch in "two weeks", with "one week to finish the whole design" including UI, animations, illustration, edge cases, error states and branding. Toing (larger, Swiggy-like flow) had "two weeks" total for design, iteration and visuals. Category images are A/B tested per user cohort and changed when they don't convert (no numbers given).
Takeaways: Snacc shipped in two weeks by reusing Swiggy's system; Keep AI images consistent with a fixed silhouette; Error and empty screens deserve a mascot and playful copy; Fix AI tells by hand, because users spot them; Refresh images and A/B test them by cohort; Hand off motion as Lottie or video with values
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: give empty, error and offline states (no questions left, no internet, sync failed) one consistent character and warm copy instead of a generic icon. Design process: for new surfaces, fork only the colour tokens of the existing design system rather than building new components, and hand off motion as Lottie or a video with easing values plus a quick on-device tuning session with engineers.

Key points.title: Snacc shipped in two weeks by reusing Swiggy's system
Key points.detail: Snacc, a Gen Z app where Swiggy cooks the food itself, went from idea to launch in 'two weeks', with 'one week to finish the whole design': UI, animation, illustration, edge cases, error states and branding. It was built on Swiggy's design system. The main change was a separate DLS where the primary orange token became a fluorescent green, hex CAFE33. Designers sat next to engineers and checked each screen's feasibility, like whether a hard shadow was possible. A co-founder reviewed everything in one meeting, which cut out rounds of approvals.

Key points.title: Keep AI images consistent with a fixed silhouette
Key points.detail: Swiggy has 90 to 100 cuisine filter images. They moved from Blender and Cinema 4D (one designer, too slow) to Adobe Firefly, then ChatGPT images and Nano Banana Pro. To keep them consistent they drew silhouettes of the same bowl, plate and glass in one isometric view and gave them as references, plus small prompt details like 'garnished with a single coriander leaf on top'. When Firefly couldn't make a crispy dosa, they ran a night-time design hackathon to crack it.

Key points.title: Error and empty screens deserve a mascot and playful copy
Key points.detail: Snacc used a ginger cat, chosen because Gen Z memes are mostly about cats. It appears cutting a cucumber when items are sold out, holding a skateboard when veg mode has no results, and holding a plug when the internet is off. Toing used its delivery-partner character for 'only in Pune for now' and kitchen-closed screens, with copy like 'we'll be back piping hot'. The team believes 'error screens shouldn't be boring', because users arrive with intent and get frustrated. For OnCourse, empty and offline states could use one consistent character.

Key points.title: Fix AI tells by hand, because users spot them
Key points.detail: For Snacc's food videos they used Kling 3.0 through Higgsfield, with simple English prompts and many variations. They rejected versions where a cherry rotated as it fell, smoke appeared, or a hand levitated, and used negative prompts. For the Toing mascot, the AI kept adding an extra thumb, so it was removed in Photoshop. The designer says these details 'give it away' as AI, and people now call out AI content everywhere. For the second Snacc menu they shot real food in the office so orders would match the pictures.

Key points.title: Refresh images and A/B test them by cohort
Key points.detail: Swiggy refreshes category images every few months. If imagery stays the same it 'becomes this blind spot', and each refresh improves quality. Real photo shoots for hundreds of items would be 'an operational nightmare' and costly. They A/B test images and change them when they don't convert for a user cohort (no numbers given). Food videos were added for 25 to 30 of 60 to 70 items because motion looked more appetizing than still images.

Key points.title: Hand off motion as Lottie or video with values
Key points.detail: Designers never send raw files to engineers. Assets and Lottie JSON files are uploaded to ImageKit, and the link goes to the configuration team. For UI interactions built in code, they share a Jitter or After Effects video plus easing and duration values. Then a 'PP session' tests it on a real phone to fix things like a 2px difference or wrong easing. The designer also taught the team Jitter presets so small animations don't wait on motion designers.

Title: This is how a top Consumer Designer designs in Figma (John, Plaid)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with John, Plaid)
Bottom line: Keep the reasoning behind design options inside the Figma file itself, on labelled cards with pros and cons, and run an async polish review before anything ships.
What they did: Plaid's Figma files separate an 'end to end' page (static screens plus prototype, the page engineers use) and a 'polish' page from a messy 'workspace' page where designers explore freely and leave comments. Each exploration gets a title card with pros and cons, and John uses custom callout components (e.g. 'from @so-and-so, and here's why we went this way') because resolved comments lose their context; options are laid out left to right from minimal to dense, including worst-case truncation and wrapped text. Experiments live on a page per quarter, each with a card listing OKR, experiment name, description, hypothesis, effort and impact estimates and ship date, with control and variants beside it. Before handoff, a panel of designers does an async, non-blocking 'polish review' (accessibility, design-system colours, type sizes, padding, copy with the content strategist, e.g. using the international phone input), after which the work is marked ready for dev.
Takeaways: Give every option a title card with pros and cons; Record decisions on the canvas, not only in comments; Split a clean handoff page from a messy workspace; Lay options out from minimal to dense, with worst cases; Keep one experiment card per test; Run an async polish review before 'ready for dev'
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: in each Figma file, keep a 'handoff' page and a 'workspace' page, and label every Paywall or Onboarding option with a title card and pros/cons before crit. Design process: keep a per-quarter experiments page with one card per test (goal, hypothesis, effort, impact, ship date, control vs variant), and add a short async polish pass by another designer (contrast, tokens, copy) before marking ready for dev.

Key points.title: Give every option a title card with pros and cons
Key points.detail: A Plaid designer, Ian, started the habit and John adopted it. Each concept gets a title, often a literal one like 'we added the new account at the bottom of the list', plus pros and cons. Anyone popping in can see what works and why. In crit John can open with 'I feel like this is strong in this aspect and weak in this one, but what do others feel?' For OnCourse, label each paywall or onboarding option this way before a review.

Key points.title: Record decisions on the canvas, not only in comments
Key points.detail: Once a comment is resolved, 'that context is lost forever'. John uses custom callout components, for example noting that an idea came from a named colleague and why the team went that way. He sometimes leaves important comment threads unresolved on purpose so others see the debate and the decision; one he showed was 10 months old and still referenced. Jay notes this protects knowledge when designers leave or go on holiday.

Key points.title: Split a clean handoff page from a messy workspace
Key points.detail: Plaid's files have an 'end to end' page with static screens and a prototype, which engineers use, and a 'polish' page. A separate 'workspace' page has 'not that many rules', so designers can explore and comment freely. John keeps things tidy by resolving comments right after crits and making the suggested explorations. Many teams touch each product, so a clear structure lets others jump in.

Key points.title: Lay options out from minimal to dense, with worst cases
Key points.detail: Within a concept, John groups sub-concepts left to right: super minimal, minimal, bank-oriented, then robust 'where we just throw everything into your face'. He pushes each one to edge cases: 'the worst case scenario', with lots of truncation and wrapped text. A red 'work in progress' section marks very conceptual ideas so people don't get caught up in details.

Key points.title: Keep one experiment card per test
Key points.detail: Experiments live on a Figma page per quarter. Each has a card with the OKR, experiment name, description, hypothesis, effort estimate, impact estimate and ship date, with the control and variants beside it. John says partners often have only a Google Doc link or a screenshot from Slack. So designers should recap the 'TL;DR', link the doc, and give one well-documented source of truth.

Key points.title: Run an async polish review before 'ready for dev'
Key points.detail: Before handoff, a panel of designers does a final review that is async and 'not meant to be a blocker'. It doesn't revisit first principles. It checks details like accessibility, design-system colors, type sizes, padding and margins. Copy gets reviewed too: John tagged the content strategist to drop the word 'instantly' and split a sentence, and a reviewer suggested the international phone input. After this the work is marked ready for dev.

Title: The 2 Question Rule that makes Design Crits effective (John, Descript)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with John, Descript)
Bottom line: Crits get better when each review type has a clear scope and the room must ask two clarifying questions before anyone gives feedback.
What they did: Descript's head of design split reviews into three: a designers-only craft crit, a cross-functional review of work in progress (all of design and product, with a facilitator), and a formal go/no-go design review; crit does not count as approval. A 'crit vibes' guide, co-written with the team, coaches presenters to set the stage and the audience to lead with curiosity, and the facilitator enforces a 'two question entry fee': the group must ask two clarifying questions before feedback opens. Crit slots are filled in the Monday weekly (he sits in the silence until someone volunteers), crits are recorded and notes shared via Notion AI, and a weekly 'creator challenge' has designers make a video with the product to feel its paper cuts. For AI, the Notion hub has a vibe-coding setup guide for the monorepo, PRs and Figma Make, his personal Cursor rules to copy, and a custom ChatGPT 'UI writing GPT' trained on voice and tone guidelines that suggests button and screen copy from a screenshot.
Results: Team is "about nine" (seven IC designers plus the head of design and a lead researcher). PMs send "messages every week now saying how much they enjoyed" the cross-functional review (anecdotal).
Takeaways: Room asks two clarifying questions before any feedback; Three review types, each with its own scope; Design principles must take a side on dilemmas; Weekly creator challenge makes designers feel paper cuts; A voice-and-tone GPT drafts UI copy from screenshots; Catalyst gets async buy-in without meetings
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: in OnCourse crits, the presenter sets context first and the room must ask two clarifying questions before any feedback; keep crit separate from go/no-go sign-off. Design process: build a copy helper (a Claude project or skill) loaded with OnCourse voice and tone, and paste a screenshot of a Paywall or Notifications screen to get button and headline options. Design process: once a week, each designer does a real NEET-PG practice session in the app and logs the paper cuts they hit.

Key points.title: Room asks two clarifying questions before any feedback
Key points.detail: Descript calls it the 'two question entry fee'. After the designer presents, the facilitator stops the room. The group has to ask two contextual questions in total before anyone gives opinions. John says it has 'done so much more than you think a simple two questions would do', because people often misread work they saw live for 30 minutes. For OnCourse crits, the facilitator can enforce this in one line: 'Who's got our two questions?'

Key points.title: Three review types, each with its own scope
Key points.detail: Descript splits reviews into a designers-only craft crit, a cross-functional review of work in progress (all of design and all of product, with a facilitator), and a formal go/no-go 'Design Review'. Crit is not the place to question roadmaps or to make go/no-go calls. Being seen in crit does not count as approval. This stopped side debates about project decisions from taking over UX feedback.

Key points.title: Design principles must take a side on dilemmas
Key points.detail: John contrasts this with hollow principles like 'create a seamless user experience'. Descript's principles answer its recurring 'design dilemmas', such as novice versus pro users. Examples: 'don't slow the flow', 'easing the curve' and 'great within reach'. One says automation is meant to move creators 'as quickly as possible to the part of the process they actually care about'. A PM now cites them in her own strategy docs. OnCourse could write principles that settle its own debates, like beginner versus topper students.

Key points.title: Weekly creator challenge makes designers feel paper cuts
Key points.detail: Each Monday John sets a challenge: make a video with Descript. Doing a real task under time pressure makes small paper cuts hard to ignore. He calls it 'one of the most reliable ways for us to surface areas of improvement', and it is also fun. For OnCourse, each designer could do a timed NEET-PG practice session every week and log what hurt.

Key points.title: A voice-and-tone GPT drafts UI copy from screenshots
Key points.detail: Descript's AI-native hub in Notion has a vibe-coding setup guide (monorepo, PRs, Figma Make) and John's personal Cursor rules for designers to copy. The team built a custom ChatGPT 'UI writing GPT' trained on Descript's voice and tone guidelines. A designer pastes a screenshot and asks what a button should be called. It fills the gap until they hire a content designer.

Key points.title: Catalyst gets async buy-in without meetings
Key points.detail: Catalyst is a Notion request-for-comment built by founder Andrew Mason, based on Shishir Mehrotra's rituals. You state the proposal and a target date, then tag a 'brain trust'. Each piece of feedback is its own row that people can upvote. Reviewers give a 'pulse' from strongly aligned to strongly unaligned. You can go ahead as long as no one is strongly unaligned. Anyone, including ICs, can start one. The design principles went through it before rollout.

Title: How I Design at Granola (Pawin)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Pawin, Granola)
Bottom line: Block out flows in low fidelity first, then go app to Figma to code: capture the live app into Figma, edit it, paste a PNG into a Claude Code agent, and test one prototype link with A/B/C switchers on weekly user calls.
What they did: The Granola designer blocks out flows in Whimsical's wireframe mode (keyboard shortcuts for buttons, avatars) to think about content and hierarchy, because AI prototypes make you 'narrow down too early'. The app, not Figma, is the source of truth: he uses the html.to.design plugin ('capture current page') to pull the running web build into Figma as editable layers, edits there, copies the frame as a PNG and pastes it into Conductor (Claude Code agents, each in its own git worktree so parallel agents don't clash) with prompts like 'add Granola as an option to the CRM list... use this custom copy... place start of list'. Prototypes use real React components with a screen picker at the bottom and A/B/C variants per screen; he archives versions in plain language ('move this version to archive, duplicate it, call it V3') and shares one Vercel preview link with a share token. He runs four to six user calls a week (context, screen share of their setup, then click-through), includes realistic context screens like a fake payment step, and the team killed a collaborative notes feature after taking it away from internal users and finding they didn't miss it.
Results: He does "four to six user research calls in a week"; Granola's target is that "every single person should be speaking to a user once a week". Collaborative notes was removed after testing with "tens maybe hundreds of users over a multi-month period" (qualitative).
Takeaways: One prototype link with a screen picker and A/B/C variants; Take a feature away to see if anyone misses it; The live app, not Figma, is the source of truth; Start low-fi because AI prototypes narrow too early; Add context screens so testers are in the right mindset; Calm UI hides controls until they are needed
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: build Paywall and Onboarding prototypes in the real React Native web build with a bottom screen picker and A/B/C variants per screen, share one preview link, and use it on weekly student calls. Design process: run separate Claude Code sessions in git worktrees (e.g. via Conductor) so several design explorations can run in parallel without overwriting each other. Onboarding: include a realistic context step (e.g. 'you just bought the plan') in test prototypes so students react in the right mindset.

Key points.title: One prototype link with a screen picker and A/B/C variants
Key points.detail: Pawin asked his agent to add a screen picker at the bottom of a coded prototype. Each screen can switch between A, B and C versions of the copy or graphics. It uses Granola's real React components, so students would click through real UI. He manages versions in plain language ('move this version to archive, duplicate it, call it V3') and shares one Vercel preview link with a share token. OnCourse could test paywall or onboarding variants the same way on student calls.

Key points.title: Take a feature away to see if anyone misses it
Key points.detail: Granola built and shipped many versions of collaborative notes to internal users and design partners. Explaining a merged, shared note right before a meeting was too hard. Then they turned it off for their own staff, and people said they 'didn't really miss it that much'. People cared more about notes being shared automatically. They removed the code after testing with 'tens maybe hundreds of users over a multi-month period'.

Key points.title: The live app, not Figma, is the source of truth
Key points.detail: Pawin says anything in Figma is out of date 'within a week if not a couple of days'. He uses the html.to.design plugin ('capture current page') to bring the running web build into Figma as editable layers. He edits there, copies the frame as a PNG, and pastes it into Conductor with 'build this out'. Conductor gives each Claude Code agent its own git worktree, so parallel agents don't overwrite each other's files.

Key points.title: Start low-fi because AI prototypes narrow too early
Key points.detail: He blocks out flows in Whimsical's wireframe mode with keyboard shortcuts (F for frame, B for button). That keeps him on content and hierarchy, not visual details. He says Claude Design or Cursor prototypes 'make you narrow down too early' because you lock into one direction. Claude Design helps a bit because it gives six or eight options by default.

Key points.title: Add context screens so testers are in the right mindset
Key points.detail: His test prototype starts with a fake payment page, even though it isn't being tested. It places the person at the right point in their life as a customer ('you've just paid, you've got special access'). He thinks about where people are in time, for example right before a meeting, which is 'such a high stress moment'. OnCourse tests could open with a realistic step like 'you just bought the plan' or 'your exam is in 30 days'.

Key points.title: Calm UI hides controls until they are needed
Key points.detail: Granola puts a lot of work into tiny components. A connected chip hides its X until hover, so it isn't 'this giant monster kind of pill' with a check and an X showing at once. Title: How I Built Pocket FM's Prototyping Playground (Harsha)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Harsha, Pocket FM)
Bottom line: Strip the real production app down to a backend-free playground on the real design system, then wrap setup, sharing, deploys and team knowledge in agent skills so any designer can prototype in code with real content.
What they did: Harsha took Pocket FM's web app (and later the native app), removed the backend, analytics and ad SDKs, and kept the real design system components as a shared 'console' repo with a gallery of every designer's demos, auto thumbnails, versions and attached code-handoff docs; demos pull real show data through documented APIs instead of lorem ipsum. Setup is a skill: an 'onboarding' skill checks the Mac, Xcode tools, Homebrew/node, GitHub access, creates a per-designer branch stored in a config file and starts the server; a 'push my work' skill commits, opens a PR to the QA branch, waits for the VPN-only deploy, returns a link and posts to a Slack channel. One CLAUDE.md (symlinked into .claude, .agents for Cursor/Codex) tells agents to use Figma terms (auto layout, frames, fill/hug, constraints), pull the latest before editing someone's demo, and 'don't over code, be calm and learning oriented'; plus skills for DialKit sliders on every demo, Agentation pin comments with a background 'watch mode' agent, a Mobbin skill that knows Pocket FM's domain, a design-system MCP to check which Figma components exist in code, motion skills (Emil Kowalski's web animation design, a motion design skill with iOS HIG curves), and simulator/phone-build skills. A 'learnings' side agent reads each chat transcript on push and appends unsaid rules (e.g. button noise defaults, 'don't render the iOS status bar from Figma') to a shared file in GitHub.
Results: First version of the playground took "less than a week"; used by "around 20 product designers" across four products (Pocket FM, UGC, writer, anime). No metric outcomes cited.
Takeaways: Build the playground on the production app and design system; Prototype with real content, not lorem ipsum; Treat designers as users: setup and sharing are skills; Live knobs and pinned comments replace re-prompting; A side agent turns repeated corrections into shared learnings; A Mobbin skill grounds agents in real UX patterns
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: set up an OnCourse playground repo on the real React Native components with real question/lesson content, an onboarding skill and a 'push and give me a link' skill. Design process: add a CLAUDE.md rule to use Figma terms (auto layout, fill, hug) and a learnings file that collects repeated corrections from sessions. Practice: prototype answer-feedback and streak-celebration motion with live sliders for duration and easing before handing off.

Key points.title: Build the playground on the production app and design system
Key points.detail: Harsha took Pocket FM's web app and removed the backend, analytics and ad SDKs. That left a light 'skeleton' with the real design system components wired in. He asked the tech team for the design system repo, and the first version took 'less than a week'. He chose this over building from scratch because 'there's an entire front-end team' who already built the screens. Later they did the same with the native iOS app.

Key points.title: Prototype with real content, not lorem ipsum
Key points.detail: The playground pulls real show trailers and metadata through APIs documented in skills. Harsha says 'we're a content company and content is our game and we can't mock it every time'. Real data shows true description lengths and edge cases. For OnCourse, prototypes should use real questions, explanations and video titles, because long medical text breaks layouts.

Key points.title: Treat designers as users: setup and sharing are skills
Key points.detail: Harsha watched a designer struggle with GitHub, so he wrote an 'onboarding' skill. It checks the Mac, Xcode tools, Homebrew and node, and GitHub access. It creates a per-designer branch saved in a config file and starts the server. A 'push my work' skill commits, opens a PR to the QA branch, waits for the VPN-only deploy, returns a link and posts in Slack. The shared CLAUDE.md tells agents to use Figma words (auto layout, frames, fill, hug) and to 'be calm and learning oriented'.

Key points.title: Live knobs and pinned comments replace re-prompting
Key points.detail: Every demo gets DialKit sliders, so a designer can change gap, width or animation delay directly. Harsha says asking the agent each time 'is wasting tokens and wasting time'. Agentation gives a Figma-like cursor to pin comments on elements. A background 'watch mode' agent picks up each pin and makes the change live, with no copy and paste. He uses a faster model for these quick loops.

Key points.title: A side agent turns repeated corrections into shared learnings
Key points.detail: On every push, a script reads the chat transcript and pulls out 'unsaid rules'. Examples: the button defaults to medium noise texture and must be passed 'noise none', and 'don't render the iOS status bar from Figma'. These get appended to a shared learnings file in GitHub, so every designer's agent knows them. If a rule keeps coming up, Harsha moves it into a skill.

Key points.title: A Mobbin skill grounds agents in real UX patterns
Key points.detail: Harsha built one screen, then asked Codex to 'look at Mobbin for references and make the password screen'. It studied real password screens before building the next steps. The skill knows Pocket FM is an entertainment app, so it filters for apps like Spotify. He can also ask it to 'look for something fresh' from another industry. He says the answers are better than asking a model what a password screen needs.
