Title: 7 Senior Designers Show How They Collect Design Inspiration (Shopify, DuckDuckGo, Webflow designers)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay, compilation)
Bottom line: To avoid 'AI slop', keep a daily habit of saving good work and, for each project, crop and highlight the exact parts of references you care about so people and coding agents know what inspired you.
What they did: A Shopify designer spends about 10 minutes most mornings bookmarking into Mobbin boards (real flows) and Pinterest (taste), uses Shopify's internal 'Studio' (an internal Dribbble), and for an AI content tool builds a FigJam mood board of Mobbin screenshots with yellow highlights on the specific element (e.g. Midjourney's control panel and gallery sorting) so crops can be handed to a code agent. A DuckDuckGo design engineer uses Mobbin's motion clips instead of screen-recording apps himself; others use Mobbin flows (search an app, open Flows, copy screens into Figma) for competitive audits of navigation, search, steppers, filters, settings and error pages, while trying real apps to feel motion. One designer notes dark mode in good apps uses a dark background with lighter cards, not black cards on gray.
Takeaways: Highlight and crop the exact part that inspired you; Save good work daily and prune it to build taste; Check standard patterns first, then decide where to deviate; Study motion from curated clips, not your own recordings; Try the real app, and pull whole flows fast; Dark mode: dark background with lighter cards
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: keep a shared Mobbin/Pinterest board per OnCourse screen and crop plus annotate the exact element before pasting references into Claude Code or Cursor. Onboarding: before redesigning, pull 5–10 onboarding flows from Mobbin and mark which parts to copy and where OnCourse should deviate. Home: check the dark theme follows the dark background with lighter cards pattern.

Key points.title: Highlight and crop the exact part that inspired you
Key points.detail: A Shopify designer exploring an AI content tool builds a FigJam mood board of Mobbin screenshots. He marks the specific element in yellow, such as Midjourney's control panel and gallery sorting. He says full screenshots have 'too much information' to show what you mean. Cropping helps teammates, and a code agent can be given exactly that crop. For OnCourse, crop the element before pasting a reference into Claude Code.

Key points.title: Save good work daily and prune it to build taste
Key points.detail: The Shopify designer spends about 10 minutes most mornings over coffee bookmarking into Mobbin and Pinterest boards: 'garbage in, garbage out'. Another designer saves everything in mymind, from UI and type to baseball and stamps. Saving and later removing things 'builds your taste'. A teammate's quote sets the stakes: with AI, 'everyone's a seven out of 10 designer now'.

Key points.title: Check standard patterns first, then decide where to deviate
Key points.detail: A Webflow designer uses Mobbin early to see 'what the industry standards are', because 'a lot of things don't need reinvention', like access control. He studies Airbnb's account settings for how sections and toggles nest. He warns that a pattern may not fit your own context and its constraints. Another designer cross-checks navigation, search, steppers and filters across many apps before locking a pattern.

Key points.title: Study motion from curated clips, not your own recordings
Key points.detail: A DuckDuckGo design engineer says motion is what 'gets axed off the end' of timelines. He used to screen-record apps on his phone and pick them apart, which was hard. Now Mobbin's motion clips are his 'most used tool' for visual inspiration. He also watches how tools he uses daily handle thinking states and transitions.

Key points.title: Try the real app, and pull whole flows fast
Key points.detail: One team tries apps themselves because screenshots don't show motion, transitions or feel. For breadth, they search an app on Mobbin (WhatsApp in the demo), open Flows, right-click to copy screens and paste into Figma. That covers a lot of ground quickly for competitor research, including fun cases like error pages.

Key points.title: Dark mode: dark background with lighter cards
Key points.detail: A designer shows that good apps make the background darker and put lighter cards on top. It is easier on the eyes than 'this black abyss'. Nextdoor's light mode uses a gray background with white cards. The instinct to use black cards on gray is the opposite of what users are used to. OnCourse can check its dark theme against this.

Title: 12 Senior Designers Show Their Engineering Handoff Process (Figma, Firefox, Slack, Shopify, Intercom designers)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay, compilation)
Bottom line: Good handoff explains why, every state and edge case, and motion as a storyboard, all in one clearly marked spec; teams designing in code now hand off a branch, PR or preview link instead.
What they did: Figma-based teams keep a separate 'specs' page with only 'ready for dev' sections, an overview and jobs-to-be-done at the top, states, hover/click interactions, long/short text, localization, empty and error states, odd spacing called out explicitly, accessibility screen-reader order, and dated update pages when specs change; one uses a spacing-measure component mapped to size tokens, another writes a grid of every permutation of a side panel and the functionality on-screen because PRDs drift. Firefox splits 'intended design' from what ships in release one after talking to engineering; one designer drew a motion storyboard with in-between keyframes, exact pixel math (pill expands to 343px) and fade timings. Others share a Loom walkthrough plus a live prototype link, or use Magic Patterns to get to 70% for alignment then go back to Figma for the source-of-truth specs. Shopify and Intercom designers instead save to a branch, share a live link with in-browser comments, and open a draft PR plus an experimental build that engineers fork.
Results: Intercom designer: engineers often say "Oh, great. I can use 80% of that" when handed a coded prototype PR. No measured outcomes.
Takeaways: Code handoff: branch, preview link and draft PR; Keep one clearly marked 'ready for dev' spec; Put final requirements on the design itself; Storyboard motion with keyframes and exact numbers; Explain the why, every state and odd spacing; Split the intended design from release one
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: hand off each OnCourse screen as a draft PR plus a preview build, with a short spec note covering why, every state (empty, error, loading, offline) and long Hindi/English text. Practice: write the answer reveal and next-question transition as a keyframe storyboard with timings before engineers build it. Paywall: list every permutation (trial, expired, renewal, discount) in one grid so nothing is missed.

Key points.title: Code handoff: branch, preview link and draft PR
Key points.detail: A Shopify designer saves work to a branch and shares a live link where people leave comments in the browser. Engineers can fork his last commit and 'think with the same materials' instead of translating Figma. An Intercom designer runs a skill that opens a draft PR and an experimental build link. Engineers often say 'Oh, great. I can use 80% of that.' This fits OnCourse, where prototypes are built in the real app.

Key points.title: Keep one clearly marked 'ready for dev' spec
Key points.detail: A Slack designer keeps a separate 'specs' page apart from scratch work, with every section marked ready for dev. She adds small notes like 'edit and remove only shows up if you have permissions'. Another designer uses the green ready-for-dev flag as the only signal and greys out older ideas. Both say they never want to assume engineers 'can read my mind'.

Key points.title: Put final requirements on the design itself
Key points.detail: A Lattice designer writes the functionality on the screens because PRDs and tech docs drift out of date. For a side panel with many states, she made a grid of every permutation, from most collapsed to most expanded. She keeps the designs pixel perfect with system variables, so Dev Mode gives correct specs. Her notes cover only what Dev Mode can't, like 'not needed for milestone one'.

Key points.title: Storyboard motion with keyframes and exact numbers
Key points.detail: A startup designer drew a transition storyboard for an assistant that grows from a button to a pill to a chat. It shows made-up in-between frames, the math ('expands to 343 pixels', the pill moves down by half the padding), and which elements fade in when. He also shared Figma and Principle prototypes. OnCourse could spec the answer reveal or streak animation this way.

Key points.title: Explain the why, every state and odd spacing
Key points.detail: A Figma designer's spec starts with an overview and why it is being built. It covers states, hover and click, long and short text, localization, and empty and error states. She calls out spacing that breaks the grid, like a 2px gap, because Dev Mode won't flag it. After staging feedback she adds a dated page with what changed and keeps the old one for context.

Key points.title: Split the intended design from release one
Key points.detail: Firefox's address bar spec covers secure and insecure sites, reader mode, long URLs, top and bottom bars, landscape, iPad, and screen-reader order. Pages hold the ideal 'intended design'. After talking with engineering, they make a separate first-release version without the hard parts, like translucency. This keeps the vision without blocking shipping.

Title: Inside Lovable's Design Team (Arthur)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Arthur, Lovable)
Bottom line: At Lovable the code base is the source of truth, designers explore wide with an agent in Paper, refine by hand, and the deliverable is a PR or a feature behind a flag, not a spec file.
What they did: Arthur has dropped Figma about 99% for Paper: he captures live production UI with the Paper Snapshot Chrome extension, asks the agent for variants (e.g. '15 variants' of a credits card), picks one and refines manually, leaves comments on the canvas and pastes the comment link to the agent (over the Paper MCP), which applies and resolves them. Lovable's Pulse design system is being mirrored in Paper as themes and tokens, but CI fails code that uses raw hex values, so explorations don't need to be perfect. Designers ship their own PRs through an internal 'Lovable on Lovable' setup: prompt plus a circled screenshot ('turn this button into custom button with plus icon to avoid confusion with close') produces a PR with before/after screenshots that an engineer approves. Crits are booked in an internal tool called Throughline with async comments on a FigJam board; he also built an internal SVG logo hub with a blur preview and a Slack bot so engineers stop asking for connector logos.
Results: Arthur has shipped "like I think 130 PRs" since joining; a small button fix went "from a problem statement to being merged" in "I would say 10 minutes"; Lovable has "over 100 connectors"; design team is "plus 20 people".
Takeaways: Code is the source of truth, and CI enforces tokens; Let the agent go wide, then refine by hand; Canvas comments become the agent's instructions; The deliverable is a PR or a feature flag; Plain cost wording beats clever phrasing; Design for user intent, not a catalog
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: let designers ship small polish PRs with a before/after screenshot and an engineer approval, and add a lint check that flags raw hex colors outside the design tokens. Design process: capture crit comments where the agent can read them (canvas comments or a markdown file) instead of FigJam stickies. Paywall: use plain cost wording like Lovable's 'this uses credits' instead of clever phrasing.

Key points.title: Code is the source of truth, and CI enforces tokens
Key points.detail: Arthur says in 10 years he never saw Figma and code truly match, because both keep moving. So Lovable treats the code base as the source of truth. Explorations in Paper can use raw hex values, because CI fails any code that doesn't use the Pulse design system tokens. Designers don't need perfect files for handoff. OnCourse could add a lint check for raw colors.

Key points.title: Let the agent go wide, then refine by hand
Key points.detail: For a card warning that Google Maps API calls cost credits, he asked the agent for '15 variants' and picked one. The agent made it 'way too complex', so he went 'full manual' in Paper, option-dragging and simplifying. His advice to junior designers: fundamentals like color, type, rhythm and layout are what let you judge the options. Otherwise you settle for 'good enough'.

Key points.title: Canvas comments become the agent's instructions
Key points.detail: In Paper he leaves comments on the canvas, copies the comment link, and gives it to the agent over the Paper MCP. The agent reads the comment and its position, makes the change and resolves the thread. A colleague asked how a FigJam crit would reach the agent, so he now makes sure feedback can be 'consumed and captured as context'.

Key points.title: The deliverable is a PR or a feature flag
Key points.detail: Arthur has shipped 'like I think 130 PRs' since joining. With an internal 'Lovable on Lovable' setup, he prompted 'turn this button into custom button with plus icon to avoid confusion with close' with a circled screenshot. It opened a PR with before and after screenshots. An engineer approved it, and it went 'from a problem statement to being merged' in about 10 minutes. He says the new handoff is 'something I shipped behind a feature flag, go and try it out'.

Key points.title: Plain cost wording beats clever phrasing
Key points.detail: Early versions of the credits card didn't make the cost clear to normal users. The final version just says 'this uses credits'. He says 'we don't use any complicated language'. For OnCourse paywall and renewal screens, state the cost or limit in the plainest words.

Key points.title: Design for user intent, not a catalog
Key points.detail: The connectors dialog was built to get many connectors live, and Lovable now has 'over 100'. An AI audit helped him see past his own tunnel vision. Users don't say 'connect to Stripe', they say 'I want to sell stuff'. The redesign asks what you want to do and groups the sidebar by goals like 'store and sync data'. OnCourse could group content by goals like 'revise weak topics' instead of subject lists.

Title: Wealthsimple’s AI Native Design Process (Danny, Wealthsimple)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Danny, Wealthsimple)
Bottom line: Use a canvas tool (Claude Design, Paper) to go wide fast, then build the chosen idea in the real codebase with Claude Code in plan mode, so teammates react to a working thing and engineers get a pre-reviewed PR.
What they did: Danny lays his tools on a spectrum from explore to refine: Cosmos and Mobbin for references (often from outside finance, e.g. Suno or Spotify for 'help people find stocks'), Claude Design for throwaway high-fidelity clickable concepts, Paper plus Claude Code (via the Paper MCP) to have Claude draw five concepts on a canvas he can then edit by hand, and Conductor (a GUI over Claude Code that gives each task its own git worktree) to build in the Wealthsimple front-end monorepo. For an advanced-trading 'mode switch' he drew resting and hover states of a notch-style 'back to home' control in Figma, pasted the Figma selection links into Claude Code, and asked it to 'use the Figma MCP to read the designs of the selections below', always with plan mode on and 'use the ask user question tool to make sure you understand'. He sometimes opens a second tab to have another model review the plan before it builds. Before tagging an engineer on a PR he runs the team's shared 'do code review' skill, which starts eight subagents (dead code, performance, security, best practices) and returns review notes.
Results: Building the notch prototype in code took about the same time as Figma ('about equal'), but the time to useful feedback was 'much much faster' because people could click a link in the real app. The idea was not shipped, but the prototype let the team judge it without engineering time.
Takeaways: Always start in plan mode and read the plan; Tell the model to interview you first; Canvas tools for going wide, code for precision; Code prototypes speed up feedback, not building; Review your own PR before tagging an engineer; Find references outside your own industry
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Add a 'review my PR' step to Sainath's Claude Code flow (a code-review skill or subagent pass) before engineers are tagged, and hand off with a Screen Studio clip plus the PR, not a Figma file. Design process: Start every prototype prompt in plan mode with 'use the ask user question tool', and paste Figma selection links (Figma MCP) for resting and active states. Practice: Prototype the MCQ answer-reveal and next-question transition in the real React Native app rather than Figma, since motion is exactly what Danny says Figma prototypes can't show.

Key points.title: Always start in plan mode and read the plan
Key points.detail: Danny says he almost never starts without plan mode. He spends most of his time reading the plan. It is like two teammates agreeing on how a feature works before writing code. Reading it catches misreadings, and lets him strip out tests and instrumentation the model adds to a 'scrappy prototype'. Sometimes he opens a second tab and has another model review the plan first.

Key points.title: Tell the model to interview you first
Key points.detail: He ends prompts with 'use the ask user question tool to make sure you fully understand'. The model then asks a form of questions, like platform, deliverable and flow screens. It 'will ask you things that are details that you had in your head' but didn't write down. In Claude Design it asked him to confirm mobile, a clickable prototype, and a loading state between steps.

Key points.title: Canvas tools for going wide, code for precision
Key points.detail: He lays out his tools on a spectrum from explore to refine. Cosmos and Mobbin come first, then Figma, Claude Design and Paper for throwaway concepts. Conductor or Claude Code in the real monorepo is for when he has conviction or needs exact interaction and motion. Claude Design is great for exploring but 'you can't ship this', because it isn't connected to the codebase.

Key points.title: Code prototypes speed up feedback, not building
Key points.detail: For an advanced-trading mode switch, he drew a notch-style 'back to home' control in Figma. Then he had Claude build it in the real app from Figma MCP links to the resting and hover frames. Building took 'about equal' time to a Figma prototype. But getting useful feedback was 'much much faster', because people clicked through the real app. The idea didn't ship, but the team judged it without engineering time.

Key points.title: Review your own PR before tagging an engineer
Key points.detail: Wealthsimple has a shared skills marketplace with a 'do code review' skill. It starts eight subagents that check dead code, performance, security and best practices. Danny runs it before asking for review, because engineers now review far more code from non-engineers. He hands off with a short video voice-over (before versus proposed) plus the PR, then pairs with an engineer on fixes.

Key points.title: Find references outside your own industry
Key points.detail: He tries not to spend much time on competitors. To help people find stocks to invest in, he looked at Suno, Spotify and Apple Music, where curation and merchandising are core. He thinks 'some of the best ideas are coming from' outside finance. OnCourse could look at music or video apps for how to surface the right topic or test next.

Title: Claude Code Workflow for Design Teams (Alan and Becky, Beyond Identity)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Alan and Becky, Beyond Identity)
Bottom line: Rebuild your app as a front-end-only sandbox on the real design system, keep a short CLAUDE.md of rules learned while working, and put every design option behind an in-app switcher so stakeholders review one link.
What they did: Alan, head of design, first built an 'AI version' of the Figma design system in Claude over a weekend by asking Claude to 'walk me through every single step of building a design system from scratch that will work in AI' and pasting Figma screenshots as it asked; it produced a Storybook-like site and checked WCAG contrast. Following advice from Ryo Lu at Cursor, he then rebuilt the whole app page by page from screenshots as a sandbox with mock data; engineering was impressed and connected it to the production design system. His CLAUDE.md grew from corrections ('MUI components only', 'use the theme tokens', one chart library, one icon library, don't redraw logos as SVGs), and he later had Claude shrink it from about 1,000 lines to under 200; an 'audit design system' skill flags hard-coded colors, spacing and accessibility issues. Becky's sandbox includes admin and end-user views, sign-up, and even a simulated terminal using real code, plus a hidden control panel with dropdowns for option, variant, state (empty or filled) and placement; reviewers pull her branch and leave pinned comments through a VS Code plugin Alan built.
Takeaways: Rebuild the app as a front-end sandbox; Put every option and state behind one switcher; Write CLAUDE.md rules as mistakes happen, then trim; Simulate engineer-owned surfaces so designers can improve them; Use color only where it means action; Make a skill only for work you repeat
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Add a dev-only 'design switcher' overlay to the React Native app that flips between options and states (empty, filled, error, new user vs. returning) so crits and PMs review one build. Design process: Keep OnCourse's CLAUDE.md as a short list of rules learned from real mistakes (existing components only, theme tokens, one icon set), and add an audit skill that flags hard-coded colors and spacing before handoff. Home: Show the main number large and the change from last week small and muted, and keep red only for things that need action today, the way Becky treated her dashboard cards.

Key points.title: Rebuild the app as a front-end sandbox
Key points.detail: Following advice from Ryo Lu at Cursor, Alan rebuilt the whole Beyond Identity app page by page from screenshots as a front end with mock data. He calls it about 95% right: "close enough is good enough." Engineering liked it and connected it to the real production design system, so designers explore on real components without touching production. For OnCourse, a mock-data copy of the app gives a safe place to try screens before they reach the real build.

Key points.title: Put every option and state behind one switcher
Key points.detail: Becky built a hidden control panel in her sandbox with dropdowns for option, variant, state (empty or filled) and placement. Stakeholders review one link instead of "15 different links", and she points them to the exact combination she wants feedback on. Changes stay local to the option, like duplicating a Figma page, so nothing flips globally. A dev-only switcher for OnCourse states (new user, returning, empty, error) would make crits much faster.

Key points.title: Write CLAUDE.md rules as mistakes happen, then trim
Key points.detail: Alan did not define rules up front. When Claude built a table that looked different from other pages, he told it to reuse patterns, and Claude wrote rules: MUI components only, theme tokens, one chart library, one icon library, never redraw logos as SVGs. When the file reached about 1,000 lines he asked Claude to optimize it for the next designer, and it came down to under 200. He treats Claude as "a really eager junior designer" who needs notes and feedback.

Key points.title: Simulate engineer-owned surfaces so designers can improve them
Key points.detail: Becky's sandbox includes a simulated terminal that runs the real code, including error states like a policy-denied alert. Without it she would have to ask IT to set up a security rule just to see the flow. Alan says CLI-style UI is now something designers must care about: copy, containers and layout in the terminal can be improved and proposed back in the same repo.

Key points.title: Use color only where it means action
Key points.detail: On the usage card, the main count (847 active sessions) is large and the change (14%) is small and muted. Upward trends are lighter and downward trends dimmer, instead of green and red. Red was added later only for detections and alerts that need action now, because "if colors are overused, you can kind of lose the value and meaning of them." For an OnCourse home screen, keep red for what needs doing today.

Key points.title: Make a skill only for work you repeat
Key points.detail: Alan's "audit design system" skill scans files for hard-coded colors, spacing and accessibility issues and ranks them critical or not. He runs it after a batch of changes or after a PM has edited the sandbox. He warns that Claude will happily generate "a thousand design skills", but you should only build one when you notice you'd otherwise repeat a task.

Title: 7 Top Designers Show How They Do Design Critiques (Figma, Slack, Ramp, CNN, Firefox, Hex designers)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay, compilation)
Bottom line: Good crits are set up by the presenter: state the goal, the phase and the exact feedback you want, collect feedback silently in writing, then discuss, and replay what changed last time.
What they did: A Figma designer structures crit files as context slides (goal, research, hypothesis, timeline, a 'what I need today' slide), then explorations with full-page layouts beside them, then an appendix; the crit is 30 minutes, 15–20 presenting while people drop comment pins silently, then she speed-reads the comments and sums up themes aloud; she also adds a 'riff zone', a disclaimer slide for wild ideas, and a summary of feedback acted on last time. Hex runs a weekly hour in FigJam: 2–3 minutes of context, a 5–6 minute timer for silent stickies under 'what resonates, why' and 'what could be better, why', then the presenter leads discussion. Another team's leader split reviews into craft crit, cross-functional review and go/no-go design review, wrote 'crit vibes', and requires a 'two question entry fee' where the audience asks two clarifying questions before any opinions. CNN's Jennifer demos Cursor prototypes with a version switcher and deploys each git branch to its own URL using a Cursor command ('setup multi-branch deployment'); Slack runs crits as a Slack thread with a feedback legend and a moderator who reads questions back; Ramp gathers async feedback on coded prototypes, then moves to Figma for the 'craft portion'.
Takeaways: Show the feedback you need on a visible frame; Collect silent written feedback before anyone talks; Charge a two-question entry fee before opinions; Keep crit, cross-functional review and go/no-go separate; Open each crit with what changed since last time; Deploy each prototype branch to its own URL
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: Start each OnCourse crit with a 'what I need today' frame and a short 'changed since last crit' list, then a 5-minute silent comment round before any discussion. Design process: Adopt the two-question entry fee and a separate go/no-go review, so crit stays about whether the UX works. Design process: Deploy each prototype branch (e.g. Paywall or Onboarding variants) to its own preview URL so reviewers comment async on the real build.

Key points.title: Show the feedback you need on a visible frame
Key points.detail: The Figma designer adds a "what do I need today" slide to her crit file. In one example it asks for detailed visual and interaction feedback and missed states and edge cases, and says "no thank you" to wild direction changes already discussed. She also uses an axis from "structural exploration" to "implementation" to show which phase each part is in. Putting it on a frame means people can come back to it during the crit, unlike a spoken request.

Key points.title: Collect silent written feedback before anyone talks
Key points.detail: At Figma a crit is 30 minutes: 15–20 minutes of presenting while people drop comment pins, then about 10 minutes of talk where the presenter speed-reads the comments and sums up themes aloud. Hex gives 2–3 minutes of context, then a 5–6 minute FigJam timer for silent stickies under "what resonates, why" and "what could be better, why", because "some people, notably me, are just louder than others." Slack live-tweets the crit in a thread with a feedback legend, and a moderator reads questions back to the presenter.

Key points.title: Charge a two-question entry fee before opinions
Key points.detail: After a designer presents, the audience must ask two clarifying questions in total before anyone gives opinions. The facilitator stops the room to enforce it. The leader says it helps because a 30-minute presentation is hard to absorb live, and questions often play back what people heard or surface missing context about scope. It reminds people that good feedback is tied to the strategy, not "dumping whatever's on your brain."

Key points.title: Keep crit, cross-functional review and go/no-go separate
Key points.detail: One design leader wrote a guide with three review types: a craft-focused crit for designers only, a cross-functional review of work in progress, and a formal design review for go/no-go. Roadmap debates kept creeping into conversations that should be about whether the UX works. It also stops designers assuming that being seen in crit means approval. She also wrote "crit vibes", tips for both presenters (set the stage) and reviewers (lead with curiosity).

Key points.title: Open each crit with what changed since last time
Key points.detail: The Figma designer starts with a summary of the last crit: the decisions made and the feedback she acted on. People work on many projects and can't remember what was said a week or two ago. Showing which feedback was used also makes reviewers feel heard, so they keep giving it. She also adds a "disclaimer" slide before wild ideas so engineers don't rabbit-hole on feasibility, and a "riff zone" where others can remix her frames.

Key points.title: Deploy each prototype branch to its own URL
Key points.detail: CNN's Jennifer used to lay out every drag-and-drop micro-interaction by hand across hundreds of component types. Now she demos a Cursor prototype with a version switcher and deploys each git branch to its own GitHub Pages URL using a Cursor command she runs as "setup multi-branch deployment." She notes Netlify and Vercel do branch URLs too, with Vercel easiest but costliest. Ramp also gathers async feedback on coded prototypes, then moves to Figma for the "craft portion."

Title: Agentic Design Process at Mercury (Carol, Mercury)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Carol, Mercury)
Bottom line: When designing an AI assistant, prototype with the real model and system prompt as early as possible, link answers straight into the right screen, and make anything with real consequences need an explicit tap to confirm.
What they did: Carol designed Mercury's 'Command', an agent that lets users start from intent ('compare this month to last month') instead of the sidebar; answers link into the real page with filters set or the transaction open, and the links are generated by the back end so the model can't invent them. She sketched the mental model in Figma, then vibe-coded a chat prototype in Cursor because turn-by-turn chat can't be felt in Figma; a deterministic prototype hit a ceiling, so she paired with her PM on one wired to a real model and system prompt, and concluded 'the system prompt in a way is the product' and the team should work in prod. For money movement the agent first asks follow-up questions in plain text, then shows a draft object labelled 'Draft' with edit, cancel and send buttons, because real money must be confirmed deterministically. Thinking states were cut from a full stream of chain of thought to a single line ('searching for card data') that users can expand, after people found plain 'thinking' felt slow and the full stream too much.
Takeaways: Prototype AI features against the real model and prompt; Link answers straight into the right screen; Confirm real actions with buttons, not chat; Show thinking as one changing, expandable line; Craft crit catches small hierarchy inconsistencies; Every shipped feature goes live in a public demo
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: If OnCourse adds an AI 'ask about my prep' box, have answers deep-link into the exact Practice set, weak topic or Lesson with filters applied, generated from app data rather than by the model. Today's plan: When an assistant changes the plan (e.g. reschedules mocks), show it as a labelled draft with Edit, Cancel and Confirm buttons before it's applied. Design process: Prototype any AI tutor or explanation feature against the real model and system prompt, not canned replies, and use a single-line expandable 'thinking' state.

Key points.title: Prototype AI features against the real model and prompt
Key points.detail: Carol first vibe-coded a chat prototype in Cursor because the feedback was that you can't feel turn-by-turn chat in Figma. But it was deterministic, so it gave canned answers and "hit a wall" on the real question: how the system responds to different questions. She then paired with her PM on a version wired to a real model and system prompt, and concluded "the system prompt in a way is the product." For any OnCourse AI tutor, test with the real prompt early, not scripted replies.

Key points.title: Link answers straight into the right screen
Key points.detail: Command flips banking from "find it in the sidebar" to "lead with intent." Ask for this month vs last month and the summary links to the Insights page with the right filters set; ask for top transactions and the link opens the Transactions page with that transaction open. The links are generated by the back end so the model can't invent them. An OnCourse assistant could link to the exact weak topic or practice set the same way.

Key points.title: Confirm real actions with buttons, not chat
Key points.detail: For a transfer, the agent first asks follow-up questions in plain text so it doesn't feel heavy, with multiple-choice options being added. It then shows a draft object labelled "Draft" with Edit, Cancel and Send, and only moves money after a tap. Carol says this is "real money that's being moved," unlike a casual chat with Claude. The Draft label came from COO Jason asking that object states (editing, draft, created) be clearer.

Key points.title: Show thinking as one changing, expandable line
Key points.detail: The team tried streaming the full chain of thought and tool calls, but a 10–20 second wait filled the page with text. A plain "thinking" label made people feel it was too slow. They landed on one line that flips through summaries like "searching for card data" and "searching for transaction details," which users can expand to see the full steps.

Key points.title: Craft crit catches small hierarchy inconsistencies
Key points.detail: In a biweekly craft crit, a designer pointed out that a data card used several different type weights, so the eye didn't know where to look. The fix used one weight and one size and "looks a lot cleaner." Carol also dropped an invoice-file preview from the invoice card: it repeated information already in the text and its document text clashed with the UI text.

Key points.title: Every shipped feature goes live in a public demo
Key points.detail: Mercury runs a public demo site anyone can try without signing up. "Is it live in demo, with the right data?" is an item on every launch checklist. It helps sales and hiring: Carol browsed it before joining. Mercury also uses a 0–5 design quality scale agreed with product and engineering, and she aimed Command at a four or five.

Title: How I use Claude Code as a Designer at Shopify (Caston)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Caston, Shopify)
Bottom line: Diverge fast in throwaway vanilla HTML with Claude Code, then converge inside a design-system playground repo and share a live link instead of Figma specs.
What they did: Caston starts each project with a FigJam board of Mobbin screenshots where he highlights the exact part he likes (so people and agents know what inspired him), plus a project folder with markdown context (merchant pains, requirements) and a vanilla HTML wireframe made with Claude Code. He then opens Shopify's 'playground' (a clone of the admin wired to the real design system and the internal Quick hosting, mock DB and AI proxy), dictates a plan to Claude Code in plan mode on Opus, and gives it three inputs at once: the spoken brief, a screenshot of the wireframe, and the wireframe folder dragged into the terminal. He runs several Claude tabs in parallel on separate concerns (one for visuals, one for a Quick DB for images, one for an LLM integration, plus a variant A/B switcher in the rough prototype), starting with only the core surface before adding scope. He shares with 'dev save', which makes an internal link with built-in comments, and hands PM and engineering the branch commit so they fork and edit the same code; he also built a set of 26 markdown commands for the team (e.g. one that aligns tokens with accessibility or checks empty states).
Results: "what might have taken a few days of effort for a version is now like few hours of effort"; "projects have shrunk from like months to days and weeks"; on a recent project the prototype "has given 80% to the developer", with the remaining 20% being polish and string internationalization; the time spent maintaining a Figma artifact for the end-to-end experience is "down to zero".
Takeaways: Give Claude a spoken brief, a screenshot and code; Diverge in throwaway HTML, converge in the real system; Highlight the exact part of each reference; Build the main surface first, then add scope; Prototype AI features with a live LLM; Share a live link and let partners fork the code
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: keep a per-feature folder with a CONTEXT.md (student pains from support/PostHog, requirements) and a throwaway HTML wireframe, then prompt Claude Code in plan mode with brief + screenshot + folder before touching the real React Native screens. Design process: write small markdown slash commands for the team, such as 'check every state' (empty, loading, error) and 'check tokens and contrast', and run them on each prototype. Practice: prototype any AI explanation or doubt-solving feature against a real LLM endpoint rather than static mocks.

Key points.title: Give Claude a spoken brief, a screenshot and code
Key points.detail: In the Shopify playground, Caston dictates a plan to Claude Code in plan mode on Opus 4.6, for example a "generate" button that opens a full-screen surface with a controls panel. He pastes a screenshot of his rough wireframe because "pictures are also very helpful for the model," then drags the wireframe's HTML folder into the terminal. Language, picture and code together give Claude enough to plan. Plan mode then asks him questions back, which he says helps him think.

Key points.title: Diverge in throwaway HTML, converge in the real system
Key points.detail: Each project starts with a folder holding markdown context (real merchant pains, requirements) and a vanilla HTML wireframe built with Claude Code. He explores there because it is fast and "unconstrained by the design system," and he even asks for a variant A/B switcher in it. Only when the idea is clear does he move to the playground, a clone of the Shopify admin on the real design system, which becomes "the converging artifact that I share with people."

Key points.title: Highlight the exact part of each reference
Key points.detail: Caston collects Mobbin screenshots in FigJam and draws yellow highlights on the bit he likes, such as Midjourney's control panel or how it sorts generations. Without that, "there's too much information in these screenshots" for a teammate or an agent to know what inspired you. He crops screenshots to that part before giving them to Claude.

Key points.title: Build the main surface first, then add scope
Key points.detail: He first asked only for the full-screen overlay with a close button, not the whole feature set. Too much scope early makes Claude write a lot of code and makes it "hard to precisely make sure that the main surface is correct," like starting with rectangles in Figma. He then runs separate Claude tabs for separate concerns (visuals, a Quick database for images, an LLM hookup) and never two tabs on the same code, because they'd overlap.

Key points.title: Prototype AI features with a live LLM
Key points.detail: He wires the prototype to Shopify's internal AI proxy because for AI-first features "it's very difficult to do this statically like in Figma," since conversations are open-ended. Using the working prototype also exposed gaps, such as a "from gallery" button that was a dead end and streaming text he disliked. He replaced the stream with four pulsing skeleton squares while images generate. For OnCourse, any AI explanation feature should be tested against a real model.

Key points.title: Share a live link and let partners fork the code
Key points.detail: Typing "dev save" creates an internal link with built-in comments, like a Figma prototype link. He gives PM and engineering the last commit so they can fork it: his PM changed parameters and his engineer added a real AI back end, then he merged their branches back. On a recent project the prototype "has given 80% to the developer," and time spent maintaining Figma specs is "down to zero." He also shared 26 markdown commands with the team, such as one that checks tokens for accessibility or thinks through empty states.

Title: How Razorpay Designers use AI to Ship 8 Projects a Month (PJ and Mina)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with PJ and Mina, Razorpay)
Bottom line: Align on how a flow works with ugly Claude artifacts first, then restyle it with the design system MCP, and walk reviews through in the user's voice from a written design doc.
What they did: For every M or L project (2 to 3 weeks or more) Razorpay designers write a design doc (brief, product and business goals, competitive insights, personas, user stories and narrative) and present walkthroughs to their design head in the user's voice ('I am a merchant with a D2C clothing brand, this morning I want to see my orders...') before showing screens, with all feedback written into a thread. PJ uses Figma only for 'visual note taking': a board with a visual audit of the current flow, 1:1 notes, and competitor screenshots from Mobbin, which he shares with Claude as one big visual prompt. Claude then builds functional artifacts (e.g. a 4-step flow vs a long form) that he uses only to align stakeholders on structure; once aligned, he converts to Blade via the design system MCP, giving one Figma screenshot to match the visual language. Small changes skip Figma entirely: PJ codes them and raises a PR, and PMs now send PRDs as markdown files in GitHub PRs. They run agents from Warp with OpenCode and Claude, and dictate long prompts with Whisper.
Results: Designers are expected to close "7 to 8 line items per head in a month" and were given a goal to "raise 10 to 15 PRs this month"; a handoff for a big project "takes about an hour"; a typical problem statement gets "a week" minimum.
Takeaways: Agree on how it works before how it looks; Walk reviewers through the flow in the user's voice; Use a Figma board as one big visual prompt; Write a design doc for every medium or large project; Ship small changes as PRs, not Figma handoffs; Run recurring sessions so the team learns together
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: in crits, walk through screens as a NEET-PG aspirant ('I'm three months from the exam and opened the app at 6 am to see today's plan') before showing UI, and capture all feedback in one written thread. Today's plan: first build two unstyled Claude artifacts of different structures (e.g. single scrolling list vs stepped sessions) to agree on how it works, then restyle in the real components. Design process: for small copy or spacing fixes, raise the PR directly instead of a Figma handoff.

Key points.title: Agree on how it works before how it looks
Key points.detail: For bigger projects PJ asks Claude for rough artifacts and says "I honestly don't care how it looks right now but I care about how it works." He showed two: a flow with four steps along the top and a single long form. He uses them to settle structure with stakeholders (steps or long form, how to section it, whether to show a preview). Only then does he restyle in Blade, Razorpay's design system, via its MCP, giving Claude one Figma screenshot to match the visual language.

Key points.title: Walk reviewers through the flow in the user's voice
Key points.detail: Their design head, Sony, pushes designers not to say "I click this button and it opens a modal." Instead they narrate as the user: "I am a merchant, I have a D2C brand, I sell clothes, and this morning the first thing I wanted to see was how many orders I got." Product and business goals and why this problem matters come before any screen. Sony writes all feedback into a thread so the designer can keep presenting and revisit it later.

Key points.title: Use a Figma board as one big visual prompt
Key points.detail: PJ now uses Figma for "visual note taking": a visual audit of what's wrong in the current flow, notes from a 1:1, and competitor screenshots from Mobbin. Together these become "a very visual and very extensive prompt" that he shares with Claude, explaining what he thinks, what competitors do and what the PM thinks. The ideation then happens in Claude artifacts, not Figma frames.

Key points.title: Write a design doc for every medium or large project
Key points.detail: Any project of about 2–3 weeks or more gets a design doc: brief, product goals, business goals, competitive insights, personas and problems. The format isn't standardized; Mina likes a user-story and narrative tab. They often write it with Claude and share it before or after the walkthrough. Sony runs four or five open slots a week where designers can bring projects for review.

Key points.title: Ship small changes as PRs, not Figma handoffs
Key points.detail: For a small rewards change PJ coded it and raised a PR, telling the PM "Figma not available." Designers were set a goal to raise "10 to 15 PRs this month" and track planned PRs in a sheet. PMs now send PRDs as markdown files in GitHub PRs. When a big project still needs a handoff, it "takes about an hour."

Key points.title: Run recurring sessions so the team learns together
Key points.detail: A maker session is a formal slot where someone presents a tool, project or way of thinking, such as two designers walking through a new agentic dashboard. That led to a builder day where everyone set up their laptops for front-end work, built a design and got a PR merged. AI open hours are an informal slot to bring any problem and solve it together. The team pace is high: 7 to 8 line items per designer each month.

Title: How Deel Designers Start Prototyping Before PRDs (Chris)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Chris, Deel)
Bottom line: Validate the concept with cheap, deliberately rough prototypes and deep discovery first, and only then spend Claude Code tokens on a high-fidelity prototype in a design-system repo.
What they did: Chris starts some projects from the solution: he builds rough Lovable or Claude Design concepts (e.g. dragging transactions onto invoices vs a fixed transaction with a list of matches for reconciliation), records a 2-minute video for stakeholders and tests with internal users; the side-by-side concept won because it 'prevent[s] more errors'. Deel's engineers built a 'UI playground' repo with many markdown instructions that act as guardrails so Claude only uses the real design system; Chris clones it next to the team's production repo and tells Claude to read the playground rules and implement small changes (a color, a tracking event) as real PRs. He does long discovery in a Figma 'brain dump' (problem context, maps, PRD excerpts) and feeds it to Claude as screenshots for diagrams and plain text for prose to save tokens. When Claude invents a component, he pastes the Storybook link and says 'you are inventing this, please do it correctly with this component'; handoff is a dev-environment link plus a video walkthrough, followed by iterative fixes as engineers find edge cases.
Results: A concept test "takes me like half of a day or... like two hours prompting" and he gets "full validation of the concept... in one day or two days"; Deel has about 90 designers and roughly 4,500 engineers.
Takeaways: Keep concept prototypes rough so people judge the idea; Put design-system guardrails in a shared repo; Spend Claude Code tokens only after the concept is clear; Do deep discovery because decisions have second-order effects; Feed context as text for prose, screenshots for diagrams; Spot invented components and correct with the Storybook link
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: create a shared 'prototype guardrails' markdown (allowed components, tokens, no new primitives) in the OnCourse repo so Claude Code and Cursor prototypes stay on-system, and correct drift by pasting the real component file. Practice: test two rough interaction concepts (e.g. how students review wrong answers) with a few students over a 2-minute video before building the polished version. Design process: hand off with a live build link plus a short video walkthrough instead of static specs.

Key points.title: Keep concept prototypes rough so people judge the idea
Key points.detail: For reconciliation, Chris built two rough Lovable concepts: dragging transactions onto invoices, and a fixed transaction on the left with possible matches beside it. He tested with internal users and the side-by-side one won because it "prevent[s] more errors" (numbers changing while dragging were easy to miss). He keeps them looking unlike Deel on purpose: at high fidelity "people start playing around and you won't get the correct feedback." A test takes "half of a day" or "two hours prompting," and he gets validation in one or two days.

Key points.title: Put design-system guardrails in a shared repo
Key points.detail: Deel's engineers built a "UI playground" repo with many markdown instructions that keep Claude on the real design system. Chris clones it next to his team's production repo and tells Claude to read the playground rules and implement a change in the real repo. He uses this for small PRs like a color change or a new tracking event. For OnCourse, one shared guardrails file would keep every designer's Claude prototype on real components.

Key points.title: Spend Claude Code tokens only after the concept is clear
Key points.detail: Chris ideates first in plain-language Claude chats, Claude Design or Lovable, then moves to Claude Code in the UI playground. He says don't "burn your tokens building software when you don't have enough clear concept in your mind." The concept should be tested and approved by stakeholders and pressure-tested by other designers first. Without discovery "you're going to waste tokens... and deliver more slop."

Key points.title: Do deep discovery because decisions have second-order effects
Key points.detail: His Figma files are "brain dumps": problem context, maps, PRD excerpts and early versions. For the checks module he sat in long meetings with the people who do it by hand and ran a Slack channel with 23 stakeholders. He does this because in a payments product "you can make a decision in this platform that ends up in someone not being paid on time." Knowing the data (invoice vs statement) decides how detailed each table row must be.

Key points.title: Feed context as text for prose, screenshots for diagrams
Key points.detail: Chris gives Claude his discovery before it builds a prototype. He pastes prose like the problem statement as plain text because "text waste[s] less tokens," and uses screenshots for maps and diagrams. His PM also generated an early prototype from the same discovery, and they shaped the surface together.

Key points.title: Spot invented components and correct with the Storybook link
Key points.detail: When Claude makes a component that isn't in the system, a trained designer can tell from the corners, color or type. Chris copies the Storybook link for the right component and tells Claude "you are inventing this, please do it correctly with this component." Handoff is a dev-environment link plus a video walkthrough, then a run of small fixes as engineers find edge cases.

Title: AI Native Designer shows his Growth Design Process (Clint, Givebutter)
Creator: Sneak Peek (Jay with Clint, Givebutter)
Bottom line: Hunt friction weekly by pairing what users say (Enterpret) with what they do (Hex), prototype fast, and ship small A/B/C tests to learn quickly, including that your assumption was wrong.
What they did: Each week Clint pulls nuggets from Granola meeting notes, pastes them into Claude to generate prompts, then runs them in Enterpret with a fixed add-on framework (summarize feedback and patterns, focus on missed opportunities, draft a brainstorm doc by opportunity area with user stories and citations, suggest experiments), and checks behavior via a Hex agent in a shared Slack channel ('talk to data'). He uses Claude Code to invent new things freely (e.g. four CRM onboarding module concepts, each with a built-in state switcher for first visit, partial progress, completed and returning user, plus a 'growth team test' badge) and Magic Patterns, which is wired to Givebutter's Storybook, to refine existing flows on real components. He shares a Loom under 5 minutes in a Slack thread with prototype links, then has Claude send approved screens to a one-Figma-file-per-quarter team file. The team A/B/C tested three ways to ask 'are you switching from another tool?' (dropdown plus yes/no, one-tap options, 'which tool are you coming from').
Results: Tests went "from concept to... working prototype to... ready for deployment" "within 2 days"; only "something like 17%" of users confirmed they were switching in one experiment "and even lower in another", disproving the 'switcher intent' assumption; the 'what tool are you coming from' one-tap variant "tested the best" but "none of them were actually successful"; "we learned within 2 weeks that we were wrong versus... 2 months".
Takeaways: A failed test can reveal a wrong mental model; Pair what users say with what they do; Use one reusable prompt framework for feedback queries; Build a state switcher into every prototype; Ask onboarding questions as one-tap choices; Refine with real components, invent without them
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: A/B test asking prep stage (e.g. 'which exam and attempt are you preparing for') as one-tap options instead of dropdowns, and check whether the answer really predicts behavior before personalizing on it. Home: prototype a 'getting started' checklist with explicit states (first visit, partial, done, returning 'since you were last here') and a state switcher for review. Design process: run a weekly friction hunt pairing support/review feedback with PostHog funnels, and share findings as a sub-5-minute Loom with prototype links.

Key points.title: A failed test can reveal a wrong mental model
Key points.detail: Givebutter assumed users who had another fundraising tool were switching to Givebutter ("switcher intent") and built onboarding questions and dashboard prompts around it. In testing, only "something like 17%" confirmed they were switching, "and even lower in another experiment." Clint says "the issue wasn't in the UI, but it was our mental model." Because concept to deploy-ready took two days, "we learned within 2 weeks that we were wrong" instead of in months, and they moved to a survey that adapts per user.

Key points.title: Pair what users say with what they do
Key points.detail: Clint's weekly "friction hunting" uses Enterpret for "the emotional texture behind the problem," pulling feedback from Intercom, Gong, G2 and the mobile app. Hex then checks whether "these feelings [are] reflected in the actual behavior." He can ask Hex questions from a shared Slack channel called "talk to data," such as the median actions before a first donation, and others see and reuse the answers. For OnCourse, that means pairing support and review comments with PostHog funnels before picking a problem.

Key points.title: Use one reusable prompt framework for feedback queries
Key points.detail: He pastes Granola meeting notes into Claude to get prompts grouped by theme, then runs them in Enterpret with a fixed add-on: summarize feedback and patterns, focus on missed opportunities, draft a brainstorm doc by opportunity area with user stories and citations, and suggest experiments. The readout gives five opportunity areas and links to real Intercom chats and Gong recordings, so he can hear users. One suggested experiment: a "your donors are now in your CRM" modal the day after a campaign closes.

Key points.title: Build a state switcher into every prototype
Key points.detail: For CRM onboarding, Claude Code produced four module concepts, each with a switcher for first visit, partial progress, completed ("you're in good shape") and returning user ("here's what happened since you were last here"). A top bar shows where you are in the prototype, and a "growth team test" badge tells anyone it's shared with who to ask. He shares it as a Loom under 5 minutes in a Slack thread with prototype links, an async meeting that saves everyone a 30-minute call.

Key points.title: Ask onboarding questions as one-tap choices
Key points.detail: The team A/B/C tested three ways to ask about switching: a dropdown plus yes/no, one-tap options (moving from another tool, brand new, not sure), and one-tap "what tool are you coming from." The last "tested the best," but "none of them were actually successful" at getting the signal they wanted. The next version asks a handful of questions that change by who signs up, using GuideStar's nonprofit data. For OnCourse onboarding, prefer one tap over dropdown plus confirm.

Key points.title: Refine with real components, invent without them
Key points.detail: Clint asks whether he is going to refine or invent. To refine an existing flow, like a donation picker, he uses Magic Patterns, which is wired to Givebutter's Storybook so the result matches production and he can hand the link straight to an engineer. To explore something new he uses Claude Code and breaks away from the design system. Approved screens are sent back to Figma, into one team file per quarter, an idea taken from Firefox's team.

Title: Dylan Field live at Figma's Config: Intuition, simplicity, and the future of design (Dylan Field)
Creator: Lenny's Podcast (Lenny Rachitsky with Dylan Field)
Bottom line: Keep the simple things simple and the complex things possible, and ship a 'minimally awesome product' fast so feedback starts early.
What they did: Field reads feedback about Figma everywhere (Twitter/X, support channels) and pushes the team to dig for the root problem behind a request ('they say X but want Y or Z'). Leaders regularly revisit whole systems where 'we made all the right local decisions and yet together they're too complex'. For launches Figma uses 'quality, features, deadline, choose two': FigJam and Figma Slides shipped fast to get feedback, while Dev Mode needed many rebuilds before it clearly added value for developers. Early on he ran long user studies with designers he admired and treated them as feedback sessions, not a growth hack.
Results: Figma took "three and a half years to launch" and about five years to its first paying customer, which Field calls "way too long, don't do that." Dev Mode looks simpler than FigJam but "took at least three times as long."
Takeaways: Treat intuition as a hypothesis generator, then find data to support or kill each idea; many good local decisions can still add up to a too-complex system, so review the whole; pick two of quality, features and deadline, and never drop quality for good; concrete artifacts and examples win arguments with leaders better than abstract pitches; AI 'make design' features give you the most obvious answer, so unique craft becomes the differentiator
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: once a quarter, walk the whole app end to end and list places where separate screen decisions add up to too much (for example, how many entry points Home, Today's plan and Practice give for the same MCQ session). Practice: keep the default path to one tap ('Start today's questions') and put filters, subject choice and timed mode behind an opt-in. Design process: when a student asks for a feature in support or reviews, write down the underlying problem before designing anything.
